xstate: XState’s state machines and actors for C++

xstate is a header-only port of XState 5.33.2, Stately’s library of state machines and actors, to C++20, one of the libraries of webcpp. A machine is loaded from the JSON config XState’s createMachine takes, and run through XState’s pure functions or as an actor.

This page teaches xstate as Stately’s documentation teaches XState: each concept, why it exists, its smallest example, its variations and its rules. Every program it shows was compiled and run, natively and for wasm32-wasip2 and wasm32-wasip3, and printed the output shown under it. Every program is also proven against XState: its twin, the same program written for XState 5.33.2, prints the same output, or the output of a difference xstate makes on purpose, unless it shows something XState does not have (How the port is proven). The reference lists every name the headers declare.

Introduction

This chapter says what xstate is and why it exists, how its two layers share the work, how the port is proven against XState, and what a program needs to use it. A quick start then builds a first program, and the last section says how the rest of the page is laid out.

Overview

XState is Stately’s library of state machines, statecharts and actors for JavaScript and TypeScript. It models logic as event-driven state machines, and runs them as actors that send each other events. xstate ports XState 5.33.2 to C++20, header-only, in the namespace webcpp::xstate. Its machines are the ones a person writes for XState: a config is JSON with the shape of XState’s, loaded when the program runs rather than compiled into it. xstate runs a machine as XState does, transition for transition: through XState’s pure functions, one microstep at a time when its caller bounds the work of an event, or as an actor that invokes and spawns children, sends other actors events, hears its children finish, waits on timers and asks the host program for work done outside it.

xstate’s actor layer is built on webcpp’s xactor, a deterministic actor system whose actors exchange messages one at a time each, on one thread, in an order that depends only on the order the messages were sent, each execution with a budget of fuel, and with no time but the host’s.

In this documentation, XState is always Stately’s library, and xstate the port of its machines and actors.

A first look

Stately’s XState page introduces the library with a counter: a machine whose context holds a count, three events that change it, an actor that runs the machine, and a subscription that prints the count after each event. In xstate the counter is this program:

#include <webcpp/xstate/actors.hpp>

#include <boost/json.hpp>

#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <utility>

namespace xstate = webcpp::xstate;

namespace {

/** An assign that adds `step` to the context's count. */
xstate::assign_action adding(std::int64_t step) {
    auto add = [step](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<boost::json::object> {
        const boost::system::result<const boost::json::value&> count = args.context.try_at("count");
        if (!count.has_value()) {
            return count.error();
        }
        const boost::system::result<std::int64_t> number = count->try_as_int64();
        if (!number.has_value()) {
            return number.error();
        }
        return boost::json::object{{"count", *number + step}};
    };
    return xstate::assign_action{.assignment = std::move(add)};
}

/** An assign that sets the count to the event's `value`. */
xstate::result<boost::json::object> set_count(const xstate::action_args& args) {
    const boost::json::value* value = args.event.payload.if_contains("value");
    if (value == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"count", *value}};
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
        "context": {"count": 0},
        "on": {
            "INC": {"actions": "increment"},
            "DEC": {"actions": "decrement"},
            "SET": {"actions": "set"}
        }
    })");
    xstate::implementations implementations;
    implementations.actions.emplace("increment", adding(1));
    implementations.actions.emplace("decrement", adding(-1));
    implementations.actions.emplace("set", xstate::assign_action{.assignment = set_count});
    const xstate::result<xstate::machine> count_machine =
        xstate::create_machine(config, std::move(implementations));
    if (!count_machine.has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }

    xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 100});
    const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> count_actor = system.create_actor(*count_machine);
    if (!count_actor.has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }
    if (!system.start(*count_actor).has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }

    const xstate::result<void> subscribed =
        system.subscribe(*count_actor, [](const xstate::snapshot& state) {
            const boost::system::result<const boost::json::value&> count =
                state.context.try_at("count");
            if (count.has_value()) {
                std::cout << boost::json::serialize(*count) << '\n';
            }
        });
    if (!subscribed.has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }

    const xstate::event inc{.type = "INC", .payload = {}};
    const xstate::event dec{.type = "DEC", .payload = {}};
    const xstate::event set{.type = "SET", .payload = {{"value", 10}}};

    if (!system.send(*count_actor, inc).has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }
    // prints 1
    if (!system.send(*count_actor, dec).has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }
    // prints 0
    if (!system.send(*count_actor, set).has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }
    // prints 10
    return 0;
}

It prints:

1
0
10

Three things in it are xstate’s own, and each has a section of this chapter:

  • The config is JSON, and JSON holds no function. XState’s assign takes a function that computes the new count; here the config names an action, increment, and implementations binds that name to C++ code, an assign_action, as XState’s setup registers an action under a name. This is machines as JSON, implementations by name.

  • create_machine returns a result: the machine, or the reason the config was refused. Every call that can fail does the same, and the program checks each one, where XState would throw. An implementation returns a result too; when adding finds no integer count, its failure puts the actor in the status error, as an exception thrown by an assigner does in XState. This is errors as values.

  • The actor lives in an actor_system the program creates. XState’s createActor makes an actor and the system that runs it in one call; in xstate, create_actor makes an actor in a system, and start, send and subscribe are XState’s, with the actor as their first argument. The system is built with a budget of fuel, which bounds the work of each execution a call opens, one for each input the call applies; here each start and send opens one, and 100 units are far more than this counter needs. This is the actor layer.

Why xstate

A state machine names every state a process can be in and, for each state, every event it accepts and where that event leads, so a move it does not list never happens, and its logic can be read, drawn and tested as a whole. A statechart adds what larger processes need, nested and parallel states, history, delays and actions, and the actor model runs many machines together, each reaching the others only by events (Core concepts). XState brings both to JavaScript and TypeScript, and Stately Studio draws, edits and simulates XState’s machines. xstate brings the same machines to C++, for a program, native or WebAssembly, whose logic reacts to events.

A machine in xstate is data, and that is what lets XState’s machines run in C++. Its config is the JSON a person writes for XState’s createMachine, or exports from Stately Studio, read when the program runs. What JSON can say, states, transitions, guards and actions by name, delays and invokes, means in xstate what it means in XState. What JSON cannot hold, the code of an action, a guard, a delay or an invoked actor, the program registers in its implementations under the name the config gives it, as XState’s setup registers it (Machines as JSON, implementations by name). So the same machine runs on XState in JavaScript and on xstate in C++, each with implementations of its own, and What JSON imposes lists the few places where JSON gives a config another form. And a program can run machines that did not exist when it was compiled.

From such a config, xstate does what XState does:

  • It loads the machine, with the implementations the program registers by name, and refuses at once every config XState refuses (Machines).

  • It runs the machine as XState’s algorithm does: transition selection, the exit and entry sets, history, done events, eventless transitions, raised and delayed events, and output (Events and transitions).

  • It offers XState’s pure functions, initial_transition, transition and the others, which compute one snapshot from another and change nothing (Pure transitions and the macrostep cursor).

  • It returns to its caller every action the machine does not perform itself, as XState’s transition does, for the caller to execute (Custom actions).

  • It writes a machine’s definition as XState’s machine.toJSON() writes it, and loads it back (The definition).

  • It runs machines as XState’s actors: children invoked and spawned, events between actors, a child’s done and error events reaching its parent, timers, host actors, systemIds and emitted events (Actors: xstate on xactor).

It adds two things that a C++ program running machines it did not write needs, and XState does not have. Under the pure functions is the macrostep cursor, which runs one microstep per call, so that its caller bounds the work an event may cause; the actor layer bounds every call the same way, with fuel. And nothing in a run depends on the world outside it: a machine reads no clock, a delayed event waits on a clock its caller moves, and actors run on one thread in the order their messages were sent, so the same inputs give the same run (Two layers).

Why header-only

A program includes <webcpp/xstate.hpp> for machines, or <webcpp/xstate/actors.hpp> for actors, and compiles nothing of xstate’s own: there is no library to build, version, install or link. The headers are compiled with the program, by its compiler and with its flags, so a build with flags of its own, without exceptions or with a sanitizer, needs no second build of the library.

The reason is portability. The same headers build the same way wherever a C++20 compiler does, natively or as a WebAssembly component, with no build of their own to port to each target and no binary to match to each compiler. Every program of this documentation is built and run natively, with GCC, Clang and MSVC, and for wasm32-wasip2 and wasm32-wasip3 with the Clang of wasi-sdk, under wasmtime, with exceptions on every target: whether a program uses them is its own choice. xstate throws nothing, and its headers compile without them (Errors as values).

The dependencies follow the same rule. Boost.System, which gives xstate its result and its error codes, is header-only, and so are xactor and Boost.Asio, which xactor includes outside a WASI build for its Asio driver (xactor’s Asio driver). Boost.JSON is compiled by the program itself, once: one of its translation units includes <boost/json/src.hpp> (Requirements). No Boost library is built.

Two layers

XState separates a machine, the logic, from the actor that runs it: a machine’s transition computes the next snapshot and returns the actions to execute, and the actor executes them. xstate draws its line at the same place, and puts each side behind a header of its own.

Layer Header What it holds What it depends on

Machine core

<webcpp/xstate.hpp>

machines, snapshots, XState’s pure functions, the macrostep cursor, the simulated clock, a machine’s definition as JSON

the standard library, Boost.JSON and Boost.System

Actor layer

<webcpp/xstate/actors.hpp>

actor_system: actors, children, host actors, timers, the systemId registry, emitted events, subscriptions

the machine core and xactor, which includes Boost.Asio’s headers outside a WASI build

actors.hpp includes xstate.hpp, so a program that uses actors includes the one header. The machine core includes nothing of xactor and runs no actor, so a program that only steps machines does not depend on xactor. It knows XState’s actors as data all the same: implementations.actors holds the actors a machine may invoke and spawn, and snapshot.children lists its children. The entry of a state that invokes, or a spawnChild, resolves into an xstate.spawnChild action, and the exit of that state, or a stopChild, into xstate.stopChild; the core returns them, with the sends, for its caller to execute. The actor layer is that caller. The core resolves an action into a value and the layer executes it, as XState splits each action into resolve and execute.

Both layers run the same machine. This one is a dog: wakes up takes it from asleep to stretching, whose eventless transition, always, takes it on to awake, whose entry action is bark. No implementation holds bark, so it is a custom action, which the machine returns to whatever runs it:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "dog",
    "initial": "asleep",
    "states": {
        "asleep": {"on": {"wakes up": "stretching"}},
        "stretching": {"always": "awake"},
        "awake": {"entry": "bark"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> dog = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!dog.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::event wakes_up{.type = "wakes up", .payload = {}};

The machine core

create_machine(config, implementations) builds a machine from XState’s config. A machine never changes once it is created, and copying one is cheap. Where a machine is, its state value, its context, its status and the rest, is a snapshot, a plain value the caller keeps, copies or stores.

The core holds XState’s pure functions, each named after XState’s in snake case. get_initial_snapshot, initial_transition and get_initial_microsteps compute where a machine starts, and get_next_snapshot, transition and get_microsteps where an event takes it from a snapshot; get_next_transitions, and can, XState’s snapshot.can, say what it could do. None of them changes anything. transition, initial_transition and the microstep functions also return every action the machine does not perform itself, such as a custom action, a delayed event or a send to another actor, for the caller to execute, as XState’s transition returns them; get_next_snapshot and get_initial_snapshot return the snapshot alone.

Under those functions is the one primitive xstate adds, the macrostep cursor. An event runs one macrostep: the transitions the event selects, then every eventless transition and every raised event that follows, until the machine is stable again. Each of those steps is a microstep. XState runs a macrostep to its end inside one call. xstate’s begin(machine, snapshot, event), and begin_initial(machine, input) for the initial macrostep, return a cursor instead, whose next() runs exactly one microstep and reports whether that microstep settled the macrostep, and whose done() says when one has. The dog’s wakes up, one microstep at a time:

const xstate::snapshot asleep = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*dog);
xstate::macrostep step = xstate::begin(*dog, asleep, wakes_up);
while (!step.done()) {
    const xstate::progress made = step.next();
    std::cout << "microstep: " << boost::json::serialize(made.step.snapshot.value) << ' '
              << types_of(made.step.actions) << '\n';
}
std::cout << "settled: " << boost::json::serialize(step.result().snapshot.value) << '\n';

It prints:

microstep: "stretching" []
microstep: "awake" [bark]
settled: "awake"

wakes up takes two microsteps: the first moves the dog to stretching, and the second takes its eventless transition to awake, whose entry action bark comes back with that microstep. XState’s getMicrosteps returns both at once; the cursor hands them over one at a time, so its caller may stop between two and resume later, since the cursor is a value and a copy of it resumes exactly where the original stopped. The caller pays for each call and stops when it chooses. The library never stops a macrostep on its own: a cycle of eventless transitions never settles, and the caller’s fuel is the only bound. The functions that compute where a machine goes are the cursor run to its end, without a bound.

The core never reads a clock either. Entering a state with after returns its delayed event as an action, a built-in xstate.raise with a delay. The caller hands it to a simulated_clock it owns, XState’s SimulatedClock, which keeps the event until the caller moves time forward and then gives it back, for the caller to send to the machine. The clock schedules only that built-in delayed raise: a custom action stays the caller’s, whatever its type or params.

Pure transitions and the macrostep cursor covers the functions, the cursor and its fuel.

The actor layer

actor_system runs machines as XState’s actors. It is XState’s createActor and its actor system in one: the host creates an actor from a machine, starts it, sends it events, reads its snapshot and subscribes to it. The machine invokes and spawns children, its sendTo, sendParent and forwardTo reach other actors, its children’s done and error events reach it, its timers fire when the host brings the time with clock_tick, and a host_actor, xstate’s counterpart of XState’s fromPromise, waits until the host resolves or rejects it. What the core returns, the layer executes: it creates the child of a spawnChild, delivers the event of a sendTo, arms a timer for a delayed raise or send, and hands a custom action to the host’s on_action. The dog, run as an actor:

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<void> acting =
    system.on_action([](xstate::actor_ref, const xstate::action& custom) {
        std::cout << "custom action: " << custom.type << '\n';
    });
if (!acting.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> dog_actor = system.create_actor(*dog);
if (!dog_actor.has_value() || !settled(system.start(*dog_actor)) ||
    !settled(system.send(*dog_actor, wakes_up))) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::snapshot* now = system.snapshot_of(*dog_actor);
if (now == nullptr) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << "actor: " << boost::json::serialize(now->value) << '\n';

It prints:

custom action: bark
actor: "awake"

The same machine and the same event lead to the same snapshot. The custom action bark reaches the host’s on_action, where XState’s actor calls the function setup registered under that name.

The layer runs on xactor, webcpp’s header-only actor system, which already is the system XState’s actors need (xactor’s model): a scheduler on one thread that holds one FIFO mailbox per actor and one FIFO queue of the actors that have work, and whose every turn hands one message to its actor, so that the order of deliveries depends only on the order messages were sent; fuel for each execution; timers; and a lifecycle, under XState’s names. A second actor system inside xstate would duplicate all of it. Every message an actor sends is queued and handled in a turn of its own, where XState handles an event at once, nested in the sender’s call, when its actor is running and idle (Interleaving across actors).

Fuel reaches the actors too. A host call that delivers something opens an execution for each input it applies, and resume() one for each parked actor besides; each execution has the budget’s fuel. Every microstep costs one unit of it, and so does every message an actor sends and every timer it arms. An actor that runs out parks with what it has left to do, until resume() gives it more; XState has no such bound (Fuel). Time is the host’s too: a timer fires when the host calls clock_tick, never on its own.

Actors covers the layer, its fuel and its time included.

Which to use

  • The pure functions, when the caller keeps the snapshot between events and the work of one event needs no bound: a test, or a program that loads a snapshot, applies one event and stores what it leads to.

  • The cursor, when the work of each event must be bounded, or watched one microstep at a time.

  • The actor layer, when machines invoke or spawn other machines, send each other events, wait on timers, or wait on work the host program does.

Machines as JSON, implementations by name

A config in xstate is a boost::json::value holding what XState’s createMachine takes: id, initial, context, states, on, always, after, entry, exit, invoke, tags, output and the rest. Where XState’s config holds a function, an action, a guard, a delay, the logic of an invoked actor, xstate’s config names it, and implementations maps each name to its C++ code. implementations is what XState’s setup({ actions, guards, delays, actors }) gives a machine. The counter of the first look registers its three actions this way.

There are three reasons for this:

  • A machine is data. It is loaded when the program runs, from a file, a request or a store, and needs no compiler. Its config has the shape of the one a person writes for XState’s createMachine.

  • JSON cannot hold a function, and neither can a boost::json::value: a C++ lambda has no place in the config either. A name is the bridge between the data and the code, and XState already has it: an action or a guard registered with setup is referenced by its name, with params, in the config.

  • Names are checked when the machine is created. A guard, a named delay or an actor that the config names and the implementations do not hold is refused then, with an error, where XState accepts the machine and fails later, or never, when it runs (A config is refused when it is created). An action name the implementations do not hold is not an error: it is a custom action, which the machine returns to the caller with its params. That is how the caller’s own effects leave the machine.

An action is registered as one of XState’s built-in action creators: assign_action, raise_action, log_action, send_parent_action, cancel_action, spawn_child_action, stop_child_action, send_to_action, forward_to_action and emit_action, each holding what XState’s creator takes, a C++ function where XState’s takes a JavaScript one. A guard is a predicate, and a delay a function that returns milliseconds. implementations.context computes the initial context from the input, XState’s context: ({ input }) => ..., and implementations.inputs and implementations.outputs compute an invoked child’s input and a final state’s output.

XState’s higher-order guards, not, and, or and stateIn, are functions in XState too; xstate writes them as JSON objects, {"type": "xstate.not", "guards": [...]} and the like (Higher-order guards). Machines and Actions cover each of these, and What JSON imposes lists every place where a JSON config differs from a JavaScript one.

Errors as values

xstate reports every failure as a value. Every call that can fail returns an xstate::result<T>, Boost.System’s result with an error_code; xstate’s own codes are xstate::errc, of the category webcpp.xstate. Where XState throws, xstate returns an error instead. At creation, it refuses a config XState refuses, and some that XState accepts and throws on only when it runs them, such as a guard the implementations do not hold or an entry that is null (A config is refused when it is created). While a machine runs, the error of an implementation that fails is in the snapshot’s status and error, as XState’s actor keeps the error of an implementation that threw.

There are two reasons for this. A caller reaches a value only through its result, so a failure cannot pass unseen. And xstate builds where exceptions are off: its headers compile without them, which the lint checks by compiling every public header, and every test and example, without them (Why header-only).

The actor layer refuses the calls it cannot take with xactor’s webcpp::xactor::errc::invalid_argument, of the category webcpp.xactor, and changes nothing: a start, send, stop, status_of, subscribe or on_emitted whose address names no actor, a stop of a child, an answer to a request no longer pending, and a call that changes the system made from inside a callback the host registered; xstate::errc has no invalid_argument. One refusal of the layer is xstate’s own: create_actor refuses a systemId another running actor holds with errc::system_id_taken, of the category webcpp.xstate. snapshot_of, child_of, parent_of, id_of and get refuse nothing: they answer nullptr, none or an empty view for what they do not find (Creating an actor, Options, Watching an actor).

How the port is proven

xstate’s reference is xstate@5.33.2, commit fbee62e7c1586315ed478c2fedf530d7e0ff5a3e. It is a port of XState’s algorithm, not a semantics of its own: transition selection, the exit and entry sets, history, done events, eventless transitions, raised and delayed events and output are translated function by function, and every ported function names, in its comment, the TypeScript function it ports. So a difference from XState points at one function on each side.

Where xstate departs from XState, it does so on purpose, for one of four reasons: XState’s behaviour belongs to JavaScript, JSON cannot say what XState’s config says, xactor runs actors differently, or xstate checks earlier than XState. So a config or a name is refused when the machine is created; a name stands where XState holds a function; an error is returned where XState throws; a host actor stands where XState awaits a promise; an event waits in a queue where XState delivers it to an idle actor at once, nested in its sender’s call; and fuel bounds the work XState leaves unbounded. The text says so where it matters, and Where xstate differs from XState gathers the cases, each with its reason.

A port is right when it does what the original does, so XState itself is the judge, twice. The oracle holds the library to what XState does, case by case; the twins hold this documentation to it, program by program. How xstate is tested tells how both run.

XState as the oracle

XState’s own tests are ported to cases written as JSON, one file per test file of XState’s, each with the tests it leaves out and why. Further cases pin what XState does where its own tests are silent, such as a machine whose root is a history node, an event of the type * or a timer armed twice under one id. The scripts of test/oracle/ run every case on XState 5.33.2 and record what XState produced: oracle.mjs the machine cases, one macrostep at a time through machine.transition, which XState’s pure functions call, and actors.mjs the actor cases, on XState’s actors. xstate’s test suites run the same cases and compare, microstep by microstep, the event, the transitions, the actions and the snapshot. The actor cases are compared actor by actor: the events each actor processed and the snapshot each left, the events it emitted, its status, and the host’s pending requests.

What XState produced is committed, so xstate’s suites run without Node. The oracle lane, b2 libs/xstate/test/oracle//oracle, runs the scripts on XState again, and fails when what XState produces is no longer what the suites hold.

The oracle runs XState’s development build, as XState’s own test suite does. That build makes checks the production build leaves out. Three of them can meet a JSON machine, and xstate makes them too: it refuses an event of the type * sent from outside, a transition that declares a truthy cond, and a forwardTo whose target resolves to no actor (The checks of XState’s development build).

A twin for every example

Every program of example/xstate and example/actors, the programs of this documentation that use xstate, has a twin in test/oracle/twins: a JavaScript program that does on XState 5.33.2 what the C++ program does on xstate. The oracle lane runs every twin on XState’s development build and compares what it prints with what the C++ program printed:

  • 114 twins print the same output, the one this page shows under the program.

  • 22 twins print something else, on purpose. Their program shows a place where xstate differs from XState, and the twin’s output, committed beside it, is what XState does there; Where xstate differs from XState shows both outputs, and why xstate differs.

  • 10 programs have no twin, because XState has nothing that does what they show: the macrostep cursor, fuel, a machine created again from its definition, an event read from JSON and the like. test/oracle/twins/without-twin.txt gives the reason for each.

So every program of this page that XState can run has run on XState, and printed what the page shows, or what Where xstate differs from XState explains.

What is not ported

These parts of XState 5.33.2 have no counterpart in xstate yet:

  • enqueueActions.

  • Callback actors, fromCallback, and observable actors, fromObservable and fromEventObservable.

  • fromTransition.

  • The persistence of actors: getPersistedSnapshot, and an actor created from a persisted snapshot. A machine’s snapshot is a value its caller may store, and resolve_state, XState’s machine.resolveState, brings it back; Pure transitions and the macrostep cursor shows it.

  • toPromise and waitFor.

  • syncSnapshot, and with it an invoke’s onSnapshot: the config accepts onSnapshot, but the actor layer sends no child’s snapshot to its parent, so no child’s snapshot ever takes that transition.

  • spawn inside assign.

  • machine.provide(): a machine takes its implementations once, from create_machine, and the same config created again with other implementations is the machine provide would return; Machines shows it.

xactor on its own leaves four things to the library built on it (what xactor leaves out): a child’s done and error reaching its parent, invoke, a registry of named actors, and the inspection of state changes. xstate’s actor layer builds all four for machines (Actors: xstate on xactor).

Requirements

  • A C++20 compiler. xstate’s tests and examples are built and run natively, and for wasm32-wasip2 and wasm32-wasip3 with the Clang of wasi-sdk, under wasmtime (Targets).

  • xstate’s headers and xactor’s, libs/xstate/include and libs/xactor/include in a webcpp checkout. The machine core needs only xstate’s; the actor layer needs xactor’s too. Nothing of xstate is compiled on its own (Why header-only).

  • webcpp’s configuration, libs/config/include in a webcpp checkout, which xstate’s and xactor’s headers include first.

  • Boost 1.92.0’s headers. Every value a machine holds, its config, its context, an event’s payload, an action’s params, is a Boost.JSON value; results and error codes are Boost.System’s. Outside a WASI build, xactor includes Boost.Asio’s headers for its Asio driver.

  • Boost.JSON’s definitions, compiled once. Boost.JSON’s headers declare and <boost/json/src.hpp> defines, so exactly one translation unit of the program includes that header; webcpp’s is tools/boost_json.cpp.

  • Without exceptions, a definition of boost::throw_exception. xstate throws nothing: it is built and tested with exceptions on, on every target, and its headers compile without them. Whether a program uses them is its own choice. Without them, Boost’s code still names boost::throw_exception, and the program defines it: webcpp’s tools/throw_exception.cpp does it with a report on the standard error and an abort, since in such a build a throw is a defect, never a condition. A program built with exceptions needs nothing here, since Boost defines the function then.

  • Nothing else: no threads, and no global or static mutable state. A machine never reads a clock, a file or the network: the same machine and the same events give the same run.

Installing xstate sets this up, and compiles a first program.

Quick start

This section builds a first program. It creates a machine, a toggle, from the JSON config XState’s createMachine takes, steps it with XState’s pure functions, runs the same machine as an actor that receives events, and then grows it with a delayed transition, context and input. It follows Stately’s quick start step by step, with one step of its own, the pure functions. Each block of code comes from a whole program of the repository, and the output under it is what that program printed.

Installing xstate

xstate is header-only, so installing it puts directories on a program’s include path, and nothing is built but the program (Requirements lists what the program provides). In a webcpp checkout they are libs/xstate/include, webcpp’s configuration, libs/config/include, and, for the actor layer, libs/xactor/include, beside Boost 1.92’s headers. From the root of the checkout, with the program of the next two sections, libs/xstate/example/xstate/qs_toggle.cpp, copied as toggle.cpp, this command builds it:

clang++ -std=c++20 -I libs/xstate/include -I libs/config/include toggle.cpp \
    tools/boost_json.cpp -o toggle

tools/boost_json.cpp is the one translation unit that includes <boost/json/src.hpp>; without it the link misses Boost.JSON’s definitions. A compiler that does not find Boost on its default include path is given Boost’s include directory with -isystem, which makes Boost’s headers system headers, so the compiler’s warnings stay on the program’s own code: for Homebrew’s Boost, the one under /opt/homebrew/opt/boost. A program that uses the actor layer adds -I libs/xactor/include. GCC takes the same options.

Without exceptions, the program also needs a definition of boost::throw_exception, which Boost.System and Boost.JSON name: webcpp’s tools/throw_exception.cpp defines its two overloads, reports what was thrown on the standard error and aborts, since in such a build a throw is a defect, never a condition:

clang++ -std=c++20 -fno-exceptions -DBOOST_NO_EXCEPTIONS -I libs/xstate/include \
    -I libs/config/include toggle.cpp tools/boost_json.cpp tools/throw_exception.cpp \
    -o toggle

A program built with exceptions on needs none of -fno-exceptions, -DBOOST_NO_EXCEPTIONS or throw_exception.cpp, since Boost defines the function itself then.

Building with b2

In the checkout, b2 libs/xstate/example builds this program with every other program of libs/xstate/example/, runs each, and compares what it prints with the output this page shows, which is the <name>.expected beside it (Testing). A b2 project uses xstate through /webcpp/xstate//xstate, which adds xstate’s headers, xactor’s, Boost’s, and Boost.JSON’s definitions, compiled once per variant, to whatever names it:

exe toggle : toggle.cpp /webcpp/xstate//xstate ;

Create a machine

A machine is the logic of an actor: the states it can be in, the events each state accepts, and where each event leads. This one, a toggle, is in one of two states, Inactive or Active, and the event toggle moves it from one to the other.

XState takes the config as a JavaScript object. xstate takes the same config as JSON, read at run time by create_machine: a C++ program has no object literal to write it in, and as data a config can come from a file, a request or Stately Studio’s export. JSON cannot hold a function, so the program gives the machine’s code in the second argument, the implementations: an action’s, for one, under the name the config gives the action. This config needs no code, and its implementations are empty (Handle context data, Implementations).

The examples of this page begin with the core’s header, Boost.JSON’s, and an alias for the namespace:

#include <webcpp/xstate.hpp>

#include <boost/json.hpp>

#include <iostream>

namespace xstate = webcpp::xstate;

Then the machine:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "toggle",
    "initial": "Inactive",
    "states": {
        "Inactive": {"on": {"toggle": "Active"}},
        "Active": {"on": {"toggle": "Inactive"}}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> toggle_machine = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!toggle_machine.has_value()) {
    std::cout << "refused: " << toggle_machine.error().message() << '\n';
    return 1;
}

create_machine returns a result<machine>: the machine, or the error that refused the config, such as invalid_config for a compound state without initial or unknown_target for a target that names no state. Where XState throws, xstate returns an error; and some configs XState accepts, failing only when it runs them, xstate refuses when the machine is created (A config is refused when it is created). A machine never changes once created, and copying one is cheap: it is a handle to data its copies share. What creation refuses tells what refuses a config.

Step it with pure functions

Before it runs as an actor, the machine can be stepped by hand, which suits a caller that keeps the state itself: a request handler that loads a snapshot, applies an event and stores the result, or a test. A snapshot is where a machine is: its state value, its context and its status. XState’s pure functions compute one snapshot from another. initialTransition returns the snapshot a machine starts in, and transition the snapshot an event leads to, each with the actions the step returned for the caller to execute. They change nothing and keep nothing: the caller holds the snapshot and passes it back with the next event. xstate has the same functions, initial_transition and transition, which return a std::pair:

const auto [initial_state, initial_actions] = xstate::initial_transition(*toggle_machine);
std::cout << "Value: " << boost::json::serialize(initial_state.value) << " ("
          << initial_actions.size() << " actions)\n";

const xstate::event toggle{.type = "toggle", .payload = {}};
const auto [next_state, actions] = xstate::transition(*toggle_machine, initial_state, toggle);
std::cout << "Value: " << boost::json::serialize(next_state.value) << " (" << actions.size()
          << " actions)\n";

const auto [last_state, last_actions] = xstate::transition(*toggle_machine, next_state, toggle);
std::cout << "Value: " << boost::json::serialize(last_state.value) << " ("
          << last_actions.size() << " actions)\n";

It prints:

Value: "Inactive" (0 actions)
Value: "Active" (0 actions)
Value: "Inactive" (0 actions)

An event is a type and a payload, empty here. The toggle has no actions, so every list is empty; Actions shows what they hold and who executes them.

An event’s macrostep is all the work it causes: one or more microsteps, each a set of transitions taken together, until no eventless transition is enabled and no raised event is queued (Microsteps). Each of these functions runs an event’s macrostep to its end at once. Under them is xstate’s one primitive, the macrostep cursor: begin returns a cursor whose next() runs exactly one microstep, so the caller decides how much work an event may cost, paying for each microstep and stopping where it wants. A machine whose eventless transitions never settle never returns from transition; only the cursor bounds it (The macrostep cursor).

Create an actor and send events

An actor is a running process: it receives events, one at a time, and each event may change its snapshot and make it send events of its own. A machine is the logic an actor runs.

XState’s createActor makes an actor from a machine. In xstate, actors live in an actor_system, which runs them on xactor, and the program names each by the actor_ref the system returns. XState makes a system for each root actor implicitly; xstate makes it explicit because the system owns what a host must decide: the fuel its actors may spend, the time, and the systemIds its actors share (Creating an actor). xactor runs the actors on one thread: each actor has a FIFO mailbox, the actors that have work wait in one FIFO queue, and each turn hands one message to its actor, so the order of deliveries depends on nothing but the order the messages were sent (xactor’s guarantee 2). With fuel bounding each execution, the same inputs make the same run and no run is unbounded. The system’s create_actor, subscribe, start and send are XState’s createActor, actor.subscribe, actor.start and actor.send, and its snapshot_of is actor.getSnapshot. An actor needs the actor layer’s header, <webcpp/xstate/actors.hpp>. The same toggle, as an actor:

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 1000});

/** Whether a call that delivers ran to its end: no error, and no actor left parked. */
const auto settled = [](const xstate::result<xstate::run_outcome>& ran) {
    return ran.has_value() && *ran == xstate::run_outcome::settled;
};

const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*toggle_machine);
if (!actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::result<void> subscribed =
    system.subscribe(*actor, [](const xstate::snapshot& snapshot) {
        std::cout << "Value: " << boost::json::serialize(snapshot.value) << '\n';
    });
if (!subscribed.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

if (!settled(system.start(*actor))) {  // logs "Inactive"
    return 1;
}

const xstate::event toggle{.type = "toggle", .payload = {}};
if (!settled(system.send(*actor, toggle))) {  // logs "Active"
    return 1;
}
if (!settled(system.send(*actor, toggle))) {  // logs "Inactive"
    return 1;
}

const xstate::snapshot* now = system.snapshot_of(*actor);
if (now == nullptr) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << "Now: " << boost::json::serialize(now->value) << '\n';

It prints:

Value: "Inactive"
Value: "Active"
Value: "Inactive"
Now: "Inactive"

  • A call runs the system. start and send, like every call that delivers something, run the system until nothing is left to do before they return, as XState’s send processes the event at once, unless an actor is parked: then the call is held, in order, until resume(). Each returns a result<run_outcome>: settled when no actor is left parked, out_of_fuel when one is, or an error, such as xactor’s invalid_argument, of the category webcpp.xactor, for an actor the system does not know (Errors as values).

  • Fuel. The budget the system is created with, {.fuel = 1000}, is the fuel of each execution a call opens; a start or a send opens one. Every microstep costs one unit, and so does every message an actor sends and every timer it arms. When an execution runs out, the call returns out_of_fuel and leaves the actor parked, its work kept and its snapshot the last one it settled in; resume() continues it. XState has no fuel, and an actor whose eventless transitions never settle runs forever there (Fuel, parking and resume, Fuel). The example’s settled takes an error and out_of_fuel alike as a failure, and returns 1.

  • Start. start constructs the actor and runs its initial macrostep, so snapshot_of returns nullptr until then. XState’s createActor already constructs it, and its getSnapshot() answers before start() (The root is constructed on start).

  • Subscribers. A subscriber hears each snapshot the actor settles in while it is active, and the one it is done in, whether the event took a transition or not, as XState’s does. It runs inside the actor’s turn: it may read the system, with snapshot_of for one, but a call from it that changes the system, a send included, returns invalid_argument and changes nothing, where XState accepts a send from a subscriber and handles it once the update in progress is done (Watching an actor, A callback that calls the system back).

Actors covers the rest: children, messages between actors, actors the host answers for, time, and what fuel guarantees.

Use delayed transitions

A delayed transition is taken when its state has been active for a given time, with no event. A state lists its delayed transitions under after, keyed by the delay in milliseconds. Here Active goes back to Inactive two seconds after it was entered, unless a toggle leaves it first, which cancels the delay.

The machine never reads a clock. Entering Active arms a timer, which waits until the host brings the time: clock_tick(2000) moves the system’s time to 2000 milliseconds and fires the timers due by then. XState’s actors schedule delays with JavaScript’s setTimeout unless they are given another clock, such as its SimulatedClock; an xstate actor has no clock but the host’s (In the actor layer, Delayed events and time).

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "toggle",
    "initial": "Inactive",
    "states": {
        "Inactive": {"on": {"toggle": "Active"}},
        "Active": {
            "on": {"toggle": "Inactive"},
            "after": {"2000": "Inactive"}
        }
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> toggle_machine = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!toggle_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 1000});
const auto settled = [](const xstate::result<xstate::run_outcome>& ran) {
    return ran.has_value() && *ran == xstate::run_outcome::settled;
};

const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*toggle_machine);
if (!actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::result<void> subscribed =
    system.subscribe(*actor, [](const xstate::snapshot& snapshot) {
        std::cout << "Value: " << boost::json::serialize(snapshot.value) << '\n';
    });
if (!subscribed.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

if (!settled(system.start(*actor))) {  // logs "Inactive"
    return 1;
}
const xstate::event toggle{.type = "toggle", .payload = {}};
if (!settled(system.send(*actor, toggle))) {  // logs "Active"
    return 1;
}
if (!settled(system.clock_tick(1000))) {  // logs nothing
    return 1;
}
if (!settled(system.clock_tick(2000))) {  // logs "Inactive"
    return 1;
}

It prints:

Value: "Inactive"
Value: "Active"
Value: "Inactive"

At 1000 milliseconds the timer is not due, and nothing happens. At 2000 it fires. An after is an event the state raises with a delay when it is entered, xstate.after.2000.toggle.Active here, and cancels when it is left; the delayed transition is a transition on that event, as in XState (In the machine core).

Handle context data

Context is the data a machine carries beside its state: here, how many times the toggle became Active. A context that is data stays in the config, as JSON: "context": {"count": 0} is XState’s context: { count: 0 }, and it is the context the machine starts with. An assign action updates it: on entering Active, incrementCount adds one to the count.

In XState the update is a function written inline in the config, which JSON cannot hold. In xstate the config names the action, and the program registers it under that name in implementations.actions, as XState’s setup({ actions }) registers implementations by name (Implementations). An assign_action receives an action_args, the context, the event and the action’s params, and returns the members it changes, which it merges into the context, as XState’s assign does (Assign).

An implementation returns a result. A failure stops the macrostep and leaves the snapshot it began from, its status error, where XState’s function would throw (Failures are values).

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "toggle",
    "context": {"count": 0},
    "initial": "Inactive",
    "states": {
        "Inactive": {"on": {"toggle": "Active"}},
        "Active": {
            "entry": "incrementCount",
            "on": {"toggle": "Inactive"},
            "after": {"2000": "Inactive"}
        }
    }
})");

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actions.emplace(
    "incrementCount",
    xstate::assign_action{
        .assignment =
            [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<boost::json::object> {
            const std::optional<std::int64_t> count = integer_at(args.context, "count");
            if (!count.has_value()) {
                return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(
                    xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
            }
            return boost::json::object{{"count", *count + 1}};
        },
    });

const xstate::result<xstate::machine> toggle_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!toggle_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 1000});
const auto settled = [](const xstate::result<xstate::run_outcome>& ran) {
    return ran.has_value() && *ran == xstate::run_outcome::settled;
};

const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*toggle_machine);
if (!actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::result<void> subscribed =
    system.subscribe(*actor, [](const xstate::snapshot& snapshot) {
        std::cout << "State: " << boost::json::serialize(snapshot.value) << ' '
                  << boost::json::serialize(snapshot.context) << '\n';
    });
if (!subscribed.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::event toggle{.type = "toggle", .payload = {}};
if (!settled(system.start(*actor))) {
    return 1;
}
if (!settled(system.send(*actor, toggle))) {  // Active, count 1
    return 1;
}
if (!settled(system.clock_tick(2000))) {  // Inactive, count 1
    return 1;
}
if (!settled(system.send(*actor, toggle))) {  // Active, count 2
    return 1;
}

It prints:

State: "Inactive" {"count":0}
State: "Active" {"count":1}
State: "Inactive" {"count":1}
State: "Active" {"count":2}

The action reads the count with integer_at, which returns none where a member is missing or is not an integer. Boost.JSON’s accessors that check, such as at and as_int64, throw on a mismatch, and a throw aborts a program built without exceptions; if_object, if_contains and is_int64 answer with a pointer or a bool instead, and try_at and try_as_int64 with a boost::system::result:

/** The integer `key` holds in the object `json`; none when it holds no integer. */
std::optional<std::int64_t> integer_at(const boost::json::value& json, std::string_view key) {
    const boost::json::object* object = json.if_object();
    if (object == nullptr) {
        return std::nullopt;
    }
    const boost::json::value* member = object->if_contains(key);
    if (member == nullptr || !member->is_int64()) {
        return std::nullopt;
    }
    return member->get_int64();
}

Context covers context one part at a time: its initial value, assign, how guards and actions read it, and how an actor holds it.

Add input

Input is the data an actor is created with. Here it is the most times the toggle may become Active, maxCount, and the initial context is computed from it. A guard is a condition a transition is taken under: countBelowMax lets toggle activate the toggle only while the count is below that maximum.

In XState both are functions written in the config. In xstate the config names the guard, and the program registers it under that name in implementations.guards, as it registers the action: a predicate of an action_args that returns a result<bool> (Guards). The context function, which a config cannot name, goes in implementations.context: it receives the input and returns the initial context, a result<boost::json::value>, in place of the config’s context. A failure it returns, or a value that is not an object, fails the actor’s initial macrostep and leaves it in the status error (Initial context from the input, A context that is not an object). The input is the input of the actor_options given to create_actor, as XState’s is an option of createActor:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "toggle",
    "initial": "Inactive",
    "states": {
        "Inactive": {
            "on": {
                "toggle": {"guard": "countBelowMax", "target": "Active"}
            }
        },
        "Active": {
            "entry": "incrementCount",
            "on": {"toggle": "Inactive"},
            "after": {"2000": "Inactive"}
        }
    }
})");

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.context =
    [](const boost::json::value& input) -> xstate::result<boost::json::value> {
    const std::optional<std::int64_t> max_count = integer_at(input, "maxCount");
    if (!max_count.has_value()) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::value>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"count", 0}, {"maxCount", *max_count}};
};
implementations.guards.emplace(
    "countBelowMax", [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<bool> {
        const std::optional<std::int64_t> count = integer_at(args.context, "count");
        const std::optional<std::int64_t> max_count = integer_at(args.context, "maxCount");
        if (!count.has_value() || !max_count.has_value()) {
            return xstate::failure<bool>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
        }
        return *count < *max_count;
    });
implementations.actions.emplace(
    "incrementCount",
    xstate::assign_action{
        .assignment =
            [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<boost::json::object> {
            const std::optional<std::int64_t> count = integer_at(args.context, "count");
            if (!count.has_value()) {
                return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(
                    xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
            }
            return boost::json::object{{"count", *count + 1}};
        },
    });

const xstate::result<xstate::machine> toggle_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!toggle_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 1000});
const auto settled = [](const xstate::result<xstate::run_outcome>& ran) {
    return ran.has_value() && *ran == xstate::run_outcome::settled;
};

const xstate::actor_options options{
    .input = boost::json::object{{"maxCount", 1}},
    .id = std::nullopt,
    .system_id = std::nullopt,
};
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*toggle_machine, options);
if (!actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::result<void> subscribed =
    system.subscribe(*actor, [](const xstate::snapshot& snapshot) {
        std::cout << "State: " << boost::json::serialize(snapshot.value) << ' '
                  << boost::json::serialize(snapshot.context) << '\n';
    });
if (!subscribed.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::event toggle{.type = "toggle", .payload = {}};
if (!settled(system.start(*actor))) {
    return 1;
}
if (!settled(system.send(*actor, toggle))) {  // Active, count 1
    return 1;
}
if (!settled(system.clock_tick(2000))) {  // after 2000 ms: Inactive
    return 1;
}
if (!settled(system.send(*actor, toggle))) {  // count is not below maxCount: stays
    return 1;
}

It prints:

State: "Inactive" {"count":0,"maxCount":1}
State: "Active" {"count":1,"maxCount":1}
State: "Inactive" {"count":1,"maxCount":1}
State: "Inactive" {"count":1,"maxCount":1}

The last toggle finds a count of 1, not below a maxCount of 1, so the guard refuses it and the snapshot stays; the subscriber hears it all the same. Input and output covers input, and output, the data an actor is done with.

How to read this documentation

The page goes from a first program to every name in the library. After this introduction, each chapter takes one part, and the appendices gather what a reader looks up:

  • State machines takes a machine one concept at a time, as Stately’s documentation does: the core concepts, machines, states, context, transitions, actions, input and output, and then the pure functions, the macrostep cursor and fuel.

  • Actors: xstate on xactor runs machines as actors: creating them, invoking and spawning children, the messages between actors, the system, time, host actors and fuel.

  • Testing tests machines and actors, and tells how xstate itself is tested against XState.

  • Guarantees lists what xstate promises whatever its caller does, each promise under a number that the code and the tests cite.

  • Reference lists every name xstate declares, from the Doc Comments of its headers.

  • From XState to C++ shows how each of XState’s JavaScript spellings is written in C++.

  • Where xstate differs from XState lists every place where xstate departs from XState, each with its reason.

  • Rationale gives the design decisions, each with its reason.

  • Glossary defines the page’s terms.

Every program on the page is compiled and run by b2 libs/xstate/example, which compares what it prints with the output committed beside it, and the page shows the program’s source and that output, so neither can drift from the library. Every program that uses xstate, and does what XState can do, also runs on XState, as its twin (A twin for every example).

The C++ examples write namespace xstate = webcpp::xstate;. Names follow XState’s, in snake case: createMachine is create_machine, getNextSnapshot is get_next_snapshot, and setup({ actions }) is implementations. An actor is named by the actor_ref its system returned, so XState’s actor.send(event) is system.send(actor, event). An event is xstate::event{.type, .payload}, XState’s { type, ...payload }. From XState to C++ gives each of these spellings, with its reason.

xactor, which the actor layer runs on, is taught alone on its own page: its scheduler, turns, fuel, timers and drivers. This page names xactor where the actor layer leans on it, and links that page there.

State machines

A machine in xstate is the logic of one process: the states it can be in, the events it reacts to, where each event takes it and what it does on the way. It is built from two things:

  • a config, the JSON object XState’s createMachine takes, read when the program runs, from a file, a request or a string in the code;

  • implementations, the C++ code of the actions, guards, delays and actors the config names, registered under those names.

create_machine(config, implementations) checks the two together and builds a machine, an immutable value: it never changes, and its copies share its data. A machine does not hold where it is either. That is a snapshot, a plain value its caller keeps, so one machine serves any number of snapshots and runs at once.

A machine runs in one of two ways. Its caller can step it with the pure functions, XState’s initialTransition, transition and their relatives, each of which computes the next snapshot from a snapshot and an event and returns the actions for the caller to execute; under them, the macrostep cursor runs one microstep per call, so that the caller bounds the work of each event. The last section of this chapter, Pure transitions and the macrostep cursor, covers both. Or an actor runs it: the actor keeps the snapshot, executes the actions, runs children and exchanges events with other actors, which is the subject of the next chapter, Actors: xstate on xactor. This chapter’s examples use the pure functions, which show what a machine does one event at a time and need nothing else.

The sections go from the ideas to the details. Core concepts explains the parts of a statechart in plain words, with one small example each. Machines shows how a machine is created, what its config holds and how its implementations are registered. States, Context, Events and transitions, Actions and Input and output then take each part of a config in depth, and Pure transitions and the macrostep cursor the functions that run it.

Core concepts

A statechart describes what one process does when something happens: the states it can be in, the events it reacts to, and what each event changes. This section explains its parts in plain words, one part at a time, each with the smallest program that shows it, and the sections after it take each part in depth. The other idea xstate rests on, the actor model, which describes how many such processes live together, each reaching the others only by events, opens the next chapter (The actor model).

The examples follow a dog through its day, as Stately’s introduction does. Each one runs its machine with two of the core’s pure functions: get_initial_snapshot gives where the machine is when it starts, and get_next_snapshot where an event takes it from there.

State machines and statecharts

A state machine models how a process goes from state to state when an event occurs. It lists every state the process can be in, every event it reacts to, and, for each state and event, where the process goes next.

Writing this down makes the impossible states visible, since a state that is not listed cannot happen, and the unwanted moves too, since a move that is not listed is never taken. The same state and the same event always lead to the same next state, so a machine is simple to test.

A statechart is a state machine extended for larger processes: a state can contain states (hierarchy), several states can be active at once (parallel states), a state can remember where it was (history), and the process carries data beside its state (context). XState implements statecharts, and xstate runs the same ones, from the same config written as JSON, with a name wherever XState’s config would hold a function (Machines as JSON, implementations by name). What is not ported lists what it does not run yet, and Where xstate differs from XState where it differs. As in Stately’s documentation, "machine" here means a statechart.

In xstate, a machine is the tree of state nodes its config describes, together with the implementations the config names, and it never changes once it is created. Where the machine is at one moment is a separate value, its snapshot (The snapshot). Each event computes a new snapshot from the previous one, and the machine stays as it was.

States

A state is a mode the process is in, such as asleep or awake. Without parallel states (Parallel states), a machine is in exactly one state at each level at a time: a dog is asleep or awake, never both and never neither. There are finitely many of them, which is why such a machine is called a finite state machine.

A config lists the states as the members of states, and names with initial the one the machine enters when it starts:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "dog",
    "initial": "asleep",
    "states": {
        "asleep": {},
        "awake": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> dog = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!dog.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::snapshot first = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*dog);
std::cout << "value: " << boost::json::serialize(first.value) << '\n';
std::cout << std::boolalpha << "asleep: " << first.matches("asleep") << '\n';
std::cout << "awake: " << first.matches("awake") << '\n';

It prints:

value: "asleep"
asleep: true
awake: false

create_machine reads the JSON config, the object XState’s createMachine takes, with the implementations the config names, none here, so {}. It returns a result: the machine, or the error that refused the config and no machine. A config that cannot be a machine is refused at once, so the program checks the result before it uses the machine (What creation refuses). get_initial_snapshot returns where the machine is when it starts, its snapshot, whose value names the current state, and matches asks whether the snapshot is in a given state. get_initial_snapshot, and get_next_snapshot below, are the short forms of initial_transition and transition, XState’s initialTransition and transition, that return the snapshot alone (The snapshot alone).

A machine whose root has states of its own, and is not parallel, names one initial state, and only one, or it would not know where to start: create_machine refuses such a config when it leaves initial out, as XState’s createMachine refuses it. A parent state (Parent states) names its initial child the same way, under the same rule. Two kinds of state need no initial: one without children, such as asleep, and a parallel state, the root included, which enters all its children at once (Parallel states). Creating a machine says more about create_machine, Initial states about the initial state, and Matching a state value about matches.

Events and transitions

An event is something that happened: the dog wakes up, the dog falls asleep. It has a type, a string, and may carry data. A transition is a move from one state, its source, to another, its target, when an event of a given type happens. Transitions are what make a machine react: for each state, they say which events matter there and where each one leads. A state lists its transitions in on, by event type:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "dog",
    "initial": "asleep",
    "states": {
        "asleep": {"on": {"wakes up": "awake"}},
        "awake": {"on": {"falls asleep": "asleep"}}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> dog = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!dog.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::snapshot now = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*dog);
for (const std::string_view type : {"wakes up", "wakes up", "falls asleep"}) {
    const xstate::event happened{.type = std::string(type), .payload = {}};
    now = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*dog, now, happened);
    std::cout << type << " -> " << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';
}

It prints:

wakes up -> "awake"
wakes up -> "awake"
falls asleep -> "asleep"

get_next_snapshot computes the next snapshot from a snapshot and an event, and changes neither. The second wakes up arrives in awake, which has no transition for it, so the dog stays awake: when neither the current state nor any state that contains it has a transition for an event, the event changes nothing, and the snapshot stays as it was.

An xstate::event holds the type and a JSON object, its payload. XState’s event is one flat object, { type: 'wakes up', ...payload }, and event_from_json reads that form. Events and transitions each have a section of their own, Events and Transitions.

One event can cause more than one step: after its transition, the machine may take eventless transitions (always) and events it raised itself. Each such step is a microstep; all of them, until the machine is stable, are one macrostep, the unit in which a machine handles an event. get_next_snapshot runs a whole macrostep in one call, as XState does. The macrostep cursor under it runs one microstep per call instead, so that its caller decides how much work an event may cost (The machine core, The macrostep cursor).

Actions

An action is an effect: something the machine does as it moves, such as notifying, logging or saving, as opposed to where it goes. The machine says when an effect happens; the code that performs it lives outside the states and transitions. Most actions are fire and forget: the machine neither waits for them nor reads their result. The exception is the built-in assign, whose result the machine merges into its context (Context). A state has entry actions, run when it is entered, and exit actions, run when it is left; a transition has actions of its own, run as it is taken:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "dog",
    "initial": "asleep",
    "states": {
        "asleep": {
            "exit": "stretch",
            "on": {"wakes up": {"target": "awake", "actions": "yawn"}}
        },
        "awake": {"entry": {"type": "bark", "params": {"times": 2}}}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> dog = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!dog.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::snapshot asleep = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*dog);
const xstate::event wakes_up{.type = "wakes up", .payload = {}};
const auto [awake, actions] = xstate::transition(*dog, asleep, wakes_up);
std::cout << "value: " << boost::json::serialize(awake.value) << '\n';
for (const xstate::action& returned : actions) {
    std::cout << "the caller executes " << returned.type;
    if (!returned.params.is_null()) {
        std::cout << ' ' << boost::json::serialize(returned.params);
    }
    std::cout << '\n';
}

It prints:

value: "awake"
the caller executes stretch
the caller executes yawn
the caller executes bark {"times":2}

In one move the exit actions come first, then the transition’s, then the entry actions: stretch, yawn, bark. A JSON config cannot hold a function, so in xstate an action is a name, with optional params, where XState’s config may also hold the function itself (Functions become names). What the name does is decided outside the config. stretch, yawn and bark have no implementation: they are custom actions, and transition returns them, in order and with their params, for the caller to execute, as XState’s pure transition returns every action and executes none.

The built-in actions, XState’s assign, raise, sendTo and the others, are registered by name in implementations, and xstate resolves them: assign changes the context and is never returned, a raise without a delay queues its event in the macrostep, and every built-in but assign comes back resolved, under XState’s name (xstate.raise, xstate.sendTo, xstate.spawnChild and so on), for the actor layer or the caller to execute. Built-in and custom actions lists them all, and Custom actions covers custom actions.

Context

The finite states say which mode the process is in; they cannot count, or hold a name. Context holds that data: a JSON object that travels with the state, the extended state of a statechart. Only an assign action changes it, by merging the object its implementation returns into the context, as JavaScript’s Object.assign does, so every change to the data is an action the config names. Here each gets treat runs eatTreat, which counts the treat:

/** One more treat: the partial context `eatTreat` merges into the context. */
xstate::result<boost::json::object> eat_treat(const xstate::action_args& args) {
    const boost::json::object* context = args.context.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* treats =
        context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("treats");
    if (treats == nullptr || !treats->is_int64()) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"treats", treats->get_int64() + 1}};
}
xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actions.emplace("eatTreat", xstate::assign_action{.assignment = eat_treat});

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "dog",
    "initial": "begging",
    "context": {"treats": 0},
    "states": {
        "begging": {"on": {"gets treat": {"actions": "eatTreat"}}}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> dog = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!dog.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::snapshot now = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*dog);
print(now);
const xstate::event gets_treat{.type = "gets treat", .payload = {}};
for (int treat = 0; treat < 2; ++treat) {
    now = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*dog, now, gets_treat);
    print(now);
}

It prints:

"begging" {"treats":0}
"begging" {"treats":1}
"begging" {"treats":2}

eat_treat computes the update: it is the function XState’s assign takes. An assign_action holds it, registered in implementations.actions under the name the config uses, eatTreat, as XState’s setup registers it. It receives an action_args: the context as it is when the action runs, the event, and the action’s params. It returns a result: when it cannot compute the update, here when treats is missing or not an integer, it returns an error rather than throwing, and the macrostep fails, leaving the snapshot it began from with the status error.

The transition on gets treat has no target, so the dog stays begging and only the action runs. Stately calls this a self-transition: doing something, not going somewhere. Without a target, the state is neither exited nor entered again (Self-transitions and reenter).

A config without context, or with null, starts from {}, as in XState. Any other context that is not an object, false, a number, a string or a list, is kept as written, and an assign on it fails with implementation_failed, where XState starts a falsy one from {} and makes any other an object at its first assign (A context that is not an object). Updating context with assign covers assign, and Initial context from the input how an input sets the first context.

Parent states

A parent state, or compound state, contains states of its own, its children, and is active while one of them is. A state without children is atomic. Parents exist so that what several states share is written once: a transition of the parent applies whichever child is active. The dog arrives home from walking or from running, and the transition is written once, on onAWalk, which names its initial child, entered with it:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "walk",
    "initial": "waiting",
    "states": {
        "waiting": {"on": {"leave home": "onAWalk"}},
        "onAWalk": {
            "initial": "walking",
            "states": {
                "walking": {"on": {"speed up": "running"}},
                "running": {"on": {"slow down": "walking"}}
            },
            "on": {"arrive home": "walkComplete"}
        },
        "walkComplete": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> walk = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!walk.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::snapshot now = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*walk);
for (const std::string_view type : {"leave home", "speed up", "arrive home"}) {
    const xstate::event happened{.type = std::string(type), .payload = {}};
    now = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*walk, now, happened);
    std::cout << type << " -> " << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << std::boolalpha
              << ", on a walk: " << now.matches("onAWalk") << '\n';
}

It prints:

leave home -> {"onAWalk":"walking"}, on a walk: true
speed up -> {"onAWalk":"running"}, on a walk: true
arrive home -> "walkComplete", on a walk: false

The state value of a parent state is an object that names its active child, {"onAWalk":"walking"}, nested as deep as the states are; an atomic state at the top is a string. matches("onAWalk") holds for every child of onAWalk. Sharing a transition, or an entry or exit action, through the parent is what keeps a large machine small. They are taken in depth in Parent states.

Parallel states

A parallel state has several children, its regions, all active at once. Each region has its own states, its own initial state and its own transitions, and moves independently of the others: the dog walks or runs, and, at the same time, wags its tail or does not. Without parallel states, each combination would need a state of its own.

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "onAWalk",
    "type": "parallel",
    "states": {
        "activity": {
            "initial": "walking",
            "states": {
                "walking": {"on": {"speed up": "running", "sees a squirrel": "running"}},
                "running": {"on": {"slow down": "walking"}}
            }
        },
        "tail": {
            "initial": "notWagging",
            "states": {
                "notWagging": {"on": {"sees a squirrel": "wagging"}},
                "wagging": {"on": {"calms down": "notWagging"}}
            }
        }
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> walk = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!walk.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::snapshot now = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*walk);
std::cout << "initial: " << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';
for (const std::string_view type : {"sees a squirrel", "slow down"}) {
    const xstate::event happened{.type = std::string(type), .payload = {}};
    now = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*walk, now, happened);
    std::cout << type << " -> " << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';
}

It prints:

initial: {"activity":"walking","tail":"notWagging"}
sees a squirrel -> {"activity":"running","tail":"wagging"}
slow down -> {"activity":"walking","tail":"wagging"}

The machine is parallel at its root, "type": "parallel", and its state value names the active child of each region. One event can move several regions in the same step: sees a squirrel makes the dog run and wag at once. slow down concerns activity only, and tail stays where it is. They are taken in depth in Parallel states.

History states

A history state remembers which child of its parent was active when the parent was left. A transition that targets it goes back to that child, where a transition that targets the parent enters the parent’s initial child, so a process that is interrupted can resume where it was:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "walk",
    "initial": "onAWalk",
    "states": {
        "onAWalk": {
            "initial": "walking",
            "states": {
                "walking": {"on": {"speed up": "running"}},
                "running": {"on": {"slow down": "walking"}},
                "previous": {"type": "history"}
            },
            "on": {"smells something": "sniffing"}
        },
        "sniffing": {"on": {"carry on": "onAWalk.previous", "start over": "onAWalk"}}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> walk = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!walk.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::snapshot now = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*walk);
for (const std::string_view type :
     {"speed up", "smells something", "carry on", "smells something", "start over"}) {
    const xstate::event happened{.type = std::string(type), .payload = {}};
    now = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*walk, now, happened);
    std::cout << type << " -> " << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';
}

It prints:

speed up -> {"onAWalk":"running"}
smells something -> "sniffing"
carry on -> {"onAWalk":"running"}
smells something -> "sniffing"
start over -> {"onAWalk":"walking"}

The dog was running when it smelled something, so carry on, which targets onAWalk.previous, takes it back to running; start over targets onAWalk itself and enters its initial child, walking. A history state is never active: it only redirects the transitions that target it. What each history state remembers is part of the snapshot.

A shallow history, the default, remembers the parent’s active child; a deep one, "history": "deep", every active state below the parent. Until the parent has been left once, the history state has nothing to remember, and the transition enters its default: the history state’s own target, or else the parent’s initial child. History states are taken in depth in History states.

Final states

A final state is where a process ends. When a machine enters a final state at its top level, it is done: its status becomes done, and it produces its output, the output of its config. A machine that is done has finished its work, and whoever runs it can stop sending it events and read the result:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "walk",
    "initial": "waiting",
    "states": {
        "waiting": {"on": {"leave home": "onAWalk"}},
        "onAWalk": {"on": {"arrive home": "walkComplete"}},
        "walkComplete": {"type": "final"}
    },
    "output": {"walked": true}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> walk = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!walk.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::snapshot now = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*walk);
for (const std::string_view type : {"leave home", "arrive home"}) {
    const xstate::event happened{.type = std::string(type), .payload = {}};
    now = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*walk, now, happened);
