    std::cout << type << " -> " << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << ", "
              << status_name(now.status) << '\n';
}
if (now.output.has_value()) {
    std::cout << "output: " << boost::json::serialize(*now.output) << '\n';
}

It prints:

leave home -> "onAWalk", active
arrive home -> "walkComplete", done
output: {"walked":true}

status_name, a function of the program, spells the status. A snapshot’s status is active while the machine runs, done once it has reached a final state at its top level, and error once it has failed, for example when an implementation returned an error or a child’s error found no transition (Failures are values). The output here is a fixed JSON value; one computed from the context and the event is registered by name, the root’s id, in implementations.outputs (A final state’s output).

A final state inside a parent state completes that parent instead: the machine raises the event xstate.done.state.<id>, <id> being the parent’s, which the parent’s onDone transition takes. The parent stays active until a transition leaves it. A parallel state is complete once every region is in a final state. Final states are taken in depth in A parent state is done, A parallel state is done and When the machine is done.

The snapshot

A snapshot is where a machine is at one moment, with everything needed to compute what it does next. In xstate it is a plain value, xstate::snapshot, which the program keeps, copies or stores, and hands back with the next event. The machine never changes; each event yields a new snapshot.

Member What it holds

value

the state value, a string or an object of the active states

context

the context

status

active, done or error

output

the output, once the machine is done

error, error_value

why the machine failed

tags

the tags of the active states, each once

nodes

the active state nodes, by their place in the machine, in XState’s order

history

what each history state remembers

children

the child actors, each as its id and its src

The dog leaves home, and the program reads the snapshot it is in:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "walk",
    "initial": "waiting",
    "context": {"dog": "Rex"},
    "states": {
        "waiting": {"on": {"leave home": "onAWalk"}},
        "onAWalk": {
            "tags": ["outside"],
            "initial": "walking",
            "states": {
                "walking": {"on": {"speed up": "running"}},
                "running": {}
            },
            "on": {"arrive home": "waiting"}
        }
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> walk = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!walk.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::snapshot waiting = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*walk);
const xstate::event leave_home{.type = "leave home", .payload = {}};
const xstate::snapshot out = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*walk, waiting, leave_home);
const xstate::result<bool> can_arrive =
    xstate::can(*walk, out, xstate::event{.type = "arrive home", .payload = {}});
const xstate::result<bool> can_leave = xstate::can(*walk, out, leave_home);
if (!can_arrive.has_value() || !can_leave.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

std::cout << "value: " << boost::json::serialize(out.value) << '\n';
std::cout << "context: " << boost::json::serialize(out.context) << '\n';
std::cout << "status: " << status_name(out.status) << '\n';
const boost::json::array tags(out.tags.begin(), out.tags.end());
std::cout << "tags: " << boost::json::serialize(tags) << '\n';
std::cout << std::boolalpha << "matches onAWalk: " << out.matches("onAWalk") << '\n';
std::cout << "has tag outside: " << out.has_tag("outside") << '\n';
std::cout << "can arrive home: " << *can_arrive << '\n';
std::cout << "can leave home: " << *can_leave << '\n';

It prints:

value: {"onAWalk":"walking"}
context: {"dog":"Rex"}
status: active
tags: ["outside"]
matches onAWalk: true
has tag outside: true
can arrive home: true
can leave home: false

A tag names a group of states, so code can ask about the group, with has_tag, without naming each state in it (Tags). can asks whether an event would take a transition that does something, one with a target or an action, before sending it (Whether an event would do anything); it returns a result, since a guard it evaluates may fail.

A snapshot names its active states by their place in the machine, so it is read with the machine that computed it. The order of nodes is not cosmetic: it decides which eventless transition a parallel state takes first. To persist a snapshot, keep its value and context, and rebuild it with resolve_state, which restores those two, and from the value the active states and their tags, but nothing else: the status comes from the value, done or active, never error, and the output, the error, what history states remember and the children are not restored (Persisted state). XState’s snapshot has one more status, stopped; in xstate, whether an actor was stopped is the actor’s status, kept apart from its snapshot (Actors). States takes each member in turn (The snapshot).

Machines

A state machine describes how something behaves: the states it can be in, and the event that takes it from one state to another. A machine is the logic of an actor, not the actor itself. It holds no current state: the state it is in lives in a snapshot, and a running instance of it is an actor. Any number of snapshots and actors are made from one machine, each independent of the others.

A machine is built from two things: a config, the description XState’s createMachine(config) takes, and implementations, the code the config names. xstate reads the config as JSON and takes the implementations by name. This section shows how a machine is created, what its config holds, how implementations are registered and why by name, why a machine never changes, what creation refuses, how to find a state node, and how a machine is written out as XState’s definition and loaded back.

Creating a machine

create_machine(config, implementations) builds a machine from a config, a boost::json::value, and the implementations the config names. It returns a result<machine>: the machine, or the error that refused the config (What creation refuses). Stately’s feedback machine has two states, question and thanks, and goes from the first to the second on the event feedback.good:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "feedback",
    "initial": "question",
    "states": {
        "question": {
            "on": {
                "feedback.good": {"target": "thanks"}
            }
        },
        "thanks": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!feedback.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::snapshot question = xstate::initial_transition(*feedback).first;
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(question.value) << '\n';

const xstate::event good{.type = "feedback.good", .payload = {}};
const xstate::snapshot thanks = xstate::transition(*feedback, question, good).first;
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(thanks.value) << '\n';

It prints:

"question"
"thanks"

Boost.JSON parses the config from a string; a program may as well read it from a file or a request. It names no implementation, so the second argument is empty, {}. Once has_value() says the result holds a machine, *feedback is that machine. initial_transition and transition are XState’s pure functions initialTransition and transition: each returns, as a pair, the snapshot the machine reaches and the actions its caller executes, and changes nothing else, so .first is the snapshot. Pure transitions and the macrostep cursor has all of them and the cursor they are built on. Stately’s page runs the machine as an actor, with createActor; in xstate an actor_system does that, as Actors shows.

The config

A config describes the machine: its states, the transitions between them, the actions they run, its context. In xstate it is the object XState’s createMachine takes, written as JSON. JSON holds data only, where XState’s config, a JavaScript object, may also hold functions: an inline action, a guard written as an arrow function, a context computed from the input. That is a choice, for three reasons:

  • A config is data a person writes, or exports from Stately Studio, and a program loads at run time, from a file, a database or a request, with nothing to compile.

  • The JSON is XState’s config: xstate’s tests run their configs on XState itself and compare the two, one microstep at a time (Testing). Only XState’s higher-order guards, functions there, take a JSON form of xstate’s (Higher-order guards and stateIn).

  • C++ has no object literal that holds functions. A config holding C++ code would be C++ code too, compiled into the program.

What a function does in XState’s config, a name does in xstate’s: the config names the function, and the implementations hold it (Implementations). An action or a guard is named as XState’s JSON writes it, "entry": "notify", or {"type": "notify", "params": {...}} with fixed params, which the implementation reads from its action_args together with the context and the event. A higher-order guard is a JSON object, {"type": "xstate.not", "guards": [...]} and the like. Appendix A maps each function XState’s config may hold to its form in xstate (Functions become implementations registered by name), and Functions become names gives the three that cannot keep what they do in XState.

The members xstate reads, on any state unless the table says otherwise:

Member What it is Section

id

The state’s id; on the root, the machine’s id

State nodes and ids

states, initial

The child states, by key, and the child a compound state starts in: its key, or {"target": "<key>", "actions": [...]}, which may also carry a meta and a description

States

type

atomic, compound, parallel, final or history; without it, a state with children is compound, one whose history is truthy as JavaScript reads it is a history state, and any other is atomic, as in XState: a history of false, null, "" or 0 leaves it atomic

States

history, target

A history state’s depth, deep for "deep" and shallow otherwise, as in XState, and its default target

States

context

On the root: the initial context. A null one, or none, is {}, as in XState; any other value that is not an object is kept as written, even false, 0 or "", which XState makes {} (A context that is not an object)

Context

on

The transitions, by event type

Events and transitions

always, after

The eventless transitions, and the delayed ones by delay

Events and transitions

onDone

The transition a compound or parallel state takes when it is done

States

entry, exit

The actions run when the state is entered and when it is left

Actions

invoke

The actors the state runs while it is active, src naming each

Actors

output

On a final state, its output; on the root, the machine’s

Input and output

tags, meta, description

Data the state carries for its readers: its tags, a string or a list of strings; its meta, any value, a null one being none; and its description, a string

States

version

On the root: the machine’s version, which its definition repeats on every node; a machine loaded from a definition has the definition’s

The definition

A transition is a target, an object (target, actions, guard, reenter, description, meta) or a list of them (Events and transitions). A target names a sibling of the transition’s state by its key, or a state below that sibling by a path of keys joined by dots, "red.stop"; a state below the transition’s own state by a path that starts with a dot, ".child"; or any state by its id, "#id" (Targets). states, on and after are read in the order JavaScript enumerates an object’s keys, as XState reads them: a key that is an array index, such as "500", first, by number, then the rest as written (State nodes and ids).

xstate reads no other member of a transition but cond, XState v4’s name for guard: a truthy cond refuses the machine, as XState’s development build refuses it (What creation refuses). types, which only TypeScript reads, and schemas, which XState keeps on the machine without using, are left unread. So is options: XState uses its maxIterations to throw on a macrostep that never settles, and in xstate the bound is the fuel of the caller that drives the cursor (Fuel). So is XState’s route, which lets the event {"type": "xstate.route", "to": "#<id>"} reach, from any state, a state that has an id and a route; in xstate that event selects no transition.

Implementations

Implementations are the code a machine runs that is not its states and transitions: actions, the side effects; guards, the conditions a transition is taken on; delays, the time before a delayed transition; and actors, what a state invokes. Three more compute a value: the initial context from the input, an invoked child’s input, and a final state’s output.

implementations holds them by name, as XState’s setup({ actions, guards, delays, actors }) registers them, so that the config refers to each with a string. In xstate a name is the only way, because a JSON config holds nothing else, and registering by name gives three things:

  • The config stays data, XState’s own, and to_json writes the machine back as XState’s definition (The definition).

  • One config runs with different implementations (A machine is immutable).

  • Creation checks the names the config uses: a guard, an after delay or an actor the implementations do not hold refuses the machine (What creation refuses), where XState fails only when it first needs the name, or never (A config is refused when it is created). A delay that an action implementation names in its delay is not checked: one that is not registered means no delay, as in XState.

An action is the exception: an action name the implementations do not hold is not an error. It is a custom action, which xstate returns to its caller to execute, as XState’s transition returns it (Custom actions). That is how a caller’s own effects, a log line, a request, a write, reach it.

Stately’s setup example registers two assign actions, increment and decrement, which the config names under on:

/** The context's count plus `step`, as an assign merges it into the context. */
xstate::result<boost::json::object> add(const xstate::action_args& args, std::int64_t step) {
    const boost::json::object* context = args.context.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* count = context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("count");
    const std::int64_t* value = count == nullptr ? nullptr : count->if_int64();
    if (value == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"count", *value + step}};
}

const xstate::assign_action increment{
    .assignment = [](const xstate::action_args& args) { return add(args, 1); },
};
const xstate::assign_action decrement{
    .assignment = [](const xstate::action_args& args) { return add(args, -1); },
};
xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actions.emplace("increment", increment);
implementations.actions.emplace("decrement", decrement);

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "context": {"count": 0},
    "on": {
        "inc": {"actions": "increment"},
        "dec": {"actions": "decrement"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> counter = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!counter.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::snapshot now = xstate::initial_transition(*counter).first;
for (const std::string_view type : {"inc", "inc", "dec"}) {
    const xstate::event sent{.type = std::string(type), .payload = {}};
    now = xstate::transition(*counter, now, sent).first;
    std::cout << type << ' ' << boost::json::serialize(now.context) << '\n';
}

It prints:

inc {"count":1}
inc {"count":2}
dec {"count":1}

increment and decrement are each an assign_action, holding an assigner that returns the members to change, and emplace registers each in implementations.actions under the name the config uses. xstate merges what an assigner returns into the context as Object.assign does, and fails with implementation_failed on a context that is not an object (A context that is not an object). A context and an event are JSON values, which no compiler checks, as XState’s types let TypeScript check them; so an implementation checks what it reads before it reads it, as add does, and returns implementation_failed when the context is not what it expects.

Guards and delays are registered the same way, in implementations.guards and implementations.delays. After Stately’s example, a delayed transition is guarded by canAccess and delayed by shortDelay; its action, trackAccess, is left unregistered:

/** Whether the context's role is "admin". */
xstate::result<bool> can_access(const xstate::action_args& args) {
    const boost::json::object* context = args.context.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* role = context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("role");
    return role != nullptr && role->is_string() && role->get_string() == "admin";
}

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.guards.emplace("canAccess", can_access);
implementations.delays.emplace("shortDelay", [](const xstate::action_args&) {
    return xstate::result<std::uint64_t>(250);
});

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "access",
    "context": {"role": "admin"},
    "initial": "checking",
    "states": {
        "checking": {
            "after": {
                "shortDelay": {
                    "guard": "canAccess",
                    "actions": "trackAccess",
                    "target": "allowed"
                }
            }
        },
        "allowed": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> access = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!access.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const auto [checking, entry_actions] = xstate::initial_transition(*access);
for (const xstate::action& entry : entry_actions) {
    std::cout << entry.type << ' ' << boost::json::serialize(entry.params) << '\n';
}

const xstate::event delayed{.type = "xstate.after.shortDelay.access.checking", .payload = {}};
const auto [allowed, actions] = xstate::transition(*access, checking, delayed);
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(allowed.value);
for (const xstate::action& taken : actions) {
    std::cout << ' ' << taken.type;
}
std::cout << '\n';

It prints:

xstate.raise {"event":{"type":"xstate.after.shortDelay.access.checking"},"id":"xstate.after.shortDelay.access.checking","delay":250}
"allowed" xstate.cancel trackAccess

Entering checking returns the delayed xstate.raise of its after event, whose delay, 250, shortDelay resolved. A delay is always a function, here one that ignores its arguments, where XState’s delays also takes a plain number. The example sends the after event itself, as a clock would once the delay has passed; delayed transitions in the machine core shows the simulated_clock that does it. canAccess lets the transition through, leaving checking returns the xstate.cancel of the delayed event, and trackAccess, which nothing implements, comes back as a custom action.

implementations is a value: a module that adds its own entries to another’s copies it and inserts them, where XState’s setup.extend adds implementations to an existing setup. It holds seven members:

Member Keyed by What it holds Section

actions

action name

XState’s setup({ actions }): one of xstate’s built-in actions, assign_action, raise_action, log_action, send_to_action and the others, with the functions it resolves with

Actions

guards

guard name

XState’s setup({ guards }): a predicate, which returns result<bool>

Events and transitions

delays

delay name

XState’s setup({ delays }): a delay_maker, which returns the delay in milliseconds, result<std::uint64_t>

Events and transitions

actors

src

XState’s setup({ actors }): a machine_actor, a machine run as a child, or a host_actor, work the host does, in place of fromPromise

Actors

context

(one function)

XState’s context: ({ input }) => ...: a context_maker, which returns the initial context for the input, in place of the config’s context. A value that is not an object fails the initial macrostep with implementation_failed, where XState merges it into {} (A context that is not an object)

Context

inputs

invoke id

An invoke’s input: ({ context, event }) => ...: a value_maker

Input and output

outputs

state id

A final state’s output: ({ context, event }) => ..., or, by the root’s id, the machine’s: a value_maker

Input and output

Built-in and custom actions lists the built-in actions, each with what the core returns for it. The machine core runs no actor itself: entering a state that invokes one resolves into an xstate.spawnChild action and leaving it into an xstate.stopChild, an invoke’s onDone and onError are transitions on xstate.done.actor.<id> and xstate.error.actor.<id>, and the actor layer runs the child and delivers those events (Invoking actors).

The context’s function receives the input. Every other function the implementations hold receives an action_args: the context as it is when the function runs, the event of the microstep, and the params the config gave the action or the guard, null when it gave none. The root’s output is the one exception to the event: it receives the done event that completed the machine, as XState’s does. For a compound root, that is the done event of the top-level final state, which carries that state’s output; for a parallel root, it is the root’s own done event, which carries none (The machine’s output and its final state). Each function returns a result, and an error it returns stops the macrostep, which leaves the snapshot it began from with the status error, where XState’s implementation would have thrown (Failures are values).

Three rules hold for the implementations, each checked at creation:

  • An implementation holding an empty function, a default-constructed std::function, refuses the machine with invalid_config: calling it would abort in a build without exceptions. An optional function left out holds none: a log_action without a value is a log of the context and the event, as in XState.

  • An inputs entry names an invoke whose config gives no input, and an outputs entry a final state, or the root, whose config gives no output; any other is invalid_config.

  • Every actor the config names, by an invoke’s src or through a spawn_child_action it names as an action, is an entry of actors; any other is unknown_actor. A registered spawn_child_action the config never names is not checked, as XState’s setup accepts it.

A machine is immutable

A machine never changes once it is created. The state it is in lives in a snapshot, a value of its own, so one machine serves any number of snapshots and actors at once, and nothing one of them does reaches another. A machine is a handle to data its copies share: copying one copies a pointer, not the tree, so a cursor, an actor or a machine_actor keeps a copy. The transitions a microstep reports point into the machine, and stay valid while any copy of it lives.

To run one config with other implementations, create a second machine from it. create_machine takes the whole set of implementations, so a program that changes some of them copies the first machine’s, registry(), and replaces the entries that change. XState’s machine.provide does this in one call; xstate has no provide (What is not ported).

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "context": {"count": 0},
    "on": {
        "inc": {"actions": "increment"}
    }
})");

const xstate::assign_action plus_one{
    .assignment = [](const xstate::action_args& args) { return add(args, 1); },
};
xstate::implementations adds_one;
adds_one.actions.emplace("increment", plus_one);
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> counter = xstate::create_machine(config, adds_one);
if (!counter.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::assign_action plus_ten{
    .assignment = [](const xstate::action_args& args) { return add(args, 10); },
};
xstate::implementations adds_ten = counter->registry();
adds_ten.actions.insert_or_assign("increment", plus_ten);
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> by_ten = xstate::create_machine(config, adds_ten);
if (!by_ten.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const auto increment_once = [](const xstate::machine& machine) {
    const xstate::snapshot initial = xstate::initial_transition(machine).first;
    const xstate::event inc{.type = "inc", .payload = {}};
    return xstate::transition(machine, initial, inc).first.context;
};
std::cout << "counter " << boost::json::serialize(increment_once(*counter)) << '\n';
std::cout << "byTen " << boost::json::serialize(increment_once(*by_ten)) << '\n';

It prints:

counter {"count":1}
byTen {"count":10}

add is the function of the previous section’s example. by_ten starts from a copy of the implementations of counter, in which insert_or_assign replaces increment and keeps any other entry. Both machines are created from one parsed config; neither changes the other, nor the config.

What creation refuses

A config is checked once, when the machine is created, and a config that is not a machine gives no machine: create_machine returns the error instead. Every machine comes from create_machine, which create_machine_from_definition calls too, so a machine that exists has passed every check, and a mistake in a config shows when the config is loaded, not when an event first reaches it.

The error is a value, not an exception. xstate throws no exception of its own, and builds with exceptions turned off, which the lint checks; where XState throws, xstate returns an error. result<T> is boost::system::result<T, boost::system::error_code>; its error is a code of the category webcpp.xstate, one of the values of errc, and message() spells its name. Check has_value() before using a result.

Here a transition is guarded by isValid, which the implementations do not hold:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "initial": "editing",
    "states": {
        "editing": {
            "on": {
                "submit": {"guard": "isValid", "target": "submitted"}
            }
        },
        "submitted": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> form = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!form.has_value()) {
    const boost::system::error_code& error = form.error();
    std::cout << error.category().name() << ": " << error.message() << '\n';
}

It prints:

webcpp.xstate: unknown_guard

xstate finds the missing name when the machine is loaded, before any event. XState creates this machine and starts it, and throws only when submit arrives and the guard is evaluated (A config is refused when it is created). XState refuses some configs in createMachine, others only when the machine starts or an event reaches the broken part, and accepts some; xstate refuses each of those below at creation, and the last column says what XState does with it:

The config, or the implementations Error XState

Is not a JSON object, or has a member xstate cannot read, such as an id or a tag that is not a string, a type xstate does not know, or a history target that is not a string or a list of strings

invalid_config

Accepts each of these at creation: a list is a machine with no state, a non-string id or tag and an unknown type run, and a history target that is not a string throws a TypeError when the history state is entered

Has an entry, exit or actions that is null, or a tags that is null

invalid_config

Reads it, as its toArray does, as a list that holds null: the machine runs with the null tag, and fails when it runs the null action

Has a compound state without initial

invalid_config

Throws in createMachine

Has an on key of ""

invalid_config

Throws in createMachine: an eventless transition is always

Has a transition that declares a truthy cond, renamed guard in XState v5

invalid_config

Throws in createMachine, in its development build

Has a transition target that names no state

unknown_target

Throws in createMachine

Has a history state, below the root, whose target names no state

unknown_target

Throws when the history state is entered

Has an initial that names no child

unknown_target

Throws when the state is entered, the root’s when the machine starts

Has a higher-order guard without a guards list, an xstate.not with other than one operand, or an xstate.stateIn without stateValue

invalid_config

No counterpart: these are functions in XState

Names a guard the implementations do not hold

unknown_guard

Throws when the guard is evaluated

Has an after key that is not digits alone but starts with a digit, a sign or a dot, such as 1.5, -5 or 1e3

invalid_config

Reads a key JavaScript takes as a number as that number, a delay of 1.5, -5 or 1000 milliseconds, and any other as a delay’s name

Names, as an after key, a delay the implementations do not hold

unknown_delay

Takes the delayed transition at once, as if it had no delay

Invokes an actor the implementations do not hold, or spawns one through an action it names

unknown_actor

Creates no child, and fails where something reads it

Has a state whose default entry leads back to it: a history state whose default target is an ancestor whose initial states lead back to the history

invalid_config

Overflows its stack when it enters the state

Has an invoke whose src is not a string

invalid_config

Takes inline actor logic, which JSON cannot hold

Implementations: one holds an empty function

invalid_config

No counterpart

Implementations: an inputs entry names no invoke, an outputs entry names neither a final state nor the root, or either names one whose config already gives its input or output

invalid_config

No counterpart

Some members hold any value, as in XState: a state’s meta, the root’s version, the output of a final state or of the root, and a transition’s meta and description. Two values are dropped, where XState keeps them: a state’s meta that is null, which xstate reads as no meta, and a state’s description that is not a string, an exception to the first row.

One config is accepted as XState accepts it: a machine whose root is itself a history state, which has no parent to resolve its default target against. A microstep that needs that default fails with unknown_target, where XState throws (History states).

What creation cannot see fails later, and as a value too: an implementation that returns an error fails the microstep that calls it, and the snapshot it leaves has the status error (Actions).

State nodes and ids

A machine is a tree of state nodes, one for the root and one for each state of its config, and a node holds everything the config says of its state. A program reads the nodes to show a machine, to name a state in a target or a query, or to read what a snapshot’s active states are.

xstate keeps the nodes in one list, in document order: the root first, a parent before its children, and the children in the order JavaScript enumerates the keys of states, as XState reads them. A key that is an array index, such as "0" or "2", comes first, by number, and the others follow as the config writes them: the children b, 10 and 2 are listed 2, 10, b. A node is named by its index in that list, so the tree holds no pointer: size() is the number of nodes, node(index) one of them, for an index below size(), and root() is node(0).

A state_node holds what XState’s StateNode holds once it is initialised: its key in its parent’s states, its id, its path of keys from the root, its type, the index of its parent, its children, its entry and exit actions, its transitions and invokes, its tags, meta, output and description. A state’s id is the id its config gives, or, without one, the machine’s id and the state’s path, joined by dots; the machine’s id, id(), is the root’s id, (machine) when the config gives none, as in XState. An explicit id names its own node only: below, the children of playing, whose id is active, are player.playing.normal and player.playing.fast.

std::string_view type_name(xstate::node_type type) {
    switch (type) {
        case xstate::node_type::atomic: return "atomic";
        case xstate::node_type::compound: return "compound";
        case xstate::node_type::parallel: return "parallel";
        case xstate::node_type::final: return "final";
        case xstate::node_type::history: return "history";
    }
    return "unknown";
}

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "player",
    "initial": "stopped",
    "states": {
        "stopped": {"on": {"play": "playing"}},
        "playing": {
            "id": "active",
            "initial": "normal",
            "states": {"normal": {}, "fast": {}},
            "on": {"stop": "stopped"}
        },
        "done": {"type": "final"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> player = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!player.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

for (std::size_t index = 0; index < player->size(); ++index) {
    const xstate::state_node& node = player->node(index);
    std::cout << index << ' ' << node.key << ' ' << node.id << ' ' << type_name(node.type)
              << '\n';
}

const xstate::result<std::size_t> active = player->node_by_id("active");
if (!active.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<std::size_t> fast = player->child(*active, "fast");
if (!fast.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<std::size_t> found = player->node_by_id("#active.fast");
if (!found.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << player->node(*fast).id << ' ' << player->node(*found).id << '\n';

It prints:

0 player player compound
1 stopped player.stopped atomic
2 playing active compound
3 normal player.playing.normal atomic
4 fast player.playing.fast atomic
5 done player.done final
player.playing.fast player.playing.fast

Each line gives a node’s index, key, id and type, and type_name spells the type. The index is the node’s order in XState, as long as no two nodes of the machine share an id. Three functions find a node, each returning its index as a result<std::size_t>:

  • node_by_id(id) is XState’s getStateNodeById. The # is optional, and a path after the id walks down from that node: #active.fast is the child fast of the node whose id is active.

  • child(node, key) is the child of node whose key is key, a dot being part of the key.

  • node_by_path(from, path) is XState’s getStateNodeByPath: a path of keys relative to from, or an id when it starts with #.

A backslash escapes a dot in an id or a path: #foo\.bar names the node whose id is foo.bar, where #foo.bar names the child bar of the node foo. A name that finds no node is the error unknown_state, where XState’s getStateNodeById throws.

The machine also keeps what it was created from: config() is the config, registry() the implementations, and context() the config’s context, an empty object when the config gives none or null. The reference lists every member of machine (webcpp::xstate::machine).

The definition

A machine’s definition is the machine written out as JSON, once its config has been read: every node with its id, key, type, initial transition and children, its transitions with their targets resolved to lists of #id, its entry and exit actions, its order (the root’s is written -1), its invokes and its tags. It is what a program stores, sends or hands to a tool when it needs the machine as data, every target already resolved. XState writes it with machine.toJSON(), which JSON.stringify(machine) calls, and to_json(machine) writes the same definition:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "toggle",
    "initial": "inactive",
    "states": {
        "inactive": {"on": {"toggle": "active"}},
        "active": {"on": {"toggle": "inactive"}}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> toggle = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!toggle.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const boost::json::value definition = xstate::to_json(*toggle);
for (const std::string_view pointer : {
         "/id",
         "/order",
         "/initial/target",
         "/states/inactive/type",
         "/states/inactive/order",
         "/states/inactive/on/toggle/0/target",
         "/states/inactive/on/toggle/0/source",
     }) {
    boost::system::error_code missing;
    const boost::json::value* found = definition.find_pointer(pointer, missing);
    if (found == nullptr) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << pointer << ' ' << boost::json::serialize(*found) << '\n';
}

It prints:

/id "toggle"
/order -1
/initial/target ["#toggle.inactive"]
/states/inactive/type "atomic"
/states/inactive/order 1
/states/inactive/on/toggle/0/target ["#toggle.active"]
/states/inactive/on/toggle/0/source "#toggle.inactive"

The program reads the definition with JSON pointers: the root’s order is -1, a state’s own type is written even where its config leaves it out, and a transition’s target and source are ids. to_json writes XState’s definition key for key, with two exceptions. It leaves out the two values creation drops, a state’s meta that is null and a description that is not a string, which XState writes (What creation refuses). And it adds the higher-order guards, which XState cannot write: they are functions in XState, and JSON.stringify leaves a function out. The members of an object may come in another order than XState’s, so compare two definitions as JSON values, with ==, and not as text.

create_machine_from_definition(definition, implementations, context) loads a definition back, one to_json wrote or one XState wrote. A definition holds names, not code, so the implementations are given again; and it holds no context, so the context is given too. It returns a result<machine>. Here a toggle is written out, stored as text, and loaded back:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "toggle",
    "version": "1.0",
    "initial": "inactive",
    "context": {"presses": 0},
    "states": {
        "inactive": {"on": {"toggle": "active"}},
        "active": {"on": {"toggle": "inactive"}}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> toggle = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!toggle.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const std::string stored = boost::json::serialize(xstate::to_json(*toggle));

boost::system::error_code malformed;
const boost::json::value definition = boost::json::parse(stored, malformed);
if (malformed) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> reloaded = xstate::create_machine_from_definition(
    definition, xstate::implementations(), toggle->context());
if (!reloaded.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::snapshot initial = xstate::initial_transition(*reloaded).first;
const xstate::event pressed{.type = "toggle", .payload = {}};
const xstate::snapshot next = xstate::transition(*reloaded, initial, pressed).first;
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(next.value) << ' ' << boost::json::serialize(next.context)
          << '\n';
std::cout << std::boolalpha << (xstate::to_json(*reloaded) == definition) << '\n';

It prints:

"active" {"presses":0}
true

The reloaded machine takes the original’s step, starts from the context it was given, and writes the definition it was loaded from, the toggle’s version on every node included. XState has no function that creates a machine from a definition.

The loader refuses with invalid_config what XState never writes: a value that is not an object, and a state whose states, on, invoke, entry or exit does not have the JSON type a definition gives it, an object of state objects, an object of lists of transition objects, a list of invoke objects, a list of actions; and, in a state that has states, an initial whose first target is not a string. From any other object it rebuilds the config the definition describes and creates the machine with create_machine, which checks it as it checks any config (What creation refuses): an id that is not a string, or a type xstate does not know, is invalid_config there. So is an entry, exit, actions or tags list that holds null, the list XState writes for one of them that is null, which creation refuses in a config too. A compound state’s initial is rebuilt from its first target, # and the id of a child, with the actions, meta and description of the written initial transition; a target that names none of the children leaves the state without an initial, which is invalid_config too, where a config’s initial that names no child is unknown_target.

Three members repeat what the rest of the definition says and are not read, whatever they hold: key, order and transitions; nor is the version of a state below the root, which repeats the root’s. The root’s version becomes the machine’s, which to_json writes on every node again.

A definition does not hold all of a config either. The definition, XState’s and so the one to_json writes, leaves out the context, the eventless transitions (always) and a history state’s default target; two states may share an id when a key holds a dot; and an entry or exit action named xstate.raise or xstate.cancel, a custom action, cannot be told from the raise and cancel an after adds, which the definition writes under those names, so the loader drops it with them. Given the original’s context, a machine loaded from a definition takes the original’s steps and writes the same definition whenever the original has none of those; one loaded from a definition XState wrote writes it without the two values to_json leaves out. A definition XState wrote has no higher-order guard either: the transition comes back unguarded, and the reloaded machine takes it whatever the guard would have decided. One to_json wrote keeps the guard.

The sections that follow take the config apart: States, Context, Events and transitions, Actions and Input and output.

States

A state is a mode of a machine: what it is doing now, and so which events it reacts to and how. A video player is paused or playing; a feedback form is prompting the user, showing a form, thanking them or closed. A machine is in one of these states at a time, out of a set fixed when the machine is written, which is why they are called finite (a parallel state counts as one, made of its regions). It moves between them only through the transitions its config declares, so an impossible state, a form being filled in and submitted at the same time, cannot happen.

States nest. A state with child states is a parent state, a state whose children are all active at once is a parallel state, and the machine itself is the root of that tree. The active states and the context, the machine’s data (Context), make up the machine’s whole condition, which xstate, as XState, calls a snapshot.

This section covers the snapshot and how to read it, then each kind of state: initial, parent, parallel, final and history states, and the tags, meta data and descriptions a state carries.

The examples step their machines with the core’s pure functions (Pure transitions and the macrostep cursor). An example that prints only snapshots calls get_initial_snapshot and get_next_snapshot, which return the snapshot alone; one that also prints the actions a step returns calls initial_transition and transition, which return both, as XState’s initialTransition and transition do. XState 5.33.2 deprecates its getInitialSnapshot and getNextSnapshot in favour of those two; xstate keeps both pairs. An actor hands out the same snapshots, through snapshot_of in xstate’s actor layer (Snapshots and status). Each program is in example/xstate/, named after its topic: states_finite.cpp, states_snapshot.cpp and so on.

Finite states

A config lists the machine’s states under states, each by its key, and names the one the machine starts in with initial. The snapshot’s value says which state is active, here by its key.

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "feedback",
    "context": {"name": "", "email": "", "feedback": ""},
    "initial": "prompt",
    "states": {
        "prompt": {"on": {"feedback.good": "thanks", "feedback.bad": "form"}},
        "form": {"on": {"feedback.submit": "thanks"}},
        "thanks": {"on": {"feedback.close": "closed"}},
        "closed": {"type": "final"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!feedback.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::snapshot first = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*feedback);
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(first.value) << '\n';  // the finite state
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(first.context) << '\n';

const xstate::event good{.type = "feedback.good", .payload = {}};
const xstate::snapshot next = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*feedback, first, good);
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(next.value) << '\n';

It prints:

"prompt"
{"name":"","email":"","feedback":""}
"thanks"

The snapshot holds both halves of the machine’s condition: value, the finite state, and context, the data no finite set of states could enumerate, such as what the user typed (Context). The event feedback.good moved the machine from prompt to thanks; the context did not change, as no action assigned to it.

Each key under states is a state node, and the machine itself is the root node. A node has an id: the one its config gives with id, or else the machine’s id and the node’s path joined by dots, feedback.prompt here. A machine without an id is (machine), as in XState. machine::node_by_id finds a node by its id and machine::node reads it (State nodes and ids). An id does not change the state value; it is another way for a transition to name the state (Targets).

The snapshot

A snapshot is where a machine is at one moment: its state value, its context, whether it still runs, and what it produced. xstate’s snapshot is a plain struct: XState’s snapshot without its machine, its node objects, its children’s actor objects and the methods that read them. You keep it, copy it, store it, and hand it back to the function that computes the next one.

It holds no pointer into its machine: it names the active state nodes by their index in the machine. A value that points nowhere has no lifetime to manage, so it can wait between two requests or two microsteps, and a copy is independent of the original. A query that needs the tree of nodes takes the machine as an argument instead, as every pure function does (get_meta, can), where XState’s snapshot carries its machine and reads it through its methods.

Two rules follow from this. A snapshot’s nodes are indexes into the machine that computed it, so a snapshot is read and advanced only with that machine, or with one created from the same config. And its members are public so they can be read: the next step reads both value, to select an event’s transitions, and nodes, to select eventless ones and to exit and enter states, so a snapshot edited by hand is not one xstate computed. To put a machine in a given state, build the snapshot with resolve_state (Persisted state).

Member What it holds XState

value

The state value: which states are active (The state value). xstate computes it from nodes, so the two never disagree.

value

context

The context, a boost::json::value (Context).

context

status

status::active while the machine runs, status::done once it has reached a top-level final state, or every region of a parallel root has (When the machine is done), status::error once a step has failed.

status, which has a fourth value, 'stopped'

output

The machine’s output once it is done, when it has one; none otherwise, where XState’s is undefined (Output).

output

error

Why the machine failed, when status is error: the code a failing implementation returned, or one of xstate’s errc (webcpp::xstate::errc). Empty otherwise.

error, the value an implementation threw

error_value

When error is actor_failed, the failed child’s error, if its error event carried one (Done and error events).

error

nodes

The active state nodes, root included, by their index in the machine, in XState’s order.

_nodes, internal

history

What each history state remembers, by the history node’s id (History states).

historyValue

tags

The tags of the active nodes, each once, in the order of nodes (Tags).

tags, a Set

children

The machine’s child actors, as (id, src) pairs, in the order JavaScript enumerates XState’s children object. The core only records them: its caller runs them, from the xstate.spawnChild and xstate.stopChild actions a step returns (Actors).

children, each child’s ActorRef by its id

XState’s 'stopped' is the status of a stopped actor, and the status its transition gives a snapshot that receives the event xstate.stop. In xstate the actor layer reports a stopped actor through status_of (Snapshots and status), and the core runs xstate.stop as any other event (Events).

Its queries are matches (Matching a state value), has_tag (Tags) and remembered (History states); get_meta(machine, snapshot) (Meta and descriptions) and can(machine, snapshot, event) (Whether an event would do anything) take the machine. A snapshot is rebuilt from a state value and a context with resolve_state (Persisted state); XState’s toJSON of a snapshot has no counterpart.

XState’s mapState(snapshot, mapper), which Stately’s page on states shows, walks the active nodes from each state without children up to the root and calls, for each one, the map function the mapper object gives for its path. xstate has no mapState: a program reads snapshot.nodes and maps each node by its id or its path, machine.node(index), as describe does in the example below.

The example prints the members of a snapshot before and after an event that completes the machine:

std::string_view name_of(xstate::status status) {
    switch (status) {
        case xstate::status::active: return "active";
        case xstate::status::done: return "done";
        case xstate::status::error: return "error";
    }
    return "unknown";
}

/** Prints what a snapshot holds, naming its active nodes by their ids. */
void describe(const xstate::machine& owner, const xstate::snapshot& now) {
    boost::json::array nodes;
    for (const std::size_t node : now.nodes) {
        nodes.emplace_back(owner.node(node).id);
    }
    const boost::json::array tags(now.tags.begin(), now.tags.end());
    std::cout << "value: " << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';
    std::cout << "context: " << boost::json::serialize(now.context) << '\n';
    std::cout << "status: " << name_of(now.status) << '\n';
    std::cout << "nodes: " << boost::json::serialize(nodes) << '\n';
    std::cout << "tags: " << boost::json::serialize(tags) << '\n';
    if (now.status == xstate::status::done && now.output.has_value()) {
        std::cout << "output: " << boost::json::serialize(*now.output) << '\n';
    }
}

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "feedback",
    "context": {"feedback": ""},
    "initial": "form",
    "states": {
        "form": {
            "tags": ["visible"],
            "initial": "invalid",
            "states": {
                "invalid": {"on": {"feedback.valid": "valid"}},
                "valid": {}
            },
            "on": {"feedback.submit": "thanks"}
        },
        "thanks": {"type": "final"}
    },
    "output": {"sent": true}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!feedback.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::snapshot first = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*feedback);
describe(*feedback, first);

const xstate::event submit{.type = "feedback.submit", .payload = {}};
describe(*feedback, xstate::get_next_snapshot(*feedback, first, submit));

It prints:

value: {"form":"invalid"}
context: {"feedback":""}
status: active
nodes: ["feedback","feedback.form","feedback.form.invalid"]
tags: ["visible"]
value: "thanks"
context: {"feedback":""}
status: done
nodes: ["feedback.thanks","feedback"]
tags: []
output: {"sent":true}

The first snapshot is in form, and in its initial child invalid; nodes lists every active node, from the root down, and tags the one tag form carries. feedback.submit takes the machine to thanks, a final child of the root, so the machine is done: its status is done and its output is the config’s output.

The order of nodes is XState’s, and xstate keeps it because it is not cosmetic: it decides the order in which the regions of a parallel state take their eventless transitions. The nodes a microstep keeps keep their place, those it exits leave, and those it enters are appended in document order; a microstep that ends with the same active nodes, and in which no history state records anything, keeps the order it had. Once a step completes the machine, XState sorts the nodes in reverse document order, a child before its parent, and so does xstate: feedback.thanks before feedback.

Document order is the order of the states in the config as XState reads it: a parent before its children, and siblings in the order JavaScript enumerates the keys of states, a key that is an array index, such as 0 or 10, first, by number, then the rest as written. A parallel state whose config writes its regions b, 10, 2 and a enters them in the order 2, 10, b, a.

The state value

The state value names the active states in JSON, the same JSON XState writes, its keys in the same order:

  • the key of the active child, a string, when that child has no children of its own;

  • an object when it has: the child’s key, and under it the child’s own value (Parent states);

  • an object with one member per region for a parallel state (Parallel states);

  • {} for a machine that has no states but its root.

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "feedback",
    "initial": "question",
    "states": {
        "question": {"on": {"next": "form"}},
        "form": {
            "initial": "invalid",
            "states": {"invalid": {}, "valid": {}},
            "on": {"settings": "settings"}
        },
        "settings": {
            "type": "parallel",
            "states": {
                "display": {"initial": "bright", "states": {"bright": {}, "dim": {}}},
                "theme": {"initial": "dark", "states": {"dark": {}, "light": {}}}
            }
        }
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!feedback.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::snapshot now = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*feedback);
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';

const xstate::event next{.type = "next", .payload = {}};
now = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*feedback, now, next);
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';

const xstate::event settings{.type = "settings", .payload = {}};
now = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*feedback, now, settings);
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';

const boost::json::value counting_config = boost::json::parse(R"({"id": "counting"})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> counting = xstate::create_machine(counting_config, {});
if (!counting.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*counting).value) << '\n';

It prints:

"question"
{"form":"invalid"}
{"settings":{"display":"bright","theme":"dark"}}
{}

An object value writes its keys in the order JavaScript enumerates an object’s keys, as XState’s value is a JavaScript object: a key that is an array index first, by number, then the rest in the order of nodes. The parallel state whose config writes its regions b, 10, 2 and a (The snapshot) writes them 2, 10, b, a in its value when it is entered, and 2, 10, a, b when it is the root and a step completes the machine, as that step sorts nodes in reverse document order. The regions of a parallel state take an event’s transitions in the order of its value’s keys, and their eventless transitions in the order of nodes.

Stately’s page on states says the value of a machine without states is null; XState 5.33.2 writes {}, and so does xstate.

Matching a state value

snapshot.matches(value) says whether the machine is in a state: whether the value given is the snapshot’s value or a part of it, as XState’s snapshot.matches does. A string names a state by its key, or a nested one by its path with dots, "form.invalid"; an object names nested and parallel states, and needs to list only the ones it tests. matches_state(parent, child) says whether the state value child is parent or a state within it, XState’s matchesState; snapshot.matches(v) is matches_state(v, snapshot.value).

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "feedback",
    "initial": "question",
    "states": {
        "question": {"on": {"feedback.bad": "form"}},
        "form": {"initial": "invalid", "states": {"invalid": {}, "valid": {}}}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!feedback.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::event bad{.type = "feedback.bad", .payload = {}};
const xstate::snapshot now =
    xstate::get_next_snapshot(*feedback, xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*feedback), bad);
std::cout << "value: " << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';

const boost::json::value tested = boost::json::parse(R"([
    "question",
    "form",
    {"form": "invalid"},
    {"form": "valid"},
    "form.invalid"
])");
std::cout << std::boolalpha;
for (const boost::json::value& value : tested.get_array()) {
    std::cout << boost::json::serialize(value) << ": " << now.matches(value) << '\n';
}

const boost::json::value playing =
    boost::json::parse(R"({"track": "playing", "volume": "normal"})");
const boost::json::value track_playing = boost::json::parse(R"({"track": "playing"})");
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(track_playing) << " in " << boost::json::serialize(playing)
          << ": " << xstate::matches_state(track_playing, playing) << '\n';

It prints:

value: {"form":"invalid"}
"question": false
"form": true
{"form":"invalid"}: true
{"form":"valid"}: false
"form.invalid": true
{"track":"playing"} in {"track":"playing","volume":"normal"}: true

"form" matches because the machine is in form, whichever child of form is active; {"form": "valid"} does not, because the active child is another. The last line tests a part of the value of a parallel state: {"track": "playing"} is within {"track": "playing", "volume": "normal"}. The order of the arguments matters, the value tested first: the same two values the other way round do not match. When the question is what the machine is doing rather than where it is, a tag survives a reorganisation of the states better than a state value (Tags).

Initial states

A machine starts in its initial state, the child of the root that initial names. A parent state names one too: entering the parent enters its initial child, and, when that child is a parent, the child’s own initial child, and so on until every active branch reaches a state without children. A machine has at most one initial state, so it always knows where to start. A parallel state, the root included, has none: entering it enters every region (Parallel states).

/** The types of a list of actions, as a JSON array. */
boost::json::array types_of(const std::vector<xstate::action>& actions) {
    boost::json::array types;
    for (const xstate::action& one : actions) {
        types.emplace_back(one.type);
    }
    return types;
}

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "light",
    "initial": "green",
    "states": {
        "green": {"on": {"timer": "yellow"}},
        "yellow": {"on": {"timer": "red", "emergency": "red.stop"}},
        "red": {
            "initial": {"target": "walk", "actions": "beep"},
            "states": {"walk": {}, "wait": {}, "stop": {}}
        }
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> light = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!light.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::snapshot green = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*light);
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(green.value) << '\n';

const xstate::event timer{.type = "timer", .payload = {}};
const xstate::snapshot yellow = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*light, green, timer);
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(yellow.value) << '\n';

const auto [walk, walk_actions] = xstate::transition(*light, yellow, timer);
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(walk.value) << ' ' << types_of(walk_actions) << '\n';

const xstate::event emergency{.type = "emergency", .payload = {}};
const auto [stop, stop_actions] = xstate::transition(*light, yellow, emergency);
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(stop.value) << ' ' << types_of(stop_actions) << '\n';

It prints:

"green"
"yellow"
{"red":"walk"} ["beep"]
{"red":"stop"} []

timer targets red, so the machine enters red and its initial child walk. initial may be an object, {"target", "actions"}: its actions run when the parent is entered through its initial state, and only then. So timer returns beep, and emergency, which targets red.stop directly, does not. beep has no implementation, so it comes back to the caller to execute (Actions), and types_of lists the types of the actions a step returned. Both transitions start from the same yellow snapshot: a snapshot is a value, and nothing stops a caller from computing two futures of it.

A parent state must name its initial state, even when every transition targets one of its children, and the name must be one of its children. create_machine refuses the machine otherwise:

const boost::json::value without_initial = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "initial": "red",
    "states": {
        "red": {"states": {"walk": {}, "wait": {}}}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> first = xstate::create_machine(without_initial, {});
if (first.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << first.error().message() << '\n';

const boost::json::value unknown_initial = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "initial": "nowhere",
    "states": {"red": {}}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> second = xstate::create_machine(unknown_initial, {});
if (second.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << second.error().message() << '\n';

It prints:

invalid_config
unknown_target

The first config, a parent without initial, is invalid_config; the second, an initial that names no child, is unknown_target. XState’s createMachine refuses the first too, and accepts the second, which throws only when the state is first entered (A config is refused when it is created). xstate refuses both when the machine is created, with every other config error it can detect there, so a mistake in a config shows before the machine runs. Two are left to run time: the #id of an xstate.stateIn guard that names no state, found when the guard is evaluated (Higher-order guards and stateIn), and the default of a history state that is the machine’s root (Shallow and deep history).

Parent states

A state can contain states, its children, which are active only while it is. A parent state is also called a compound state. Grouping states under a parent lets them share what is common to them: a transition every child takes, an entry or exit action, a sub-process with its own initial state and its own end.

The machine is a parent state too, the root, and it is always active. A machine may have no states besides the root: its transitions are then the root’s, which run actions and target no state, and its state value is {} (The state value).

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "machine",
    "initial": "parent",
    "states": {
        "parent": {
            "initial": "child1",
            "states": {
                "child1": {"on": {"next": "child2"}},
                "child2": {
                    "initial": "grandchild1",
                    "states": {"grandchild1": {}, "grandchild2": {}}
                }
            },
            "on": {
                "next": ".child2.grandchild2",
                "restart": ".child1"
            }
        }
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> nested = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!nested.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::snapshot now = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*nested);
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';

const xstate::event next{.type = "next", .payload = {}};
now = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*nested, now, next);  // child1's own transition
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';

now = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*nested, now, next);  // the parent's transition
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';

const xstate::event restart{.type = "restart", .payload = {}};
now = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*nested, now, restart);
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';

It prints:

{"parent":"child1"}
{"parent":{"child2":"grandchild1"}}
{"parent":{"child2":"grandchild2"}}
{"parent":"child1"}

The first next is handled by child1, the deepest active state, whose own transition goes to child2 and so into its initial child grandchild1. The second next finds no transition in grandchild1 or child2, and reaches parent, whose transition targets grandchild2. restart targets child1 from the parent.

Three rules govern transitions on parent states:

  • An event is offered to the deepest active state first, then to its parent, and so on up to the root; the first one with an enabled transition for the event takes it (Selecting a transition).

  • A transition that targets a parent enters the parent’s initial state, and that state’s initial state, down to a state without children.

  • A parent’s transition targets its own descendants with a path that starts with a dot: .child1, .child2.grandchild2 (Targets).

A parent state also ends: when one of its final children is reached, the parent is done, and its onDone transition is taken (A parent state is done).

Parallel states

A parallel state’s children, its regions, are all active at the same time, where a parent state has one active child. Parallel states model aspects of a system that change independently, such as a player’s track and its volume. Entering a parallel state enters every region, exiting it exits every region, and an event reaches every region: each region with a transition for it takes it, all in one microstep. A parallel state has "type": "parallel" and needs no initial.

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "player",
    "type": "parallel",
    "states": {
        "track": {
            "initial": "paused",
            "states": {
                "paused": {"on": {"PLAY": "playing"}},
                "playing": {"on": {"STOP": "paused", "RESET": "paused"}}
            }
        },
        "volume": {
            "initial": "normal",
            "states": {
                "normal": {"on": {"MUTE": "muted"}},
                "muted": {"on": {"UNMUTE": "normal", "RESET": "normal"}}
            }
        }
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> player = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!player.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::snapshot now = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*player);
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';

now = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*player, now, xstate::event{.type = "PLAY", .payload = {}});
now = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*player, now, xstate::event{.type = "MUTE", .payload = {}});
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';

const xstate::event reset{.type = "RESET", .payload = {}};
const std::vector<xstate::microstep> steps = xstate::get_microsteps(*player, now, reset);
if (steps.empty()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::snapshot& after = steps.back().snapshot;
std::cout << steps.size() << " microstep: " << boost::json::serialize(after.value) << '\n';

It prints:

{"track":"paused","volume":"normal"}
{"track":"playing","volume":"muted"}
1 microstep: {"track":"paused","volume":"normal"}

The value of a parallel state is an object with one member per region. PLAY reaches both regions and only track handles it; MUTE only volume. RESET is handled by both regions, in a single microstep, which get_microsteps shows: that microstep’s transitions lists the two transitions taken (The microsteps of an event).

A parallel state is done when every one of its regions is (A parallel state is done).

Final states

A final state, "type": "final", is a state where a piece of work is complete. A final child completes its parent; a final child of the root completes the machine. A machine may have several final states, or none, if it runs for as long as it lives.

A parent state is done

When a parent’s final child is entered, the parent is done: the machine raises the event xstate.done.state.<parent id>, and the parent’s onDone is a transition on that event. It is taken in the same macrostep, so the caller of transition sees only where it led.

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "coffee",
    "initial": "preparation",
    "states": {
        "preparation": {
            "initial": "weighing",
            "states": {
                "weighing": {"on": {"weighed": "grinding"}},
                "grinding": {"on": {"ground": "ready"}},
                "ready": {"type": "final"}
            },
            "onDone": "brewing"
        },
        "brewing": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> coffee = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!coffee.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::event weighed{.type = "weighed", .payload = {}};
const xstate::snapshot grinding =
    xstate::get_next_snapshot(*coffee, xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*coffee), weighed);
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(grinding.value) << '\n';

const xstate::event ground{.type = "ground", .payload = {}};
for (const xstate::microstep& step : xstate::get_microsteps(*coffee, grinding, ground)) {
    std::cout << "microstep: " << boost::json::serialize(step.snapshot.value) << '\n';
}

It prints:

{"preparation":"grinding"}
microstep: {"preparation":"ready"}
microstep: "brewing"

ground takes two microsteps, which get_microsteps returns one by one. The first enters ready, the final child; the second runs the raised event xstate.done.state.coffee.preparation, whose onDone transition leaves preparation for brewing. Each microstep also carries its event, step.event, which XState’s getMicrosteps does not return (The microsteps of an event). A final state may have an output, which travels in the done event (A final state’s output).

A parallel state is done

A parallel state is done when every one of its regions is in a final state: the machine then raises the parallel state’s own done event, and its onDone is taken.

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "coffee",
    "initial": "preparing",
    "states": {
        "preparing": {
            "type": "parallel",
            "states": {
                "grindBeans": {
                    "initial": "grindingBeans",
                    "states": {
                        "grindingBeans": {"on": {"BEANS_GROUND": "beansGround"}},
                        "beansGround": {"type": "final"}
                    }
                },
                "boilWater": {
                    "initial": "boilingWater",
                    "states": {
                        "boilingWater": {"on": {"WATER_BOILED": "waterBoiled"}},
                        "waterBoiled": {"type": "final"}
                    }
                }
            },
            "onDone": "makingCoffee"
        },
        "makingCoffee": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> coffee = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!coffee.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::snapshot now = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*coffee);
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';

const xstate::event beans_ground{.type = "BEANS_GROUND", .payload = {}};
now = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*coffee, now, beans_ground);
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';

const xstate::event water_boiled{.type = "WATER_BOILED", .payload = {}};
now = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*coffee, now, water_boiled);
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';

It prints:

{"preparing":{"grindBeans":"grindingBeans","boilWater":"boilingWater"}}
{"preparing":{"grindBeans":"beansGround","boilWater":"boilingWater"}}
"makingCoffee"

After BEANS_GROUND one region is in its final state and the other is not, so preparing waits. WATER_BOILED completes the second region, and preparing is done.

When the machine is done

A final child of the root completes the machine, and so does a parallel root once each of its regions is in a final state. In the same microstep the snapshot’s status becomes done and its output is computed: the root’s output, a fixed value in the config, or one an implementation computes from the context and the done event (Output). The snapshot keeps the state value of the final state.

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "process",
    "initial": "running",
    "states": {
        "running": {"on": {"finish": "complete"}},
        "complete": {"type": "final"}
    },
    "output": {"message": "Process completed."}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> process = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!process.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::snapshot now = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*process);
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << ' ' << name_of(now.status) << '\n';

now = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*process, now, xstate::event{.type = "finish", .payload = {}});
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << ' ' << name_of(now.status) << '\n';
if (now.status == xstate::status::done && now.output.has_value()) {
    std::cout << "output: " << boost::json::serialize(*now.output) << '\n';
}

It prints:

"running" active
"complete" done
output: {"message":"Process completed."}

finish takes the machine to complete, a final child of the root, so its status becomes done and its output is the config’s output; name_of, a function of the program, spells the status. As XState does, the machine then resolves the exit actions of every active node, in reverse document order (The snapshot): it applies those it executes itself, such as an assign, and returns the others to its caller. After them it returns one xstate.stopChild for each child its snapshot still lists, which the snapshot keeps; the core runs no child, so stopping it is the caller’s work (Stopping a child).

A machine that is done receives no more events: an actor stops there (Actors). The pure functions do not check the status, as XState’s do not: from a done snapshot, get_next_snapshot takes the transition an event selects, and the status stays done. A caller that drives the core itself stops sending events once the status is done.

A final state should have no transitions, as Stately’s page on final states says, but neither XState 5.33.2 nor xstate enforces it: a final state that declares a transition takes it. Leave final states without transitions.

History states

A history state is a pseudostate: it is never active itself. A transition that targets it enters, instead, the children its parent had active when the parent was last exited, so a machine can resume where it left off. When the parent has never been exited, it enters the history state’s target, when it has one, or else the parent’s initial state, or, when the parent is a parallel state, every one of its regions.

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "checkout",
    "initial": "cart",
    "states": {
        "cart": {"on": {"checkout": "payment.hist"}},
        "payment": {
            "initial": "card",
            "states": {
                "card": {"on": {"switch": "paypal"}},
                "paypal": {"on": {"switch": "card"}},
                "hist": {"type": "history"}
            },
            "on": {"next": "address"}
        },
        "address": {"on": {"back": "payment.hist"}}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> checkout = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!checkout.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::snapshot now = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*checkout);
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';

for (const std::string_view type : {"checkout", "switch", "next"}) {
    const xstate::event happened{.type = std::string(type), .payload = {}};
    now = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*checkout, now, happened);
    std::cout << type << ": " << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';
}

const std::vector<std::size_t>* remembered = now.remembered("checkout.payment.hist");
if (remembered == nullptr) {
    return 1;
}
boost::json::array ids;
for (const std::size_t node : *remembered) {
    ids.emplace_back(checkout->node(node).id);
}
std::cout << "remembered: " << boost::json::serialize(ids) << '\n';

now = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*checkout, now, xstate::event{.type = "back", .payload = {}});
std::cout << "back: " << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';

It prints:

"cart"
checkout: {"payment":"card"}
switch: {"payment":"paypal"}
next: "address"
remembered: ["checkout.payment.paypal"]
back: {"payment":"paypal"}

checkout targets payment.hist before payment was ever exited, so the machine enters the initial state of payment, card. next exits payment while paypal is active, and the history state records it; back returns to paypal. The snapshot’s history holds what each history state remembers, and remembered(id) returns it for one history node, as node indexes, or nullptr before the history state has recorded anything; XState’s is historyValue[id], the node objects.

A history state is "type": "history", and shallow unless it says "history": "deep"; "history": "shallow" and "history": true say shallow. A node with no type, no children and a history member is a history state too, when that member is truthy as JavaScript reads it, as in XState: a history of false, null, "" or 0 leaves the node atomic.

Shallow and deep history

A shallow history state remembers its parent’s active children only: entering one of them again enters that child’s initial state. A deep history state remembers the active states without children below its parent, so the whole nested configuration comes back.

/** The ids of the nodes a history node remembers, none when it has not recorded. */
boost::json::array remembered_ids(const xstate::machine& owner, const xstate::snapshot& now,
                                  std::string_view history_id) {
    const std::vector<std::size_t>* remembered = now.remembered(history_id);
    if (remembered == nullptr) {
        return {};
    }
    boost::json::array ids;
    for (const std::size_t node : *remembered) {
        ids.emplace_back(owner.node(node).id);
    }
    return ids;
}

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "player",
    "initial": "powered",
    "states": {
        "powered": {
            "initial": "radio",
            "states": {
                "radio": {
                    "initial": "stopped",
                    "states": {
                        "stopped": {"on": {"play": "playing"}},
                        "playing": {"on": {"stop": "stopped"}}
                    }
                },
                "shallow": {"type": "history"},
                "deep": {"type": "history", "history": "deep"}
            },
            "on": {"power": "standby"}
        },
        "standby": {
            "on": {
                "resume": "powered.shallow",
                "resumeDeep": "powered.deep"
            }
        }
    }
})");
