const xstate::result<xstate::machine> player = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!player.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::snapshot standby = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*player);
for (const std::string_view type : {"play", "power"}) {
    const xstate::event happened{.type = std::string(type), .payload = {}};
    standby = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*player, standby, happened);
}
const boost::json::array shallow = remembered_ids(*player, standby, "player.powered.shallow");
const boost::json::array deep = remembered_ids(*player, standby, "player.powered.deep");
std::cout << "shallow remembers " << shallow << '\n';
std::cout << "deep remembers " << deep << '\n';

for (const std::string_view type : {"resume", "resumeDeep"}) {
    const xstate::event resume{.type = std::string(type), .payload = {}};
    const xstate::snapshot resumed = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*player, standby, resume);
    std::cout << type << ": " << boost::json::serialize(resumed.value) << '\n';
}

It prints:

shallow remembers ["player.powered.radio"]
deep remembers ["player.powered.radio.playing"]
resume: {"powered":{"radio":"stopped"}}
resumeDeep: {"powered":{"radio":"playing"}}

Both resumptions start from the same standby snapshot. The shallow history state remembers radio, so it enters radio and its initial child stopped; the deep one remembers radio.playing, and enters it.

Three more rules:

  • A history state whose default leads back to it, a target that is an ancestor whose initial chain reaches the history state again, would never finish entering: create_machine refuses it with invalid_config, where XState overflows its stack when it enters it.

  • A machine whose root is itself a history state has no parent to resolve its default against. The machine is created, and a microstep that needs the default, the first one included, fails with unknown_target, where XState’s initial snapshot reports a TypeError as its error (A config is refused when it is created, Failures are values).

  • resolve_state builds a snapshot from a state value and a context, and from nothing else, so none of its history states has recorded anything. XState restores what they remember through the persistence of its actors, which xstate does not port (Persisted state). When what a history state remembers must survive a pause, keep the snapshot itself, a value the program holds between two events.

Tags

A tag is a name a state carries to say what kind of state it is, such as loading or visible: several states may share it, and a state may carry several. A state lists its tags under tags, one string or a list of strings; create_machine refuses any other tags, null included, with invalid_config (What creation refuses). The snapshot’s tags holds the tags of every active node, each once, and has_tag(tag) says whether one of them is the tag given, as XState’s snapshot.hasTag does.

/** Prints a snapshot's value, its tags, and whether one of them is "visible". */
void show(const xstate::snapshot& now) {
    const boost::json::array tags(now.tags.begin(), now.tags.end());
    std::cout << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << ' ' << tags << " visible: " << std::boolalpha
              << now.has_tag("visible") << '\n';
}

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "feedback",
    "initial": "prompt",
    "states": {
        "prompt": {"tags": ["visible"], "on": {"feedback.good": "thanks"}},
        "thanks": {
            "tags": ["visible"],
            "initial": "celebrating",
            "states": {"celebrating": {"tags": ["visible", "confetti"]}},
            "on": {"feedback.close": "closed"}
        },
        "closed": {"tags": "hidden"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!feedback.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::snapshot now = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*feedback);
show(now);

const xstate::event good{.type = "feedback.good", .payload = {}};
now = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*feedback, now, good);
show(now);

const xstate::event close{.type = "feedback.close", .payload = {}};
now = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*feedback, now, close);
show(now);

It prints:

"prompt" ["visible"] visible: true
{"thanks":"celebrating"} ["visible","confetti"] visible: true
"closed" ["hidden"] visible: false

In thanks, both thanks and its child celebrating carry visible, and the snapshot lists it once, in the order of the active nodes. closed writes its one tag as a string. A tag answers what the machine is doing without naming where it is: code that asks has_tag("visible") keeps working when the states are renamed or nested differently, where a test of a state value would need to change. XState types its tags with setup({ types }); a JSON config has no types, so xstate’s tags are any strings.

Meta and descriptions

meta is static data a state carries for whoever reads the machine, such as the text a view shows in that state: any JSON, which the machine never reads itself. get_meta(machine, snapshot) collects the meta of every active node that has one, by the node’s id, as XState’s snapshot.getMeta() does. It takes the machine because the meta belongs to the nodes, and the snapshot names its nodes by index.

A description is a string that documents a state for the people who read the machine; Stately’s editor shows it beside the state. A transition may have a description and a meta too. xstate keeps each where the config put it, a state’s description in state_node::description, and writes them in the machine’s definition (The definition), except a state’s meta that is null and a state’s description that is not a string, which it drops (A state’s null meta, and a description that is not a string).

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "feedback",
    "initial": "prompt",
    "meta": {"title": "Feedback"},
    "states": {
        "prompt": {
            "description": "Waits for the user to rate the experience.",
            "meta": {"content": "How was your experience?"},
            "on": {"feedback.good": "thanks"}
        },
        "thanks": {"meta": {"content": "Thank you for your feedback!"}}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!feedback.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::snapshot now = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*feedback);
std::cout << xstate::get_meta(*feedback, now) << '\n';

const xstate::event good{.type = "feedback.good", .payload = {}};
now = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*feedback, now, good);
std::cout << xstate::get_meta(*feedback, now) << '\n';

const xstate::result<std::size_t> prompt = feedback->node_by_id("feedback.prompt");
if (!prompt.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << feedback->node(*prompt).description.value_or("") << '\n';

It prints:

{"feedback":{"title":"Feedback"},"feedback.prompt":{"content":"How was your experience?"}}
{"feedback":{"title":"Feedback"},"feedback.thanks":{"content":"Thank you for your feedback!"}}
Waits for the user to rate the experience.

The root’s meta is in both results, because the root is always active; the meta of prompt and then of thanks follows the active state. The description of prompt is read from its node, an optional string.

Context

A machine’s finite states say which mode it is in: idle or loading, inactive or active. Most machines also carry data that no finite set of states holds well: a count, the text of a form, a user’s id, the last error. That data is the machine’s context, which statecharts call extended state. It lives in the snapshot, beside the state value, and it is available in every state.

The context never changes in place. An assign action computes a new one, the microstep that runs it returns a new snapshot that holds it, and the snapshot it began from keeps the old one. The context is optional: a machine that only needs its finite states leaves it out, and its snapshots then hold an empty object.

In xstate the context is JSON, a boost::json::value, and in practice an object. The smallest example is a machine with an initial context, and the snapshot it starts in:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "feedback",
    "context": {"feedback": "Some feedback", "rating": 5}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback_machine = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!feedback_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::snapshot snapshot = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*feedback_machine);
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(snapshot.context) << '\n';

It prints:

{"feedback":"Some feedback","rating":5}

The config’s context is the one XState’s createMachine takes, written in JSON. get_initial_snapshot, XState’s getInitialSnapshot, computes the snapshot a machine starts in (Pure transitions and the macrostep cursor), and the snapshot’s context is a boost::json::value, which boost::json::serialize writes. Stately’s own page reads the context through an actor and its subscription; that program is in Context in an actor.

Initial context

The config’s context is the initial context of every snapshot the machine starts in. xstate copies it into each one, so every snapshot owns its context and no two snapshots, or two actors, share one. XState hands every actor the config’s object itself, which is why Stately’s page warns that mutating it may change the context of other actors; a boost::json::value held by value leaves nothing for that warning to guard.

A machine without a context, or with "context": null, starts with an empty object, as XState’s does:

const boost::json::value no_context = boost::json::parse(R"({"id": "toggle"})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> toggle = xstate::create_machine(no_context, {});
if (!toggle.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*toggle).context) << '\n';

It prints:

{}

Write the context as an object. xstate keeps any other value as written, false, a number, a string or a list, and an assign on it fails with implementation_failed. XState starts a context of false, 0 or "" as {}, and its assign, which merges with JavaScript’s Object.assign, drops a context of true or a number and spreads a string or a list into numbered members (A context that is not an object).

Lazy initial context

Some context is not known when the machine is written: a timestamp, an id, anything that must be computed when the machine starts. XState takes the context as a function for that, which runs once for each actor, when the actor is created, so that each actor computes its own. A function cannot be JSON, so xstate takes it from the implementations, as it takes all the code a machine names: implementations.context, a context_maker. When it is set, it replaces the config’s context.

It runs at the start of every initial macrostep: in each get_initial_snapshot, initial_transition, get_initial_microsteps and begin_initial, and when an actor is constructed. A child is constructed when its parent resolves the spawn of an invoke or a spawn_child_action. A root is constructed on start, not on create_actor, which runs nothing; XState’s createActor runs the function at once (The root is constructed on start).

/** The caller's clock, in milliseconds: xstate reads none. */
std::uint64_t now = 1000;
xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.context =
    [&now](const boost::json::value& /*input*/) -> xstate::result<boost::json::value> {
    return boost::json::object{{"feedback", "Some feedback"}, {"createdAt", now}};
};
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({"id": "feedback"})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!feedback_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

now = 2000;
const xstate::snapshot first = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*feedback_machine);
now = 3000;
const xstate::snapshot second = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*feedback_machine);
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(first.context) << '\n'
          << boost::json::serialize(second.context) << '\n';

It prints:

{"feedback":"Some feedback","createdAt":2000}
{"feedback":"Some feedback","createdAt":3000}

The machine was created while now was 1000, and each snapshot holds the time at which it was computed. xstate itself never reads a clock, and a context_maker that read one would make the initial snapshot depend on the moment it ran, so the time here comes from a variable the function captures, where Stately’s page reads Date.now(). A program whose results must follow from what it is given passes the time in the input (Initial context from the input).

Initial context from the input

The input is the data a machine is started with, as a function is called with its arguments; Input and output covers it whole. The initial context is often computed from it: a user’s id, a default rating. XState’s context function receives { input }. xstate’s context_maker receives the input itself, a boost::json::value, null when none was given. The input is the second argument of get_initial_snapshot, initial_transition, get_initial_microsteps and begin_initial, and the input of an actor’s actor_options.

xstate::result<boost::json::value> initial_feedback(const boost::json::value& input) {
    const boost::json::object* given = input.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* rating =
        given == nullptr ? nullptr : given->if_contains("defaultRating");
    if (rating == nullptr || !rating->is_number()) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::value>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"feedback", ""}, {"rating", *rating}};
}

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.context = initial_feedback;
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({"id": "feedback"})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!feedback_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const boost::json::value input = boost::json::parse(R"({"defaultRating": 5})");
const xstate::snapshot snapshot = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*feedback_machine, input);
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(snapshot.context) << '\n';

It prints:

{"feedback":"","rating":5}

initial_feedback checks the input before it reads it, and returns an error when the input lacks what it needs: xstate throws no exception, and where XState’s function throws, xstate’s returns the error as a value. A context that cannot be computed fails the initial macrostep on its first next(), before any state is entered: the snapshot’s status is error, its error the code the function returned, and its context an empty object, the snapshot XState’s getInitialSnapshot returns when its function throws. The same machine without an input:

const xstate::snapshot without = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*feedback_machine);
std::cout << (without.status == xstate::status::error ? "error " : "active ")
          << boost::json::serialize(without.context) << '\n';

It prints:

error {}

An actor takes the same input in its options, as XState’s createActor(machine, { input }) does (Options):

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> feedback_actor =
    system.create_actor(*feedback_machine, {.input = input});
if (!feedback_actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.start(*feedback_actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::snapshot* started = system.snapshot_of(*feedback_actor);
if (started == nullptr) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(started->context) << '\n';

It prints:

{"feedback":"","rating":5}

Three rules hold for the function:

  • It returns an object. Any other value fails the initial macrostep with implementation_failed, where XState merges whatever its function returns into an empty object (A context that is not an object).

  • It takes the input only. XState also hands it spawn and self; an xstate context cannot spawn a child (The context function).

  • An empty std::function is refused by create_machine with invalid_config, because calling it would abort in a build without exceptions.

Updating context with assign

The context changes through one action: assign. Like any action, it is named by a transition, an entry or an exit, and runs when that transition is taken or that state entered or left (Assign). Its implementation is an assigner: a function of the action_args that returns a partial update, an object. The update is merged into the context as Object.assign merges it: each of its members replaces the context’s member of that name, or is added, and every other member is kept.

XState writes an assign in the config or in the actions of setup. xstate registers it by name, as an assign_action in implementations.actions, because a config is JSON and a function is not. Here update_feedback copies the event’s feedback into the context:

xstate::result<boost::json::object> update_feedback(const xstate::action_args& args) {
    const boost::json::value* feedback = args.event.payload.if_contains("feedback");
    if (feedback == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"feedback", *feedback}};
}

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actions.emplace("updateFeedback",
                                xstate::assign_action{.assignment = update_feedback});
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "feedback",
    "context": {"feedback": "Some feedback", "rating": 5},
    "on": {"feedback.update": {"actions": "updateFeedback"}}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!feedback_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::snapshot initial = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*feedback_machine);
const xstate::event update{
    .type = "feedback.update",
    .payload = {{"feedback", "Some other feedback"}},
};
const auto [next, actions] = xstate::transition(*feedback_machine, initial, update);
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(initial.context) << '\n'
          << boost::json::serialize(next.context) << '\n'
          << actions.size() << " actions\n";

It prints:

{"feedback":"Some feedback","rating":5}
{"feedback":"Some other feedback","rating":5}
0 actions

The update named feedback only, so rating was kept. The event’s members other than type are its payload, args.event.payload (Events). transition returned no action: the library runs an assign while it computes the microstep and never returns it to the caller, as XState does. The snapshot initial still holds the context it had.

XState’s assign takes either a function that returns the update, assign(({ context, event }, params) => ({ ... })), or an object of property assigners and fixed values. An xstate assigner is the function form: it builds every member of the update itself, as update_feedback builds feedback. XState’s assigner also receives spawn, self and system, and can put an actor it spawns in the context. An xstate assigner receives only the action_args, a context holds no actor, and a child is spawned by a spawn_child_action (Spawning actors, The context function).

The rules of an assign:

  • The merge is shallow, as the merge of Object.assign is: a member that holds an object is replaced whole, not merged.

  • An update adds and replaces members; it removes none. Set a member to null to clear it.

  • The context must be an object (Initial context).

  • An assigner that returns an error fails the macrostep, and no assign of that macrostep reaches the context (A snapshot is a value).

  • create_machine refuses an assign_action whose assignment is empty, with invalid_config.

How guards and actions read the context

Every function of the implementations but the context function, which receives the input (Initial context from the input), receives an action_args: context, the context as it is when the implementation runs; event, the microstep’s event; and params, the params the config gave the action or the guard, null when it gave none. These are the three XState hands an implementation, the first two in its first argument and params in its second. The machine’s output is the one exception to event, as in XState: it receives the done event that completed the machine, that of the top-level final state that completed it or, for a parallel root, the root’s own (The machine’s output and its final state).

  • A guard runs while its transition is selected, before any action of the microstep, and reads the context of the snapshot the microstep starts from.

  • An action reads the context as the actions before it in the same microstep left it, in XState’s order: the exit actions, the transitions’ actions, the entry actions (Actions). Two assigns in one microstep apply in order, each to the context the one before it left.

  • The eventless transitions are selected again after the microstep of an event, and after the microstep of an eventless transition when it changed the snapshot; a microstep that ran an assign has changed it, whatever values the assign wrote. So an always guarded on the context sees, in the same macrostep, the context an assign left (Eventless transitions).

A counter shows the first two. belowLimit guards inc, add adds its param by, and report is a log whose value is the count it sees. Each reads its numbers with integer_at, which returns the integer an object holds under a key, or none:

/** The integer `object` holds under `key`, or none when it holds no integer there. */
std::optional<std::int64_t> integer_at(const boost::json::value& object, std::string_view key) {
    const boost::json::object* members = object.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* found = members == nullptr ? nullptr : members->if_contains(key);
    if (found == nullptr || !found->is_int64()) {
        return std::nullopt;
    }
    return found->get_int64();
}

xstate::result<bool> below_limit(const xstate::action_args& args) {
    const std::optional<std::int64_t> count = integer_at(args.context, "count");
    const std::optional<std::int64_t> limit = integer_at(args.context, "limit");
    if (!count.has_value() || !limit.has_value()) {
        return xstate::failure<bool>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return *count < *limit;
}

xstate::result<boost::json::object> add(const xstate::action_args& args) {
    const std::optional<std::int64_t> count = integer_at(args.context, "count");
    const std::optional<std::int64_t> by = integer_at(args.params, "by");
    if (!count.has_value() || !by.has_value()) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"count", *count + *by}};
}

xstate::result<std::optional<boost::json::value>> report(const xstate::action_args& args) {
    const std::optional<std::int64_t> count = integer_at(args.context, "count");
    if (!count.has_value()) {
        return xstate::failure<std::optional<boost::json::value>>(
            xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return std::optional<boost::json::value>(*count);
}

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.guards.emplace("belowLimit", below_limit);
implementations.actions.emplace("add", xstate::assign_action{.assignment = add});
implementations.actions.emplace("report",
                                xstate::log_action{.value = report, .label = std::nullopt});
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "counter",
    "context": {"count": 0, "limit": 2},
    "on": {
        "inc": {
            "guard": "belowLimit",
            "actions": ["report", {"type": "add", "params": {"by": 1}}, "report"]
        }
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> counter = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!counter.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::snapshot now = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*counter);
for (int sent = 0; sent < 3; ++sent) {
    auto [next, actions] =
        xstate::transition(*counter, now, xstate::event{.type = "inc", .payload = {}});
    boost::json::array logged;
    for (const xstate::action& returned : actions) {
        const boost::json::object* params = returned.params.if_object();
        if (returned.type != "xstate.log" || params == nullptr) {
            continue;
        }
        if (const boost::json::value* value = params->if_contains("value")) {
            logged.push_back(*value);
        }
    }
    std::cout << boost::json::serialize(next.context) << " logged "
              << boost::json::serialize(logged) << '\n';
    now = std::move(next);
}

It prints:

{"count":1,"limit":2} logged [0,1]
{"count":2,"limit":2} logged [1,2]
{"count":2,"limit":2} logged []

Each inc that was taken logged the count twice: report ran before add and after it, and saw each context. The third inc found the count at the limit: the guard was false, no transition was taken, and nothing ran or was returned. report is returned as xstate.log, its value resolved from the context at its turn (Log).

A custom action, one the implementations do not hold, is returned to the caller with the params the config gave it, and nothing of the context, where XState’s carries the context it ran with in its info (Custom actions). The code that executes it reads the context from a snapshot, which holds it as a whole microstep left it: the snapshot of the microstep that returned the action, from the cursor or get_microsteps, holds the context after every action of that microstep (Microsteps). A value that must be computed from the context at the action’s turn is computed by a registered implementation, as the value of report is here.

A snapshot is a value

A snapshot is a plain C++ value: the state value, the context, the status and the rest. A transition never changes the snapshot it begins from; it returns a new one. The same event taken twice from the same snapshot gives two snapshots equal member by member, and the first is still there, to be used again or stored. A counter whose inc adds one, and whose set increments, then assigns the count its event carries, and fails without one:

xstate::result<boost::json::object> increment(const xstate::action_args& args) {
    const boost::json::object* context = args.context.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* count = context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("count");
    if (count == nullptr || !count->is_int64()) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"count", count->get_int64() + 1}};
}

xstate::result<boost::json::object> set_count(const xstate::action_args& args) {
    const boost::json::value* count = args.event.payload.if_contains("count");
    if (count == nullptr || !count->is_int64()) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"count", *count}};
}

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actions.emplace("increment", xstate::assign_action{.assignment = increment});
implementations.actions.emplace("setCount", xstate::assign_action{.assignment = set_count});
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "counter",
    "context": {"count": 0},
    "on": {
        "inc": {"actions": "increment"},
        "set": {"actions": ["increment", "setCount"]}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> counter = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!counter.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::event inc{.type = "inc", .payload = {}};
const xstate::snapshot first = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*counter);
const xstate::snapshot second = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*counter, first, inc);
const xstate::snapshot again = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*counter, first, inc);
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(first.context) << ' '
          << boost::json::serialize(second.context) << ' '
          << boost::json::serialize(again.context) << '\n';

It prints:

{"count":0} {"count":1} {"count":1}

A failure keeps the snapshot a macrostep began from too. When an implementation fails, the macrostep ends in that snapshot, its status error and its error the code the implementation returned: no assign of the failed macrostep reaches the context, not even one that ran before the failure. That is the snapshot XState’s actor keeps, where its pure functions throw (When an implementation fails, Failures are values). A set without a count, from the snapshot second:

const xstate::snapshot failed =
    xstate::get_next_snapshot(*counter, second, xstate::event{.type = "set", .payload = {}});
std::cout << (failed.status == xstate::status::error ? "error " : "active ")
          << boost::json::serialize(failed.context) << '\n';

It prints:

error {"count":1}

The count is 1, the count of second: increment ran and made it 2, then setCount failed, and the increment was dropped with the rest of the macrostep.

Since a snapshot is a value, its caller keeps it where it likes: in a variable, a queue, a map of sessions. Its state value and its context are JSON, so they can be stored, in a database or across two requests, and resolve_state(machine, value, context) builds a snapshot back from them, as XState’s machine.resolveState({ value, context }) does. It returns a result and refuses a value that names no state with unknown_state. It restores the value and the context and nothing else: the status comes from the value, done or active, never error, and the output, what history states remember and the children are not restored (Persisted state). Inside a macrostep, the snapshot of each microstep holds the context as that microstep left it, and the macrostep cursor hands each one to its caller (The macrostep cursor).

Context in an actor

An actor keeps the snapshot for its caller: it starts in the initial snapshot, takes each event sent to it, and keeps the snapshot each macrostep settles in. Stately’s page shows the context through an actor that a listener watches. Here the actor is one of xstate’s actor_system, and its machine updates the context with update_feedback, the assigner of Updating context with assign:

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actions.emplace("updateFeedback",
                                xstate::assign_action{.assignment = update_feedback});
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "feedback",
    "context": {"feedback": "Some feedback"},
    "on": {"feedback.update": {"actions": "updateFeedback"}}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!feedback_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> feedback_actor = system.create_actor(*feedback_machine);
if (!feedback_actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<void> subscribed =
    system.subscribe(*feedback_actor, [](const xstate::snapshot& state) {
        std::cout << boost::json::serialize(state.context) << '\n';
    });
if (!subscribed.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.start(*feedback_actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::event update{
    .type = "feedback.update",
    .payload = {{"feedback", "Some other feedback"}},
};
if (!system.send(*feedback_actor, update).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

It prints:

{"feedback":"Some feedback"}
{"feedback":"Some other feedback"}

subscribe hands its listener each snapshot the actor settles in while it is active, and the one it is done in, as XState’s subscribe does; snapshot_of returns the latest. The listener runs inside the actor’s turn: it may read the system, but a call from it that changes the system, a send among them, is refused with xactor’s invalid_argument and changes nothing, where XState accepts a send from a subscriber and handles it after the update in progress (A callback that calls the system back). Actors, their fuel (Fuel, parking and resume) and their children are the subject of Actors.

Context and types

XState types the context with TypeScript, in setup({ types: { context } }), and the compiler checks every implementation against it. An xstate machine is loaded from JSON at run time, so no type exists for a compiler to check: the context is a boost::json::value, and each implementation checks what it reads, before it reads it. It returns an error when a member is missing or of the wrong kind, as integer_at and its callers do in How guards and actions read the context. That error is a value: it ends the macrostep in the snapshot’s status (A snapshot is a value).

Read members with if_object and if_contains, which return a null pointer when the value is not an object or the member is missing. at throws on a missing member, and in a build without exceptions the throw aborts the program.

Context cheatsheet

XState xstate

context: { feedback: '' }

"context": {"feedback": ""} in the config

context: () => ({ ... })

implementations.context, a context_maker

context: ({ input }) => ({ ... })

the same, reading its const boost::json::value& input

getInitialSnapshot(machine, input)

get_initial_snapshot(machine, input)

createActor(machine, { input })

system.create_actor(machine, {.input = input})

assign({ feedback: ({ event }) => event.feedback })

an assign_action whose assignment returns {"feedback": ...}, read from args.event.payload

assign(({ context, event }, params) => ({ ... }))

an assign_action whose assignment returns the partial update

context, event and params in an implementation

args.context, args.event (its type, and its other members in args.event.payload) and args.params

snapshot.context

snapshot.context, a boost::json::value

setup({ types: { context } })

none: each implementation checks what it reads

Events and transitions

A transition is a change from one state to another. An event is what causes it: a message the machine receives, with a type that names what happened and the data that travels with it. When a machine receives an event, it looks in its active states for the transitions that event enables. If there are some, it takes them: it leaves the states they leave, runs their actions and enters the states they reach. If there is none, nothing changes.

Transitions are deterministic: the same snapshot and the same event always lead to the same next snapshot and the same actions. That is what lets a step be computed as a plain function, tested event by event, and replayed.

This section covers the events a machine receives, the transitions of a state’s on and where they lead, how an event selects among them, event descriptors and wildcards, guards, and the two kinds of transitions no event names: eventless (always) and delayed (after) ones. The actions a transition runs are in Actions; how each microstep runs, and how a caller pays for it, in Pure transitions and the macrostep cursor.

Events

An event is an object with a type, the string that names what happened, and any other members, its payload, as an event is in XState. xstate’s event holds the two apart: type, a std::string, and payload, a boost::json::object holding every other member. Transitions match the type; the payload is data for the implementations, which receive the event as args.event. The example reads an event from JSON with event_from_json, prints its two parts, and sends it to a machine:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "feedback",
    "initial": "question",
    "states": {
        "question": {
            "on": {
                "feedback.good": {"target": "thanks"}
            }
        },
        "thanks": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!feedback.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::result<xstate::event> event = xstate::event_from_json(boost::json::parse(
    R"({"type": "feedback.good", "feedback": "This is great!", "rating": 5})"));
if (!event.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << event->type << ' ' << boost::json::serialize(event->payload) << '\n';

const xstate::snapshot question = xstate::initial_transition(*feedback).first;
const xstate::snapshot thanks = xstate::transition(*feedback, question, *event).first;
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(question.value) << " -> "
          << boost::json::serialize(thanks.value) << '\n';

It prints:

feedback.good {"feedback":"This is great!","rating":5}
"question" -> "thanks"

An event usually arrives as JSON, in the flat form XState’s actor.send takes, {"type": ..., ...payload}. event_from_json reads that form and to_json writes it, its type first. An event can also be built in C++, from its two members:

const xstate::event update{
    .type = "feedback.update",
    .payload = {{"feedback", "This is great!"}, {"rating", 5}},
};
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(xstate::to_json(update)) << '\n';

event_from_json refuses a value that is not an object, or whose type is missing or not a string, with invalid_event:

for (const std::string_view text : {
         R"({"type": "feedback.update", "rating": 5})",
         R"({"type": "*"})",
         R"({"rating": 5})",
         R"({"type": 5})",
         R"("feedback.update")",
     }) {
    boost::system::error_code parsed;
    const boost::json::value json = boost::json::parse(text, parsed);
    if (parsed) {
        return 1;
    }
    const xstate::result<xstate::event> read = xstate::event_from_json(json);
    if (!read.has_value()) {
        std::cout << text << " -> " << read.error().message() << '\n';
        continue;
    }
    std::cout << text << " -> " << read->type << ' ' << boost::json::serialize(read->payload)
              << '\n';
}

It prints:

{"type":"feedback.update","feedback":"This is great!","rating":5}
{"type": "feedback.update", "rating": 5} -> feedback.update {"rating":5}
{"type": "*"} -> * {}
{"rating": 5} -> invalid_event
{"type": 5} -> invalid_event
"feedback.update" -> invalid_event

An event of the type * is read like any other. A machine refuses it as the event of a macrostep, which a caller sends or a clock releases, and takes it only as an event it raised itself without a delay (An event of the type *).

Events whose type starts with xstate. are the machine’s own: xstate.init is the event of the initial macrostep, xstate.after.<delay>.<state id> comes back from a delayed transition (Delayed transitions), xstate.done.state.<state id> is raised when a compound or parallel state completes (Done events), and xstate.done.actor.<id> and xstate.error.actor.<id> come from invoked actors (Done and error events). They select transitions as any other event does, with two exceptions in XState that xstate does not follow yet. When xstate.init comes from outside, XState’s macrostep selects no transition for it, and when xstate.stop, the event that stops an XState actor, comes from outside, it stops the machine. xstate selects transitions for both as for any other event, so an on entry that names one, or a * transition, takes it. A caller should therefore not send xstate.init or xstate.stop, nor make up any other of these events. A caller of the machine core does deliver two kinds itself: each xstate.after... event its clock releases (In the machine core), and the done and error events of the children it runs, since the core runs none. The actor layer delivers both for its actors.

Transitions

A state’s on maps event descriptors (Event descriptors) to transitions. Each transition is written in one of three forms:

"on": {
    "feedback.good": "thanks",
    "feedback.bad": {"target": "form", "actions": "track"},
    "feedback.provide": [
        {"guard": "sentimentGood", "target": "thanks"},
        {"target": "form"}
    ]
}

  • a string, the shorthand for {"target": "thanks"};

  • an object with any of target, actions, guard, reenter, description and meta;

  • a list of strings and objects, tried in order until one is enabled (Guards).

target names the state or states the transition goes to (Targets); a transition without one is targetless. actions lists the actions it runs when it is taken (Actions), guard the condition it is taken on (Guards), and reenter whether it leaves and enters its source again (Self-transitions and reenter). description and meta are for readers and tools: xstate keeps them in the machine’s definition, which to_json writes as XState’s toJSON() does, and does nothing else with them. The root is a state too: its on handles an event in every state, unless a deeper state handles it first.

Creating the machine checks every transition, so a mistake is an error before any event runs: a target that names no state is refused with unknown_target, a guard the implementations do not hold with unknown_guard, and an on key that is the empty string with invalid_config, as XState refuses it and asks for always instead. invalid_config also refuses a transition that declares cond, XState v4’s name for guard, with a value JavaScript reads as true, as XState’s development build does, and an actions that is null, which XState accepts as a list that holds null, and then throws when it takes the transition (What creation refuses lists them all).

Selecting a transition

An event selects its transitions starting from the deepest active states:

  1. Start at each active atomic state, a state with no children.

  2. Take the first of its transitions for the event that is enabled: one without a guard, or whose guard passes.

  3. If it has none, look in its parent, and so on up to the root.

  4. If no state up to the root has one, the event changes nothing.

In a parallel state each region selects on its own, so one event can take a transition in each region (Parallel states). The parallel state’s own transitions, and its ancestors’, are tried only when no region selected one. When the transitions selected in two regions would exit a common state, as two that leave the parallel state would, only the first is taken, in the order the state value lists the regions.

In the editor below, escape means three things: in menu it closes the menu, in text it closes the editor, and in saving it does nothing.

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "editor",
    "initial": "editing",
    "states": {
        "editing": {
            "initial": "text",
            "on": {"escape": "closed"},
            "states": {
                "text": {"on": {"menu.open": "menu", "save": "saving"}},
                "menu": {"on": {"escape": "text"}},
                "saving": {"on": {"escape": {}}}
            }
        },
        "closed": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> editor = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!editor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const std::vector<std::vector<std::string_view>> runs{
    {"menu.open", "escape", "escape"},
    {"save", "escape"},
};
for (const std::vector<std::string_view>& run : runs) {
    xstate::snapshot now = xstate::initial_transition(*editor).first;
    std::cout << "start " << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';
    for (const std::string_view type : run) {
        const xstate::event happened{.type = std::string(type), .payload = {}};
        now = xstate::transition(*editor, now, happened).first;
        std::cout << type << " -> " << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';
    }
}

It prints:

start {"editing":"text"}
menu.open -> {"editing":"menu"}
escape -> {"editing":"text"}
escape -> "closed"
start {"editing":"text"}
save -> {"editing":"saving"}
escape -> {"editing":"saving"}

In menu, its own escape is taken: the deepest state wins. In text, which has no escape, the parent’s is taken and the editor closes. saving declares escape with no target and no actions: a forbidden transition. It is selected, so the search stops there and the parent’s escape is never looked at, and it changes nothing: the editor cannot be closed while it saves. Leaving the event out of saving would have let the parent take it.

An event that selects no transition, or only a forbidden one, changes nothing in its own microstep. The eventless transitions are still selected after it, with that event (Eventless transitions), so the macrostep settles at its first microstep with the snapshot unchanged unless one of them now passes, for example one whose guard reads the event. can(machine, snapshot, event), XState’s snapshot.can(event), says beforehand whether an event would take a transition that has a target or actions (Whether an event would do anything); for escape in saving it says no.

Targets

A target is written relative to the state that declares the transition, its source:

Target Names

"b"

the sibling b of the source

"b.two"

the child two of the sibling b: a path of keys, separated by dots

".other"

the child other of the source; from the root, ".a" names the top-level state a

"#c"

the state whose id is c, anywhere in the machine; "#c.other" continues from it as a path

The root has no siblings, so a target declared on the root starts with . or #: "a" there is refused with unknown_target, as XState refuses it and suggests ".a".

A state’s id is its id member, or, without one, the machine’s id followed by the state’s path, joined by dots: in the machine below, #machine.b.two names the state two.

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "machine",
    "initial": "a",
    "on": {"reset": ".a"},
    "states": {
        "a": {"on": {"next": "b", "deep": "b.two"}},
        "b": {
            "initial": "one",
            "on": {"next": "#c"},
            "states": {"one": {}, "two": {}}
        },
        "c": {
            "id": "c",
            "initial": "child",
            "on": {"next": ".other"},
            "states": {"child": {}, "other": {}}
        }
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> machine = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::snapshot now = xstate::initial_transition(*machine).first;
std::cout << "start " << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';
for (const std::string_view type : {"next", "next", "next", "reset", "deep"}) {
    const xstate::event happened{.type = std::string(type), .payload = {}};
    now = xstate::transition(*machine, now, happened).first;
    std::cout << type << " -> " << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';
}

It prints:

start "a"
next -> {"b":"one"}
next -> {"c":"child"}
next -> {"c":"other"}
reset -> "a"
deep -> {"b":"two"}

a goes to its sibling b, and entering b, a compound state, enters its initial child one. one has no next, so the next of b is taken, to the state whose id is c, which enters child. c then goes to its own child other. reset, on the root, returns to a from anywhere, and deep names a child of a sibling, so b is entered at two instead of its initial child.

Multiple targets

A transition may name several targets, as a list under target, when each is in a different region of a parallel state (Parallel states): it moves every region it names in one microstep. The list goes under target; a list in the place of the transition is a list of transitions, of which the first enabled is taken.

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "settings",
    "type": "parallel",
    "on": {
        "set.dark.custom": {"target": [".mode.dark", ".theme.custom"]},
        "set.light": {"target": ".mode.light"}
    },
    "states": {
        "mode": {
            "initial": "light",
            "on": {"mode.light": ".light"},
            "states": {
                "light": {"on": {"toggle": "dark"}},
                "dark": {"on": {"toggle": "light"}}
            }
        },
        "theme": {
            "initial": "default",
            "states": {
                "default": {"on": {"change": "custom"}},
                "custom": {"on": {"change": "default"}}
            }
        }
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> settings = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!settings.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::snapshot now = xstate::initial_transition(*settings).first;
std::cout << "start " << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';
for (const std::string_view type :
     {"set.dark.custom", "set.light", "set.dark.custom", "mode.light"}) {
    const xstate::event happened{.type = std::string(type), .payload = {}};
    now = xstate::transition(*settings, now, happened).first;
    std::cout << type << " -> " << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';
}

It prints:

start {"mode":"light","theme":"default"}
set.dark.custom -> {"mode":"dark","theme":"custom"}
set.light -> {"mode":"light","theme":"default"}
set.dark.custom -> {"mode":"dark","theme":"custom"}
mode.light -> {"mode":"light","theme":"custom"}

set.dark.custom moves both regions. set.light names one target, yet it also sends theme back to default. A transition leaves every active state inside its domain: its source, when every target is inside the source and it does not reenter, or else the nearest state that contains the source and every target. It enters its targets, their ancestors up to the domain and, of each parallel state among those ancestors or the domain, every region that holds no target, at its initial state. set.light is declared on the root, so its domain is the root: it leaves both regions, and entering mode again under the parallel root enters theme at its initial state. Stately’s page on transitions says such a transition leaves the other region as it is; XState 5.33.2 resets it, and xstate does what XState does. To move one region and keep the others, declare the transition in that region: mode.light, in mode, has mode as its domain, and theme keeps custom.

Self-transitions and reenter

A transition whose targets are inside its source, the source itself included, does not leave the source by default: the source’s exit and entry actions do not run, and the actors it invokes keep running. Only the states below the source are left and entered. With reenter: true the domain is above the source, so the source is left and entered again: its actions run, and its invoked actors are stopped and started again. A transition without a target leaves and enters no state, whatever its reenter says, as in XState.

A self-transition is one that stays in its source, and there are three kinds:

Transition The source’s children The source’s entry and exit actions The source’s invoked actors

targetless, no target

kept as they are

not run

keep running

targeted, the source as its target

left and entered at their initial states

not run

keep running

re-entering, a target and reenter: true

left and entered at their initial states

run

stopped and started again

The machine below names an entry and an exit action for each state. None has an implementation, so each is returned to the caller in the order it runs (Custom actions), and the output shows what each transition left and entered. types_of, a helper of the program, writes the types of a list of actions as [a, b]:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "machine",
    "initial": "parentState",
    "states": {
        "parentState": {
            "entry": "enterParent",
            "exit": "exitParent",
            "initial": "someChildState",
            "on": {
                "event.targetless": {"actions": "notify"},
                "event.normal": {"target": ".someChildState"},
                "event.thatReenters": {"target": ".otherChildState", "reenter": true},
                "event.self": {"target": "parentState"},
                "event.selfReenters": {"target": "parentState", "reenter": true}
            },
            "states": {
                "someChildState": {"entry": "enterSome", "exit": "exitSome"},
                "otherChildState": {"entry": "enterOther", "exit": "exitOther"}
            }
        }
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> machine = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

auto [now, actions] = xstate::initial_transition(*machine);
std::cout << "start " << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << ' ' << types_of(actions) << '\n';
for (const std::string_view type : {
         "event.thatReenters",
         "event.targetless",
         "event.self",
         "event.normal",
         "event.selfReenters",
     }) {
    const xstate::event happened{.type = std::string(type), .payload = {}};
    std::tie(now, actions) = xstate::transition(*machine, now, happened);
    std::cout << type << " -> " << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << ' ' << types_of(actions)
              << '\n';
}

It prints:

start {"parentState":"someChildState"} [enterParent, enterSome]
event.thatReenters -> {"parentState":"otherChildState"} [exitSome, exitParent, enterParent, enterOther]
event.targetless -> {"parentState":"otherChildState"} [notify]
event.self -> {"parentState":"someChildState"} [exitOther, enterSome]
event.normal -> {"parentState":"someChildState"} [exitSome, enterSome]
event.selfReenters -> {"parentState":"someChildState"} [exitSome, exitParent, enterParent, enterSome]

  • event.thatReenters goes from parentState to its child otherChildState, and re-enters: parentState is left and entered too.

  • event.targetless runs notify and nothing else; otherChildState stays.

  • event.self targets parentState itself: its child is left and its initial child entered, and the entry and exit actions of parentState itself do not run.

  • event.normal targets .someChildState, the active child: the child is inside the domain, so it is left and entered again.

  • event.selfReenters re-enters parentState and everything in it.

In XState v4 a re-entering transition was called external, and the default one internal.

Event descriptors

The key of an on entry is an event descriptor: it says which event types its transitions take. Most descriptors are a type and match only that type. Two forms match more. A wildcard is a catch-all, for the events a state does not name; a partial descriptor handles a family of events named with a common prefix, such as every feedback. event, in one place:

  • *, the wildcard, matches every event type, the machine’s own included;

  • a partial descriptor, a prefix and then .*, matches every type that starts with the prefix’s dot-separated tokens: feedback.* matches feedback, feedback.good and feedback.bad.rude, and not feedbacks.

* is a wildcard only as the whole descriptor, or as the last token after a dot when no earlier token is * itself. A * inside a longer token is a plain character: mou*se.* is a partial descriptor and matches mou*se.x. Any other descriptor that holds a *, such as mouse*, *.click, mouse.*.click or mouse.*.*, matches only an event of exactly that type. xstate writes no warning about any of them, where XState’s development build writes a console warning about a descriptor that ends in .* and holds another *, such as mouse.*.* or mou*se.*, the first time a state looks up the transitions of an event type (The checks of XState’s development build).

One event can match several descriptors of one state. Their transitions are tried in this order: those of the descriptor equal to the event’s type, then those of each matching wildcard descriptor, the longest first, so feedback.bad.* before feedback.* before *. The first enabled transition is taken, and only when none is does the search go up to the parent.

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "feedback",
    "initial": "prompt",
    "states": {
        "prompt": {
            "on": {
                "feedback.good": "thanks",
                "feedback.*": "form",
                "feedback.bad.*": "apology",
                "*": "other"
            }
        },
        "thanks": {},
        "form": {},
        "apology": {},
        "other": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!feedback.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::snapshot prompt = xstate::initial_transition(*feedback).first;
for (const std::string_view type : {
         "feedback.good",
         "feedback.bad",
         "feedback.bad.rude",
         "feedback.meh",
         "feedback",
         "feedbacks",
         "mouse.click",
         "*",
     }) {
    const xstate::event happened{.type = std::string(type), .payload = {}};
    const xstate::snapshot next = xstate::transition(*feedback, prompt, happened).first;
    if (next.status == xstate::status::error) {
        std::cout << type << " -> " << next.error.message() << '\n';
        continue;
    }
    std::cout << type << " -> " << boost::json::serialize(next.value) << '\n';
}

It prints:

feedback.good -> "thanks"
feedback.bad -> "apology"
feedback.bad.rude -> "apology"
feedback.meh -> "form"
feedback -> "form"
feedbacks -> "other"
mouse.click -> "other"
* -> invalid_event

feedback.bad is matched by feedback.bad.*, which is longer than feedback.*; feedbacks is not the token feedback, so only * matches it. Since the wildcard matches the machine’s own events too, a * transition in an active child state takes the xstate.after... event of its parent’s delayed transition before the parent sees it: the deepest state is tried first.

An event of the type *

An event may not have the type * when it comes from outside the machine. The macrostep that takes one settles at once with the snapshot it began from, its status error and its error invalid_event, which is the last line the example prints. XState’s development build throws there, An event cannot have the wildcard type ('*'), and xstate returns the error as a value (The checks of XState’s development build).

A raised event of the type * that the machine queues itself, a raise without a delay, is not refused: its type is the descriptor * exactly, so * transitions take it, and no partial descriptor matches it, as in XState. A delayed one comes back from the clock as a macrostep of its own and is refused like an event from outside, and an actor sent one, or receiving its own delayed one, fails with invalid_event, as XState’s actor ends in error.

Guards

A guard is a condition a transition checks before it is taken: a guarded transition is enabled only when its guard passes. Guards let one event lead to different states depending on data: the event’s payload, the context, or the params the config gives the guard. A guard decides and changes nothing.

In XState a guard is a function, inline in the config or named in setup({ guards }). A JSON config cannot hold a function, so in xstate every guard is a name, and implementations.guards maps each name to a predicate: a function of the action_args every implementation receives, the context, the event and the params, that returns a result<bool>. A guard is written as its name, or as an object with a type, its name, and params, a JSON value that reaches the guard as args.params, null when the config gives none; guards with the same name share one implementation, and their params tell one use from another. XState’s params may also be a function of the context and the event, which JSON cannot hold: an xstate guard reads both from its args.

When one event has a list of transitions, they are tried in order, and the first enabled one is taken; a last transition without a guard is the default, taken when no guard before it passes. integer_at, a helper of the program, returns the integer a JSON object holds under a key, or none:

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.guards.emplace(
    "sentimentGood", [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<bool> {
        const std::optional<std::int64_t> rating = integer_at(args.event.payload, "rating");
        return rating.has_value() && *rating >= 4;
    });
implementations.guards.emplace(
    "sentimentBad", [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<bool> {
        const std::optional<std::int64_t> rating = integer_at(args.event.payload, "rating");
        return rating.has_value() && *rating <= 2;
    });
implementations.guards.emplace(
    "isValid", [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<bool> {
        const boost::json::object* params = args.params.if_object();
        const std::optional<std::int64_t> max_length =
            params == nullptr ? std::nullopt : integer_at(*params, "maxLength");
        const boost::json::value* feedback = args.event.payload.if_contains("feedback");
        if (!max_length.has_value() || feedback == nullptr || !feedback->is_string()) {
            return xstate::failure<bool>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
        }
        const std::size_t length = feedback->get_string().size();
        return length > 0 && std::cmp_less_equal(length, *max_length);
    });
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "feedback",
    "initial": "prompt",
    "states": {
        "prompt": {
            "on": {
                "feedback.provide": [
                    {"guard": "sentimentGood", "target": "thanks"},
                    {"guard": "sentimentBad", "target": "form"},
                    {"target": "neutral"}
                ]
            }
        },
        "form": {
            "on": {
                "submit": {
                    "guard": {"type": "isValid", "params": {"maxLength": 50}},
                    "target": "submitting"
                }
            }
        },
        "thanks": {},
        "neutral": {},
        "submitting": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback =
    xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!feedback.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::snapshot prompt = xstate::initial_transition(*feedback).first;
for (const std::int64_t rating : {5, 1, 3}) {
    const xstate::event provide{.type = "feedback.provide", .payload = {{"rating", rating}}};
    const xstate::snapshot next = xstate::transition(*feedback, prompt, provide).first;
    std::cout << "rating " << rating << " -> " << boost::json::serialize(next.value) << '\n';
}

const xstate::event bad{.type = "feedback.provide", .payload = {{"rating", 1}}};
const xstate::snapshot form = xstate::transition(*feedback, prompt, bad).first;
for (const std::string_view text : {"", "Too slow."}) {
    const xstate::event submit{.type = "submit", .payload = {{"feedback", text}}};
    const xstate::snapshot next = xstate::transition(*feedback, form, submit).first;
    std::cout << "feedback " << boost::json::serialize(boost::json::value(text)) << " -> "
              << boost::json::serialize(next.value) << '\n';
}

const xstate::event no_feedback{.type = "submit", .payload = {}};
const xstate::snapshot failed = xstate::transition(*feedback, form, no_feedback).first;
std::cout << "no feedback -> " << boost::json::serialize(failed.value);
if (failed.status == xstate::status::error) {
    std::cout << " error " << failed.error.message();
}
std::cout << '\n';

It prints:

rating 5 -> "thanks"
rating 1 -> "form"
rating 3 -> "neutral"
feedback "" -> "form"
feedback "Too slow." -> "submitting"
no feedback -> "form" error implementation_failed

A rating of 3 passes neither guard, so the default is taken. In form, an empty feedback does not pass isValid: no transition is enabled and the machine stays. A guard whose input is wrong, here a submit without feedback, returns an error rather than a guess, and the macrostep fails with it (When a guard cannot run): the last line is the snapshot it began from, form, its status error and its error implementation_failed. XState’s transition throws there instead, Unable to evaluate guard 'isValid' ..., followed by the message of the TypeError its guard raised (Failures are values).

Higher-order guards and stateIn

XState composes guards with and, or and not, and tests the machine’s state with stateIn. All four are functions in XState, which JSON cannot hold, so xstate writes each as an object whose type names it:

{"type": "xstate.and", "guards": ["isValid", "isAuthorized"]}
{"type": "xstate.or", "guards": ["isAuthorized", "isGuest"]}
{"type": "xstate.not", "guards": ["isGuest"]}
{"type": "xstate.stateIn", "stateValue": {"form": "submitting"}}

An operand in guards is a guard in any form: a name, an object with params, or another higher-order guard. and passes when every operand passes, and or when one does; like XState’s, both stop at the first operand that decides, so an operand after it is not evaluated. not takes exactly one operand. A not with any other number of operands, or an and or or without a guards list, is refused with invalid_config.

stateIn passes when the snapshot is in stateValue: a state value, matched as snapshot.matches matches it, or a string that starts with #, which passes when the state with that id is active. It tests the whole machine’s state, not the source’s, which is mostly useful in a parallel state, where one region depends on another. In the editor below, save needs the network region online and the role of an owner or an admin, and edit refuses a guest:

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.guards.emplace(
    "hasRole", [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<bool> {
        const boost::json::object* params = args.params.if_object();
        const boost::json::value* wanted =
            params == nullptr ? nullptr : params->if_contains("role");
        if (wanted == nullptr || !wanted->is_string()) {
            return xstate::failure<bool>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
        }
        const boost::json::value* role = args.event.payload.if_contains("role");
        return role != nullptr && *role == *wanted;
    });
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "editor",
    "type": "parallel",
    "states": {
        "document": {
            "initial": "dirty",
            "states": {
                "dirty": {
                    "on": {
                        "save": {
                            "guard": {
                                "type": "xstate.and",
                                "guards": [
                                    {"type": "xstate.stateIn", "stateValue": {"network": "online"}},
                                    {
                                        "type": "xstate.or",
                                        "guards": [
                                            {"type": "hasRole", "params": {"role": "owner"}},
                                            {"type": "hasRole", "params": {"role": "admin"}}
                                        ]
                                    }
                                ]
                            },
                            "target": "saved"
                        }
                    }
                },
                "saved": {
                    "on": {
                        "edit": {
                            "guard": {
                                "type": "xstate.not",
                                "guards": [{"type": "hasRole", "params": {"role": "guest"}}]
                            },
                            "target": "dirty"
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
        },
        "network": {
            "initial": "offline",
            "states": {
                "offline": {"on": {"connect": "online"}},
                "online": {}
            }
        }
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> editor = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!editor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const std::vector<std::pair<std::string_view, std::string_view>> steps{
    {"save", "owner"}, {"connect", ""},   {"save", "guest"},
    {"save", "admin"}, {"edit", "guest"}, {"edit", "owner"},
};
xstate::snapshot now = xstate::initial_transition(*editor).first;
for (const auto& [type, role] : steps) {
    xstate::event happened{.type = std::string(type), .payload = {}};
    std::cout << type;
    if (!role.empty()) {
        happened.payload.emplace("role", role);
        std::cout << ' ' << role;
    }
    now = xstate::transition(*editor, now, happened).first;
    std::cout << " -> " << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';
}

It prints:

save owner -> {"document":"dirty","network":"offline"}
connect -> {"document":"dirty","network":"online"}
save guest -> {"document":"dirty","network":"online"}
save admin -> {"document":"saved","network":"online"}
edit guest -> {"document":"saved","network":"online"}
edit owner -> {"document":"dirty","network":"online"}

to_json writes these guards in the form above, so a machine loaded back from its definition keeps them, where XState’s machine.toJSON() writes nothing in their place, since they are functions (Higher-order guards).

When a guard cannot run

  • A guard name the implementations do not hold is refused when the machine is created, with unknown_guard. XState accepts the machine and throws when it first evaluates the guard; xstate refuses a name it cannot resolve at creation (A config is refused when it is created).

  • A guard that returns an error fails the macrostep: it settles at once, with the snapshot it began from, its status error and its error the one the guard returned. XState’s pure functions throw there, and its actor keeps the snapshot from before the event, in error, as xstate’s does.

  • A stateIn whose #id names no state is accepted when the machine is created; evaluating it fails the macrostep with unknown_state, where XState’s getStateNodeById throws. A state value that names no state does not pass.

Eventless transitions

An eventless transition is taken without an event: whenever its state is active and its guard passes, right after the microstep that made it so. It is declared under a state’s always, in any of the forms of a transition in on. It fits a change that follows from a condition rather than from a trigger: the kettle below boils when its temperature, which events update, goes above 100, whatever event raised it.

updateTemperature is an assign that copies the event’s temperature into the context (Updating context with assign); turnOffLight has no implementation, so it is a custom action, returned to the caller. isBoiling reads the context with integer_at, the helper of the quick start (Handle context data), which returns the integer an object holds under a key, or none. The example prints, for each event, every microstep of its macrostep, with the state value it left and the actions it returned, written by the types_of of Self-transitions and reenter:

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.guards.emplace(
    "isBoiling", [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<bool> {
        const std::optional<std::int64_t> temperature = integer_at(args.context, "temperature");
        if (!temperature.has_value()) {
            return xstate::failure<bool>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
        }
        return *temperature > 100;
    });
implementations.actions.emplace(
    "updateTemperature",
    xstate::assign_action{
        .assignment =
            [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<boost::json::object> {
            const boost::json::value* temperature =
                args.event.payload.if_contains("temperature");
            if (temperature == nullptr) {
                return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(
                    xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
            }
            return boost::json::object{{"temperature", *temperature}};
        },
    });
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "kettle",
    "initial": "lukewarm",
    "context": {"temperature": 80},
    "on": {"temp.update": {"actions": "updateTemperature"}},
    "states": {
        "lukewarm": {"on": {"boil": "heating"}},
        "heating": {"always": {"guard": "isBoiling", "target": "boiling"}},
        "boiling": {
            "entry": "turnOffLight",
            "always": {
                "guard": {"type": "xstate.not", "guards": ["isBoiling"]},
                "target": "heating"
            }
        }
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> kettle = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!kettle.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const std::vector<std::pair<std::string_view, boost::json::object>> events{
    {"temp.update", {{"temperature", 105}}},
    {"boil", {}},
    {"temp.update", {{"temperature", 90}}},
};
xstate::snapshot now = xstate::initial_transition(*kettle).first;
for (const auto& [type, payload] : events) {
    const xstate::event happened{.type = std::string(type), .payload = payload};
    std::cout << type << ':';
    for (const xstate::microstep& micro : xstate::get_microsteps(*kettle, now, happened)) {
        std::cout << ' ' << boost::json::serialize(micro.snapshot.value) << ' '
                  << types_of(micro.actions);
        now = micro.snapshot;
    }
    std::cout << '\n';
}

It prints:

temp.update: "lukewarm" []
boil: "heating" [] "boiling" [turnOffLight]
temp.update: "boiling" [] "heating" []

The first update raises the temperature to 105 while the kettle is lukewarm, which has no eventless transition: one microstep. boil takes two: its own transition to heating, and then, since the temperature is already above 100, the eventless transition of heating to boiling. The macrostep settles in boiling, so heating is a transient state there: the machine passes through it and never rests in it. The last update is a targetless transition of the root. Its microstep lowers the temperature in the context, and the eventless transitions, selected after every event’s microstep, now find that the guard of boiling passes.

The rules, which are XState’s:

  • To select the eventless transitions, the machine walks up from each active atomic state and takes the first eventless transition whose guard passes. Those it finds run as one microstep, before the next raised event is taken.

  • It selects them after the macrostep’s first microstep, the event’s or the initial one, and after each raised event’s. After a microstep of eventless transitions, it selects them again only when that microstep changed the snapshot: the active states, the history, the context (an assign ran), the children (a spawn or a stop) or the status. XState compares snapshot objects; xstate states the rule. So an unguarded targetless always whose actions change nothing runs once per macrostep and once more after each raised event; one that assigns runs forever.

  • Their guards and actions receive the macrostep’s event: the external one, or the raised event the machine took last. Each microstep reports it as microstep.event.

  • A transient state is never a settled snapshot: the actor layer’s subscribers do not see it (Watching an actor), as XState’s do not. The cursor and get_microsteps report every microstep, so the machine core shows it. A delayed transition with a delay of 0 does not run inside the macrostep: its event comes back from the clock, so the macrostep settles in its state first (Delayed transitions).

A macrostep that never settles

An eventless transition that is always enabled and always changes the snapshot never lets its macrostep settle: two states whose always lead to each other, or an unguarded always that assigns. Stately advises a target that differs from the current state, or a guard that turns false. Stately’s page says an unguarded, targetless always always loops; in XState 5.33.2, as in xstate, it loops only when its actions change the snapshot.

xstate never stops such a macrostep on its own: the functions that run a macrostep to its end, transition and get_next_snapshot among them, never return. The cursor runs one microstep per next(), so its caller decides how many it pays for. Here it pays for five, and the two states of the cycle take turns:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "loop",
    "initial": "idle",
    "states": {
        "idle": {"on": {"start": "ping"}},
        "ping": {"always": "pong"},
        "pong": {"always": "ping"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> loop = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!loop.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::snapshot idle = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*loop);
xstate::macrostep step = xstate::begin(*loop, idle, {.type = "start", .payload = {}});
std::size_t spent = 0;
for (std::size_t fuel = 5; fuel > 0 && !step.done(); --fuel) {
    const xstate::progress made = step.next();
    ++spent;
    std::cout << boost::json::serialize(made.step.snapshot.value) << '\n';
}
std::cout << (step.done() ? "settled" : "not settled") << " after " << spent << " microsteps\n";

It prints:

"ping"
"pong"
"ping"
"pong"
"ping"
not settled after 5 microsteps

The cursor is still valid when the fuel runs out, and a later next() resumes it where it stopped (Fuel). What a caller may do then is shown with the cursor (Out of fuel in a cycle).

XState bounds such a macrostep only through the config’s options.maxIterations: once that many microsteps have followed the event’s own with the machine still active, the macrostep throws, even when it would settle there, and without the option transition never returns. xstate does not read options, and the fuel of the caller that drives the cursor is the bound (Fuel).

Delayed transitions

A delayed transition is taken when its state has been active for a given time. It is declared under a state’s after, whose keys are delays and whose values are transitions in any of the forms of on. Leaving the state before the time has passed cancels it. Delayed transitions make timeouts and retries part of the machine.

A delay is written as a key of after:

  • a whole number of milliseconds, such as "5000";

  • the name of a delay of implementations.delays, a delay_maker: a function of the action_args that returns the milliseconds, XState’s setup({ delays }). It is computed each time the state is entered, from the context of that moment. XState’s delays also maps a name to a number; in xstate a constant named delay is a delay_maker that returns that number.

A name the implementations do not hold is refused when the machine is created, with unknown_delay; XState takes such a delay as no delay at all, and the transition is taken in the same macrostep (A config is refused when it is created). A key that is not all digits and starts with a digit, a sign or a dot, such as "1.5", "-1" or "1e3", is refused with invalid_config, because time in xstate is whole milliseconds written as digits; XState reads "1e3" and "+5" as numbers (Time in whole milliseconds). A key that starts with a space is a name to xstate, where XState reads " 5" as 5.

In the machine core

The machine core never reads a clock. Entering a state with after returns, for each delay, the action xstate.raise of the event xstate.after.<delay>.<state id>, <delay> being the number or the delay’s name, with its delay in milliseconds, computed for a named one, and with that type as its id; leaving the state returns xstate.cancel of that id. The state’s delayed transitions are transitions on that event.

Keeping time out of the machine makes a step a function of the snapshot and the event alone, so the same events give the same steps in a test and in production. Time is one more input, which the caller brings when it chooses: a caller that keeps a snapshot between two requests keeps its clock beside it, and moves the time when the next request comes.
