In the game below, the initial macrostep returns the raise, and pushing the button the cancel, before logSuccess. print_actions writes the actions a step returns, each with its params:

/** Prints a macrostep's actions, one a line: its type, and its params when it has some. */
void print_actions(std::string_view macrostep, const std::vector<xstate::action>& actions) {
    std::cout << macrostep << ":\n";
    for (const xstate::action& one : actions) {
        std::cout << "  " << one.type;
        if (!one.params.is_null()) {
            std::cout << ' ' << boost::json::serialize(one.params);
        }
        std::cout << '\n';
    }
}
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "game",
    "initial": "waitingForButtonPush",
    "states": {
        "waitingForButtonPush": {
            "after": {
                "5000": {"target": "timedOut", "actions": "logThatYouGotTimedOut"}
            },
            "on": {
                "PUSH_BUTTON": {"actions": "logSuccess", "target": "success"}
            }
        },
        "success": {},
        "timedOut": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> game = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!game.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const auto [waiting, entered] = xstate::initial_transition(*game);
print_actions("initial macrostep", entered);
const xstate::event push{.type = "PUSH_BUTTON", .payload = {}};
print_actions("PUSH_BUTTON", xstate::transition(*game, waiting, push).second);

It prints:

initial macrostep:
  xstate.raise {"event":{"type":"xstate.after.5000.game.waitingForButtonPush"},"id":"xstate.after.5000.game.waitingForButtonPush","delay":5000}
PUSH_BUTTON:
  xstate.cancel {"sendId":"xstate.after.5000.game.waitingForButtonPush"}
  logSuccess

These are the actions, with the same params, that XState’s initialTransition and transition return.

Entering a state with several delays returns their raises in the order JavaScript enumerates the keys of after, as XState reads them: a key that is an array index, such as "500", first, by number, then the others as written. So with "1000" written before "500", the raise of 500 comes first.

A simulated_clock keeps the delayed events: XState’s SimulatedClock with its scheduler, as a value the caller owns. apply schedules each delayed raise and applies each cancel among the built-in actions a step returns; a custom action is the caller’s, whatever the config named it, and apply leaves it alone. set and increment move the time, never backwards: set to an earlier time is refused with invalid_config, where XState’s SimulatedClock throws (The core’s clock hands over the due events). pop_due takes out the earliest event whose time has come, by deadline and then in the order it was scheduled, and the caller delivers it as a macrostep of its own, whose actions go to the clock before the next pop_due. Due events come out one at a time, so an event scheduled while another is delivered is ordered as XState orders it, and one that a delivery cancels never comes out. Delayed events and the simulated clock lists the clock’s members. An actor does all of this itself (In the actor layer).

The same program goes on with two players. execute hands each action a step returns to the clock and runs the custom ones, which here print their name; advance moves the clock to a time and delivers each event that comes due by then:

/** Hands each action to the clock and runs the custom ones, which here print their name. */
void execute(const std::vector<xstate::action>& actions, xstate::simulated_clock& clock) {
    for (const xstate::action& one : actions) {
        clock.apply(one);
        if (!one.builtin) {
            std::cout << one.type << '\n';
        }
    }
}

/** Moves the clock to `time` and delivers each event that comes due, a macrostep each. */
xstate::result<xstate::snapshot> advance(const xstate::machine& machine, xstate::snapshot now,
                                         xstate::simulated_clock& clock, std::uint64_t time) {
    if (const xstate::result<void> moved = clock.set(time); !moved.has_value()) {
        return moved.error();
    }
    while (const std::optional<xstate::event> due = clock.pop_due()) {
        auto [next, actions] = xstate::transition(machine, now, *due);
        execute(actions, clock);
        now = std::move(next);
    }
    return now;
}
/** A player who never pushes. */
{
    xstate::simulated_clock clock;
    auto [now, actions] = xstate::initial_transition(*game);
    execute(actions, clock);
    std::cout << "at 0: " << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';
    for (const std::uint64_t time : {4999, 5000}) {
        const xstate::result<xstate::snapshot> later = advance(*game, now, clock, time);
        if (!later.has_value()) {
            return 1;
        }
        now = *later;
        std::cout << "at " << time << ": " << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';
    }
}

/** A player who pushes the button at 1000. */
{
    xstate::simulated_clock clock;
    auto [now, actions] = xstate::initial_transition(*game);
    execute(actions, clock);
    std::cout << "at 0: " << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';
    const xstate::result<xstate::snapshot> pushed = advance(*game, now, clock, 1000);
    if (!pushed.has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::tie(now, actions) =
        xstate::transition(*game, *pushed, {.type = "PUSH_BUTTON", .payload = {}});
    execute(actions, clock);
    std::cout << "at 1000: " << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';
    const xstate::result<xstate::snapshot> later = advance(*game, now, clock, 6000);
    if (!later.has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "at 6000: " << boost::json::serialize(later->value) << '\n';
}

It prints:

at 0: "waitingForButtonPush"
at 4999: "waitingForButtonPush"
logThatYouGotTimedOut
at 5000: "timedOut"
at 0: "waitingForButtonPush"
logSuccess
at 1000: "success"
at 6000: "success"

The first player’s timer comes due at 5000: advance delivers its event, the delayed transition is taken, and logThatYouGotTimedOut runs. The second player pushes at 1000; leaving waitingForButtonPush cancels the timer, so nothing comes due at 6000.

In the actor layer

An actor of actor_system arms a timer for each built-in delayed raise its machine returns, and removes it for each built-in cancel; a custom action goes to the host’s on_action whatever its name (Custom actions). Time is the host’s: clock_tick(now) moves the system’s time to now, in milliseconds from 0, and releases the timers due by then one at a time, in (deadline, arming) order, running the system after each, so a timer’s transition can cancel a later timer of the same tick, as XState’s SimulatedClock does. A stopped actor’s timers never fire. clock_tick does not refuse a time before the last one: it sets the time back, and a timer armed afterwards counts from it, where the core’s simulated_clock refuses to go back and XState’s SimulatedClock throws (A tick earlier than the last). Pass a time that never decreases.

The machine below retries with a delay that grows with each attempt, and gives up after the third. The delay timeout is computed from the context each time attempting is entered. It, the guard and the assign read the context with the kettle’s integer_at (Eventless transitions):

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.delays.emplace(
    "timeout", [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<std::uint64_t> {
        const std::optional<std::int64_t> attempts = integer_at(args.context, "attempts");
        if (!attempts.has_value() || *attempts < 0) {
            return xstate::failure<std::uint64_t>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
        }
        return static_cast<std::uint64_t>(*attempts) * 1000;
    });
implementations.guards.emplace(
    "canRetry", [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<bool> {
        const std::optional<std::int64_t> attempts = integer_at(args.context, "attempts");
        if (!attempts.has_value()) {
            return xstate::failure<bool>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
        }
        return *attempts < 3;
    });
implementations.actions.emplace(
    "countAttempt",
    xstate::assign_action{
        .assignment =
            [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<boost::json::object> {
            const std::optional<std::int64_t> attempts = integer_at(args.context, "attempts");
            if (!attempts.has_value()) {
                return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(
                    xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
            }
            return boost::json::object{{"attempts", *attempts + 1}};
        },
    });
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "retry",
    "initial": "attempting",
    "context": {"attempts": 1},
    "states": {
        "attempting": {
            "after": {
                "timeout": [
                    {
                        "guard": "canRetry",
                        "actions": "countAttempt",
                        "target": "attempting",
                        "reenter": true
                    },
                    {"target": "failed"}
                ]
            }
        },
        "failed": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> retry = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!retry.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*retry);
if (!actor.has_value() || !system.start(*actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
for (const std::uint64_t now : {0, 1000, 2999, 3000, 6000}) {
    if (!system.clock_tick(now).has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }
    const xstate::snapshot* state = system.snapshot_of(*actor);
    if (state == nullptr) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "at " << now << ": " << boost::json::serialize(state->value) << ' '
              << boost::json::serialize(state->context) << '\n';
}

It prints:

at 0: "attempting" {"attempts":1}
at 1000: "attempting" {"attempts":2}
at 2999: "attempting" {"attempts":2}
at 3000: "attempting" {"attempts":3}
at 6000: "failed" {"attempts":3}

The timer armed at 0 is due at 1000. Its transition counts the attempt and re-enters attempting: the exit cancels the timer that fired, and the entry arms a new one with the delay of the new context, 2000 milliseconds, due at 3000, so nothing happens at 2999. At 6000 canRetry does not pass, and the second transition, the default, is taken. Without reenter: true the transition would not leave attempting, its entry would not run again, and no timer would be armed after the first: Stately’s example of a dynamic delay omits it, and so retries once.

In XState an actor takes its clock from its options, a SimulatedClock in tests and the real timers otherwise. The actor layer reads no clock at all: clock_tick is how time passes, in tests and in production (Delayed events and time).

Actions

An action is an effect a machine causes as it moves from state to state: it updates the context, sends an event, writes a log line, or asks your program to do something. Actions are fire-and-forget: the machine does not wait for one to finish. A machine runs actions in three places: on a transition, listed in its actions; when it enters a state, listed in the state’s entry; and when it leaves a state, listed in the state’s exit.

In XState an action is a function, and setup({ actions }) gives a name to the functions a config refers to. A JSON config cannot hold a function, so in xstate every action a config writes is a name, with optional params, and the implementations given to create_machine decide what each name is:

  • A name the implementations hold is a built-in action: one of XState’s action creators, assign, raise, sendTo, log, emit and the others, registered as a value that says what it does. The library resolves it.

  • Any other name is a custom action: an effect of your program. The machine core returns it to its caller, in order, as XState’s transition() returns its actions; the actor layer hands it to the callback your program gives on_action.

The split keeps the machine core pure. Resolving a microstep computes the next snapshot and the list of effects, and performs no effect outside the snapshot: your program performs the custom ones, and the actor layer, or your program when it calls the core itself, the built-in ones that reach other actors, timers and listeners.

Entry, exit and transition actions

Entry actions run on every transition that enters their state, exit actions on every transition that leaves it, and a transition’s actions on that transition. Each of entry, exit and a transition’s actions holds one action or a list of them. create_machine refuses a null one with invalid_config; XState reads it as a list that holds null, and fails when it runs it. A transition with no target runs its actions and nothing else: it leaves and enters no state, even with reenter: true. A transition whose target is its source or one of the source’s descendants does not leave the source either, and the source’s exit and entry actions run only when it sets reenter: true (Self-transitions and reenter).

The machine below lists a custom action at each place: exitAction when it leaves question, track on the transition, showConfetti when it enters thanks. None has an implementation, so each one is returned:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "feedback",
    "initial": "question",
    "states": {
        "question": {
            "exit": "exitAction",
            "on": {
                "feedback.good": {"target": "thanks", "actions": "track"}
            }
        },
        "thanks": {"entry": "showConfetti"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!feedback.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::snapshot question = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*feedback);
const auto [thanks, actions] =
    xstate::transition(*feedback, question, {.type = "feedback.good", .payload = {}});
std::cout << "feedback.good:";
for (const xstate::action& one : actions) {
    std::cout << ' ' << one.type;
}
std::cout << '\n';

It prints:

feedback.good: exitAction track showConfetti

The machine left question, took the transition, and entered thanks: the exit action first, then the transition’s, then the entry action.

A machine that only reacts to events, with no states, is written with transitions that have actions and no target (Assign is one; Self-transitions and reenter has the rules).

Nested states and the root

A transition may leave and enter several states at once: a state and its ancestors, up to the root, which is a state too. The machine below nests asking in question, gives the root entry and exit actions, and ends in a final state:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "feedback",
    "initial": "question",
    "entry": "rootEntry",
    "exit": "rootExit",
    "states": {
        "question": {
            "initial": "asking",
            "entry": "enterQuestion",
            "exit": "exitQuestion",
            "states": {
                "asking": {
                    "entry": "enterAsking",
                    "exit": "exitAsking",
                    "on": {
                        "feedback.good": {"target": "#feedback.thanks", "actions": "track"}
                    }
                }
            }
        },
        "thanks": {"type": "final", "entry": "showConfetti", "exit": "exitThanks"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!feedback.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const auto [initial, initial_actions] = xstate::initial_transition(*feedback);
std::cout << "initial:";
for (const xstate::action& one : initial_actions) {
    std::cout << ' ' << one.type;
}
std::cout << '\n';

const auto [next, actions] =
    xstate::transition(*feedback, initial, {.type = "feedback.good", .payload = {}});
std::cout << "feedback.good:";
for (const xstate::action& one : actions) {
    std::cout << ' ' << one.type;
}
std::cout << '\n';

It prints:

initial: rootEntry enterQuestion enterAsking
feedback.good: exitAsking exitQuestion track showConfetti exitThanks rootExit

The order is XState’s, and it is fixed within a microstep. It follows the document order of the states: a parent before its children, and siblings in the order XState reads the keys of states. That is the order JavaScript enumerates an object’s keys in: a key that is an array index, such as "0" or "2", first, by number, then the rest as written. A microstep runs:

  1. the exit actions of the states it leaves, in reverse document order, so a child before its parent; each state’s exit actions are followed by an xstate.stopChild for each child it invokes;

  2. the actions of the transitions it takes, each transition’s in the order listed. When parallel regions take several, the transitions an event selects come in the order of the regions in the state value, whose keys are in the order JavaScript enumerates them, and eventless ones in the order of the active atomic states in nodes (The state value);

  3. the entry actions of the states it enters, in document order, so a parent before its children; each state’s entry actions are followed by the spawns of the children it invokes, then, when it is entered by default and its initial is an object with actions, those actions. A compound state is entered by default when no target of the transition is inside it, and it then enters its initial child.

Document order is not depth. When a parallel state is left and entered again, every state of its second region is left before any of its first, and every state of its first region is entered before any of its second.

The root’s entry actions run in the machine’s first microstep, before those of the states it enters. When a transition reaches a final state of the root, the machine is done, and in that same microstep the exit actions of every state still active run, in reverse document order, the root’s last: that is why exitThanks and rootExit follow showConfetti. Stately’s documentation says a top-level final state cannot have exit actions; XState 5.33.2 runs them when the machine completes, and xstate does the same.

Action objects and params

An action in a config is a string, its name, or an object with a type, its name, and optional params, a JSON value for that use of it. Actions with the same type share one implementation; their params tell one use from another. Here the transition lists two actions with params: track, which has no implementation, and addRating, an assign that adds its param by to the rating:

const xstate::assigner add_rating =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<boost::json::object> {
    const boost::json::object* params = args.params.if_object();
    const boost::json::object* context = args.context.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* by = params == nullptr ? nullptr : params->if_contains("by");
    const boost::json::value* rating =
        context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("rating");
    if (by == nullptr || !by->is_int64() || rating == nullptr || !rating->is_int64()) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"rating", rating->get_int64() + by->get_int64()}};
};
xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actions.emplace("addRating", xstate::assign_action{.assignment = add_rating});

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "feedback",
    "initial": "question",
    "context": {"rating": 0},
    "states": {
        "question": {
            "on": {
                "feedback.good": {
                    "target": "thanks",
                    "actions": [
                        {"type": "track", "params": {"response": "good"}},
                        {"type": "addRating", "params": {"by": 5}}
                    ]
                }
            }
        },
        "thanks": {"entry": "showConfetti"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback =
    xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!feedback.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::snapshot question = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*feedback);
const auto [thanks, actions] =
    xstate::transition(*feedback, question, {.type = "feedback.good", .payload = {}});
for (const xstate::action& one : actions) {
    std::cout << one.type;
    if (!one.params.is_null()) {
        std::cout << ' ' << boost::json::serialize(one.params);
    }
    std::cout << '\n';
}
std::cout << "context " << boost::json::serialize(thanks.context) << '\n';

It prints:

track {"response":"good"}
showConfetti
context {"rating":5}

track has no implementation: it is a custom action, returned with the params the config gave it. addRating is a built-in, an assign_action (Built-in and custom actions, Assign), so it changed the context and was not returned; its implementation read its params from args.params. showConfetti, written as a string, has no params, and its params is null.

Every action implementation, and every guard, delay and value maker, receives an action_args, which XState hands an action as ({ context, event }, params):

context

The context as it is when the action runs: an assign earlier in the same microstep has already changed it.

event

The microstep’s event.

params

The params the config gave the action or the guard, null when it gives none.

XState also takes params as a function of the context and the event, computed when the action runs. JSON holds no function, so xstate’s params are the fixed value the config writes. An implementation that needs the context or the event reads them from its action_args. A caller executing a custom action finds the event in the microstep that returned it, and the context as that whole microstep left it, after any assign listed after the action (How guards and actions read the context). A value that must be computed at the action’s turn is computed by a registered implementation (Actions).

Built-in and custom actions

Each built-in action is one alternative of action_implementation, registered under the name the config uses, with XState’s arguments as its members. The machine core resolves it as XState resolves the action creator and returns it as XState’s transition() returns it: an action of the same type xstate.*, whose params are XState’s less what is not JSON or has no value. An actor reference is left out, and a targetId or an id names the actor instead; an id, a delay or a label with no value is left out.

There are two exceptions, both sends whose receiver depends on where the machine runs. XState’s pure functions run the machine as an inert actor, which has no parent and a fresh system of its own; xstate’s core returns the send for its caller to resolve:

  • On a send or a forward to the parent, a sendParent or a target #_parent, XState’s transition() throws; xstate returns an xstate.sendTo to #_parent (sendParent without a parent).

  • On a send or a forward to a systemId, which XState names with ({ system }) => system.get('notifier'), the inert actor’s system knows only the children the call itself spawns. For any other systemId, even one a child of the snapshot holds, a forwardTo throws in XState’s development build (The checks of XState’s development build), and a sendTo goes to the inert actor itself, with no targetId. xstate returns an xstate.sendTo whose targetId is #system:notifier (Targets that name actors).

Each built-in, what the core returns for it, and what the actor layer then does:

XState Registered as Returned to the caller Run by the actor layer

assign(...)

assign_action

never: the context changes

-

raise(event)

raise_action

xstate.raise {event}, the event already queued

nothing more

raise(event, { id, delay })

raise_action with a delay

xstate.raise {event, id, delay}

arms a timer

cancel(id)

cancel_action

xstate.cancel {sendId}

cancels the timer

sendTo(target, event, { id, delay })

send_to_action

xstate.sendTo {targetId, event, id, delay}

delivers the event once the macrostep has settled, or arms a timer

sendParent(event, { id, delay })

send_parent_action

xstate.sendTo to #_parent

as a sendTo

forwardTo(target, { id, delay })

forward_to_action

xstate.sendTo of the microstep’s event

as a sendTo

log(value, label)

log_action

xstate.log {value, label}

hands it to on_log

emit(event)

emit_action

xstate.emit {event}

hands the event to the actor’s listeners once the macrostep has settled

spawnChild(src, { id, systemId, input })

spawn_child_action

xstate.spawnChild {id, src, input, systemId}

creates the child (Spawning actors)

stopChild(id)

stop_child_action

xstate.stopChild {id}

stops the child (Stopping a child)

a function of your program

nothing

{type, params} as the config names it

hands it to on_action

The name decides, not the type a config writes. A config may name an action xstate.raise; if the implementations hold no such name, it is a custom action, returned with that type, as XState returns it. action::builtin tells the two apart. In an entry or an exit, an action named xstate.raise or xstate.cancel does not survive the machine’s definition: create_machine_from_definition cannot tell it from the raise and cancel an after adds, and drops it (The definition).

XState’s documentation warns that its built-in action creators are not imperative: calling assign(...) inside a custom action does nothing. In xstate a custom action runs in your program, outside the machine: it cannot change the context or send an event, and constructing an xstate::assign_action{...} there does nothing. Only a built-in registered under a name the config uses acts on the machine.

Every implementation returns a result. An error is the implementation’s failure, where XState’s would throw: the macrostep settles at once with the snapshot it began from, its status error and its error the code the implementation returned (When an implementation fails).

xstate has no inline action function and no params function, because JSON holds no function (Functions become names). It has no enqueueActions yet (What is not ported lists what xstate does not have yet). It has no machine.provide: create_machine plays that role, and the same config created with other implementations is another machine (A machine is immutable).

Custom actions

A custom action is how a machine asks your program to do something: send an email, write to a database, show confetti. The machine names it and your program implements it. In XState the implementation is a function of setup({ actions }); in xstate it is code of yours that runs the action the machine returns, here a function execute that reads the type and the params:

/** Runs a custom action the machine returned; one it does not know does nothing. */
void execute(const xstate::action& custom) {
    if (custom.type == "track") {
        const boost::json::object* params = custom.params.if_object();
        const boost::json::value* response =
            params == nullptr ? nullptr : params->if_contains("response");
        std::cout << "tracking " << (response == nullptr ? "-" : boost::json::serialize(*response))
                  << '\n';
        return;
    }
    if (custom.type == "showConfetti") {
        std::cout << "confetti!\n";
    }
}

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "feedback",
    "initial": "question",
    "states": {
        "question": {
            "on": {
                "feedback.good": {
                    "target": "thanks",
                    "actions": [
                        {"type": "track", "params": {"response": "good"}}
                    ]
                }
            },
            "exit": [{"type": "exitAction"}]
        },
        "thanks": {"entry": [{"type": "showConfetti"}]}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!feedback.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::event good{.type = "feedback.good", .payload = {}};

With the pure functions, transition returns the actions and the caller runs them, in order. Each carries its name and its params, where XState’s returned actions carry the function to run as exec:

const xstate::snapshot question = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*feedback);
const auto [thanks, actions] = xstate::transition(*feedback, question, good);
std::cout << "returned:";
for (const xstate::action& one : actions) {
    std::cout << ' ' << one.type;
}
std::cout << '\n';
for (const xstate::action& one : actions) {
    execute(one);
}

An actor runs its custom actions while its macrostep is resolved, as XState’s actor runs them: the actor layer hands each to the callback given to on_action, here one that calls execute:

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<void> acting =
    system.on_action([](xstate::actor_ref, const xstate::action& custom) { execute(custom); });
if (!acting.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*feedback);
if (!actor.has_value() || !system.start(*actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << "the actor:\n";
if (!system.send(*actor, good).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

It prints:

returned: exitAction track showConfetti
tracking "good"
confetti!
the actor:
tracking "good"
confetti!

execute did nothing for exitAction: it ignores a type it does not know, as XState’s actor does nothing for an action that has no implementation.

  • The core returns a macrostep’s actions in order: transition and initial_transition return all of them, and the cursor returns each microstep’s in its microstep::actions, which macrostep_result::actions gathers. Run each action once: either each microstep’s as it comes, or the result’s at the end (Executing actions as they come has the details).

  • The actor layer hands each custom action to on_action as its microstep is resolved, with the actor that returned it. That is before the macrostep’s sends and emitted events, which wait until it has settled (Emitting events shows the order). An actor’s initial custom actions reach on_action when the actor starts, as XState runs them on start().

  • When a macrostep fails, the custom actions it resolved before the failure have already reached on_action, as XState’s actor has run them. The initial macrostep is the exception: an actor whose initial macrostep fails hands over none of its custom actions, as XState’s start() runs none for an actor born failed.

  • on_action holds one callback for the whole system, and a second call replaces the first. The callback runs inside the actor’s turn, while the system runs: it may call the members that read the system, but a call from it to one that changes the system, a send or a resolve among them, returns xactor’s invalid_argument and changes nothing. XState accepts a send made from an action’s function: one to the actor running the action is handled once the event in progress is done, and one to another actor that is idle is handled at once, before the function returns (A callback that calls the system back, Watching an actor).

  • An actor’s custom action reaches on_action with its type and the params the config wrote, nothing more: no context and no event, which XState hands an action’s function in its first argument, info. What must be computed from the context or the event at the action’s turn is computed by a registered built-in, an emit_action whose event_maker builds the event the host’s listener reads, or a log_action (Emitting events, Log).

Assign

assign updates the context, and it is the only action that does: the context is never written in place. Its implementation is an assigner, a function of action_args that returns the members to change as an object. Here addValue adds the event’s value to the count, and an actor’s listener prints each context the actor settles in:

const xstate::assigner add_value =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<boost::json::object> {
    const boost::json::object* context = args.context.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* count =
        context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("count");
    const boost::json::value* value = args.event.payload.if_contains("value");
    if (count == nullptr || !count->is_int64() || value == nullptr || !value->is_int64()) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"count", count->get_int64() + value->get_int64()}};
};
xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actions.emplace("addValue", xstate::assign_action{.assignment = add_value});

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "context": {"count": 0, "unit": "clicks"},
    "on": {"increment": {"actions": "addValue"}}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> count_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!count_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> count_actor = system.create_actor(*count_machine);
if (!count_actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<void> subscribed =
    system.subscribe(*count_actor, [](const xstate::snapshot& state) {
        std::cout << boost::json::serialize(state.context) << '\n';
    });
if (!subscribed.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.start(*count_actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.send(*count_actor, {.type = "increment", .payload = {{"value", 3}}}).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.send(*count_actor, {.type = "increment", .payload = {{"value", 2}}}).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

It prints:

{"count":0,"unit":"clicks"}
{"count":3,"unit":"clicks"}
{"count":5,"unit":"clicks"}

  • The library merges the object an assigner returns into the context as Object.assign does: the members it returns are replaced or added, and the others kept, as unit is. XState’s two forms, an object of property assigners and a function returning part of the context, are both this one.

  • The assigner receives the context as a const reference and cannot mutate it, which XState’s documentation can only ask of you.

  • An assign is never returned to the caller: its effect is the new context. The actions after it in the same microstep see the context it left (Log shows it).

  • An assign needs a context that is an object. A config with no context, or a null one, starts with {}; any other value that is not an object (false, true, a number, a string, a list) is kept as written, and an assign on it fails the macrostep with implementation_failed. XState starts false, 0 and "" as {} too; an assign drops true or a nonzero number and spreads a string or a list into numbered members (A context that is not an object). An assigner that returns an error fails the macrostep with that error’s code; the assigner of addValue returns implementation_failed when the event has no integer value.

  • This machine has no states: its root takes the event increment with a transition that has actions and no target, and the action addValue handles it.

Context covers the context itself: its initial value, input and how a snapshot holds it.

Raise

A raise sends an event to the machine itself. The event goes to the macrostep’s internal queue, first in, first out. The machine takes it once no eventless transition is enabled, before the macrostep settles, so before any event from outside, which waits for the next macrostep (Eventless transitions). In the loader below, entering loading raises started, which carries the attempt the context holds:

const xstate::event_maker started =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<xstate::event> {
    const boost::json::object* context = args.context.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* attempt =
        context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("attempt");
    if (attempt == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<xstate::event>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return xstate::event{.type = "started", .payload = {{"attempt", *attempt}}};
};
xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actions.emplace(
    "announce",
    xstate::raise_action{.event = started, .id = std::nullopt, .delay = std::nullopt});

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "loader",
    "initial": "idle",
    "context": {"attempt": 1},
    "states": {
        "idle": {"on": {"load": "loading"}},
        "loading": {"entry": "announce", "on": {"started": "running"}},
        "running": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> loader = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!loader.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::snapshot idle = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*loader);
for (const xstate::microstep& step :
     xstate::get_microsteps(*loader, idle, {.type = "load", .payload = {}})) {
    std::cout << boost::json::serialize(step.snapshot.value);
    for (const xstate::action& one : step.actions) {
        std::cout << ' ' << one.type << ' ' << boost::json::serialize(one.params);
    }
    std::cout << '\n';
}

It prints, one line per microstep:

"loading" xstate.raise {"event":{"type":"started","attempt":1}}
"running"

load took two microsteps in one macrostep. The first entered loading, whose entry raised started; the second took started to running. The event a raise makes may depend on the context and the event: its event_maker receives action_args, as XState’s event function does.

A raise without a delay is returned too, as xstate.raise with its event, as XState returns it. It asks nothing of the caller: the macrostep has already queued the event.

Delayed raise, ids and cancel

With a delay, a raise is not queued: the event waits until the delay has passed, then starts a macrostep of its own. The delay is a number of milliseconds, or the name of a delay of implementations.delays, a function of action_args computed when the action resolves; a name the implementations do not hold is no delay, as in XState, and the event is raised at once. An id names the waiting event, and a cancel_action of the same id cancels it. Here scheduleNudge raises nudge after 1000 milliseconds, under the id nudge, and cancelNudge cancels it:

const xstate::event_maker nudge =
    [](const xstate::action_args&) -> xstate::result<xstate::event> {
    return xstate::event{.type = "nudge", .payload = {}};
};
const xstate::raise_action schedule_nudge{
    .event = nudge,
    .id = "nudge",
    .delay = xstate::delay_ref{std::uint64_t{1000}},
};
xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actions.emplace("scheduleNudge", schedule_nudge);
implementations.actions.emplace("cancelNudge", xstate::cancel_action{.id = "nudge"});

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "reminder",
    "initial": "waiting",
    "states": {
        "waiting": {
            "on": {
                "remind": {"actions": "scheduleNudge"},
                "dismiss": {"actions": "cancelNudge"},
                "nudge": "nudged"
            }
        },
        "nudged": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> reminder =
    xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!reminder.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

The machine core keeps no time. It returns the delayed raise and the cancel, with their params:

const xstate::snapshot waiting = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*reminder);
for (const std::string_view type : {"remind", "dismiss"}) {
    const auto [next, actions] =
        xstate::transition(*reminder, waiting, {.type = std::string(type), .payload = {}});
    for (const xstate::action& one : actions) {
        std::cout << type << ": " << one.type << ' ' << boost::json::serialize(one.params)
                  << '\n';
    }
}

An actor keeps the timers, and the host brings the time:

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*reminder);
if (!actor.has_value() || !system.start(*actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const auto print_value = [&system, &actor](std::string_view when) {
    const xstate::snapshot* now = system.snapshot_of(*actor);
    if (now == nullptr) {
        return false;
    }
    std::cout << when << ": " << boost::json::serialize(now->value) << '\n';
    return true;
};
const xstate::event remind{.type = "remind", .payload = {}};
const xstate::event dismiss{.type = "dismiss", .payload = {}};

if (!system.send(*actor, remind).has_value() || !system.send(*actor, dismiss).has_value() ||
    !system.clock_tick(1000).has_value() || !print_value("at 1000")) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.send(*actor, remind).has_value() || !system.clock_tick(2000).has_value() ||
    !print_value("at 2000")) {
    return 1;
}

It prints:

remind: xstate.raise {"event":{"type":"nudge"},"id":"nudge","delay":1000}
dismiss: xstate.cancel {"sendId":"nudge"}
at 1000: "waiting"
at 2000: "nudged"

The first nudge was cancelled before its time came; the second fired at 2000 and took the machine to nudged.

  • clock_tick(now) takes the time to move to, in milliseconds, here 1000 and then 2000, where XState’s SimulatedClock.increment takes the step to add. It fires the timers due by then one at a time, in the order of their deadlines, and runs the system after each.

  • With the pure functions, a simulated_clock is the caller’s clock: its apply schedules each built-in delayed xstate.raise a step returns and applies each built-in xstate.cancel, and ignores a custom action whatever its type, action::builtin telling them apart (Built-in and custom actions). Its pop_due gives back the due events one at a time, each to be sent as a macrostep of its own (Delayed events and the simulated clock).

  • A second timer armed under an id takes the id over: a cancel then finds the second, and the first still fires, as in XState.

  • A cancel finds a delayed send_to_action of the same actor by its id too (Sending to other actors).

  • A state’s after is built of these two actions: entering the state raises xstate.after.<delay>.<state id> with that delay, and leaving it cancels it (Delayed transitions). The raises follow the order in which XState reads the keys of after, the same as for states (Nested states and the root): an after that writes "1000" before "500" raises the 500 one first.

  • Time is whole milliseconds; XState’s SimulatedClock also takes fractions (Time in whole milliseconds).

Sending to other actors

send_to_action sends an event to another actor, as XState’s sendTo. send_parent_action sends one to the actor’s parent, as sendParent, and forward_to_action sends on the event being handled, as forwardTo. The child below counts the inc it receives and tells its parent each count:

const xstate::assigner add =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<boost::json::object> {
    const std::optional<std::int64_t> count = integer_at(args.context.if_object(), "count");
    if (!count.has_value()) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"count", *count + 1}};
};
const xstate::assigner set_count =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<boost::json::object> {
    const std::optional<std::int64_t> count = integer_at(&args.event.payload, "count");
    if (!count.has_value()) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"count", *count}};
};
const xstate::event_maker counted =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<xstate::event> {
    const std::optional<std::int64_t> count = integer_at(args.context.if_object(), "count");
    if (!count.has_value()) {
        return xstate::failure<xstate::event>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return xstate::event{.type = "counted", .payload = {{"count", *count}}};
};
xstate::implementations counter_implementations;
counter_implementations.actions.emplace("add", xstate::assign_action{.assignment = add});
counter_implementations.actions.emplace("setCount",
                                        xstate::assign_action{.assignment = set_count});
counter_implementations.actions.emplace(
    "report",
    xstate::send_parent_action{.event = counted, .id = std::nullopt, .delay = std::nullopt});

const boost::json::value counter_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "counter",
    "context": {"count": 0},
    "on": {
        "inc": {"actions": ["add", "report"]},
        "set": {"actions": ["setCount", "report"]}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> counter =
    xstate::create_machine(counter_config, counter_implementations);
if (!counter.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

integer_at reads an integer member of an object, or nothing. The parent invokes the child, sends it inc on each click and forwards it set:

const xstate::event_maker inc =
    [](const xstate::action_args&) -> xstate::result<xstate::event> {
    return xstate::event{.type = "inc", .payload = {}};
};
const xstate::assigner keep_last =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<boost::json::object> {
    const std::optional<std::int64_t> count = integer_at(&args.event.payload, "count");
    if (!count.has_value()) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"last", *count}};
};
const xstate::send_to_action send_inc{
    .target = "counter",
    .event = inc,
    .id = std::nullopt,
    .delay = std::nullopt,
};
const xstate::forward_to_action forward_set{
    .target = "counter",
    .id = std::nullopt,
    .delay = std::nullopt,
};
xstate::implementations app_implementations;
app_implementations.actors.emplace("counter", xstate::machine_actor{*counter});
app_implementations.actions.emplace("inc", send_inc);
app_implementations.actions.emplace("forwardSet", forward_set);
app_implementations.actions.emplace("keepLast", xstate::assign_action{.assignment = keep_last});

const boost::json::value app_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "app",
    "context": {"last": null},
    "invoke": {"id": "counter", "src": "counter"},
    "on": {
        "click": {"actions": "inc"},
        "set": {"actions": "forwardSet"},
        "counted": {"actions": "keepLast"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> app =
    xstate::create_machine(app_config, app_implementations);
if (!app.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

An actor of the parent takes three events, and the program prints both contexts after each:

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> app_actor = system.create_actor(*app);
if (!app_actor.has_value() || !system.start(*app_actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::event click{.type = "click", .payload = {}};
const xstate::event set{.type = "set", .payload = {{"count", 10}}};
for (const xstate::event& sent : {click, click, set}) {
    if (!system.send(*app_actor, sent).has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }
    const std::optional<xstate::actor_ref> child = system.child_of(*app_actor, "counter");
    const xstate::snapshot* parent_now = system.snapshot_of(*app_actor);
    const xstate::snapshot* child_now =
        child.has_value() ? system.snapshot_of(*child) : nullptr;
    if (parent_now == nullptr || child_now == nullptr) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << sent.type << ": app " << boost::json::serialize(parent_now->context)
              << ", counter " << boost::json::serialize(child_now->context) << '\n';
}

It prints:

click: app {"last":1}, counter {"count":1}
click: app {"last":2}, counter {"count":2}
set: app {"last":10}, counter {"count":10}

Each click made the parent send inc; the child counted and sent counted back, and the parent kept the count. set reached the child whole, its count with it.

A target is a string, read as XState reads one:

counter

The child of that id, an invoke’s or a spawned child’s.

#_counter

The same child, once it is in the snapshot’s children.

#_parent

The actor’s parent: send_parent_action sends there.

#_internal

The actor itself, which receives the event as one from outside, unlike a raised event.

#system:notifier

The actor registered under the systemId notifier, or the actor itself when none is. XState names it with a function, ({ system }) => system.get('notifier'), and sends to the actor itself when that returns nothing. A forwardTo fails the actor with unknown_target there instead, as XState’s development build throws.

  • The machine core checks a target when the action resolves. A child must be in the snapshot’s children, or, named by its bare id from an entry or initial action, be an invoke of the state being entered, whose child is spawned after the entry actions; otherwise the microstep fails with unknown_target. The parent, the actor itself and a systemId are its caller’s to find; XState’s pure functions find no parent there, and no child of the snapshot under its systemId (Built-in and custom actions). A forwardTo with an empty target fails with unknown_target.

  • The core returns xstate.sendTo with {targetId, event, id, delay}. XState’s params also hold the receiving actor, which is not JSON; here the caller finds it from targetId. The actor layer delivers the event once the sender’s macrostep has settled, so the receiver sees the sender’s new snapshot, as XState defers it for that reason.

  • With a delay, the sender arms a timer, as for a delayed raise, and a cancel_action of the same id cancels it.

  • A root actor has no parent: a send to #_parent fails it with unknown_target, as XState’s root actor fails with the error its resolution throws. The pure functions return the send all the same, as xstate.sendTo to #_parent, for their caller to deliver; XState’s pure functions throw on it, because they run the machine as an inert actor that has no parent (sendParent without a parent).

  • An actor reference is not data. Where XState puts self in an event or an input for the receiver to answer, xstate names the actor: by #_parent, by its id, or by a systemId (Sending events between actors).

  • Between actors, XState delivers an event to an idle actor at once, nested in the sender’s call stack, and queues it for a busy one. xactor queues every delivery: each actor has a mailbox, first in, first out, and the actors that have work wait in one queue, first in, first out, each turn handing one message to its actor. An actor receives what one sender sends it in the order sent, but the order between senders may differ from XState’s (Interleaving across actors).

Log

log_action writes a log line: XState’s log(value, label). Its value is a value_maker, a function of action_args that returns the value, or none for JavaScript’s undefined; without one, the value is {context, event}, as in XState. Its label is an optional string. The counter below logs a fixed message, its count under a label, and the default value:

const xstate::assigner add =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<boost::json::object> {
    const boost::json::object* context = args.context.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* count =
        context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("count");
    if (count == nullptr || !count->is_int64()) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"count", count->get_int64() + 1}};
};
const xstate::value_maker message =
    [](const xstate::action_args&) -> xstate::result<std::optional<boost::json::value>> {
    return std::optional<boost::json::value>("incremented");
};
const xstate::value_maker count =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<std::optional<boost::json::value>> {
    const boost::json::object* context = args.context.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* found =
        context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("count");
    if (found == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<std::optional<boost::json::value>>(
            xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return std::optional<boost::json::value>(*found);
};
xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actions.emplace("add", xstate::assign_action{.assignment = add});
implementations.actions.emplace("logMessage",
                                xstate::log_action{.value = message, .label = std::nullopt});
implementations.actions.emplace("logCount",
                                xstate::log_action{.value = count, .label = "count"});
implementations.actions.emplace(
    "logAll", xstate::log_action{.value = std::nullopt, .label = std::nullopt});

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "context": {"count": 0},
    "on": {
        "increment": {"actions": ["add", "logMessage", "logCount", "logAll"]}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> counter = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!counter.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

The core returns each log as an action; an actor hands it to the callback given to on_log:

const xstate::event increment{.type = "increment", .payload = {}};

const xstate::snapshot initial = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*counter);
const auto [next, actions] = xstate::transition(*counter, initial, increment);
for (const xstate::action& one : actions) {
    std::cout << one.type << ' ' << boost::json::serialize(one.params) << '\n';
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<void> logging = system.on_log(
    [](xstate::actor_ref, const boost::json::value* value, std::string_view label) {
        if (!label.empty()) {
            std::cout << label << ": ";
        }
        std::cout << (value == nullptr ? "undefined" : boost::json::serialize(*value)) << '\n';
    });
if (!logging.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*counter);
if (!actor.has_value() || !system.start(*actor).has_value() ||
    !system.send(*actor, increment).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

It prints the three actions transition returns, then the three lines the actor logs:

xstate.log {"value":"incremented"}
xstate.log {"value":1,"label":"count"}
xstate.log {"value":{"context":{"count":1},"event":{"type":"increment"}}}
"incremented"
count: 1
{"context":{"count":1},"event":{"type":"increment"}}

  • The core returns xstate.log with {value, label}, each left out when it has none. The actor layer hands each log to the callback given to on_log, with the actor, the value, a null pointer for undefined, and the label, empty when there is none: XState’s logger option, which receives (label, value) or (value).

  • A fixed message is a value_maker that returns it, as logMessage does for XState’s log('incremented').

  • logCount read the context after add: an action sees the context the assigns before it left.

  • The actor layer hands logs over as it hands custom actions, while the macrostep is resolved and under the same rules (Custom actions). on_log holds one callback for the whole system, which runs inside the actor’s turn as the callback of on_action does.

Emitting events

An actor emits an event for the code outside that listens to it, as an event emitter does: a machine reports what happened without knowing who listens. emit_action makes the event with an event_maker, so it may depend on the context:

const xstate::event_maker static_event =
    [](const xstate::action_args&) -> xstate::result<xstate::event> {
    return xstate::event{.type = "someStaticEvent", .payload = {{"data", 42}}};
};
const xstate::event_maker dynamic_event =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<xstate::event> {
    const boost::json::object* context = args.context.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* data =
        context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("someData");
    if (data == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<xstate::event>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return xstate::event{.type = "someDynamicEvent", .payload = {{"data", *data}}};
};
xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actions.emplace("emitStaticEvent", xstate::emit_action{.event = static_event});
implementations.actions.emplace("emitDynamicEvent",
                                xstate::emit_action{.event = dynamic_event});

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "context": {"someData": "hello"},
    "on": {
        "someEvent": {"actions": ["emitStaticEvent", "emitDynamicEvent", "track"]}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> machine = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

The listeners are the host’s: on_emitted(actor, listener) is XState’s actor.on('*', listener):

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*machine);
if (!actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<void> hearing_static =
    system.on_emitted(*actor, [](const xstate::event& emitted) {
        if (emitted.type == "someStaticEvent") {
            std::cout << "static: " << boost::json::serialize(xstate::to_json(emitted)) << '\n';
        }
    });
if (!hearing_static.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<void> hearing_any = system.on_emitted(
    *actor, [](const xstate::event& emitted) { std::cout << "any: " << emitted.type << '\n'; });
if (!hearing_any.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<void> acting =
    system.on_action([](xstate::actor_ref, const xstate::action& custom) {
        std::cout << "action: " << custom.type << '\n';
    });
if (!acting.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

if (!system.start(*actor).has_value() ||
    !system.send(*actor, {.type = "someEvent", .payload = {}}).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

It prints:

action: track
static: {"type":"someStaticEvent","data":42}
any: someStaticEvent
any: someDynamicEvent

  • on_emitted hears every event the actor emits. XState also takes the type to listen to, actor.on('someStaticEvent', ...); in xstate a listener compares type, as the first one does. XState calls the listeners of the event’s type before those of *, whatever the order they were added in, and xstate calls all of them in the order added: add the listeners that stand for typed ones first, as here, to keep XState’s order (Listeners of emitted events).

  • An actor may have several listeners, and an inspector hears each emitted event too (Inspection). xstate has no unsubscribe. on_emitted returns xactor’s invalid_argument for an address that names no actor. A listener runs inside the actor’s turn, as the callback of on_action does: a call from it that changes the system, on_emitted among them, returns invalid_argument too and changes nothing (A callback that calls the system back).

  • The core returns xstate.emit with {event}. The actor layer hands the event to the listeners once the macrostep has settled, as XState defers it: after track, a custom action listed after both emits.

  • An emitted event of the type * reaches a listener once; XState hands it twice to a listener on * (An emitted event of the type *).

  • XState’s promise, callback, observable and transition actors emit through an emit function they receive. In xstate only a machine emits, with emit_action; a host actor has no way to.

Input and output

Input is the data an actor is given when it is created. Output is the data an actor produces when it is done: the result of its work. Between the two sit the done events, which tell a state or a parent actor that what it waited on has finished, and carry the output to it.

Input exists so that one machine can start from different data: a feedback form for one user or another, a conversion of one amount or another. Without it, each starting value needs a machine of its own, built by a factory function. Output exists so that whoever waits on an actor receives its result without reading the actor’s context.

In xstate, as in XState, input and output are values, here JSON values. A value that depends on nothing stays in the config, where XState’s JSON puts it. A value XState computes with a function (a context from the input, an invoke’s input from the context, an output from the context) needs a function JSON cannot hold, so the caller registers it in implementations, as it registers actions and guards (Implementations).

An invoke’s computed input and a state’s computed output are registered under the id of the invoke or the state, and not under a name the config refers to, as an action is. In XState’s JSON an invoke’s input and a state’s output are the values themselves: a string there is the input, not the name of a function. Keyed by id, the function leaves the config as XState reads it.

A machine’s input

An actor is created with its input. XState’s createActor(machine, { input }) is actor_system::create_actor(machine, options), whose actor_options::input is a boost::json::value, null when none is given. A machine usually reads its input once, to compute its initial context: XState’s context: ({ input }) => ... is implementations.context, a context_maker that receives the input and returns the initial context, or an error.

/** The context a feedback machine starts with, read from its input. */
xstate::result<boost::json::value> feedback_context(const boost::json::value& input) {
    const boost::json::object* given = input.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* user_id = given == nullptr ? nullptr : given->if_contains("userId");
    const boost::json::value* rating =
        given == nullptr ? nullptr : given->if_contains("defaultRating");
    if (user_id == nullptr || rating == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::value>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"userId", *user_id}, {"feedback", ""}, {"rating", *rating}};
}
xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.context = feedback_context;
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "feedback",
    "initial": "prompt",
    "states": {
        "prompt": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!feedback_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> feedback_actor = system.create_actor(
    *feedback_machine, {.input = boost::json::object{{"userId", "123"}, {"defaultRating", 5}}});
if (!feedback_actor.has_value() || !system.start(*feedback_actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::snapshot* started = system.snapshot_of(*feedback_actor);
if (started == nullptr) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(started->context) << '\n';

It prints:

{"userId":"123","feedback":"","rating":5}

feedback_context checks the input before it reads it, and returns an error when the input lacks a member it needs, where XState’s function would read undefined. When implementations.context is set, the context it returns replaces the config’s context; it must be an object. Its other rules, and a machine started without the input it needs, are in Initial context from the input. XState also hands the context function spawn and self; xstate hands it the input only, so a context cannot spawn a child (The context function).

The actor copies the input when it is created and reads it once, to begin its initial macrostep: it keeps no link to the value the caller passed. To hand a running actor new data, send it an event (Events and transitions).

Input without an actor

The machine core takes an input too. Every function that starts a machine takes it as its last argument, null when it is left out: initial_transition, get_initial_snapshot and get_initial_microsteps, which are XState’s initialTransition, getInitialSnapshot and getInitialMicrosteps, and begin_initial, the cursor of the initial macrostep, which the other three run to its end (The initial macrostep). Input runs them on a machine whose context needs the input.

const boost::json::object input{{"userId", "123"}, {"defaultRating", 5}};

const xstate::snapshot started = xstate::initial_transition(*feedback_machine, input).first;
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(started.context) << '\n';

const std::vector<xstate::microstep> microsteps =
    xstate::get_initial_microsteps(*feedback_machine, input);
if (microsteps.empty()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(microsteps.back().snapshot.context) << " after "
          << microsteps.size() << " microstep\n";

It prints:

{"userId":"123","feedback":"","rating":5}
{"userId":"123","feedback":"","rating":5} after 1 microstep

The machine is the feedback machine above, run here without an actor. Its initial macrostep takes one microstep, the one that enters prompt, and get_initial_microsteps lists it with the context computed from the input, as XState’s getInitialMicrosteps does.

The xstate.init event

A machine’s initial macrostep runs for the event xstate.init. When the machine has an input, the event carries it as its member input, so every action that runs for xstate.init can read it from the event: the entry actions and initial actions of the states the machine starts in, as this entry action does, and the eventless transitions taken before any raised event, with the entry actions of the states they enter. An action that runs for an event raised during the initial macrostep, a done event among them, receives that event, which has no input.

Where XState writes the entry action as a function of the event, ({ event }) => ..., here it is a named log_action whose value is the event, read from its action_args; the actor system hands each value logged to its on_log listener (Log).

xstate::implementations implementations;
// XState's ({ event }) => console.log(event), as a log of the event.
const xstate::value_maker the_event =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<std::optional<boost::json::value>> {
    return boost::json::value(xstate::to_json(args.event));
};
implementations.actions.emplace("logEvent",
                                xstate::log_action{.value = the_event, .label = std::nullopt});
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({"entry": "logEvent"})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!feedback_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<void> logging =
    system.on_log([](xstate::actor_ref, const boost::json::value* value, std::string_view) {
        if (value != nullptr) {
            std::cout << boost::json::serialize(*value) << '\n';
        }
    });
if (!logging.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> feedback_actor = system.create_actor(
    *feedback_machine, {.input = boost::json::object{{"userId", "123"}, {"defaultRating", 5}}});
if (!feedback_actor.has_value() || !system.start(*feedback_actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

It prints:

{"type":"xstate.init","input":{"userId":"123","defaultRating":5}}

XState’s xstate.init always has the member input, undefined when there is no input, which JSON.stringify leaves out. xstate’s has it only for an input that is not null, since JSON has no undefined: given the input null, XState writes "input": null and xstate writes no input. For the same reason a machine started without an input hands its context function null, where XState hands it undefined.

Input to an invoked actor

A state that invokes an actor can give it an input. A fixed input is a value in the invoke’s config, "input", which the child receives as it is when the state is entered. A host actor, xstate’s stand-in for XState’s fromPromise, runs no code: the host reads its input from its pending request, host_request::input (Host actors). A machine child receives it as a machine created with an input does, in its implementations.context and its xstate.init event (Invoking actors).

xstate::implementations implementations;
// The fetch is the host's: a host actor, XState's fromPromise.
implementations.actors.emplace("liveFeedback", xstate::host_actor{});
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "feedback",
    "invoke": {
        "src": "liveFeedback",
        "input": {"domain": "stately.ai"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!feedback_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> feedback_actor = system.create_actor(*feedback_machine);
if (!feedback_actor.has_value() || !system.start(*feedback_actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
for (const xstate::host_request& request : system.host_requests()) {
    if (request.input.has_value()) {
        std::cout << boost::json::serialize(*request.input) << '\n';
    }
}

It prints:

{"domain":"stately.ai"}

The host reads the input from the pending request and does the work itself, where XState’s fromPromise receives the input as an argument of its function; the host then answers the request with actor_system::resolve (Actor done events).

An input computed from the context and the event

XState also computes an invoke’s input with a function, input: ({ context, event }) => ...; in xstate it is a value_maker registered in implementations.inputs under the invoke’s id. It receives the action_args every implementation receives, the context, the event that entered the state and null params, and returns the input, none for undefined (When a value is undefined), or an error.

// assign({ userId: ({ event }) => event.userId })
const xstate::assigner select_user =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<boost::json::object> {
    const boost::json::value* user_id = args.event.payload.if_contains("userId");
    if (user_id == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"userId", *user_id}};
};
// ({ context }) => ({ userId: context.userId })
const xstate::value_maker user_of_context =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<std::optional<boost::json::value>> {
    const boost::json::object* context = args.context.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* user_id =
        context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("userId");
    if (user_id == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<std::optional<boost::json::value>>(
            xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::value(boost::json::object{{"userId", *user_id}});
};

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actors.emplace("fetchUser", xstate::host_actor{});
implementations.actions.emplace("selectUser", xstate::assign_action{.assignment = select_user});
// The input of the invoke whose id is fetchUser.
implementations.inputs.emplace("fetchUser", user_of_context);
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "feedback",
    "context": {"userId": ""},
    "initial": "idle",
    "states": {
        "idle": {"on": {"user.selected": "loading"}},
        "loading": {
            "entry": "selectUser",
            "invoke": {"id": "fetchUser", "src": "fetchUser"}
        }
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!feedback_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> feedback_actor = system.create_actor(*feedback_machine);
if (!feedback_actor.has_value() || !system.start(*feedback_actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::event selected{.type = "user.selected", .payload = {{"userId", "42"}}};
if (!system.send(*feedback_actor, selected).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
for (const xstate::host_request& request : system.host_requests()) {
    if (request.input.has_value()) {
        std::cout << boost::json::serialize(*request.input) << '\n';
    }
}

It prints:

{"userId":"42"}

The input is computed when its state is entered, after the state’s entry actions and before its initial actions, as XState’s enterStates resolves them. So the input reads the user id the entry assign has just stored. The event is the one that entered the state, user.selected, which an input function could read directly as well.

The function is found by the invoke’s id, so give the invoke an id. Without one, its id is <index>.<state id>, the invoke’s position among the state’s invokes and the state’s id, as XState’s createInvokeId makes it, and the function must be registered under that: here 0.feedback.loading. Creating the machine refuses a computed input that names no invoke, and one for an invoke whose config fixes an input too (Rules).

Input to a spawned actor

A child spawned by an action receives its input from the action. XState’s spawnChild(src, { id, input }) is a spawn_child_action registered under a name, whose input is a value_maker computed when the action resolves, from the context and the event of its microstep. Without one, the child has no input; a fixed input is a function that returns it.

Stately’s page spawns inside assign, to keep the child’s reference in the context. xstate has no spawn inside assign, and an actor reference is not data: the parent names its child by its id (Spawning actors).

// ({ context }) => ({ userId: context.userId })
const xstate::value_maker user_of_context =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<std::optional<boost::json::value>> {
    const boost::json::object* context = args.context.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* user_id =
        context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("userId");
    if (user_id == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<std::optional<boost::json::value>>(
            xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::value(boost::json::object{{"userId", *user_id}});
};

// spawnChild('emailUser', { id: 'emailUser', input: ... })
const xstate::spawn_child_action spawn_email_user{
    .src = "emailUser",
    .id = "emailUser",
    .system_id = std::nullopt,
    .input = user_of_context,
};

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actors.emplace("emailUser", xstate::host_actor{});
implementations.actions.emplace("spawnEmailUser", spawn_email_user);
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "feedback",
    "context": {"userId": "123"},
    "on": {
        "feedback.submit": {"actions": "spawnEmailUser"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!feedback_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> feedback_actor = system.create_actor(*feedback_machine);
if (!feedback_actor.has_value() || !system.start(*feedback_actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.send(*feedback_actor, {.type = "feedback.submit", .payload = {}}).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
for (const xstate::host_request& request : system.host_requests()) {
    if (request.input.has_value()) {
        std::cout << boost::json::serialize(*request.input) << '\n';
    }
}

It prints:

{"userId":"123"}

The machine core returns the spawn as an xstate.spawnChild action whose params hold the child’s id and src, and its input and systemId when it has them; the actor layer creates the child from them. An invoke returns the same action when its state is entered.

Output

A machine’s output is the value it is done with. It is the output of its root, computed when the machine is done, when a top-level final state is entered or each region of a parallel root is in a final state (When the machine is done), and from then on it is the snapshot’s output, a std::optional<boost::json::value> that holds nothing while the machine is active. The root’s output is fixed in the config, the root’s "output", or computed: XState’s output: ({ context }) => ... at the root of the config is a value_maker registered in implementations.outputs under the root’s id.

// ({ input }) => ({ amount: input.amount, currency: input.toCurrency })
const xstate::context_maker from_input =
    [](const boost::json::value& input) -> xstate::result<boost::json::value> {
    const boost::json::object* given = input.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* amount =
        given == nullptr ? nullptr : given->if_contains("amount");
    const boost::json::value* currency =
        given == nullptr ? nullptr : given->if_contains("toCurrency");
    if (amount == nullptr || currency == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::value>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"amount", *amount}, {"currency", *currency}};
};
// assign({ amount: ({ event }) => event.amount })
const xstate::assigner keep_amount =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<boost::json::object> {
    const boost::json::value* amount = args.event.payload.if_contains("amount");
    if (amount == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"amount", *amount}};
};
// ({ context }) => ({ amount: context.amount, currency: context.currency })
const xstate::value_maker from_context =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<std::optional<boost::json::value>> {
    const boost::json::object* context = args.context.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* amount =
        context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("amount");
    const boost::json::value* currency =
        context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("currency");
    if (amount == nullptr || currency == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<std::optional<boost::json::value>>(
            xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::value(
        boost::json::object{{"amount", *amount}, {"currency", *currency}});
};

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.context = from_input;
implementations.actions.emplace("keepAmount", xstate::assign_action{.assignment = keep_amount});
// The machine's output: the output of its root, whose id is currency.
implementations.outputs.emplace("currency", from_context);
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "currency",
    "initial": "converting",
    "states": {
        "converting": {
            "on": {
                "amount.converted": {"target": "converted", "actions": "keepAmount"}
            }
        },
        "converted": {"type": "final"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> currency_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!currency_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const boost::json::object input{{"amount", 10}, {"fromCurrency", "USD"}, {"toCurrency", "EUR"}};
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> currency_actor =
    system.create_actor(*currency_machine, {.input = input});
if (!currency_actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<void> subscribed =
    system.subscribe(*currency_actor, [](const xstate::snapshot& snapshot) {
