        if (snapshot.status == xstate::status::done && snapshot.output.has_value()) {
            std::cout << boost::json::serialize(*snapshot.output) << '\n';
        }
    });
if (!subscribed.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::event converted{.type = "amount.converted", .payload = {{"amount", 12}}};
if (!system.start(*currency_actor).has_value() ||
    !system.send(*currency_actor, converted).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

It prints:

{"amount":12,"currency":"EUR"}

subscribe hands its listener each snapshot the actor settles in while it is active, and the one it is done in, as XState’s subscribe does; only the done one holds the output.

The root’s id is the config’s "id", (machine) when the config has none, as in XState; a machine whose output is computed is clearer with an id of its own.

A final state’s output

A final state can have an output too. When it is entered, its parent state is done (A parent state is done), and the parent’s done event, xstate.done.state.<parent id>, carries the final state’s output as its member output; the parent’s onDone reads it from the event (Done events). It is fixed in the final state’s config, or computed by a value_maker registered in implementations.outputs under the final state’s id, from the context and the event that entered the final state.

// ({ event }) => ({ grams: event.grams }), from the event that entered the final state
const xstate::value_maker dose_of_event =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<std::optional<boost::json::value>> {
    const boost::json::value* grams = args.event.payload.if_contains("grams");
    if (grams == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<std::optional<boost::json::value>>(
            xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::value(boost::json::object{{"grams", *grams}});
};
// assign({ dose: ({ event }) => event.output })
const xstate::assigner keep_dose =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<boost::json::object> {
    const boost::json::value* output = args.event.payload.if_contains("output");
    if (output == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"dose", *output}};
};

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actions.emplace("keepDose", xstate::assign_action{.assignment = keep_dose});
// The output of the final state whose id is coffee.preparation.ready.
implementations.outputs.emplace("coffee.preparation.ready", dose_of_event);
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "coffee",
    "context": {"dose": null},
    "initial": "preparation",
    "states": {
        "preparation": {
            "initial": "weighing",
            "states": {
                "weighing": {"on": {"weighed": "grinding"}},
                "grinding": {"on": {"ground": "ready"}},
                "ready": {"type": "final"}
            },
            "onDone": {"target": "brewing", "actions": "keepDose"}
        },
        "brewing": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> coffee_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!coffee_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::event weighed{.type = "weighed", .payload = {}};
const xstate::event ground{.type = "ground", .payload = {{"grams", 18}}};
xstate::snapshot snapshot = xstate::initial_transition(*coffee_machine).first;
snapshot = xstate::transition(*coffee_machine, snapshot, weighed).first;
snapshot = xstate::transition(*coffee_machine, snapshot, ground).first;
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(snapshot.value) << ' '
          << boost::json::serialize(snapshot.context) << '\n';

It prints:

"brewing" {"dose":{"grams":18}}

ready has no id of its own, so its id is the root’s id and its path, joined by dots, coffee.preparation.ready (State nodes and ids). Its output reads grams from ground, the event that entered it, and keepDose reads the output from the done event’s payload.

The machine’s output and its final state

When the root has an output, it is computed as the machine completes, from the context and the done event that completed it, as XState’s internal getMachineOutput (stateUtils.ts) computes it. For a compound root, that is the done event of the top-level final state that completed the machine, which carries that final state’s own output. So the root’s output can pass on the output of the final state that completed the machine, as ({ event }) => event.output; here it returns the whole event, to show it. When the root has no output, the machine has none, whatever its final state’s output.

/** Pays a checkout and returns its output: "error" when it is not done, "none" without one. */
std::string checkout_output(const xstate::machine& checkout) {
    const xstate::event paid{.type = "paid", .payload = {{"receiptId", "R-1"}}};
    const xstate::snapshot start = xstate::initial_transition(checkout).first;
    const xstate::snapshot done = xstate::transition(checkout, start, paid).first;
    if (done.status != xstate::status::done) {
        return "error";
    }
    if (!done.output.has_value()) {
        return "none";
    }
    return boost::json::serialize(*done.output);
}
// ({ event }) => ({ receiptId: event.receiptId })
const xstate::value_maker receipt_of_event =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<std::optional<boost::json::value>> {
    const boost::json::value* receipt_id = args.event.payload.if_contains("receiptId");
    if (receipt_id == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<std::optional<boost::json::value>>(
            xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::value(boost::json::object{{"receiptId", *receipt_id}});
};
// ({ event }) => event
const xstate::value_maker the_event =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<std::optional<boost::json::value>> {
    return boost::json::value(xstate::to_json(args.event));
};
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "checkout",
    "initial": "paying",
    "states": {
        "paying": {"on": {"paid": "receipt"}},
        "receipt": {"type": "final"}
    }
})");

xstate::implementations without_root_output;
without_root_output.outputs.emplace("checkout.receipt", receipt_of_event);
xstate::implementations with_root_output = without_root_output;
with_root_output.outputs.emplace("checkout", the_event);

const xstate::result<xstate::machine> with_output =
    xstate::create_machine(config, with_root_output);
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> without_output =
    xstate::create_machine(config, without_root_output);
if (!with_output.has_value() || !without_output.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << checkout_output(*with_output) << '\n' << checkout_output(*without_output) << '\n';

It prints:

{"type":"xstate.done.state.checkout.receipt","output":{"receiptId":"R-1"}}
none

The event names the final state, checkout.receipt, not its parent: it exists for the root’s output only, and no transition takes it. A machine whose root is a parallel state completes when each of its regions is done, and the event is then the root’s own, xstate.done.state.<root id>, without an output.

When a value is undefined

JavaScript has undefined, and JSON has not. A value_maker returns std::optional<boost::json::value>: none stands for undefined, and the member that would hold it is left out, as JavaScript’s JSON.stringify leaves it out. The snapshot then has no output, a done event no output, a child no input (host_request::input holds nothing, and the xstate.spawnChild params have no input), a log no value.

A JSON null is a value like any other, and is kept: a null output, a done event’s null output, a host actor’s null input. The exception is a machine’s input: for a machine, a null input and no input are the same, and its xstate.init has no input (The xstate.init event, undefined).

/** A snapshot's output: "error" when it is not done, "none" when it has none. */
std::string output_of(const xstate::snapshot& done) {
    if (done.status != xstate::status::done) {
        return "error";
    }
    if (!done.output.has_value()) {
        return "none";
    }
    return boost::json::serialize(*done.output);
}

// ({ input }) => input
const xstate::context_maker the_input =
    [](const boost::json::value& input) -> xstate::result<boost::json::value> { return input; };
// ({ context }) => context.total, undefined when the context has no total
const xstate::value_maker total_of_context =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<std::optional<boost::json::value>> {
    const boost::json::object* context = args.context.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* total =
        context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("total");
    if (total == nullptr) {
        return std::optional<boost::json::value>();
    }
    return std::optional<boost::json::value>(*total);
};

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.context = the_input;
implementations.outputs.emplace("order", total_of_context);
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "order",
    "initial": "placed",
    "states": {
        "placed": {"type": "final"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> order_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!order_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const std::array<boost::json::object, 3> inputs{
    boost::json::object{{"total", 42}},
    boost::json::object{},
    boost::json::object{{"total", nullptr}},
};
for (const boost::json::object& input : inputs) {
    const xstate::snapshot done = xstate::initial_transition(*order_machine, input).first;
    std::cout << boost::json::serialize(input) << " -> " << output_of(done) << '\n';
}

It prints:

{"total":42} -> 42
{} -> none
{"total":null} -> null

The order machine’s initial state is final, so the machine is done as soon as it starts. A host actor resolved with std::nullopt is a promise resolved with undefined in the same way: its done event has no output.

Done events

When something a machine waits on finishes, the machine hears it as an event, and onDone is the transition that takes it. A done event lets a parent move on when what it started has finished, without knowing the steps that finished it: the coffee machine’s preparation moves to brewing once its steps reach ready, and the order below moves on once the child that prices it is done. There are two kinds:

Event Raised or sent when Members besides type

xstate.done.state.<id>

the state <id> is done: a final child of a compound state is entered, or each region of a parallel state is in a final state

output, the final child’s output, when it has one; none for a parallel state

xstate.done.actor.<id>

the child actor whose id is <id>, invoked or spawned, is done

output, the child’s output, when it has one; actorId, the child’s id

A state’s onDone is its transition on xstate.done.state.<state id>. An invoke’s onDone is a transition of the invoking state on xstate.done.actor.<invoke id>, and its onError one on xstate.error.actor.<invoke id>, the event a child that fails sends with its error and its actorId (Done and error events). One state can have both kinds of onDone: its own, for its final child, and its invoke’s, for its child actor. A spawned child has no invoke to hold an onDone; its parent takes the child’s done event with a transition like any other, "on": {"xstate.done.actor.<id>": ...}.

State done events

A state done event is raised by the machine itself, into the macrostep’s internal queue, and runs in the same macrostep as the microstep that entered the final state; nobody sends it. The macrostep cursor shows it, since each microstep reports the event it ran for. This runs ground on the coffee machine above, from grinding:

for (const xstate::microstep& step :
     xstate::get_microsteps(*coffee_machine, snapshot, ground)) {
    std::cout << boost::json::serialize(xstate::to_json(step.event)) << " -> "
              << boost::json::serialize(step.snapshot.value) << '\n';
}

It prints:

{"type":"ground","grams":18} -> {"preparation":"ready"}
{"type":"xstate.done.state.coffee.preparation","output":{"grams":18}} -> "brewing"

The first microstep enters ready, which raises xstate.done.state.coffee.preparation with its output; the second takes the onDone of preparation to brewing. XState’s getMicrosteps returns each microstep’s snapshot and actions, but not its event, which XState shows only to an inspector, in its @xstate.microstep events.

A parallel state is done when each of its regions is in a final state (A parallel state is done). A region that is a compound state raises its own done event when its final child is entered, with that child’s output, and the parallel state’s done event follows, without an output.

Actor done events

A child actor is done when its machine is done (When the machine is done), for a machine child, or when the host answers its request with actor_system::resolve(request, output), for a host actor: the output it passes is the actor’s output, none for XState’s undefined (Host actors). Its parent then receives xstate.done.actor.<id>, with the child’s output and its id. Here a child machine computes a quote from its input, and its parent takes the quote in the invoke’s onDone:

// ({ input }) => input
const xstate::context_maker the_input =
    [](const boost::json::value& input) -> xstate::result<boost::json::value> { return input; };
// ({ context }) => ({ total: context.items * context.unitPrice })
const xstate::value_maker total_of_context =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<std::optional<boost::json::value>> {
    const boost::json::object* context = args.context.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* items =
        context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("items");
    const boost::json::value* unit_price =
        context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("unitPrice");
    if (items == nullptr || unit_price == nullptr || !items->is_int64() ||
        !unit_price->is_int64()) {
        return xstate::failure<std::optional<boost::json::value>>(
            xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::value(
        boost::json::object{{"total", items->get_int64() * unit_price->get_int64()}});
};

xstate::implementations quote_implementations;
quote_implementations.context = the_input;
quote_implementations.outputs.emplace("quote", total_of_context);
const boost::json::value quote_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "quote",
    "initial": "priced",
    "states": {
        "priced": {"type": "final"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> quote_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(quote_config, quote_implementations);
if (!quote_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
// ({ event }) => console.log(event), as a log of the event
const xstate::value_maker the_event =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<std::optional<boost::json::value>> {
    return boost::json::value(xstate::to_json(args.event));
};
// assign({ quote: ({ event }) => event.output })
const xstate::assigner keep_quote =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<boost::json::object> {
    const boost::json::value* output = args.event.payload.if_contains("output");
    if (output == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"quote", *output}};
};

xstate::implementations order_implementations;
order_implementations.actors.emplace("quote", xstate::machine_actor{*quote_machine});
order_implementations.actions.emplace(
    "logEvent", xstate::log_action{.value = the_event, .label = std::nullopt});
order_implementations.actions.emplace("keepQuote",
                                      xstate::assign_action{.assignment = keep_quote});
const boost::json::value order_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "order",
    "context": {"quote": null},
    "initial": "quoting",
    "states": {
        "quoting": {
            "invoke": {
                "id": "quote",
                "src": "quote",
                "input": {"items": 3, "unitPrice": 4},
                "onDone": {"target": "quoted", "actions": ["logEvent", "keepQuote"]}
            }
        },
        "quoted": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> order_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(order_config, order_implementations);
if (!order_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<void> logging =
    system.on_log([](xstate::actor_ref, const boost::json::value* value, std::string_view) {
        if (value != nullptr) {
            std::cout << boost::json::serialize(*value) << '\n';
        }
    });
if (!logging.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> order = system.create_actor(*order_machine);
if (!order.has_value() || !system.start(*order).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::snapshot* quoted = system.snapshot_of(*order);
if (quoted == nullptr) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(quoted->value) << ' '
          << boost::json::serialize(quoted->context) << '\n';

It prints:

{"type":"xstate.done.actor.quote","output":{"total":12},"actorId":"quote"}
"quoted" {"quote":{"total":12}}

The invoke’s input reaches the child’s implementations.context, and the output the child’s root computes reaches the parent’s onDone as event.output. The quote machine’s initial state is final, so the child is done in its initial macrostep; it reports to its parent once the parent’s own initial macrostep has settled and the parent has started it, and the parent takes onDone in a macrostep of its own, as in XState.

Rules

Creating a machine checks what implementations.inputs and implementations.outputs name, and refuses, with invalid_config, what could never be called or would contradict the config: an input that names no invoke, an input for an invoke whose config fixes one too, an output that names neither a final state nor the root, and an output for a state whose config fixes one too (What creation refuses). XState has nothing of the kind to check, since its functions sit in the config where they apply. An empty std::function, in implementations.inputs, implementations.outputs, implementations.context or the input of a spawn_child_action, is refused with invalid_config too, because calling it would abort in a build without exceptions.

const xstate::value_maker nothing =
    [](const xstate::action_args&) -> xstate::result<std::optional<boost::json::value>> {
    return std::optional<boost::json::value>();
};
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "feedback",
    "initial": "loading",
    "states": {
        "loading": {
            "invoke": {
                "id": "fetchUser",
                "src": "fetchUser",
                "input": {"userId": "42"}
            },
            "on": {"loaded": "closed", "cancel": "cancelled"}
        },
        "closed": {"type": "final"},
        "cancelled": {"type": "final", "output": "cancelled"}
    }
})");
xstate::implementations registry;
registry.actors.emplace("fetchUser", xstate::host_actor{});

xstate::implementations no_such_invoke = registry;
no_such_invoke.inputs.emplace("fetchUsers", nothing);
xstate::implementations input_twice = registry;
input_twice.inputs.emplace("fetchUser", nothing);
xstate::implementations not_final = registry;
not_final.outputs.emplace("feedback.loading", nothing);
xstate::implementations output_twice = registry;
output_twice.outputs.emplace("feedback.cancelled", nothing);
xstate::implementations final_and_root = registry;
final_and_root.outputs.emplace("feedback.closed", nothing);
final_and_root.outputs.emplace("feedback", nothing);

std::cout << "an input for no invoke: " << created(config, no_such_invoke) << '\n'
          << "an input the config fixes too: " << created(config, input_twice) << '\n'
          << "an output for a state not final: " << created(config, not_final) << '\n'
          << "an output the config fixes too: " << created(config, output_twice) << '\n'
          << "outputs for a final state and the root: " << created(config, final_and_root)
          << '\n';

It prints:

an input for no invoke: invalid_config
an input the config fixes too: invalid_config
an output for a state not final: invalid_config
an output the config fixes too: invalid_config
outputs for a final state and the root: created

created returns the error’s message, or created. A final state and the root may each have an output, fixed or computed, as the last line shows.

Once the machine runs, a computed input or output that returns an error fails the microstep that called it, as any implementation does: the macrostep settles with the snapshot it began from, its status error and its error the function’s (When an implementation fails). One that returns none leaves its member out (When a value is undefined).

Input and output cheatsheet

XState xstate, fixed xstate, computed

createActor(machine, { input })

create_actor(machine, {.input = ...})

initialTransition(machine, input)

initial_transition(machine, input), begin_initial(machine, input)

context: ({ input }) => ...

the config’s "context", which does not read the input

implementations.context

event.input in the initial macrostep

args.event.payload.if_contains("input")

invoke: { input }

the invoke’s "input"

implementations.inputs, under the invoke’s id

spawnChild(src, { id, input })

spawn_child_action::input

a final state’s output

the final state’s "output"

implementations.outputs, under the state’s id

the machine’s output

the root’s "output"

implementations.outputs, under the root’s id

snapshot.output

snapshot::output, none for undefined

event.output in onDone

args.event.payload.if_contains("output")

Pure transitions and the macrostep cursor

A pure transition function computes where a machine goes, and what it asks its caller to do, from a snapshot and an event. It starts no actor, executes no action and keeps nothing between calls: the same machine, snapshot and event always give the same result.

These functions are for a caller that keeps the snapshot itself: a server that stores each user’s snapshot between two requests, a test that checks where an event leads, a tool that shows what a machine can do next. Each needs the next step computed, not run, and holds the snapshot where it likes. XState offers them beside its actors, as initialTransition, transition and their relatives. Each call of one of XState’s that computes a step still constructs actors it never starts. One is an actor of the machine itself, whose construction resolves the machine’s initial macrostep whatever snapshot the call starts from: it runs the context function, the guards and every function a built-in action is written with, though no custom action, and constructs every child that macrostep invokes or spawns. The others are one for each child the step invokes or spawns, which the call puts in the snapshot’s children.

In xstate they are not an addition: they are the machine core. A machine is an immutable value and a snapshot a plain value the caller keeps; nothing in <webcpp/xstate.hpp> creates or runs an actor, executes a custom action, reads a clock or keeps state the caller does not hold: the snapshot, the cursor and the clock are values the caller owns. A call computes the step it is asked for and nothing else. A snapshot’s children are data, the id and the source of each child, and a step that invokes or spawns one returns an xstate.spawnChild action for its caller. The actor layer of Actors is built on them.

Every function that computes a step, transition and its relatives, is one primitive run to its end: the macrostep cursor, which xstate adds to XState. The cursor runs a macrostep one microstep per call, so its caller decides how much work an event may cost and sees each microstep on the way. The other functions ask about a snapshot and run no step. This section shows the functions first, then the cursor under them, then the clock that delayed events need.

xstate XState Returns

initial_transition(m, input)

initialTransition(m, input)

the initial snapshot and its actions

transition(m, s, e)

transition(m, s, e)

the snapshot an event leads to and its actions

get_initial_snapshot(m, input)

getInitialSnapshot(m, input)

the initial snapshot

get_next_snapshot(m, s, e)

getNextSnapshot(m, s, e)

the snapshot an event leads to

get_initial_microsteps(m, input)

getInitialMicrosteps(m, input)

each microstep of the initial macrostep

get_microsteps(m, s, e)

getMicrosteps(m, s, e)

each microstep of an event’s macrostep

can(m, s, e)

s.can(e)

whether the event selects a transition with a target or actions, as a result

get_next_transitions(m, s)

getNextTransitions(s)

every transition the snapshot could take

resolve_state(m, value, context)

m.resolveState({ value, context })

the snapshot of a state value, as a result

none

getStateNodes(node, value)

the nodes a state value names (The active state nodes)

begin_initial(m, input), begin(m, s, e)

none

a cursor over one macrostep

input is optional and null when left out. Where XState’s function takes a snapshot alone, xstate’s takes the machine too: a snapshot is plain data and does not point to its machine (The snapshot). The queries of XState’s snapshot are taught with states: snapshot::matches, and matches_state for two state values, XState’s snapshot.matches and matchesState (Matching a state value); snapshot::has_tag, XState’s snapshot.hasTag (Tags); and get_meta(machine, snapshot), XState’s snapshot.getMeta() (Meta and descriptions).

Computing the next state

The caller keeps the snapshot, and each event runs one macrostep from it. initial_transition(machine) returns the snapshot a machine starts in and the actions its initial macrostep returned. transition(machine, snapshot, event) returns the snapshot the event leads to and the actions of its macrostep: the caller keeps the snapshot for the next event and executes the actions. Both return a std::pair, which structured bindings take apart as JavaScript takes apart the [snapshot, actions] tuple of XState’s functions. types_of lists the types of the actions returned:

/** The types of `actions`, as a list: [a, b]. */
std::string types_of(const std::vector<xstate::action>& actions) {
    std::string listed = "[";
    for (const xstate::action& one : actions) {
        if (listed.size() > 1) {
            listed += ", ";
        }
        listed += one.type;
    }
    return listed + "]";
}

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "initial": "pending",
    "states": {
        "pending": {"on": {"start": {"target": "started"}}},
        "started": {"entry": {"type": "doSomething"}}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> machine = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const auto [initial_state, initial_actions] = xstate::initial_transition(*machine);
std::cout << "initial value: " << boost::json::serialize(initial_state.value) << '\n';
std::cout << "initial actions: " << types_of(initial_actions) << '\n';

const xstate::event start{.type = "start", .payload = {}};
const auto [next_state, actions] = xstate::transition(*machine, initial_state, start);
std::cout << "next value: " << boost::json::serialize(next_state.value) << '\n';
std::cout << "actions: " << types_of(actions) << '\n';

It prints:

initial value: "pending"
initial actions: []
next value: "started"
actions: [doSomething]

doSomething has no implementation, so it is a custom action: the functions return it and execute nothing (Actions). Stately’s page says the initial actions hold doSomething too, but pending has no entry action, and XState 5.33.2 returns none, as xstate does.

Neither the machine nor initial_state changes: each call returns a new snapshot. A snapshot can be kept, copied or stored, and transition called from it again gives the same result every time.

The event is an xstate::event, a type and a JSON payload, built in C++ or read with event_from_json from the flat JSON form XState’s actor.send takes, and the implementations read it as args.event (Events). The caller sends only the events that come from outside. Those the machine raises itself, a raised event or a done event, run inside the same macrostep (Actions, State done events), and a delayed event comes back from the caller’s clock, to be sent as any other (Delayed events and the simulated clock).

These functions run the macrostep to its end, however many microsteps it takes: a machine whose eventless transitions never settle never returns from them, as it never returns from XState’s. A caller that must bound the work of an event drives the cursor instead (The macrostep cursor).

Input

A machine whose initial context depends on an input takes the input as the last argument of initial_transition, get_initial_snapshot, get_initial_microsteps and begin_initial. XState writes that context as a function of the input in the config, context: ({ input }) => .... A function cannot be JSON, so xstate takes it as implementations.context, a context_maker that receives the input and returns the context (Input without an actor has the rest). name_of spells a status as XState does:

/** The name of a status, as XState spells it. */
std::string_view name_of(xstate::status status) {
    switch (status) {
        case xstate::status::active: return "active";
        case xstate::status::done: return "done";
        case xstate::status::error: return "error";
    }
    return "unknown";
}

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.context =
    [](const boost::json::value& input) -> xstate::result<boost::json::value> {
    const boost::json::object* given = input.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* count =
        given == nullptr ? nullptr : given->if_contains("initialCount");
    if (count == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::value>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"count", *count}};
};
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "initial": "pending",
    "states": {
        "pending": {"on": {"start": {"target": "started"}}},
        "started": {"entry": {"type": "doSomething"}}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> machine = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const boost::json::value input = boost::json::object{{"initialCount", 0}};
const auto [initial_state, initial_actions] = xstate::initial_transition(*machine, input);
std::cout << "value: " << boost::json::serialize(initial_state.value) << '\n';
std::cout << "context: " << boost::json::serialize(initial_state.context) << '\n';
std::cout << "status: " << name_of(initial_state.status) << '\n';

const auto [without_input, no_actions] = xstate::initial_transition(*machine);
std::cout << "without input: " << name_of(without_input.status) << ", context "
          << boost::json::serialize(without_input.context) << '\n';

It prints:

value: "pending"
context: {"count":0}
status: active
without input: error, context {}

Without an input, the context function receives null and returns an error, and initial_transition returns the snapshot the machine was about to start from, with status error and an empty context. XState reaches the same snapshot another way: its function reads a member of undefined and throws, and initialTransition catches the error into the snapshot it returns.

One case differs: xstate refuses a context function that returns anything but an object, with implementation_failed and the same snapshot, where XState merges whatever its function returns into {} with Object.assign, so a number or null starts the machine with an empty context (A context that is not an object).

The snapshot alone

get_initial_snapshot and get_next_snapshot return the snapshot without the actions. XState marks its getInitialSnapshot and getNextSnapshot deprecated in favour of initialTransition and transition; xstate keeps both, as the short form for a caller that has no use for the actions:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "light",
    "initial": "green",
    "states": {
        "green": {"on": {"TIMER": "yellow"}},
        "yellow": {"on": {"TIMER": "red"}},
        "red": {"on": {"TIMER": "green"}}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> light = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!light.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::event timer{.type = "TIMER", .payload = {}};
const xstate::event unknown{.type = "UNKNOWN", .payload = {}};

const xstate::snapshot green = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*light);
const xstate::snapshot yellow = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*light, green, timer);
const xstate::snapshot red = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*light, yellow, timer);
const xstate::snapshot still_red = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*light, red, unknown);

std::cout << boost::json::serialize(green.value) << '\n';
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(yellow.value) << '\n';
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(red.value) << '\n';
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(still_red.value) << '\n';

It prints:

"green"
"yellow"
"red"
"red"

An event no transition takes, UNKNOWN here, is not an error: its macrostep settles at once and the snapshot is unchanged. can says beforehand whether an event would do anything.

Actions

An action is something the machine asks to happen: send an email, change the context, raise an event. The pure functions resolve each action and return it, in the order XState returns it; they execute none. What comes back depends on what the action’s name stands for:

  • A name the implementations do not hold is a custom action. It comes back as the config names it: its type, and its params from the config, null when the config gives none, and builtin false, even when the config gives it the type of a built-in action, such as xstate.raise. Executing it is the caller’s work (Custom actions).

  • An assign merges its update into the context. It never comes back.

  • Every other built-in action comes back with its params resolved and builtin set: a raise as xstate.raise, a log as xstate.log, a cancel as xstate.cancel, and so on. What concerns the machine itself is done already: a raise without a delay has been processed inside the macrostep.

Here the transition on processUser names a custom action, an assign and a raise:

const xstate::assigner count_user =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<boost::json::object> {
    const boost::json::object* context = args.context.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* users =
        context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("users");
    if (users == nullptr || !users->is_int64()) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"users", users->get_int64() + 1}};
};
const xstate::event_maker started =
    [](const xstate::action_args&) -> xstate::result<xstate::event> {
    return xstate::event{.type = "STARTED", .payload = {}};
};
xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actions.emplace("countUser", xstate::assign_action{.assignment = count_user});
implementations.actions.emplace(
    "announce",
    xstate::raise_action{.event = started, .id = std::nullopt, .delay = std::nullopt});

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "initial": "idle",
    "context": {"users": 0},
    "states": {
        "idle": {
            "on": {
                "processUser": {
                    "target": "processing",
                    "actions": [
                        {"type": "sendEmail", "params": {"subject": "Processing started"}},
                        "countUser",
                        "announce"
                    ]
                }
            }
        },
        "processing": {"on": {"STARTED": "started"}},
        "started": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> machine = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::snapshot idle = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*machine);
const xstate::event process_user{
    .type = "processUser",
    .payload = {{"userId", "123"}, {"email", "user@example.com"}},
};
const auto [next_state, actions] = xstate::transition(*machine, idle, process_user);
for (const xstate::action& action : actions) {
    std::cout << action.type << ' ' << boost::json::serialize(action.params) << '\n';
}
std::cout << "value: " << boost::json::serialize(next_state.value) << '\n';
std::cout << "context: " << boost::json::serialize(next_state.context) << '\n';

It prints:

sendEmail {"subject":"Processing started"}
xstate.raise {"event":{"type":"STARTED"}}
value: "started"
context: {"users":1}

transition ran the whole macrostep: processUser took idle to processing, announce raised STARTED, and STARTED took processing to started. The raise comes back so the caller sees it, not so the caller sends STARTED again. countUser changed the context and is not in the list.

What the caller does with the built-in actions it receives:

  • An xstate.raise with a delay in its params, and an xstate.cancel, are for the caller’s clock (Delayed events and the simulated clock).

  • xstate.spawnChild, xstate.stopChild, xstate.sendTo and xstate.emit are for whatever runs the machine’s children and its listeners. The actor layer does that (Actors).

  • An xstate.log holds the value to log.

On Stately’s page, a custom action’s params are a function of the context and the event: sendEmail reads event.email. A function cannot be JSON, so xstate’s params are what the config fixes, and what comes from the event is read where the event is: each microstep reports its event beside its actions (Microsteps). Actions covers every built-in action, and Functions become names the reason for named implementations.

Microsteps

One event can move a machine more than once. The transitions the event selects run first. Then XState’s loop runs one microstep at a time: the eventless (always) transitions that are enabled, or, when none is, the next event the machine raised, until no eventless transition is enabled and no raised event is queued. Each of those steps is a microstep; together they are a macrostep (Core concepts). transition returns where the macrostep ends; get_microsteps and get_initial_microsteps return every microstep on the way.

The microsteps of an event

get_microsteps(machine, snapshot, event) returns each microstep of the macrostep an event runs, as XState’s getMicrosteps does. Here TRIGGER moves the machine, raises an event, and leads to an eventless transition:

/** The types of `actions`, as a list: [a, b]. */
std::string types_of(const std::vector<xstate::action>& actions) {
    std::string listed = "[";
    for (const xstate::action& one : actions) {
        if (listed.size() > 1) {
            listed += ", ";
        }
        listed += one.type;
    }
    return listed + "]";
}

const xstate::event_maker raised =
    [](const xstate::action_args&) -> xstate::result<xstate::event> {
    return xstate::event{.type = "RAISED", .payload = {}};
};
xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actions.emplace(
    "raiseRaised",
    xstate::raise_action{.event = raised, .id = std::nullopt, .delay = std::nullopt});

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "initial": "first",
    "states": {
        "first": {
            "on": {"TRIGGER": {"target": "second", "actions": "raiseRaised"}}
        },
        "second": {"on": {"RAISED": "third"}},
        "third": {"always": "fourth"},
        "fourth": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> machine = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::snapshot initial_state = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*machine);
const xstate::event trigger{.type = "TRIGGER", .payload = {}};
for (const xstate::microstep& micro :
     xstate::get_microsteps(*machine, initial_state, trigger)) {
    std::cout << boost::json::serialize(micro.snapshot.value) << ' ' << types_of(micro.actions)
              << '\n';
}

It prints:

"second" [xstate.raise]
"third" []
"fourth" []

TRIGGER takes first to second and raises RAISED, which takes second to third, whose eventless transition takes it to fourth: three microsteps, one macrostep. XState’s raise(...) is a call written in the config; xstate names it, raiseRaised, and registers a raise_action under that name.

XState’s microstep is a pair, [snapshot, actions]. xstate’s microstep has four members:

event

the event it ran for: the external one, a raised one, or, for an eventless transition, the event of the microstep before it.

transitions

the transitions it took, as pointers into the machine, valid while any copy of the machine lives: an empty list when the event selected none, and std::nullopt for the initial microstep, which reports none, for a microstep that failed while it ran, and for a next() on a cursor that is done.

actions

the actions it returned, in order.

snapshot

the snapshot it left.

The microsteps of the initial state

get_initial_microsteps(machine) returns each microstep of the initial macrostep, as XState’s getInitialMicrosteps does. Here the initial state has an entry action and an eventless transition:

/** The types of `actions`, as a list: [a, b]. */
std::string types_of(const std::vector<xstate::action>& actions) {
    std::string listed = "[";
    for (const xstate::action& one : actions) {
        if (listed.size() > 1) {
            listed += ", ";
        }
        listed += one.type;
    }
    return listed + "]";
}

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "initial": "a",
    "states": {
        "a": {
            "entry": "enterA",
            "always": {"target": "b", "actions": "aToB"}
        },
        "b": {"entry": "enterB"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> machine = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const std::vector<xstate::microstep> microsteps = xstate::get_initial_microsteps(*machine);
for (const xstate::microstep& micro : microsteps) {
    std::cout << boost::json::serialize(micro.snapshot.value) << ' ' << types_of(micro.actions)
              << '\n';
}

It prints:

"a" [enterA]
"b" [aToB, enterB]

The first microstep enters the initial state and returns its entry action. The second is the eventless transition of a: its action, then the entry of b. Stately’s page writes these actions as inline functions; here they are names with no implementation, which come back as custom actions, as they come back from XState’s getInitialMicrosteps. A machine with an input takes it as the second argument: get_initial_microsteps(machine, input).

Asking about a snapshot

Whether an event would do anything

can(machine, snapshot, event) says whether the event would do anything from the snapshot: whether it selects a transition that has a target or actions. It evaluates guards, as selecting a transition does, and executes nothing. It is XState’s snapshot.can(event):

const xstate::predicate has_text = [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<bool> {
    const boost::json::object* context = args.context.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* text =
        context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("text");
    if (text == nullptr || !text->is_string()) {
        return xstate::failure<bool>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return !text->get_string().empty();
};
const xstate::assigner keep =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<boost::json::object> {
    const boost::json::value* text = args.event.payload.if_contains("text");
    if (text == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"text", *text}};
};
xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.guards.emplace("hasText", has_text);
implementations.actions.emplace("keep", xstate::assign_action{.assignment = keep});

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "form",
    "initial": "editing",
    "context": {"text": ""},
    "states": {
        "editing": {
            "on": {
                "SUBMIT": {"target": "submitted", "guard": "hasText"},
                "TYPE": {"actions": "keep"},
                "IGNORE": {}
            }
        },
        "submitted": {"type": "final"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> form = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!form.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::snapshot editing = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*form);
for (const std::string_view type : {"SUBMIT", "TYPE", "IGNORE", "UNKNOWN"}) {
    const xstate::result<bool> able =
        xstate::can(*form, editing, xstate::event{.type = std::string(type), .payload = {}});
    if (!able.has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << type << ": " << (*able ? "true" : "false") << '\n';
}

const xstate::event type_hi{.type = "TYPE", .payload = {{"text", "hi"}}};
const xstate::snapshot typed = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*form, editing, type_hi);
const xstate::result<bool> submit =
    xstate::can(*form, typed, xstate::event{.type = "SUBMIT", .payload = {}});
if (!submit.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << "after TYPE, SUBMIT: " << (*submit ? "true" : "false") << '\n';

It prints:

SUBMIT: false
TYPE: true
IGNORE: false
UNKNOWN: false
after TYPE, SUBMIT: true

SUBMIT is guarded by hasText, false while the text is empty. TYPE has an action, so it does something without a target. IGNORE selects a transition that has neither a target nor actions, which changes nothing, so can is false although a transition is selected. UNKNOWN selects nothing.

can returns a result<bool>: a guard is an implementation and may fail, and the guard’s error comes back in place of an answer.

Every transition a snapshot could take

get_next_transitions(machine, snapshot) lists every transition the snapshot could take, without evaluating a guard: for each active atomic state, in the order of nodes, its own transitions and then those of each ancestor not listed yet; within a state, its event transitions in the order of the node’s transitions, which is XState’s, and then its eventless ones. It is XState’s getNextTransitions(snapshot), for a tool that shows what can happen next:

/** The ids of a transition's targets, or "(targetless)". */
std::string targets_of(const xstate::machine& owner, const xstate::transition_definition& one) {
    if (!one.target.has_value()) {
        return "(targetless)";
    }
    std::string listed;
    for (const std::size_t node : *one.target) {
        if (!listed.empty()) {
            listed += ", ";
        }
        listed += owner.node(node).id;
    }
    return listed;
}

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "form",
    "initial": "editing",
    "on": {"RESET": ".editing"},
    "states": {
        "editing": {
            "on": {
                "SUBMIT": {"target": "submitted", "guard": "hasText"},
                "TYPE": {"actions": "keep"}
            },
            "always": {"target": "submitted", "guard": "isFull"}
        },
        "submitted": {"type": "final"}
    }
})");
xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.guards.emplace("hasText", [](const xstate::action_args&) { return true; });
implementations.guards.emplace("isFull", [](const xstate::action_args&) { return false; });
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> form = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!form.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::snapshot editing = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*form);
for (const xstate::transition_definition* one : xstate::get_next_transitions(*form, editing)) {
    std::cout << '"' << one->event_type << "\" " << form->node(one->source).id << " -> "
              << targets_of(*form, *one) << '\n';
}

It prints:

"SUBMIT" form.editing -> form.submitted
"TYPE" form.editing -> (targetless)
"" form.editing -> form.submitted
"RESET" form -> form.editing

An eventless transition has the empty descriptor "", and a delayed one the type of its delayed event, xstate.after.<delay>.<state id> (Delayed transitions). A targetless transition has no target (std::nullopt), which is not the same as an empty list of targets. Both guarded transitions are listed: whether a guard holds is the question can answers. Each element points into the machine, like a microstep’s transitions.

The active state nodes

A snapshot lists its active state nodes in nodes, as indexes into the machine; machine::node(index) reads one, with its id, its key, its type and the rest of its definition (State nodes and ids):

/** Prints a snapshot's state value, then the id of each active node, in order. */
void print_nodes(const xstate::machine& owner, const xstate::snapshot& of) {
    std::cout << boost::json::serialize(of.value) << '\n';
    for (const std::size_t node : of.nodes) {
        std::cout << ' ' << owner.node(node).id;
    }
    std::cout << '\n';
}

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "player",
    "initial": "on",
    "states": {
        "off": {},
        "on": {
            "type": "parallel",
            "on": {"OFF": "#player.off"},
            "states": {
                "track": {
                    "initial": "paused",
                    "states": {
                        "paused": {"on": {"PLAY": "playing"}},
                        "playing": {}
                    }
                },
                "volume": {
                    "initial": "normal",
                    "states": {
                        "normal": {"on": {"MUTE": "muted"}},
                        "muted": {}
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> player = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!player.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::snapshot paused = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*player);
print_nodes(*player, paused);
const xstate::snapshot playing =
    xstate::get_next_snapshot(*player, paused, xstate::event{.type = "PLAY", .payload = {}});
print_nodes(*player, playing);

It prints:

{"on":{"track":"paused","volume":"normal"}}
 player player.on player.on.track player.on.track.paused player.on.volume player.on.volume.normal
{"on":{"track":"playing","volume":"normal"}}
 player player.on player.on.track player.on.volume player.on.volume.normal player.on.track.playing

The order is XState’s, the order of its snapshot’s internal _nodes (The snapshot): a node that stays active keeps its place, an exited one leaves, and an entered one is appended, so after PLAY the node playing comes last. A microstep that leaves the machine done lists the nodes in reverse document order instead, as XState’s does. The order decides which eventless transition a parallel region takes first. It also orders a state value’s keys, all but those that are array indexes: XState’s value is a JavaScript object, which enumerates such keys first, by number, and xstate writes them first too.

XState also exports getStateNodes(stateNode, stateValue), the nodes a state value names below a node, as it names them: no initial state the value leaves out, and a node repeated for each level of an object value. xstate has no counterpart. The nearest is resolve_state (Persisted state): its snapshot’s nodes are every node the value implies, completed with the initial states it leaves out, each listed once. XState’s resolveState computes the same nodes, in the same order: it completes the value first, then takes getAllStateNodes(getStateNodes(root, value)) of the completed value. Both read an object value’s keys in the order JavaScript enumerates them, array indexes first, so they agree whatever order the value writes its keys in.

Persisted state

A snapshot is a value, so a server can keep it between requests: persist it, and turn it back into a snapshot when the next event comes. resolve_state(machine, value, context) is XState’s machine.resolveState({ value, context }): it completes a state value to every node it implies and returns that snapshot, with status done when the value is a final state and active otherwise. Here the traffic light shown above (The snapshot alone), given a context, is persisted in yellow, restored, and sent TIMER:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "light",
    "initial": "green",
    "context": {"cycles": 0},
    "states": {
        "green": {"on": {"TIMER": "yellow"}},
        "yellow": {"on": {"TIMER": "red"}},
        "red": {"on": {"TIMER": "green"}}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> machine = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::event timer{.type = "TIMER", .payload = {}};
const xstate::snapshot current_state =
    xstate::get_next_snapshot(*machine, xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*machine), timer);

const std::string state_to_persist = boost::json::serialize(boost::json::object{
    {"value", current_state.value},
    {"context", current_state.context},
});

/** Later, perhaps in another process, the persisted text is read back. */
boost::system::error_code malformed;
const boost::json::value persisted = boost::json::parse(state_to_persist, malformed);
const boost::json::object* fields = persisted.if_object();
if (malformed || fields == nullptr || !fields->contains("value") ||
    !fields->contains("context")) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<xstate::snapshot> restored_state =
    xstate::resolve_state(*machine, fields->at("value"), fields->at("context"));
if (!restored_state.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const auto [next_state, actions] = xstate::transition(*machine, *restored_state, timer);
std::cout << "restored: " << boost::json::serialize(restored_state->value) << '\n';
std::cout << "context: " << boost::json::serialize(restored_state->context) << '\n';
std::cout << "next: " << boost::json::serialize(next_state.value) << '\n';

It prints:

restored: "yellow"
context: {"cycles":0}
next: "red"

resolve_state restores the value and the context, and nothing else: the status comes from the value, done or active, never error, and a done machine’s output is not restored. XState’s resolveState also reads status, output, error and historyValue from what it is given, so its round trip of a done snapshot keeps the output and xstate’s does not. A value that names a state the machine does not have is refused with unknown_state. What history states remember is not restored, and neither are the children: the snapshot starts without them.

XState’s resolveState restores what history states remember only from a live historyValue, whose members are state node objects: from what JSON.stringify made of them, a later transition to the history state enters a plain object in place of the node, and the snapshot is corrupt. XState’s actor persistence, getPersistedSnapshot and createActor with a snapshot, restores it from JSON by node id; xstate has no counterpart (What is not ported), so a caller that needs what history states remember keeps the snapshot itself, in memory.

The macrostep cursor

The macrostep cursor runs one macrostep a microstep at a time, under its caller’s control. It is xstate’s one primitive, and XState has no counterpart: XState runs a macrostep to its end inside one call, and its loop has no bound but the config’s options.maxIterations, infinite unless the config sets it (A macrostep that never settles). Without it, a machine whose eventless transitions or raised events lead back to each other never returns from transition.

That is acceptable when the machine is code the program was written with, whose author can find such a cycle before the program ships. A program that runs machines it did not write cannot. xstate loads a machine from JSON when the program runs: a user may have written it, Stately Studio exported it, a request carried it. A server runs it inside a request it must answer within a budget, and one cycle in that machine, by mistake or by intent, would hold the server’s thread for good. So the program pays for each microstep with fuel, and stops the macrostep when its budget is spent.

A cursor, macrostep, holds one macrostep in progress. Each call of next() runs exactly one microstep and reports it, with whether that microstep settled the macrostep. The caller decides whether to call next() again, and so how much an event may cost: one unit of fuel per microstep is the natural measure. The actor layer pays it, plus one unit for each message an actor sends and each timer it arms (Fuel, parking and resume). Every function above that computes a step is this cursor run to its end without a bound, so their results are the cursor’s.

One microstep at a time

begin(machine, snapshot, event) returns the cursor of the macrostep the event runs from the snapshot. With this machine, where charge is a raise_action of CHARGED, CHECKOUT takes three microsteps:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "order",
    "initial": "idle",
    "states": {
        "idle": {"on": {"CHECKOUT": {"target": "validating", "actions": "track"}}},
        "validating": {"always": "charging"},
        "charging": {"entry": "charge", "on": {"CHARGED": "confirmed"}},
        "confirmed": {"entry": "sendReceipt"}
    }
})");

Two helpers spell what a microstep returned and took. A transition names its source and its targets by their index in the machine, and machine::node reads each:

/** The types of `actions`, as a list: [a, b]. */
std::string types_of(const std::vector<xstate::action>& actions) {
    std::string listed = "[";
    for (const xstate::action& one : actions) {
        if (listed.size() > 1) {
            listed += ", ";
        }
        listed += one.type;
    }
    return listed + "]";
}

/** The transitions a microstep took, as source -> targets, or "none". */
std::string transitions_of(const xstate::machine& owner, const xstate::microstep& micro) {
    if (!micro.transitions.has_value() || micro.transitions->empty()) {
        return "none";
    }
    std::string listed;
    for (const xstate::transition_definition* one : *micro.transitions) {
        if (!listed.empty()) {
            listed += ", ";
        }
        listed += owner.node(one->source).key + " ->";
        for (const std::size_t target : one->target.value_or(std::vector<std::size_t>{})) {
            listed += ' ' + owner.node(target).key;
        }
    }
    return listed;
}

The cursor runs the microsteps one per call of next():

xstate::macrostep cursor =
    xstate::begin(*order, idle, xstate::event{.type = "CHECKOUT", .payload = {}});
std::size_t count = 0;
while (!cursor.done()) {
    const xstate::progress made = cursor.next();
    const xstate::microstep& micro = made.step;
    std::cout << ++count << ": " << micro.event.type << ", " << transitions_of(*order, micro)
              << ", " << types_of(micro.actions) << ", "
              << boost::json::serialize(micro.snapshot.value)
              << (made.settled ? ", settled" : "") << '\n';
}
const xstate::macrostep_result& settled = cursor.result();
std::cout << "result: " << boost::json::serialize(settled.snapshot.value) << ", "
          << types_of(settled.actions) << ", " << settled.microsteps << " microsteps\n";

It prints:

1: CHECKOUT, idle -> validating, [track], "validating"
2: CHECKOUT, validating -> charging, [xstate.raise], "charging"
3: CHARGED, charging -> confirmed, [sendReceipt], "confirmed", settled
result: "confirmed", [track, xstate.raise, sendReceipt], 3 microsteps

Each next() returns a progress:

step

the microstep it ran.

settled

true on the microstep after which XState’s loop would stop, no eventless transition being enabled and no raised event queued, or the machine no longer active; false on every other.

resolved_before_failure

the actions a failing microstep resolved before it failed (When an implementation fails).

The second microstep is the eventless transition of validating. It reports the event of the microstep before it, CHECKOUT, as XState does. The third ran CHARGED, which charging raised on entry.

Between two calls, the caller can read what the microstep did: the context its assigns left, the transitions it took, the actions it returned. The microstep that settles leaves the snapshot the macrostep settles in, so a caller that acts after each microstep takes its new stable state from that microstep’s snapshot.

Once done() is true, result() holds the macrostep_result: the settled snapshot, every action of every microstep in order, and the number of microsteps. Two more accessors read a cursor while it runs: current(), the snapshot the last microstep left, which is not a stable state until the macrostep settles, and began_from(), the snapshot the macrostep started from. A next() on a cursor that is done runs nothing and reports settled again. An event that selects no transition settles on the first next(), with the snapshot unchanged.

The initial macrostep

begin_initial(machine, input) returns the cursor of the initial macrostep: the microstep that enters the initial states, then XState’s loop for the event xstate.init, which carries the input. It prints with the helpers types_of and transitions_of shown above (One microstep at a time):

const xstate::context_maker from_input =
    [](const boost::json::value& input) -> xstate::result<boost::json::value> {
    const boost::json::object* given = input.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* user = given == nullptr ? nullptr : given->if_contains("user");
    return boost::json::object{{"user", user == nullptr ? boost::json::value() : *user}};
};
const xstate::predicate has_user = [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<bool> {
    const boost::json::object* context = args.context.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* user =
        context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("user");
    return user != nullptr && !user->is_null();
};
xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.context = from_input;
implementations.guards.emplace("hasUser", has_user);

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "session",
    "initial": "checking",
    "states": {
        "checking": {
            "always": [
                {"target": "signedIn", "guard": "hasUser"},
                {"target": "signedOut"}
            ]
        },
        "signedIn": {"entry": "welcome"},
        "signedOut": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> session = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!session.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const boost::json::value input = boost::json::object{{"user", "ana"}};
xstate::macrostep cursor = xstate::begin_initial(*session, input);
while (!cursor.done()) {
    const xstate::progress made = cursor.next();
    const xstate::microstep& micro = made.step;
    std::cout << boost::json::serialize(xstate::to_json(micro.event)) << ", "
              << transitions_of(*session, micro) << ", " << types_of(micro.actions) << ", "
              << boost::json::serialize(micro.snapshot.value)
              << (made.settled ? ", settled" : "") << '\n';
}
std::cout << "context: " << boost::json::serialize(cursor.result().snapshot.context) << '\n';

It prints:

{"type":"xstate.init","input":{"user":"ana"}}, none, [], "checking"
{"type":"xstate.init","input":{"user":"ana"}}, checking -> signedIn, [welcome], "signedIn", settled
context: {"user":"ana"}

begin_initial computes the context from the input before the first microstep, with implementations.context. A context that cannot be computed fails the macrostep on its first next(), as in Input. The first microstep reports no transitions, as XState reports none for it. The second is the eventless transition of checking, whose guard read the context; it reports xstate.init still. With a null input, xstate’s xstate.init has no input member, where XState’s has one that is undefined.

Fuel

Fuel is the budget a caller gives a macrostep: the caller pays for each microstep before it calls next(), and stops when the budget is spent. A cursor is a value, so stopping loses nothing. The caller keeps the cursor and calls next() again later, in the same request or in a later one the same process serves: a cursor holds its machine and points into it, so it lives in memory and is not written out as a snapshot is (Persisted state). It resumes exactly where it stopped, with the events the machine raised still queued. A copy is independent of the original and resumes from the same point. This function pays one unit of fuel per microstep:

/** Runs at most `fuel` microsteps of `cursor`, one unit each; returns the units spent. */
std::size_t run(xstate::macrostep& cursor, std::size_t fuel) {
    std::size_t spent = 0;
    while (!cursor.done() && spent < fuel) {
        cursor.next();
        ++spent;
    }
    return spent;
}

Two requests of two units each run the CHECKOUT macrostep shown above (One microstep at a time), and a copy taken between them runs too:

xstate::macrostep cursor =
    xstate::begin(*order, idle, xstate::event{.type = "CHECKOUT", .payload = {}});

const std::size_t first = run(cursor, 2);
std::cout << "first request: " << first << " microsteps, done " << cursor.done() << ", at "
          << boost::json::serialize(cursor.current().value) << '\n';

xstate::macrostep copy = cursor;

const std::size_t second = run(cursor, 2);
std::cout << "second request: " << second << " microstep, done " << cursor.done() << ", at "
          << boost::json::serialize(cursor.result().snapshot.value) << '\n';

run(copy, 2);
std::cout << "the copy: done " << copy.done() << ", at "
          << boost::json::serialize(copy.result().snapshot.value) << ", "
          << copy.result().microsteps << " microsteps\n";

It prints:

first request: 2 microsteps, done false, at "charging"
second request: 1 microstep, done true, at "confirmed"
the copy: done true, at "confirmed", 3 microsteps

The first request runs out of fuel after two microsteps, in charging, with CHARGED raised and queued. The second runs the one microstep left. The copy settles in the same snapshot after the same three microsteps: result().microsteps counts the macrostep’s microsteps, wherever they ran.

While a macrostep has not settled, its current() snapshot is not a stable state; the snapshot it began from is still the machine’s state for anything else the caller does. An initial macrostep has no such state: its began_from() is the snapshot before the machine started, whose nodes hold the root alone.

One unit a microstep is this example’s measure, not a rule: a caller may charge each microstep by what it costs, the actions it returns to execute among them.

Out of fuel in a cycle

A macrostep never settles when its eventless transitions keep enabling each other, or its raised events keep raising others: no microstep is the last (A macrostep that never settles). With the cursor, the caller sees it as a cursor still not done when its fuel is spent. Here SPIN enters left, whose always leads to right, whose always leads back to left, and the caller gives the macrostep 1000 units of fuel:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "spinner",
    "initial": "idle",
    "states": {
        "idle": {"on": {"SPIN": "left"}},
        "left": {"always": "right"},
        "right": {"always": "left"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> spinner = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!spinner.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::snapshot idle = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*spinner);

constexpr std::size_t fuel = 1000;
xstate::macrostep cursor =
    xstate::begin(*spinner, idle, xstate::event{.type = "SPIN", .payload = {}});
std::size_t spent = 0;
while (!cursor.done() && spent < fuel) {
    cursor.next();
    ++spent;
}
if (!cursor.done()) {
    std::cout << "out of fuel after " << spent << " microsteps, at "
              << boost::json::serialize(cursor.current().value) << '\n';
    std::cout << "the stable state is still "
              << boost::json::serialize(cursor.began_from().value) << '\n';
}

It prints:

out of fuel after 1000 microsteps, at "right"
the stable state is still "idle"

The cursor does not stop on its own: no microstep settles, and the caller’s fuel is the only bound. When it is spent, current() is a snapshot inside the cycle, which is not a stable state, and began_from() is the stable state the event found. What happens then is the caller’s choice: drop the event and keep that stable state, as here, report an error, or resume later with more fuel. The actor layer parks the actor until resume() gives it more (Fuel, parking and resume). XState’s transition never returns on SPIN; given an options.maxIterations of 1000, it throws Infinite loop detected instead, and its caller keeps the snapshot it passed. Where xstate differs compares the two bounds.

Executing actions as they come

A caller that executes actions microstep by microstep reads each progress.step.actions; one that executes them once the macrostep settles reads result().actions, which gathers them in order. Each action is executed from one or the other, never both, or it runs twice.

XState’s actor does both, by kind. It runs a custom action or a log as it resolves it, and holds what every other built-in action does, an emit, a send, a delayed raise, a cancel, the start of a spawned child or the stop of a started one, until the macrostep ends, then runs those in order. A raise without a delay leaves nothing to run: the macrostep has processed its event already (Actions). A stop does part of its work at once: it releases the systemIds of the child’s family, and it stops a child that has not started, so a child that a macrostep spawns and then stops never starts: its held start finds it stopped and does nothing.

The actions of an initial macrostep wait until the actor starts, and its start orders them differently. It first starts the children the settled snapshot lists whose own snapshot is active, in the order of its children, then runs the custom actions and the logs, and then what the other built-in actions do, each in the order the macrostep returned them. A child born done or failed is not active: it starts at its xstate.spawnChild, with the other built-in actions. An active child of an initial macrostep thus starts before the custom actions of that macrostep run, where a child of any later macrostep starts after them.

A caller that acts as XState’s actor executes the custom actions and the logs from each progress.step.actions, and the other built-in actions from result().actions once the macrostep has settled, unless it failed (When an implementation fails). Of those it skips a raise without a delay, and both the xstate.spawnChild and the xstate.stopChild of a child that the same macrostep spawned and stopped. Of an initial macrostep it executes nothing until it starts the machine, and then executes them as that start does: it starts first the listed children whose own snapshot is active, and does not execute their xstate.spawnChild again, then executes the custom actions and the logs, then the other built-in actions, among them the xstate.spawnChild of a child born done or failed.

One kind of action is in result().actions only: when a macrostep settles with the machine not active, done or still in the error it began from, it returns an xstate.stopChild for each child left, after every microstep’s actions and in no microstep. A macrostep that ends in a new error returns none: one an implementation fails, or one whose event is an actor’s error that no transition handles. A caller that executes microstep by microstep executes the stops once the macrostep has settled.

One more rule concerns a send to a child that the same microstep invokes. An xstate.sendTo that names, by its bare id, an invoke of the state being entered may come back before that invoke’s xstate.spawnChild, since a state’s entry actions run before its invokes spawn their children. It carries bound_at: how many of its microstep’s actions come before the point where XState binds it to the child, the end of that state’s entry actions, spawns and initial actions (XState’s retryResolveSendTo). Its target is the child that id names once the caller has executed that many of the microstep’s actions. The actor layer binds it there, and fails with unknown_target when no child has that id by then (action::bound_at, A sendTo whose child is gone).

When an implementation fails

An implementation returns a result, and when it returns an error the microstep fails. That next() settles the macrostep at once, and the snapshot is the one the macrostep began from, with status error and the implementation’s error code in error. XState’s pure transition throws instead; its actor keeps the snapshot from before the macrostep, with status error. xstate throws no exception, and a failure returned as a value lands in the snapshot the caller receives, where it cannot be missed (Failures are values). The machine below returns custom actions alone. A cursor loop that executes them as they come does with them what XState’s actor does, and prints what an actor of XState prints for the same machine (name_of is the helper of the input example):

/** Executes a custom action, the only kind this machine returns for its caller to run. */
void execute(const xstate::action& action) {
    if (action.builtin) {
        return;
    }
    std::cout << "ran " << action.type << '\n';
}

const xstate::assigner count_attempt =
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<boost::json::object> {
    const boost::json::object* context = args.context.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* attempts =
        context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("attempts");
    if (attempts == nullptr || !attempts->is_int64()) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"attempts", attempts->get_int64() + 1}};
};
const xstate::assigner fail =
    [](const xstate::action_args&) -> xstate::result<boost::json::object> {
    return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
};
xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actions.emplace("countAttempt",
                                xstate::assign_action{.assignment = count_attempt});
implementations.actions.emplace("fail", xstate::assign_action{.assignment = fail});

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "upload",
    "initial": "idle",
    "context": {"attempts": 0},
    "states": {
        "idle": {"on": {"UPLOAD": {"target": "uploading", "actions": "notify"}}},
        "uploading": {
            "always": {
                "target": "done",
                "actions": ["progress", "countAttempt", "fail"]
            }
        },
        "done": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> upload = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!upload.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::snapshot idle = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*upload);

xstate::macrostep cursor =
    xstate::begin(*upload, idle, xstate::event{.type = "UPLOAD", .payload = {}});
while (!cursor.done()) {
    const xstate::progress made = cursor.next();
    for (const xstate::action& action : made.step.actions) {
        execute(action);
    }
    for (const xstate::action& action : made.resolved_before_failure) {
        execute(action);
    }
}
const xstate::snapshot& settled = cursor.result().snapshot;
std::cout << "status: " << name_of(settled.status) << " (" << settled.error.message() << ")\n";
std::cout << "value: " << boost::json::serialize(settled.value) << '\n';
std::cout << "context: " << boost::json::serialize(settled.context) << '\n';

It prints:

ran notify
ran progress
status: error (implementation_failed)
value: "idle"
context: {"attempts":0}

The first microstep returned notify and moved to uploading. The second failed at fail, after progress had resolved and countAttempt had counted. It reports no actions, as XState’s pure functions throw; its resolved_before_failure holds progress, which XState’s actor has run by then. The context is the one the macrostep began from, attempts at 0, although notify and progress have run: actions executed as they come are not undone, so they must tolerate a macrostep that fails after them. result().actions holds notify, from the microstep before the failure, and nothing of the failing one.

A guard of an eventless transition fails differently. The cursor evaluates it after the microstep before it, to decide whether the macrostep settles, so the next() that ran that microstep reports its transitions and its actions, with the snapshot the macrostep began from in error, settles, and leaves resolved_before_failure empty; result().actions keeps those actions too. Here GO returns a custom action, an emit and a log, and the guard of the eventless transition of checking fails. The loop prints the step the cursor reported, which an actor of XState does not show, and then what XState’s actor prints for the same machine (types_of is the helper of the cursor example, name_of that of the input example):

/**
 Runs what XState's actor runs as it resolves an action: a custom action,
 and a log, which it hands to its logger.

 Tip: XState's actor holds what an emit, the other built-in action here,
 does until the macrostep ends, which a macrostep that fails never reaches.
*/
void execute(const xstate::action& action) {
    if (!action.builtin) {
        std::cout << "ran " << action.type << '\n';
        return;
    }
    if (action.type != "xstate.log" || !action.params.is_object()) {
        return;
    }
    const boost::json::value* value = action.params.get_object().if_contains("value");
    if (value == nullptr || !value->is_string()) {
        return;
    }
    const std::string_view text = value->get_string();
    std::cout << "logged: " << text << '\n';
}

const xstate::event_maker told =
    [](const xstate::action_args&) -> xstate::result<xstate::event> {
    return xstate::event{.type = "told", .payload = {}};
};
const xstate::value_maker said =
    [](const xstate::action_args&) -> xstate::result<std::optional<boost::json::value>> {
    return std::optional<boost::json::value>("say");
};
const xstate::predicate broken = [](const xstate::action_args&) -> xstate::result<bool> {
    return xstate::failure<bool>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
};
xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actions.emplace("tell", xstate::emit_action{.event = told});
implementations.actions.emplace("say",
                                xstate::log_action{.value = said, .label = std::nullopt});
implementations.guards.emplace("broken", broken);

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "order",
    "initial": "idle",
    "states": {
        "idle": {"on": {"GO": {"target": "checking", "actions": ["note", "tell", "say"]}}},
        "checking": {"always": {"target": "done", "guard": "broken"}},
        "done": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> order = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!order.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::snapshot idle = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*order);

xstate::macrostep cursor =
