    xstate::begin(*order, idle, xstate::event{.type = "GO", .payload = {}});
while (!cursor.done()) {
    const xstate::progress made = cursor.next();
    std::cout << "step: " << types_of(made.step.actions) << (made.settled ? ", settled" : "")
              << '\n';
    for (const xstate::action& action : made.step.actions) {
        execute(action);
    }
    for (const xstate::action& action : made.resolved_before_failure) {
        execute(action);
    }
}
const xstate::snapshot& settled = cursor.result().snapshot;
std::cout << "status: " << name_of(settled.status) << " (" << settled.error.message() << ")\n";
std::cout << "value: " << boost::json::serialize(settled.value) << '\n';

It prints:

step: [note, xstate.emit, xstate.log], settled
ran note
logged: say
status: error (implementation_failed)
value: "idle"

The step holds the emit, as result().actions does, and the caller drops it, since XState’s actor never delivers told: a listener of told on that actor hears nothing.

One rule covers every macrostep that fails. XState’s actor runs a log as it resolves it, and holds what every other built-in action does until the macrostep ends, all but the part of a stop that runs at once (Executing actions as they come). A macrostep that throws never gets there: nothing it held runs, and no child the macrostep spawned starts. A caller that acts as XState’s actor therefore runs, of a macrostep that fails, the custom actions and the logs, whether it reads them from progress.step.actions, resolved_before_failure or result().actions, and drops every other built-in action but for that part of a stop: of a child it started earlier, it releases the systemIds of the child’s family and leaves the child running. Of an initial macrostep that fails it runs nothing at all: XState’s actor runs the initial actions only once it has started, and the start of an actor whose initial macrostep failed runs none. The actor layer does the same (Watching an actor).

Neither that caller nor the actor layer copies XState in one respect. XState’s actor constructs a child when it resolves the spawn, so a child that a failing macrostep spawned stays constructed and never starts, and the systemIds of its family can stay registered: a stop of that child releases them only outside an initial macrostep, which holds that part of a stop too. The caller, which drops the xstate.spawnChild, never creates that child; the actor layer creates it and then stops it, which releases those systemIds (The children of a failing macrostep). The error codes are listed under errc in Reference.

Delayed events and the simulated clock

A delayed event is one the machine asks to receive later: a state’s after, or a raise_action with a delay. The machine never reads a clock, so a step stays a function of the snapshot and the event, and time is what the caller brings (Delayed transitions). Entering a state with after returns, for each of its delays, an xstate.raise whose params hold the event, its id and the delay in milliseconds; leaving the state returns an xstate.cancel of each id. A delayed raise_action comes back the same way and is not queued. Keeping the time is the caller’s work, and simulated_clock does it: XState’s SimulatedClock with the scheduler of its actor system, as a value the caller owns.

Here a light leaves green after 1000 milliseconds and yellow after 500, unless STOP takes it to red first. The caller hands every action a step returns to the clock, moves the time, and delivers each event the clock hands back as a macrostep of its own:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "light",
    "initial": "green",
    "states": {
        "green": {"after": {"1000": "yellow"}},
        "yellow": {"after": {"500": "red"}, "on": {"STOP": "red"}},
        "red": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> light = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!light.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::simulated_clock clock;
auto [now, initial_actions] = xstate::initial_transition(*light);
for (const xstate::action& returned : initial_actions) {
    clock.apply(returned);
}

const auto deliver = [&](const xstate::event& happened) {
    auto [next, actions] = xstate::transition(*light, now, happened);
    for (const xstate::action& returned : actions) {
        clock.apply(returned);
    }
    now = std::move(next);
    std::cout << "  " << happened.type << " -> " << boost::json::serialize(now.value) << '\n';
};

const std::vector<std::uint64_t> times{500, 1000, 1200, 2000};
for (const std::uint64_t time : times) {
    if (!clock.set(time).has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "at " << time << ":\n";
    if (time == 1200) {
        deliver(xstate::event{.type = "STOP", .payload = {}});
    }
    while (const std::optional<xstate::event> due = clock.pop_due()) {
        deliver(*due);
    }
}

It prints:

at 500:
at 1000:
  xstate.after.1000.light.green -> "yellow"
at 1200:
  STOP -> "red"
at 2000:

Entering green returned the raise of xstate.after.1000.light.green, which the clock released at 1000. Entering yellow then returned the raise of xstate.after.500.light.yellow, due at 1500; STOP left yellow at 1200, its exit returned the cancel, and nothing fired at 2000.

XState’s pure functions leave the same work to their caller, which keeps its timers on a SimulatedClock: setTimeout holds a function that delivers the event, and moving the time calls it. A simulated_clock holds the event itself and hands it back, so the caller delivers it and applies what that delivery returns before it takes the next (The core’s clock hands over the due events).

simulated_clock has these members:

apply(action)

schedules a built-in xstate.raise that has a delay, and cancels on a built-in xstate.cancel. A delayed built-in xstate.sendTo with an id is not the machine’s to receive: the clock holds only that id, as XState’s scheduler keys every delayed event by its id, and pop_due() never returns it. A custom action changes nothing, whatever its type (builtin tells the two kinds apart, Actions), and neither does any other action.

schedule(event, delay, id)

holds an event for delay milliseconds, under an id or none. A later schedule under the same id takes the id over: the earlier event still fires, but no cancel reaches it any more, as in XState’s scheduler.

cancel(id)

forgets the event that holds id, the latest scheduled under it. Once an event scheduled under id has fired, cancel(id) cancels nothing, as XState’s scheduler forgets the id when its timer fires.

set(time), increment(milliseconds), now()

move and read the time. set refuses to move it back, with invalid_config, where XState’s set throws. Neither set nor increment releases an event, where XState’s run the timeouts that are due: pop_due() releases them.

pop_due()

takes out the earliest event that is due, by deadline and then by the order it was scheduled in, or std::nullopt when none is.

The caller delivers each due event as a macrostep of its own and applies what that macrostep returns before the next pop_due(), so a delivered event can cancel a later one, or schedule one that is due already. Time is whole milliseconds, a std::uint64_t, where XState’s clock takes fractions (Time in whole milliseconds), and equal deadlines come out in the order they were scheduled, which is what XState’s sort does under V8 (Equal deadlines). The actor layer keeps the timers of its actors itself, released by actor_system::clock_tick(now) (Delayed events and time).

Actors: xstate on xactor

The machine core computes what a machine does and returns what it does not do itself: a child to invoke or spawn, a child to stop, an event for another actor, a timer to arm, a custom action or a log for the host (the actions a step returns). A caller that steps a machine with the pure functions executes those actions itself. The actor layer, <webcpp/xstate/actors.hpp>, executes them: it runs machines as XState’s actors, so that their children run, their events reach each other, their done and error events reach their parents, their timers fire when the host brings the time, and the work only the host can do waits for the host’s answer. The split is XState’s own: its machines resolve an action, its actors execute it.

The core includes nothing of the layer and runs no actor. It knows a machine’s actors as data, the implementations’ actors and the snapshot’s children, and resolves each invoke and spawn into the xstate.spawnChild and xstate.stopChild actions it returns; the layer is the caller that executes them. The layer runs on xactor, webcpp’s deterministic actor system: one scheduler on the host’s thread, a mailbox for each actor, fuel for each execution, and timers. The core includes nothing of xactor; the layer’s headers do. This chapter uses xactor only through the layer; xactor’s page teaches it alone.

The actor model explains the ideas first, in plain words, each with one small program, and Actors takes the layer in depth. It starts with one actor: how it is created, watched and given its input. Then come the children it invokes and spawns, the events actors send each other, the system, where an actor is found by name, time, host actors, the port’s stand-in for XState’s promises, and fuel, which bounds the work of every call. The last two sections say how the layer runs and where it differs from XState.

The actor model

The actor model is a model of concurrent computation whose building block is the actor: an independent, live object that reaches others only by messages.

  • An actor has its own state, which only it changes, in response to a message it receives.

  • It talks to other actors only by sending them messages. In XState, and in xstate, the messages are events.

  • It handles one message at a time, from its mailbox, the queue of the messages it has received.

  • It shares its state only by sending events, or by publishing snapshots to whoever subscribed to them.

  • It can create actors, its children.

These rules let each actor be understood on its own. Nothing else changes its state, and what it does depends only on the messages it receives, in the order it receives them, so a program of many processes becomes a set of small ones that talk, each of which can be tested by the events it takes and sends.

A statechart describes the logic of one actor; the actor model describes how many of them live together. When XState runs a machine, the machine becomes an actor; xstate’s actor layer does the same. This section takes the model’s ideas one at a time, each with the smallest program that shows it, and the section after it, Actors, takes each in depth.

Actors

An actor runs its logic, what XState calls actor logic: here a machine. A host_actor, whose work the host does, is the other kind of logic xstate knows (Spawning). A machine actor holds the current snapshot, takes one event at a time, and moves its snapshot on with each. Nothing outside it changes its state; the host sends it events and reads, or subscribes to, its snapshots. Here the dog that wakes up and falls asleep (Events and transitions) runs as an actor, and a listener prints each snapshot it settles in:

/** Whether a call that delivers ran to its end: no error, and no actor left parked. */
bool settled(const xstate::result<xstate::run_outcome>& ran) {
    return ran.has_value() && *ran == xstate::run_outcome::settled;
}
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "dog",
    "initial": "asleep",
    "states": {
        "asleep": {"on": {"wakes up": "awake"}},
        "awake": {"on": {"falls asleep": "asleep"}}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> dog = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!dog.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> dog_actor = system.create_actor(*dog);
if (!dog_actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<void> subscribed =
    system.subscribe(*dog_actor, [](const xstate::snapshot& snapshot) {
        std::cout << "snapshot: " << boost::json::serialize(snapshot.value) << '\n';
    });
if (!subscribed.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!settled(system.start(*dog_actor))) {
    return 1;
}
for (const std::string_view type : {"wakes up", "falls asleep"}) {
    if (!settled(system.send(*dog_actor, {.type = std::string(type), .payload = {}}))) {
        return 1;
    }
}
if (!system.stop(*dog_actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<xactor::status> ended = system.status_of(*dog_actor);
if (!ended.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << "status: " << status_name(*ended) << '\n';

It prints:

snapshot: "asleep"
snapshot: "awake"
snapshot: "asleep"
status: stopped

actor_system is XState’s createActor and the actor’s system in one. create_actor makes an actor of a machine, start runs its initial macrostep, send delivers an event, and stop ends a root actor with all its children. subscribe hands a listener each snapshot the actor settles in while it is active, and the one it is done in. A failed actor’s snapshot is not handed over, as XState hands a failure to an observer’s error rather than to its next; status_of says when an actor has failed. Each call that delivers runs the system until nothing is left to do before it returns, as XState’s send processes its event at once, and says whether everything settled or an actor ran out of fuel (The actor layer). The program’s settled checks that a call returned no error and left no actor parked; the examples below use it too. An actor’s status, active, done, error or stopped, comes from status_of, where XState writes it in the snapshot.

A listener runs inside the actor’s turn. It may read the system, with snapshot_of for example, but a call from it that changes the system, a send among them, returns invalid_argument and changes nothing; XState accepts a send from a subscriber and handles it after the update in progress (A callback that calls the system back).

Messages and mailboxes

Actors talk by sending messages; to a machine actor, a message is an event. Each actor has a mailbox, where messages wait in the order they arrived, and it takes the next one only when it has finished with the one before. A machine actor has finished with an event when its macrostep has settled, so one event never interrupts another: this is XState’s run to completion. So no event ever finds an actor halfway through another: each starts from the snapshot the one before settled in.

A machine sends an event with a send_to_action, XState’s sendTo, naming its target by id: here the owner names the child it invokes, dog. The example registers the dog’s machine as an actor, a machine_actor in implementations.actors, which is XState’s setup({ actors }), invokes it from the owner, and finds it with child_of; Spawning, next, explains all three. The owner’s throw sends the dog fetch, and the dog counts the fetches in its context:

/** One more fetch, merged into the dog's context. */
xstate::result<boost::json::object> count(const xstate::action_args& args) {
    const boost::json::object* context = args.context.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* fetched =
        context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("fetched");
    if (fetched == nullptr || !fetched->is_int64()) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"fetched", fetched->get_int64() + 1}};
}

/** The event the owner sends its dog. */
xstate::result<xstate::event> fetch(const xstate::action_args& /*args*/) {
    return xstate::event{.type = "fetch", .payload = {}};
}
xstate::implementations dog_implementations;
dog_implementations.actions.emplace("count", xstate::assign_action{.assignment = count});
const boost::json::value dog_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "dog",
    "context": {"fetched": 0},
    "on": {"fetch": {"actions": "count"}}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> dog =
    xstate::create_machine(dog_config, dog_implementations);
if (!dog.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::send_to_action throw_ball{
    .target = "dog",
    .event = fetch,
    .id = std::nullopt,
    .delay = std::nullopt,
};
xstate::implementations owner_implementations;
owner_implementations.actions.emplace("throw", throw_ball);
owner_implementations.actors.emplace("dog", xstate::machine_actor{*dog});
const boost::json::value owner_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "owner",
    "invoke": {"id": "dog", "src": "dog"},
    "on": {"play": {"actions": ["throw", "throw"]}}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> owner =
    xstate::create_machine(owner_config, owner_implementations);
if (!owner.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> owner_actor = system.create_actor(*owner);
if (!owner_actor.has_value() || !settled(system.start(*owner_actor))) {
    return 1;
}
const std::optional<xstate::actor_ref> dog_actor = system.child_of(*owner_actor, "dog");
if (!dog_actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<void> subscribed =
    system.subscribe(*dog_actor, [](const xstate::snapshot& snapshot) {
        std::cout << "dog: " << boost::json::serialize(snapshot.context) << '\n';
    });
if (!subscribed.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!settled(system.send(*owner_actor, {.type = "play", .payload = {}}))) {
    return 1;
}

It prints:

dog: {"fetched":1}
dog: {"fetched":2}

The owner sends two fetch events in one macrostep. They leave once that macrostep has settled, and the dog takes them one at a time, each a macrostep of its own, in the order they were sent.

xactor’s scheduler gives each actor a FIFO mailbox and keeps one FIFO queue of the actors that have messages waiting. Sending a message only puts it in its target’s mailbox; one turn at a time, on one thread, the scheduler hands the actor at the front of the queue its next message, and puts the actor back at the end of the queue while it has more. So a delivery is queued, never nested in the sender’s call, a run depends on nothing but the order in which messages were queued, and the same input always gives the same run (xactor’s guarantees 1 and 2). An actor receives what one sender sends it in the order sent. Between actors the order can differ from XState’s, which delivers an event to an idle actor at once, nested in the sender’s call: a subscriber of the owner here would hear the owner’s snapshot before the dog’s two, where XState’s hears it after them (Interleaving across actors).

Spawning

An actor can create actors, its children, to hand work to: a request the machine waits on, a process with states of its own, one helper for each item of a list. A machine does it in two ways. A state’s invoke starts a child when the state is entered and stops it when the state is left. A spawn_child_action, XState’s spawnChild, starts one that lives until a stop_child_action, XState’s stopChild, stops it, it ends, or its parent is done or stopped; a parent that fails leaves it running, as in XState. Either way the parent knows the child by an id and sends it events. A child that is done or fails tells its parent with an event: xstate.done.actor.<id>, with its output, or xstate.error.actor.<id>, with its error. An invoke takes these with its onDone and onError; a spawned child’s are taken under on. A child that is stopped sends no event.

Here the owner invokes its dog while it walks, and goes home when the dog has fetched its stick:

const boost::json::value dog_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "dog",
    "initial": "sniffing",
    "states": {
        "sniffing": {"on": {"finds a stick": "fetched"}},
        "fetched": {"type": "final"}
    },
    "output": {"brought": "a stick"}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> dog = xstate::create_machine(dog_config, {});
if (!dog.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actors.emplace("dog", xstate::machine_actor{*dog});
const boost::json::value owner_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "owner",
    "initial": "walking",
    "states": {
        "walking": {"invoke": {"id": "dog", "src": "dog", "onDone": "home"}},
        "home": {"type": "final"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> owner =
    xstate::create_machine(owner_config, implementations);
if (!owner.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> owner_actor = system.create_actor(*owner);
if (!owner_actor.has_value() || !settled(system.start(*owner_actor))) {
    return 1;
}
const std::optional<xstate::actor_ref> dog_actor = system.child_of(*owner_actor, "dog");
if (!dog_actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
print("owner", system.snapshot_of(*owner_actor));
print("dog", system.snapshot_of(*dog_actor));

if (!settled(system.send(*dog_actor, {.type = "finds a stick", .payload = {}}))) {
    return 1;
}
print("owner", system.snapshot_of(*owner_actor));
print("dog", system.snapshot_of(*dog_actor));

print, a helper of the program, writes who an actor is, its state value, its status, and its output when it has one. It prints:

owner: "walking", active
dog: "sniffing", active
owner: "home", done
dog: "fetched", done, output {"brought":"a stick"}

An invoke names its child by src, which the implementations register, as XState’s setup({ actors }) does: a machine_actor for a machine, or a host_actor for work done outside the machines, which XState writes as a promise. child_of finds a child by its parent and its id. When the dog reaches its final state it is done, with its output; the owner receives xstate.done.actor.dog, and its onDone takes it home. XState also takes inline logic as a src; JSON cannot hold it, so xstate takes a name only (An invoke’s src).

The same owner can spawn the same dog instead: an entry action spawns it, and the owner takes its done event under on, since onDone belongs to an invoke. The dog’s machine is the one above:

const xstate::spawn_child_action adopt{
    .src = "dog",
    .id = std::string("dog"),
    .system_id = std::nullopt,
    .input = std::nullopt,
};
xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actors.emplace("dog", xstate::machine_actor{*dog});
implementations.actions.emplace("adopt", adopt);
const boost::json::value owner_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "owner",
    "initial": "walking",
    "states": {
        "walking": {
            "entry": "adopt",
            "on": {"xstate.done.actor.dog": "home"}
        },
        "home": {"type": "final"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> owner =
    xstate::create_machine(owner_config, implementations);
if (!owner.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> owner_actor = system.create_actor(*owner);
if (!owner_actor.has_value() || !settled(system.start(*owner_actor))) {
    return 1;
}
const std::optional<xstate::actor_ref> dog_actor = system.child_of(*owner_actor, "dog");
if (!dog_actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
print("owner", system.snapshot_of(*owner_actor));

if (!settled(system.send(*dog_actor, {.type = "finds a stick", .payload = {}}))) {
    return 1;
}
print("owner", system.snapshot_of(*owner_actor));
print("dog", system.snapshot_of(*dog_actor));

It prints:

owner: "walking", active
owner: "home", done
dog: "fetched", done, output {"brought":"a stick"}

adopt is a built-in action registered by name, as throw is in Messages and mailboxes; it names the child’s src and its id. Invoking actors, Spawning actors and Host actors take each in depth.

The system

A system is the set of actors that live together: a root actor, with its children and theirs. An actor can be registered in the system under a name, its systemId, and any actor of the system can then reach it by that name alone, without holding a reference to it or knowing where it sits in the family. A name is for actors that need each other but are not parent and child: two siblings, or a service that actors in every branch of the family call.

A machine names a registered actor with the target #system:<systemId>. XState writes that target as a function of the system, ({ system }) => system.get('vet'), which a JSON config cannot hold (Targets that name actors). The host finds a registered actor with get, XState’s system.get. Here the owner invokes a vet and a dog walker, and the walker calls the vet when the dog limps:

/** The symptom event, its symptom taken from the action's params. */
xstate::result<xstate::event> symptom_event(const xstate::action_args& args) {
    const boost::json::object* params = args.params.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* symptom =
        params == nullptr ? nullptr : params->if_contains("symptom");
    if (symptom == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<xstate::event>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return xstate::event{.type = "symptom", .payload = {{"symptom", *symptom}}};
}

/** Keeps the symptom of the event being handled. */
xstate::result<boost::json::object> note(const xstate::action_args& args) {
    const boost::json::value* symptom = args.event.payload.if_contains("symptom");
    if (symptom == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"last", *symptom}};
}
xstate::implementations vet_implementations;
vet_implementations.actions.emplace("note", xstate::assign_action{.assignment = note});
const boost::json::value vet_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "vet",
    "context": {"last": null},
    "on": {"symptom": {"actions": "note"}}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> vet =
    xstate::create_machine(vet_config, vet_implementations);
if (!vet.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::send_to_action call_vet{
    .target = "#system:vet",
    .event = symptom_event,
    .id = std::nullopt,
    .delay = std::nullopt,
};
xstate::implementations walker_implementations;
walker_implementations.actions.emplace("callVet", call_vet);
const boost::json::value walker_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "walker",
    "on": {
        "sees a limp": {"actions": {"type": "callVet", "params": {"symptom": "limps"}}}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> walker =
    xstate::create_machine(walker_config, walker_implementations);
if (!walker.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::implementations owner_implementations;
owner_implementations.actors.emplace("vet", xstate::machine_actor{*vet});
owner_implementations.actors.emplace("walker", xstate::machine_actor{*walker});
const boost::json::value owner_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "owner",
    "invoke": [
        {"id": "vet", "src": "vet", "systemId": "vet"},
        {"id": "walker", "src": "walker"}
    ]
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> owner =
    xstate::create_machine(owner_config, owner_implementations);
if (!owner.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> owner_actor = system.create_actor(*owner);
if (!owner_actor.has_value() || !settled(system.start(*owner_actor))) {
    return 1;
}
const std::optional<xstate::actor_ref> walker_actor = system.child_of(*owner_actor, "walker");
if (!walker_actor.has_value() ||
    !settled(system.send(*walker_actor, {.type = "sees a limp", .payload = {}}))) {
    return 1;
}
const std::optional<xstate::actor_ref> vet_actor = system.get("vet");
if (!vet_actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::snapshot* heard = system.snapshot_of(*vet_actor);
if (heard == nullptr) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << "vet: " << boost::json::serialize(heard->context) << '\n';

It prints:

vet: {"last":"limps"}

The walker and the vet are siblings: neither holds the other, and the walker reaches the vet by its systemId alone. A systemId names one actor at a time: a second claim fails the actor that makes it, with system_id_taken, and the host’s create_actor refuses a name already held. The roots one actor_system creates share one system, where XState gives each root its own, because an actor_system owns one xactor scheduler with its registry and xstate keeps no global state; a program that wants XState’s arrangement gives each root an actor_system of its own (One system per actor_system). Its rules follow in the system’s own section.

Actors

When a machine runs as an actor, the actor keeps the machine’s snapshot, takes its events one at a time and executes what each macrostep returns. It receives events, sends events to other actors and changes its behaviour by the events it receives. It can invoke and spawn other actors, its children, and it hears from them when they are done or fail.

An actor is what a machine needs once it does not live alone. The pure functions suit one machine whose caller keeps the snapshot and executes its actions (Pure transitions and the macrostep cursor). A machine that invokes another, sends it events, waits on a timer or waits on work the host does needs something to run all of that, in order, between the host’s calls. An actor does it, and the host only creates actors, sends them events, brings the time and reads what the actors publish.

Actor logic

An actor runs its logic, what XState calls actor logic. xstate knows two kinds:

Logic Receives events Sends events Has children Input Output

A machine, machine_actor: XState’s createMachine

yes

yes

yes

yes

yes

A host actor, host_actor: in place of XState’s fromPromise

no

only its done or error event

no

yes

yes

The host creates a machine actor with create_actor, and a machine invokes or spawns one where implementations.actors names a machine_actor. A host actor is always a child, which a machine invokes or spawns where implementations.actors names a host_actor, and whose work the host does (Host actors). XState’s callback, observable and transition actors have no counterpart yet (What is not ported).

Every actor lives in an actor_system: one xactor scheduler on the host’s thread, which the host drives by calling the system. The scheduler holds a first-in first-out mailbox for each actor and a first-in first-out queue of the actors that have work, and each turn hands one message to one actor (How the layer runs). So the actor model holds as XState applies it: an actor changes only its own state, talks only by events, takes one event at a time from its mailbox, its whole macrostep, and creates children.

Creating an actor

An actor_system is XState’s createActor and the system it creates, in one object. create_actor creates an actor from a machine, not yet started; start runs its initial macrostep; send delivers an event; stop stops it with its children. XState makes a system for each root actor, implicitly; xstate makes it explicit, because the system owns what a host must decide: the fuel of each execution its calls open, the time, and the systemIds its actors share. The machine is the toggle of Stately’s page on state machine actors, and a listener prints each snapshot:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "initial": "inactive",
    "states": {
        "inactive": {"on": {"toggle": {"target": "active"}}},
        "active": {"on": {"toggle": {"target": "inactive"}}}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> toggle_machine = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!toggle_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> toggle_actor = system.create_actor(*toggle_machine);
if (!toggle_actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<void> subscribed =
    system.subscribe(*toggle_actor, [](const xstate::snapshot& snapshot) {
        std::cout << boost::json::serialize(snapshot.value) << '\n';
    });
if (!subscribed.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

if (!system.start(*toggle_actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
// logs "inactive"
const xstate::event toggle{.type = "toggle", .payload = {}};
if (!system.send(*toggle_actor, toggle).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
// logs "active"
if (!system.send(*toggle_actor, toggle).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
// logs "inactive"

if (!system.stop(*toggle_actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<xactor::status> status = system.status_of(*toggle_actor);
if (!status.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << "status: " << name_of(*status) << '\n';

It prints:

"inactive"
"active"
"inactive"
status: stopped

create_actor returns result<actor_ref>: the actor’s address on xactor, or system_id_taken (Options). Every operation names the actor by that address, through the system. subscribe hears the snapshots the actor settles in while it is active, and the one it is done in, as XState’s does: the initial one on start, then one for each event, whether it took a transition or not (Watching an actor).

The constructor takes budgets, xactor’s limits. Its one member, fuel, bounds the work of one execution, a million units by default. A call that delivers opens executions of its own, each with the whole budget: one for each input it applies and, for resume(), one for each parked actor. So one call can spend more than one budget (Fuel, parking and resume). The examples give 10'000, far more than they use, and check only that a call returned no error; a host with a tight budget also checks whether it returned settled or out_of_fuel.

Each call that delivers something, start and send here, and clock_tick, resolve, reject and resume in the later sections, runs the system until no message is left before it returns, as XState’s send processes its event at once. It returns result<run_outcome>: settled, or out_of_fuel when an actor is left parked for want of fuel (Fuel, parking and resume).

A call the system cannot take fails with xactor’s errc::invalid_argument, of the category webcpp.xactor, and changes nothing: a start, a send, a stop, a status_of, a subscribe or an on_emitted whose actor_ref names no actor of the system, a stop of a child, an answer to a request no longer pending (Host actors), and any call that changes the system made from inside a callback (Watching an actor). The other readers refuse nothing: snapshot_of, child_of, parent_of, id_of and get answer nullptr, none or an empty view for what they do not find. xstate’s own codes, such as the system_id_taken of create_actor, are xstate::errc, of the category webcpp.xstate, and none of them is invalid_argument.

The rules of an actor’s life:

  • An event sent before start waits, and runs after the initial macrostep, as XState’s mailbox holds it until the actor starts. A second start does nothing.

  • stop stops a root actor and its whole family, each after its descendants, and returns them. For a child it is xactor’s invalid_argument and changes nothing: a child is its parent’s to stop, as XState’s actor.stop() refuses one.

  • A stopped actor drops what is sent to it.

Snapshots and status

snapshot_of(actor) is a machine actor’s last snapshot (The snapshot), as XState’s getSnapshot().

  • It is published once the macrostep has settled and its actions are resolved, before the effects they deferred (sends, emits, starts, stops and timers) run. Subscribers hear it after those effects. An actor parked before that point (Fuel, parking and resume) still shows the snapshot from before; one parked while running the effects already shows the new one, which its subscribers have not heard yet.

  • It is nullptr before the actor is constructed, and for a host actor. xstate constructs a root on start, where XState’s createActor constructs it at once, so XState’s getSnapshot() has the initial snapshot before start() (The root is constructed on start).

status_of(actor) is xactor’s status: active, done, error or stopped. The snapshot’s own status has only the first three; XState’s has a fourth, 'stopped'. A stopped actor keeps its last snapshot, whose status stays what it was, and status_of says stopped where XState’s snapshot says 'stopped'.

Options

actor_options holds the options of XState’s createActor that concern one actor: input, id and system_id. The others belong to the system: logger is on_log (Watching an actor), inspect is inspect (Inspection), and clock is clock_tick (Delayed events and time). snapshot, which restores a persisted actor, has no counterpart yet. Here one actor is named and registered, and another is left unnamed:

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::actor_options options{
    .input = nullptr,
    .id = "feedback",
    .system_id = "root-id",
};
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> named = system.create_actor(*machine, options);
if (!named.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> unnamed = system.create_actor(*machine);
if (!unnamed.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << system.id_of(*named) << '\n';    // feedback
std::cout << system.id_of(*unnamed) << '\n';  // x:1

if (!system.start(*named).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const std::optional<xstate::actor_ref> found = system.get("root-id");
std::cout << std::boolalpha << (found == *named) << '\n';  // true

It prints:

feedback
x:1
true

  • id is the actor’s id, which id_of(actor) returns. Without one, the id is the actor’s session id, x:<n>, n the number of actors the system created or began to create before it. XState counts the actors of the whole process, so the two agree while the process runs one actor_system with one root (One system per actor_system). The example’s two roots agree with XState only because the first has no children: XState numbers a root’s initial children when it creates the root, xstate when it starts it (The root is constructed on start).

  • system_id registers the actor under that name at once: get(system_id) finds it, and a #system: target names it (The system). A name another running actor holds is refused with system_id_taken. The empty name registers nothing, as XState registers only a truthy one.

  • input is the machine’s input (Machine actors).

Watching an actor

The host learns what its actors do through callbacks it registers on the system.

  • subscribe(actor, f) hands f each snapshot the actor settles in while it is active, and the one it is done in: XState’s actor.subscribe. A failed actor’s snapshot is not handed over; XState hands the error to an observer’s error callback, which xstate does not have, and status_of tells it.

  • on_emitted(actor, f) hands f each event the actor emits, in order: XState’s actor.on('*', f) (Emitting events). The listener reads the event’s type.

  • on_action(f) hands f every custom action of every actor, with the actor that returned it.

  • on_log(f) hands f every log of every actor (Log), with the actor, the value, nullptr for JavaScript’s undefined, and the label: XState’s logger option. The label is empty when the log has none, where XState calls the logger with the value alone.

A custom action is one the implementations do not hold (Custom actions). XState runs it as a function of the machine; xstate hands it to the host as its type and params, because JSON cannot hold a function and the library runs no effect of its own: the host decides what greet does. Here a machine greets on entry, and answers ping by emitting pong and logging the event:

xstate::result<xstate::event> pong(const xstate::action_args& /*args*/) {
    return xstate::event{.type = "pong", .payload = {}};
}

xstate::result<std::optional<boost::json::value>> the_event(const xstate::action_args& args) {
    return std::optional<boost::json::value>(xstate::to_json(args.event));
}
xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actions.emplace("answer", xstate::emit_action{.event = pong});
implementations.actions.emplace("note",
                                xstate::log_action{.value = the_event, .label = "received"});
// greet has no implementation: it is a custom action, the host's to run.
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "entry": {"type": "greet", "params": {"name": "Ada"}},
    "on": {"ping": {"actions": ["answer", "note"]}}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> machine = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<void> acting =
    system.on_action([](xstate::actor_ref, const xstate::action& custom) {
        std::cout << "action " << custom.type << ' ' << boost::json::serialize(custom.params)
                  << '\n';
    });
if (!acting.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<void> logging = system.on_log(
    [](xstate::actor_ref, const boost::json::value* value, std::string_view label) {
        if (value != nullptr) {
            std::cout << "log " << label << ' ' << boost::json::serialize(*value) << '\n';
        }
    });
if (!logging.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*machine);
if (!actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<void> listening =
    system.on_emitted(*actor, [](const xstate::event& emitted) {
        std::cout << "emitted " << boost::json::serialize(xstate::to_json(emitted)) << '\n';
    });
if (!listening.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

if (!system.start(*actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
// logs: action greet {"name":"Ada"}
if (!system.send(*actor, {.type = "ping", .payload = {}}).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
// logs: log received {"type":"ping"}
// logs: emitted {"type":"pong"}

It prints:

action greet {"name":"Ada"}
log received {"type":"ping"}
emitted {"type":"pong"}

The order is XState’s. Custom actions and logs are handed over as each microstep’s actions are resolved, those of the initial macrostep when the actor starts; emits, like sends, wait until the macrostep has settled, as XState defers them. So note logs before answer emits, though the machine lists answer first. A macrostep that fails has handed over the custom actions and logs it resolved before the failure, as XState’s running actor has run them by then; an initial macrostep that fails hands over none, as XState’s start() runs no initial action of an actor whose construction failed.

subscribe and on_emitted add a listener of one actor, and an empty one is none; such a listener is kept as long as the system lives, with no unsubscribe. Both refuse an address that names no actor with invalid_argument, as send does. on_action, on_log and inspect hold one callback for the whole system: each call replaces the previous one, so an empty callback removes it. Each returns a result<void>.

A callback, a subscribe or on_emitted listener, the on_action or on_log callback or the inspector, runs inside an actor’s turn, while the system runs. It may call the const members, which read the system: snapshot_of, status_of, get, child_of, parent_of, id_of and host_requests. Every other member changes the system: create_actor, start, send, clock_tick, resolve, reject, resume, run_until_idle, stop, and the registrations subscribe, on_emitted, on_action, on_log and inspect. A call to one of them from a callback returns xactor’s invalid_argument and changes nothing. A host that must act on what it heard records it in the callback and acts once the call that ran the system has returned. XState accepts a send from a subscriber and handles it after the update in progress (A callback that calls the system back).

Inspection

inspect(inspector) is XState’s inspect option: it hears every actor of the system, and replaces the inspector given before. An inspector holds three callbacks, each of which may be left empty:

XState xstate

@xstate.actor, when an actor is created

started, when an actor starts

@xstate.snapshot, each snapshot with the event that caused it

settled, each macrostep a machine actor settles, with its machine, the event that began the macrostep and the snapshot

@xstate.action of the type xstate.emit, whose params hold the event, reported when the action runs; the actor’s actor.on listeners hear the event once the macrostep has settled

emitted, each event an actor emits, just before its on_emitted listeners hear it

@xstate.action of every other type: each custom action, and each built-in action but assign and enqueueActions: a send, a raise, a log, a spawn, a stop or a cancel

none in the inspector: on_action hears the custom actions and on_log the logs, and no callback hears the other built-in actions

@xstate.event and @xstate.microstep

none: the macrostep cursor gives each microstep (The macrostep cursor)

A macrostep that an unhandled error event fails is heard, with the status error and the error actor_failed, as XState inspects the snapshot that event leaves. Any other that fails while it is computed or while its actions resolve is not heard. Nor does XState inspect one where it throws, as for an implementation that fails, a systemId taken when a spawn resolves or a target that names no actor when a send resolves; where it does not fail, on a context that is not an object (A context that is not an object), its inspector hears the macrostep as any other. A macrostep whose deferred effect fails, such as a send to a child gone when it is bound (A sendTo whose child is gone), is heard with the snapshot it reached, as XState’s update inspects the snapshot it was given; snapshot_of has the status error.

Here an inspector watches the toggle of the first example, whose active state now emits activated on entry:

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<void> inspecting = system.inspect(xstate::inspector{
    .started = [](xstate::actor_ref) { std::cout << "started\n"; },
    .settled =
        [](xstate::actor_ref, const xstate::machine&, const xstate::event& cause,
           const xstate::snapshot& settled) {
            std::cout << "settled " << cause.type << ' '
                      << boost::json::serialize(settled.value) << '\n';
        },
    .emitted =
        [](xstate::actor_ref, const xstate::event& emitted) {
            std::cout << "emitted " << emitted.type << '\n';
        },
});
if (!inspecting.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*machine);
if (!actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.start(*actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.send(*actor, {.type = "toggle", .payload = {}}).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

It prints:

started
settled xstate.init "inactive"
emitted activated
settled toggle "active"

The inspector hears the actor start, then its initial macrostep settle for xstate.init. The toggle enters active, whose entry emits activated: the inspector hears the emit while the actor runs the effects of that macrostep, before the snapshot of toggle, which it hears once those effects have run.

Machine actors

A machine actor runs a machine: it receives events, sends events, has children, starts from an input and ends with an output. create_actor creates one from a machine; a machine child is a machine_actor of the implementations (Invoking actors).

Its input is actor_options::input. The machine reads it in implementations.context, XState’s context: ({ input }) => ..., which returns result<boost::json::value>. A failure it returns fails the initial macrostep with its code, and a value that is not an object fails it with implementation_failed, where XState merges whatever its function returns into an empty object (A context that is not an object). The event xstate.init carries the input too. When the machine reaches its top-level final state, the actor is done: status_of says done, its last snapshot holds the output, and it takes no more events. The output here is the context, which implementations.outputs computes under the root’s id, XState’s output: ({ context }) => context. A machine’s input and its output have sections of their own. The example is the feedback machine of Stately’s page on state machine actors, given a final state and an output.

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.context =
    [](const boost::json::value& input) -> xstate::result<boost::json::value> {
    const boost::json::object* given = input.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* rating =
        given == nullptr ? nullptr : given->if_contains("defaultRating");
    if (rating == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::value>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"rating", *rating}};
};
// By the root's id: the machine's output.
implementations.outputs.emplace(
    "feedback",
    [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<std::optional<boost::json::value>> {
        return std::optional<boost::json::value>(args.context);
    });
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "feedback",
    "initial": "question",
    "states": {
        "question": {"on": {"submit": "thanks"}},
        "thanks": {"type": "final"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!feedback_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::actor_options options{
    .input = boost::json::object{{"defaultRating", 3}},
    .id = std::nullopt,
    .system_id = std::nullopt,
};
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> feedback_actor =
    system.create_actor(*feedback_machine, options);
if (!feedback_actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<void> subscribed =
    system.subscribe(*feedback_actor, [](const xstate::snapshot& snapshot) {
        std::cout << boost::json::serialize(snapshot.context) << '\n';
    });
if (!subscribed.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.start(*feedback_actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
// logs {"rating":3}
if (!system.send(*feedback_actor, {.type = "submit", .payload = {}}).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
// logs {"rating":3}, the snapshot it is done in

const xstate::result<xactor::status> status = system.status_of(*feedback_actor);
if (!status.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::snapshot* last = system.snapshot_of(*feedback_actor);
if (last == nullptr) {
    return 1;
}
if (!last->output.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << "status: " << name_of(*status) << '\n'
          << "output: " << boost::json::serialize(*last->output) << '\n';

It prints:

{"rating":3}
{"rating":3}
status: done
output: {"rating":3}

The listener hears the initial snapshot, its context computed from the input, and the snapshot the actor is done in, after submit; that last snapshot holds the output.

Invoking actors

A state can invoke an actor: a child that starts when the state is entered and stops when the state is exited. Invoking suits work the machine orchestrates without knowing its details: a request to a server, a process with states of its own. An invoke on the root lives as long as the machine. A state’s invoke is one object or a list of them, each a child of its own.

An invoke’s members:

src

The name of an entry of implementations.actors: a machine_actor or a host_actor. XState also takes inline logic, which JSON cannot hold; a name is XState’s setup({ actors }), the logic registered there. A name the implementations do not hold is refused when the machine is created, with unknown_actor, where XState fails later.

id

How the parent knows the child: <index>.<state id> when none is given, as in XState.

input

The child’s input: a JSON value (Input to an invoked actor), or what implementations.inputs computes for the invoke’s id, in place of XState’s input function (An input computed from the context and the event).

onDone

The transition taken on xstate.done.actor.<id>, when the child is done.

onError

The transition taken on xstate.error.actor.<id>, when the child fails.

systemId

A name every actor of the system can find the child by (The system).

A machine can declare onSnapshot too, but the layer sends no xstate.snapshot.<id> event yet, so it is never taken.

The host reaches a child through its parent: child_of(parent, id) is XState’s snapshot.children[id], and the parent’s snapshot lists its children as (id, src) pairs. parent_of(child) goes the other way. Here a parent invokes a worker and takes its output when it is done.

const boost::json::value worker_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "initial": "working",
    "states": {
        "working": {"on": {"finish": "done"}},
        "done": {"type": "final"}
    },
    "output": {"result": 42}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> worker = xstate::create_machine(worker_config, {});
if (!worker.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actors.emplace("worker", xstate::machine_actor{*worker});
implementations.actions.emplace("note",
                                xstate::log_action{.value = the_event, .label = "done"});
const boost::json::value parent_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "initial": "waiting",
    "states": {
        "waiting": {
            "invoke": {
                "src": "worker",
                "id": "worker",
                "onDone": {"target": "finished", "actions": "note"}
            }
        },
        "finished": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> parent_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(parent_config, implementations);
if (!parent_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<void> logging = system.on_log(
    [](xstate::actor_ref, const boost::json::value* value, std::string_view label) {
        if (value != nullptr) {
            std::cout << label << ' ' << boost::json::serialize(*value) << '\n';
        }
    });
if (!logging.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> parent = system.create_actor(*parent_machine);
if (!parent.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.start(*parent).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
print(system, *parent);  // "waiting" ["worker"]

const std::optional<xstate::actor_ref> child = system.child_of(*parent, "worker");
if (!child.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.send(*child, {.type = "finish", .payload = {}}).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
// logs the done event onDone took
print(system, *parent);  // "finished" []

const xstate::result<xactor::status> status = system.status_of(*child);
if (!status.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << "worker: " << name_of(*status) << '\n';

print, a helper of the program, writes the parent’s state value and the ids of its children. It prints:

"waiting" ["worker"]
done {"type":"xstate.done.actor.worker","output":{"result":42},"actorId":"worker"}
"finished" []
worker: done

Entering waiting starts the worker, which the parent lists as its child. When the worker reaches its final state, the parent receives xstate.done.actor.worker with the worker’s output, and onDone logs that event and takes the parent to finished. Leaving waiting removes the worker from the parent’s children; the worker itself is done.

A child’s life follows its parent’s macrosteps, as in XState:

  • A machine child is constructed when its parent resolves the action that spawns it: its initial macrostep runs and its own children are constructed, their systemIds registered, before the parent resolves its next action, so a #system: send later in the same macrostep reaches a grandchild. It starts once the parent’s macrostep has settled, and the custom actions and logs of its initial macrostep are handed over then, none when that macrostep failed (Watching an actor).

  • A child spawned and stopped in the same macrostep never starts: XState constructs it and never starts it, so a state entered and left in one macrostep runs none of its invokes.

  • A transition that re-enters the state (reenter: true) stops its invoked children and starts new ones.

Done and error events

A child that ends tells its parent:

  • xstate.done.actor.<id>, with output and actorId, when it is done; the output is left out when it has none (Actor done events).

  • xstate.error.actor.<id>, with error and actorId, when it fails. A host actor’s error is what the host rejected it with. A machine child’s is the error of the child whose failure failed it in turn, or else the name of its own error code, such as "implementation_failed", where XState’s is the value its implementation threw.

An error event that no transition takes fails the parent too, and the error climbs unchanged: the parent’s snapshot has the status error, the error actor_failed and, as error_value, the event’s error, and the parent reports to its own parent. Here a payment fails, the checkout that invoked it has no onError, and the shop above it handles the checkout’s error. The payment is a host actor, xstate’s stand-in for XState’s promise actor, which the host answers (Host actors): host_requests() lists it as a pending request, and reject fails it with the error given, as rejecting its promise fails XState’s promise actor.

xstate::implementations checkout_implementations;
checkout_implementations.actors.emplace("charge", xstate::host_actor{});
// No onError: the payment's error fails the checkout.
const boost::json::value checkout_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "initial": "paying",
    "states": {
        "paying": {"invoke": {"src": "charge", "id": "payment"}}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> checkout =
    xstate::create_machine(checkout_config, checkout_implementations);
if (!checkout.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::implementations shop_implementations;
shop_implementations.actors.emplace("checkout", xstate::machine_actor{*checkout});
shop_implementations.actions.emplace("note",
                                     xstate::log_action{.value = the_event, .label = "shop"});
const boost::json::value shop_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "initial": "open",
    "states": {
        "open": {
            "invoke": {
                "src": "checkout",
                "id": "checkout",
                "onError": {"target": "failed", "actions": "note"}
            }
        },
        "failed": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> shop_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(shop_config, shop_implementations);
if (!shop_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<void> logging = system.on_log(
    [](xstate::actor_ref, const boost::json::value* value, std::string_view label) {
        if (value != nullptr) {
            std::cout << label << ' ' << boost::json::serialize(*value) << '\n';
        }
    });
if (!logging.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> shop = system.create_actor(*shop_machine);
if (!shop.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.start(*shop).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const std::optional<xstate::actor_ref> checkout_actor = system.child_of(*shop, "checkout");
if (!checkout_actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const std::vector<xstate::host_request> requests = system.host_requests();
if (requests.empty()) {
    return 1;
}
const boost::json::object declined{{"code", "declined"}};
if (!system.reject(requests.front(), declined).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
// logs the error event onError took

const xstate::result<xactor::status> status = system.status_of(*checkout_actor);
if (!status.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::snapshot* failed = system.snapshot_of(*checkout_actor);
if (failed == nullptr) {
    return 1;
}
if (!failed->error_value.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << "checkout: " << name_of(*status) << ' '
          << boost::json::serialize(*failed->error_value) << '\n';
std::cout << "error code: " << failed->error.message() << '\n';

It prints:

shop {"type":"xstate.error.actor.checkout","error":{"code":"declined"},"actorId":"checkout"}
checkout: error {"code":"declined"}
error code: actor_failed

The checkout’s snapshot holds the code actor_failed in error, since every failure in xstate is an error_code, and the payment’s error in error_value, which the shop’s event carries unchanged. XState’s snapshot holds the value itself in error, and has no code to print (Failures are values). A failed actor’s children keep running, as in XState; a done actor’s were stopped by its last macrostep.

Spawning actors

Invoking ties a child to a state. Some children must outlive a state, or come in a number the machine learns as it runs, one per item of a list. Those are spawned: spawn_child_action, XState’s spawnChild, creates a child that lives until a stop_child_action, XState’s stopChild, stops it, or until its parent is done or stopped; a failed parent’s children keep running, as in XState (Done and error events).

spawn_child_action holds XState’s options: src, the actor’s name in implementations.actors; id, a string, or an id_maker that computes it when the action resolves; system_id; and input, a value_maker (Input to a spawned actor). An id left out is the empty string, and the child is keyed under "", where XState keys a child spawned without an id "undefined" (A spawned child without an id). XState’s other way to spawn, spawn inside assign, keeps an actor reference in the context, which JSON cannot hold; it has no counterpart. The example is the one of Stately’s page on spawning, with its children registered by name. spawning makes each spawn action:

/** XState's spawnChild('childMachine', { id }). */
xstate::spawn_child_action spawning(std::string_view id) {
    return xstate::spawn_child_action{
        .src = "childMachine",
        .id = std::string(id),
        .system_id = std::nullopt,
        .input = std::nullopt,
    };
}
const boost::json::value child_config = boost::json::parse(R"({"id": "child"})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> child_machine = xstate::create_machine(child_config, {});
if (!child_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actors.emplace("childMachine", xstate::machine_actor{*child_machine});
implementations.actions.emplace("spawnChild1", spawning("child-1"));
implementations.actions.emplace("spawnChild2", spawning("child-2"));
implementations.actions.emplace("spawnChild3", spawning("child-3"));
implementations.actions.emplace("stopChild2", xstate::stop_child_action{.id = "child-2"});
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "entry": ["spawnChild1", "spawnChild2", "spawnChild3"],
    "on": {"STOP": {"actions": "stopChild2"}}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> parent_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!parent_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> parent = system.create_actor(*parent_machine);
if (!parent.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.start(*parent).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
print_children(system, *parent);  // ["child-1","child-2","child-3"]

const std::optional<xstate::actor_ref> child2 = system.child_of(*parent, "child-2");
if (!child2.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.send(*parent, {.type = "STOP", .payload = {}}).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
print_children(system, *parent);  // ["child-1","child-3"]

const xstate::result<xactor::status> status = system.status_of(*child2);
if (!status.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << "child-2: " << name_of(*status) << '\n';

print_children, a helper of the program, writes the ids of the parent’s children. It prints:

["child-1","child-2","child-3"]
["child-1","child-3"]
child-2: stopped

The entry spawns the three children, which the parent lists in the order they were spawned. STOP stops child-2: it leaves the list, and its status is stopped.

Stopping a child

A stop_child_action stops the child its id names. The systemIds of the child’s family are released at once, or, in an initial macrostep, when the actor starts, since that macrostep defers everything to the start. The parent forgets the child, which leaves the snapshot’s children. A started child receives the stop behind everything already sent to it: it finishes the macrostep it runs and the events that arrived before, ignores what arrives after, asks its own children to stop the same way, and stops, running no exit action. A child that has already ended ignores the stop; a failed one’s children keep running, as in XState. A child spawned and stopped in the same macrostep never starts (Invoking actors). Leaving a state stops its invoked children the same way.

Sending events between actors

A machine sends an event with a send_to_action, XState’s sendTo (Sending to other actors), whose target is a string:

XState xstate’s target

sendTo('child', event)

"child" or "#_child": the child with that id

sendParent(event)

"#_parent", or a send_parent_action

sendTo('#_internal', event)

"#_internal": the actor itself, as an event of its own

sendTo(({ system }) => system.get('name'), event)

"#system:name": the actor registered under that systemId

forwardTo('child')

a forward_to_action, which sends the event being handled

The target is resolved when the action resolves, and the event is delivered once the macrostep has settled, as XState defers its sendTo. A target that names no actor fails the sender with unknown_target, where XState throws. A #system: target under which nothing is registered sends to the actor itself, as XState’s sendTo of an undefined actor does; a forward_to_action fails there with unknown_target, as XState’s development build throws.

An actor reference is not data (Targets that name actors). XState can put self in an event, and the receiver can answer event.sender; xstate’s events hold JSON, so an answer goes to #_parent, to a child’s id or to a systemId. The example is Stately’s, where the server answers the client’s sender; here the server answers its parent, the client that invoked it.

xstate::implementations server_implementations;
// The server answers the actor that sent CODE, its parent.
const xstate::send_parent_action answer{
    .event = token,
    .id = std::nullopt,
    .delay = std::nullopt,
};
server_implementations.actions.emplace("answer", answer);
const boost::json::value server_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "server",
    "initial": "waitingForCode",
    "states": {
        "waitingForCode": {"on": {"CODE": {"actions": "answer"}}}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> auth_server_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(server_config, server_implementations);
if (!auth_server_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::implementations client_implementations;
client_implementations.actors.emplace("authServer",
                                      xstate::machine_actor{*auth_server_machine});
const xstate::send_to_action send_code{
    .target = "auth-server",
    .event = code,
    .id = std::nullopt,
    .delay = std::nullopt,
};
client_implementations.actions.emplace("sendCode", send_code);
const boost::json::value client_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "client",
    "initial": "idle",
    "states": {
        "idle": {"on": {"AUTH": {"target": "authorizing"}}},
        "authorizing": {
            "invoke": {"id": "auth-server", "src": "authServer"},
            "entry": "sendCode",
            "on": {"TOKEN": {"target": "authorized"}}
        },
        "authorized": {"type": "final"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> auth_client_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(client_config, client_implementations);
if (!auth_client_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> client = system.create_actor(*auth_client_machine);
if (!client.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<void> subscribed =
    system.subscribe(*client, [](const xstate::snapshot& snapshot) {
        std::cout << boost::json::serialize(snapshot.value) << '\n';
    });
if (!subscribed.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.start(*client).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.send(*client, {.type = "AUTH", .payload = {}}).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
// logs "idle", "authorizing", then "authorized"

It prints:

"idle"
"authorizing"
"authorized"

AUTH takes the client to authorizing, which invokes the server and, on entry, sends it CODE. The entry’s send names the state’s own invoke, which does not exist yet when the entry action is resolved; the event waits until the child has started, as in XState. The server answers TOKEN, which takes the client to authorized. Stately’s server answers after a second, with { delay: 1000 }; with .delay = xstate::delay_ref{std::uint64_t{1000}}, the token arrives when the host brings the time to 1000 (Delayed events and time).

Each actor receives what one sender sends it in the order sent. Between senders the order can differ from XState’s, which delivers an event to an idle actor at once, nested in the sender’s call, where xactor queues every delivery (Interleaving across actors).

The system

All the actors of an actor_system belong to one system. An actor registered under a systemId can be found by any other: an invoke’s systemId, a spawn’s system_id and actor_options::system_id register one. From the host, get(system_id) finds it, XState’s system.get; from a machine, a send’s target #system:<systemId> names it, where XState writes ({ system }) => system.get(id), a function JSON cannot hold. The example is the one of Stately’s page on systems: a feedback machine invokes a form and a notifier, each under a systemId, and the form notifies the notifier by name. That page’s machine registers no notifier; this one invokes one, so the event has somewhere to go.

xstate::result<xstate::event> notification(const xstate::action_args& /*args*/) {
    return xstate::event{.type = "notify", .payload = {{"message", "Form submitted!"}}};
}

/** {last: event.message} */
xstate::result<boost::json::object> keep_last(const xstate::action_args& args) {
    const boost::json::value* message = args.event.payload.if_contains("message");
    if (message == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"last", *message}};
}
xstate::implementations notifier_implementations;
notifier_implementations.actions.emplace("keep",
                                         xstate::assign_action{.assignment = keep_last});
const boost::json::value notifier_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "context": {"last": null},
    "on": {"notify": {"actions": "keep"}}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> notifier_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(notifier_config, notifier_implementations);
if (!notifier_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::implementations form_implementations;
const xstate::send_to_action notify{
    .target = "#system:notifier",
    .event = notification,
    .id = std::nullopt,
    .delay = std::nullopt,
};
form_implementations.actions.emplace("notify", notify);
const boost::json::value form_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "on": {"submit": {"actions": "notify"}}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> form_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(form_config, form_implementations);
if (!form_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::implementations feedback_implementations;
feedback_implementations.actors.emplace("formMachine", xstate::machine_actor{*form_machine});
feedback_implementations.actors.emplace("notifierMachine",
                                        xstate::machine_actor{*notifier_machine});
const boost::json::value feedback_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "invoke": [
        {"systemId": "formMachine", "src": "formMachine"},
        {"systemId": "notifier", "src": "notifierMachine"}
    ]
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> feedback_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(feedback_config, feedback_implementations);
if (!feedback_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> feedback_actor = system.create_actor(*feedback_machine);
if (!feedback_actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.start(*feedback_actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const std::optional<xstate::actor_ref> form = system.get("formMachine");
if (!form.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.send(*form, {.type = "submit", .payload = {}}).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const std::optional<xstate::actor_ref> notifier = system.get("notifier");
if (!notifier.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::snapshot* notified = system.snapshot_of(*notifier);
if (notified == nullptr) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(notified->context) << '\n';
// logs {"last":"Form submitted!"}

It prints:

{"last":"Form submitted!"}

A systemId names its actor from the actor’s creation until it is done, failed or stopped, or until a stopChild of it or of an ancestor releases it. A claim of a name another actor holds fails the claiming actor with system_id_taken, as XState throws; create_actor returns the error instead.

The roots of one actor_system share one system: their systemIds, get and the #system: targets. XState’s createActor makes a system for each root; a host that wants that creates an actor_system for each root (One system per actor_system). The host stops a system by stopping its roots: stop refuses a child.

Delayed events and time

Every after and every delayed built-in action that sends arms a timer (Delayed raise, ids and cancel): a delayed raise_action, send_to_action, send_parent_action or forward_to_action. The timer is owned by the actor that armed it, under the action’s id when it has one, and a cancel_action of that id removes it. Only built-in actions arm one: a custom action goes to on_action, whatever its type or params. The machine never reads a clock, and neither does the system: the host brings the time. clock_tick(now) moves the system’s clock to now, in milliseconds, and releases the timers due by then one at a time, by deadline and then by arming order, running the system after each. It is XState’s SimulatedClock, passed to createActor as its clock, and its set(now). The machine core’s simulated_clock is the clock of a machine run without actors: it schedules only the built-in delayed raises a step returns, and leaves a custom action to its caller, whatever its type or params (Delayed events and the simulated clock). A timer is due at the time of the last tick, 0 before any, plus its delay. The example is the delayed send and cancel of Stately’s page on actions. That page does not define someActor; here it is a child the machine invokes, which counts what it receives.

xstate::implementations some_actor_implementations;
some_actor_implementations.actions.emplace("count",
                                           xstate::assign_action{.assignment = increment});
const boost::json::value some_actor_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "context": {"count": 0},
    "on": {"someEvent": {"actions": "count"}}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> some_actor =
    xstate::create_machine(some_actor_config, some_actor_implementations);
if (!some_actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actors.emplace("someActor", xstate::machine_actor{*some_actor});
const xstate::send_to_action transmit{
    .target = "someActor",
    .event = some_event,
    .id = "someId",
    .delay = xstate::delay_ref{std::uint64_t{1000}},
};
implementations.actions.emplace("transmit", transmit);
implementations.actions.emplace("cancelIt", xstate::cancel_action{.id = "someId"});
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "invoke": {"id": "someActor", "src": "someActor"},
    "on": {
        "event": {"actions": "transmit"},
        "cancelEvent": {"actions": "cancelIt"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> machine = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*machine);
if (!actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.start(*actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
// At 0 ms: armed for 1000 ms, then cancelled.
if (!system.send(*actor, {.type = "event", .payload = {}}).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.send(*actor, {.type = "cancelEvent", .payload = {}}).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.clock_tick(1000).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
print_count(system, *actor);  // count 0

// At 1000 ms: armed for 2000 ms.
if (!system.send(*actor, {.type = "event", .payload = {}}).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.clock_tick(1999).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
print_count(system, *actor);  // count 0
if (!system.clock_tick(2000).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
print_count(system, *actor);  // count 1

print_count, a helper of the program, writes the count in the context of the child someActor. It prints:

count 0
count 0
count 1

At 0 ms, event arms a timer for 1000 ms under the id someId, and cancelEvent removes it, so nothing arrives at 1000. At 1000 ms, event arms another, due at 2000: at 1999 it has not fired, and at 2000 it has.

The rules of time:

  • Timers fire one at a time, so the handling of one can cancel a later one of the same tick, as XState’s SimulatedClock fires them. A timer armed during the tick and already due fires in the same call (A timer that falls due during clock_tick).

  • The timers of an actor that has stopped, is done or has failed never fire (Timers of an ended actor).

  • Time is whole milliseconds, where XState’s SimulatedClock takes fractions (Time in whole milliseconds).

  • Bring the time forward only. clock_tick does not refuse a time before the last one, and a timer armed after it counts from the earlier time; XState’s set throws for it, and the core’s simulated_clock refuses it with invalid_config (A tick earlier than the last).

Host actors

A host actor is a child whose work the host does: a request to a server, a file to read, anything that waits on the world outside the machines. It stands for XState’s promise actor, fromPromise, which runs asynchronous work and resolves with an output or rejects with an error. A C++ library with no event loop and no thread cannot await a promise; the host, which owns the I/O, does that work, at its own pace, and answers. A host_actor in implementations.actors registers one. Once started, a host actor is a pending request, a host_request:

Member What it holds

actor

The host actor.

parent

The actor that invoked or spawned it.

id

Its id, as its parent knows it.

src

The name it is registered under.

input

Its input; none for JavaScript’s undefined, when it was given none.

host_requests() lists the pending requests, in the order their actors started. resolve(request, output) ends the host actor done: its parent receives xstate.done.actor.<id> with the output, or without one when the output is none. reject(request, error) ends it failed: its parent receives xstate.error.actor.<id> with the error. Both run the system, as send does. The example is Stately’s user machine, whose promise fetches a user; the host rejects the first request and resolves the second. The invoke’s input, the user id of the context, is computed by user_id_of, registered under the invoke’s id getUser (An input computed from the context and the event), and the host reads it from the request.

/** The input of the invoke getUser: {userId} from the context. */
xstate::result<std::optional<boost::json::value>> user_id_of(const xstate::action_args& args) {
