    const boost::json::object* context = args.context.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* user_id =
        context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("userId");
    if (user_id == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<std::optional<boost::json::value>>(
            xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return std::optional<boost::json::value>(boost::json::object{{"userId", *user_id}});
}

/** {user: event.output} */
xstate::result<boost::json::object> assign_user(const xstate::action_args& args) {
    const boost::json::value* output = args.event.payload.if_contains("output");
    if (output == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"user", *output}};
}

/** {error: event.error} */
xstate::result<boost::json::object> assign_error(const xstate::action_args& args) {
    const boost::json::value* error = args.event.payload.if_contains("error");
    if (error == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"error", *error}};
}
xstate::implementations implementations;
// The promise is the host's work: a host actor.
implementations.actors.emplace("fetchUser", xstate::host_actor{});
implementations.inputs.emplace("getUser", user_id_of);
implementations.actions.emplace("assignUser", xstate::assign_action{.assignment = assign_user});
implementations.actions.emplace("assignError",
                                xstate::assign_action{.assignment = assign_error});
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "user",
    "initial": "idle",
    "context": {"userId": "42", "user": null, "error": null},
    "states": {
        "idle": {"on": {"FETCH": {"target": "loading"}}},
        "loading": {
            "invoke": {
                "id": "getUser",
                "src": "fetchUser",
                "onDone": {"target": "success", "actions": "assignUser"},
                "onError": {"target": "failure", "actions": "assignError"}
            }
        },
        "success": {},
        "failure": {"on": {"RETRY": {"target": "loading"}}}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> user_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!user_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*user_machine);
if (!actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.start(*actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.send(*actor, {.type = "FETCH", .payload = {}}).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::vector<xstate::host_request> requests = system.host_requests();
print_requests(requests);  // request fetchUser getUser {"userId":"42"}
if (requests.empty()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.reject(requests.front(), "Network error").has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
print(system, *actor);  // "failure", with the error

if (!system.send(*actor, {.type = "RETRY", .payload = {}}).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
requests = system.host_requests();
print_requests(requests);  // a new request
if (requests.empty()) {
    return 1;
}
const boost::json::object user{{"name", "David"}, {"location", "Florida"}};
if (!system.resolve(requests.front(), user).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
print(system, *actor);  // "success", with the user

print_requests, a helper of the program, writes each pending request’s src, id and input, and print the state value and the context. It prints:

request fetchUser getUser {"userId":"42"}
"failure" {"userId":"42","user":null,"error":"Network error"}
request fetchUser getUser {"userId":"42"}
"success" {"userId":"42","user":{"name":"David","location":"Florida"},"error":"Network error"}

FETCH enters loading, whose invoke starts the host actor, and its request appears. The rejection takes the machine to failure, with the error in its context; RETRY enters loading again, which invokes a new host actor with a new request, and its resolution takes the machine to success, with the user. The context starts with null for the user and the error: Stately’s page leaves them undefined, and JSON has no undefined.

A host actor takes no event, as XState’s promise actor ignores them. A request ends with its actor: when the invoking state is left, the host actor is stopped and its request is no longer pending, and resolve or reject of it returns xactor’s invalid_argument and changes nothing, as XState ignores a promise that settles after its actor stopped. A host actor is always a child: create_actor takes a machine.

Fuel, parking and resume

XState runs each call to its end: send returns when every macrostep it caused has settled, however long that takes, and a call that enters a cycle of eventless transitions never returns. A host that runs machines it does not trust, or must answer within a budget, cannot allow that. xstate bounds the work of each call by fuel.

The fuel of the budgets given to the constructor (Creating an actor), a million by default, is the fuel of one execution. An execution pays one unit for each microstep, before it runs, and one for each message an actor sends: an event, a child’s construction and the answer to it, a child’s start, a stop. Each timer an actor arms costs one too. Each call that delivers opens executions of its own, each with the whole budget: one for each input it applies, and one for each parked actor resume() continues. The timers a clock_tick releases all share its one execution, so the budget also bounds timers that keep arming within one tick. The start of a machine that invokes one machine child costs five: the root’s initial microstep, the child’s construction, its initial microstep, its answer and its start.

When an execution cannot pay, the actor parks: it keeps its cursor, the actions it has not resolved and the effects it has not run, and the call returns out_of_fuel. A parked actor runs nothing it has not paid for, and nothing twice. An event that reaches it waits behind what it has left, so run to completion holds: no event starts before the macrostep in progress has settled. resume() gives each parked actor a new execution and continues it where it stopped. run_until_idle() delivers nothing: it runs what is queued and returns the same outcome. Every call above already ends with it, so after one of them it only reports whether an actor is still parked.

While an actor is parked, the host’s inputs wait: start, send, clock_tick, resolve and reject are checked, then held in the order made, and return out_of_fuel. resume() applies them once the parked actors have settled, each run to its end before the next, as XState runs each call to its end. stop is never held: it is how the host ends an actor that would never settle. The example runs a chain of eventless transitions on a fuel of 3, then a cycle that never settles; it has no twin, since XState has no fuel.

// GO takes five microsteps: idle to a, then four eventless ones.
const boost::json::value chain_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "initial": "idle",
    "states": {
        "idle": {"on": {"GO": "a"}},
        "a": {"always": "b"},
        "b": {"always": "c"},
        "c": {"always": "d"},
        "d": {"always": "e"},
        "e": {"on": {"PING": "f"}},
        "f": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> chain = xstate::create_machine(chain_config, {});
if (!chain.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 3});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*chain);
if (!actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<xstate::run_outcome> started = system.start(*actor);
if (!started.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
print("start", *started, system, *actor);  // start: settled "idle"

const xstate::result<xstate::run_outcome> go =
    system.send(*actor, {.type = "GO", .payload = {}});
if (!go.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
print("GO", *go, system, *actor);  // GO: out_of_fuel "idle"

const xstate::result<xstate::run_outcome> ping =
    system.send(*actor, {.type = "PING", .payload = {}});
if (!ping.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
print("PING", *ping, system, *actor);  // PING: out_of_fuel "idle"

const xstate::result<xstate::run_outcome> resumed = system.resume();
if (!resumed.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
print("resume", *resumed, system, *actor);  // resume: settled "f"
// An eventless cycle: its initial macrostep never settles.
const boost::json::value spin_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "initial": "ping",
    "states": {
        "ping": {"always": "pong"},
        "pong": {"always": "ping"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> spin = xstate::create_machine(spin_config, {});
if (!spin.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system bounded({.fuel = 100});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> spinner = bounded.create_actor(*spin);
if (!spinner.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<xstate::run_outcome> spun = bounded.start(*spinner);
if (!spun.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
print("start", *spun, bounded, *spinner);  // start: out_of_fuel none
const xstate::result<xstate::run_outcome> again = bounded.resume();
if (!again.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
print("resume", *again, bounded, *spinner);  // resume: out_of_fuel none

if (!bounded.stop(*spinner).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<xactor::status> status = bounded.status_of(*spinner);
if (!status.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << "stop: " << name_of(*status) << '\n';  // stop: stopped

print, a helper of the program, writes the call, the outcome it returned and the state value the actor has published. It prints:

start: settled "idle"
GO: out_of_fuel "idle"
PING: out_of_fuel "idle"
resume: settled "f"
start: out_of_fuel none
resume: out_of_fuel none
stop: stopped

With a fuel of 3, the five microsteps of GO cannot be paid in one call: the actor parks after three, its snapshot still the one from before GO, and PING waits behind it. resume() pays the last two, then runs PING. The second machine’s initial macrostep never settles: its start and each resume() spend a budget of 100 and park it again, before it has published a snapshot, until stop ends it. XState has no fuel (Appendix B, Fuel): it returns from send({ type: 'GO' }) with the actor in "e", and never returns from the createActor of the second machine, since it runs the initial macrostep when it constructs the actor (The root is constructed on start). The macrostep cursor bounds a single machine the same way, one microstep for each call of next() (the cursor’s fuel).

How the layer runs

  • One thread, queued deliveries. The system runs on one xactor scheduler, on the host’s thread (xactor’s model). Each actor has a first-in first-out mailbox, and the actors that have work wait in one first-in first-out queue: a turn takes the actor at its head and hands it the first message of its mailbox, and the actor goes back to the end of the queue while its mailbox holds more. So messages to different actors are served actor by actor, in turns, and can run in another order than the one they were sent in. Nothing runs between two calls of the host, and the same calls give the same run: the order of the events, the callbacks and the timers depends on the inputs alone.

  • Run to completion, per actor. An actor runs one macrostep at a time; an event that arrives while one has not settled waits, and the waiting events run in the order they arrived, each a macrostep of its own.

  • Interleaving. XState delivers an event to an idle actor at once, nested in its sender’s call; xactor queues it. Within one actor the order is XState’s. Across actors it can differ, and so can the order of the callbacks: a parent handles the last sends of a child that is done after the child has released its systemId, and an actor’s start hands over its own initial custom actions before its initial children hand over theirs (Interleaving across actors).

  • Errors are values. No call throws: a refusal is an error code, and an actor that fails says so in its snapshot and to its parent (Failures are values).

  • The host owns the effects. Custom actions, logs, emitted events, snapshots, the work of host actors and time cross between the system and the host as data, through its calls and callbacks, and nothing else does.

Where the layer differs from XState

Within one actor, the layer keeps XState’s order. What differs, between actors and around the host’s calls, follows from running on xactor: fuel and parking (Appendix B, Fuel), deliveries queued instead of nested, a root constructed on start, one system for every root of an actor_system, time in whole milliseconds that the host brings, and callbacks that run inside an actor’s turn. Appendix B gives each with what XState does and why, in What the actor model on xactor imposes, which also names the entries of its other groups that concern actors.

Testing

A test checks that a machine’s logic does what it should: from a known state, given some events, it reaches the states it should and asks for the effects it should. Stately’s testing guide writes each test in three parts, and so does this chapter:

  • Arrange: create the machine, and the actor that runs it when the test needs one.

  • Act: send it events.

  • Assert: check the states it reached and the effects it asked for.

A test is worth its assertions only when the run it checks is the same every time. In xstate nothing in a run depends on the world outside the test:

  • There is no real clock. A delay waits on a clock the test owns, and only the test moves its time (Time).

  • There is no thread and no promise. A pure function returns when its macrostep has settled; a call of the actor system returns when its work is done, or says that it ran out of fuel; the work a promise would do is asked of the host, which the test plays (Mocking effects).

  • There is no exception. An implementation that fails puts the snapshot in error, where the test reads it (Testing failures).

  • A custom action comes back as data, with its params, so the test reads it where XState’s test registers a mock (Testing a machine).

  • Work is counted. A test can bound the microsteps an event may take, and run an actor system with every budget of fuel (Bounding a macrostep, Every fuel budget).

A machine is tested at two levels. With the machine core, <webcpp/xstate.hpp>, a test calls it as a function, a snapshot and an event in, the next snapshot and its actions out, through XState’s pure functions or the macrostep cursor (Pure transitions and the macrostep cursor). With the actor layer, <webcpp/xstate/actors.hpp>, a test runs machines as actors, with their children, their timers and their requests to the host (Actors). A program that uses xactor alone, without machines, tests its actors as xactor’s page shows. The last part of the chapter tells how xstate itself is tested, against XState (How xstate is tested).

The examples are programs that print what they check and return 1 when a check fails, which fails b2 libs/xstate/example (The examples), and each shows its whole main. In a test framework each check is an assertion; xstate’s own tests use Boost.Core’s lightweight_test, and Boost.Test for the suites that run the ported cases (The tests).

Testing a machine

The shortest test of a machine uses its pure functions: get_initial_snapshot returns the snapshot the machine starts in, and transition takes a snapshot and an event and returns the next snapshot with the actions its macrostep returned. No actor is created, and nothing runs between two calls. Stately’s first example tests a toggle that notifies each time it becomes active. On the pure functions, the test reads:

int main() {
    // 1. Arrange
    const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
        "initial": "inactive",
        "states": {
            "inactive": {"on": {"toggle": {"target": "active"}}},
            "active": {
                "entry": {"type": "notify", "params": {"message": "Active!"}},
                "on": {"toggle": {"target": "inactive"}}
            }
        }
    })");
    const xstate::result<xstate::machine> machine = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
    if (!machine.has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }

    // 2. Act
    const xstate::event toggle{.type = "toggle", .payload = {}};
    xstate::snapshot current = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*machine);
    boost::json::array notified_messages;
    for (int sent = 0; sent < 3; ++sent) {
        const auto [next, actions] = xstate::transition(*machine, current, toggle);
        for (const xstate::action& returned : actions) {
            const boost::json::value* message =
                returned.params.is_object() ? returned.params.get_object().if_contains("message")
                                            : nullptr;
            if (returned.type == "notify" && message != nullptr) {
                notified_messages.push_back(*message);
            }
        }
        current = next;
    }

    // 3. Assert
    const boost::json::value expected = boost::json::parse(R"(["Active!", "Active!"])");
    if (current.value != boost::json::value("active") ||
        boost::json::value(notified_messages) != expected) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "value: " << boost::json::serialize(current.value) << '\n';
    std::cout << "notified: " << boost::json::serialize(notified_messages) << '\n';
    return 0;
}

It prints:

value: "active"
notified: ["Active!","Active!"]

notify has no implementation, so it is a custom action, and transition returns it to its caller with its params, {"message": "Active!"}. The test is that caller, and keeps the message of each notify it is returned, where Stately’s test registers notify as a mock, a function that records the params it is called with. A function cannot be JSON, so a config names its actions and leaves the custom ones to the code that runs the machine (Custom actions); a test is such code, and needs no mock. XState’s own transition returns its custom actions the same way. An assign is the one action never returned: it changes the context, and the test asserts on snapshot.context instead.

get_initial_snapshot, transition and the other pure functions run each macrostep to its end, without a bound: on a machine whose eventless transitions never settle, they never return. A test of such a machine drives the cursor itself (Bounding a macrostep).

Testing failures

An implementation can fail: an assign handed an event without the member it needs, a guard that cannot decide. Where XState’s implementation throws, xstate’s returns an error, a result holding an error code: xstate throws nothing, and reports every error as a value. The macrostep then settles at once, with the snapshot it began from, its status error and its error the code the implementation returned. That is the snapshot XState’s actor keeps when an implementation throws, while XState’s pure functions throw instead (Failures are values). So a test of a failure needs no actor. save_age fails when the event carries no age, and the test sends save without one:

/** Keeps the event's age, and fails when the event carries none. */
xstate::result<boost::json::object> save_age(const xstate::action_args& args) {
    const boost::json::value* age = args.event.payload.if_contains("age");
    if (age == nullptr || !age->is_number()) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"age", *age}};
}

int main() {
    // 1. Arrange
    xstate::implementations implementations;
    implementations.actions.emplace("saveAge", xstate::assign_action{.assignment = save_age});
    const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
        "initial": "editing",
        "context": {"age": 0},
        "states": {
            "editing": {"on": {"save": {"target": "saved", "actions": "saveAge"}}},
            "saved": {}
        }
    })");
    const xstate::result<xstate::machine> machine = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
    if (!machine.has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }

    // 2. Act
    const xstate::snapshot editing = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*machine);
    const xstate::event save{.type = "save", .payload = {}};
    const xstate::snapshot failed = xstate::get_next_snapshot(*machine, editing, save);

    // 3. Assert
    if (failed.status != xstate::status::error ||
        failed.error != xstate::errc::implementation_failed ||
        failed.value != boost::json::value("editing")) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "status: error\n";
    std::cout << "value: " << boost::json::serialize(failed.value) << '\n';
    std::cout << "context: " << boost::json::serialize(failed.context) << '\n';
    return 0;
}

It prints:

status: error
value: "editing"
context: {"age":0}

The machine stays where it was before save: in editing, with its context unchanged. The snapshot holds the error_code the implementation returned, here implementation_failed, where XState’s actor holds the thrown Error. An implementation may return any error_code, so a test can tell its own failures apart.

An actor of xstate fails the same way, so the test carries over to the actor layer: after a send that fails, status_of(actor) holds xactor::status::error, and snapshot_of(actor) has the status error and the error code (Snapshots and status). The test reads the failure there: xstate has no error callback, and a listener subscribe registers is not handed a failed snapshot (Watching an actor). A parent hears of a child’s failure through the child’s error event (Done and error events).

Every microstep

A macrostep is everything one event causes: the transition the event selects, then every eventless transition and raised event that follows, each one microstep, until the machine is stable. A snapshot shows where the macrostep ended, and nothing of the way there. A state entered and left by an eventless (always) transition in one macrostep never appears in a snapshot: XState’s subscribers and getSnapshot() never see it, and neither does a test that asserts on the snapshot. Stately’s page suggests listening to the inspection API’s @xstate.microstep events, or changing the machine so that a zero delay replaces the always.

xstate’s cursor shows each microstep without changing the machine (The macrostep cursor). begin starts the macrostep an event runs, and each call of next() runs exactly one microstep and returns a progress: the microstep, with the snapshot it left and the actions it returned, and settled, true on the microstep that ends the macrostep and on no other. In this machine submit enters validating, which an eventless transition leaves at once:

int main() {
    const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
        "initial": "idle",
        "states": {
            "idle": {"on": {"submit": "validating"}},
            "validating": {"entry": "validate", "always": "submitted"},
            "submitted": {}
        }
    })");
    const xstate::result<xstate::machine> machine = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
    if (!machine.has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }

    const xstate::snapshot initial = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*machine);
    const xstate::event submit{.type = "submit", .payload = {}};
    xstate::macrostep step = xstate::begin(*machine, initial, submit);
    std::vector<boost::json::value> values;
    while (!step.done()) {
        const xstate::progress made = step.next();
        values.push_back(made.step.snapshot.value);
        std::cout << boost::json::serialize(made.step.snapshot.value) << ' '
                  << types_of(made.step.actions) << (made.settled ? " settled" : "") << '\n';
    }

    // The transient state was entered, then left in the same macrostep.
    const std::vector<boost::json::value> expected{"validating", "submitted"};
    if (values != expected) {
        return 1;
    }
    return 0;
}

It prints:

"validating" [validate]
"submitted" [] settled

submit entered validating, which returned its entry action validate, and the eventless transition left it in the same macrostep, which settled in submitted. get_microsteps, XState’s getMicrosteps, is the same cursor run to its end: it returns the microsteps as a list, whose last one settles, for a test that needs the list only (The microsteps of an event).

Bounding a macrostep

A cycle of eventless transitions never reaches a stable state. XState runs it until the config’s options.maxIterations, when one is set, makes the macrostep throw; by default there is no bound, and the call never returns (A macrostep that never settles). xstate never stops a macrostep on its own, and does not read that option: the caller that drives the cursor pays for each microstep and decides how many it allows, which is its fuel (Fuel). A test uses the same bound to assert that an event settles within a number of microsteps, and to report a cycle as a failure instead of hanging on it.

In this machine GO takes three microsteps, through two states that eventless transitions leave at once, and SPIN enters a cycle that never settles. settle_within runs at most fuel microsteps of a macrostep, and returns its result only when it has settled:

/**
 Runs at most `fuel` microsteps of a macrostep: its result once it has
 settled, nothing when the fuel ran out first, the cursor left where it
 stopped for its caller to resume or drop.
*/
std::optional<xstate::macrostep_result> settle_within(xstate::macrostep& step, std::size_t fuel) {
    for (std::size_t paid = 0; paid < fuel && !step.done(); ++paid) {
        step.next();
    }
    if (!step.done()) {
        return std::nullopt;
    }
    return step.result();
}

int main() {
    const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
        "initial": "idle",
        "states": {
            "idle": {"on": {"GO": "one", "SPIN": "ping"}},
            "one": {"entry": "first", "always": "two"},
            "two": {"entry": "second", "always": "three"},
            "three": {"entry": "third"},
            "ping": {"always": "pong"},
            "pong": {"always": "ping"}
        }
    })");
    const xstate::result<xstate::machine> machine = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
    if (!machine.has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }
    const xstate::snapshot idle = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*machine);

    const xstate::event go{.type = "GO", .payload = {}};
    xstate::macrostep going = xstate::begin(*machine, idle, go);
    const std::optional<xstate::macrostep_result> went = settle_within(going, 10);
    if (!went.has_value() || went->snapshot.value != boost::json::value("three")) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "GO settles in " << went->microsteps << " microsteps at "
              << boost::json::serialize(went->snapshot.value) << " with " << types_of(went->actions)
              << '\n';

    const xstate::event spin{.type = "SPIN", .payload = {}};
    xstate::macrostep spinning = xstate::begin(*machine, idle, spin);
    if (settle_within(spinning, 1000).has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "SPIN has not settled after 1000 microsteps\n";
    return 0;
}

It prints:

GO settles in 3 microsteps at "three" with [first, second, third]
SPIN has not settled after 1000 microsteps

The test learns of the cycle from a cursor that has not settled when its fuel is spent, where XState’s learns of it from the error its bound throws. The test holds that cursor, spinning, by name: it is still there, where it stopped, to resume or to drop.

Resuming a cursor

A cursor is a value. A caller that runs out of fuel keeps it, or a copy of it, and resumes it later, perhaps in a later request the same process serves; the macrostep goes on exactly where it stopped, with the raised events it had queued. A test of code that pays fuel checks that, wherever it stops, the cursor and a copy of it settle where a run without a stop settles. XState has no cursor, so this test has no twin (The XState twins). finish runs a cursor to its end, and same compares two settled macrosteps:

/** Runs the microsteps a cursor has left; the macrostep it settles. */
xstate::macrostep_result finish(xstate::macrostep& cursor) {
    while (!cursor.done()) {
        cursor.next();
    }
    return cursor.result();
}

/** Whether two settled macrosteps agree: microsteps, snapshot and actions. */
bool same(const xstate::macrostep_result& left, const xstate::macrostep_result& right) {
    return left.microsteps == right.microsteps && left.snapshot.value == right.snapshot.value &&
           left.snapshot.context == right.snapshot.context &&
           types_of(left.actions) == types_of(right.actions);
}

The test stops a cursor after every number of microsteps from 0 to the macrostep’s length, copies it there, and finishes both:

xstate::macrostep straight = xstate::begin(*machine, idle, go);
const xstate::macrostep_result expected = finish(straight);

for (std::size_t stopped = 0; stopped <= expected.microsteps; ++stopped) {
    xstate::macrostep original = xstate::begin(*machine, idle, go);
    for (std::size_t paid = 0; paid < stopped; ++paid) {
        original.next();
    }
    xstate::macrostep copy = original;
    const xstate::macrostep_result from_copy = finish(copy);
    const xstate::macrostep_result from_original = finish(original);
    if (!same(from_copy, expected) || !same(from_original, expected)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "stopped after " << stopped << ", the cursor and its copy settle at "
              << boost::json::serialize(from_copy.snapshot.value) << " with "
              << types_of(from_copy.actions) << '\n';
}

It prints:

stopped after 0, the cursor and its copy settle at "three" with [first, second, third]
stopped after 1, the cursor and its copy settle at "three" with [first, second, third]
stopped after 2, the cursor and its copy settle at "three" with [first, second, third]
stopped after 3, the cursor and its copy settle at "three" with [first, second, third]

Time

A delayed transition, after, waits for time to pass. A test that waits for real time is slow, and fails when the machine running it is slower still, so the test brings the time, as XState’s tests do with a SimulatedClock. xstate’s actor system reads no real clock: clock_tick(now) moves the system’s clock to now, in milliseconds, and the timers due by then fire one at a time. Like the set(now) of XState’s SimulatedClock, and unlike its increment(ms), it takes the time to move to, not an increment, so a second tick 510 ms after a first at 500 is clock_tick(1010) (Delayed events and time). The test runs a traffic light and checks it at 500 ms and at 1010 ms:

/** Moves the system's clock to `now`; whether the actor is then in `expected`, which it prints. */
bool tick(xstate::actor_system& system, xstate::actor_ref actor, std::uint64_t now,
          std::string_view expected) {
    if (system.clock_tick(now) != xstate::run_outcome::settled) {
        return false;
    }
    const xstate::snapshot* current = system.snapshot_of(actor);
    if (current == nullptr) {
        return false;
    }
    std::cout << "after " << now << " ms: " << boost::json::serialize(current->value) << '\n';
    return current->value == boost::json::value(expected);
}

int main() {
    const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
        "id": "light",
        "initial": "green",
        "states": {
            "green": {"after": {"1000": "yellow"}},
            "yellow": {"after": {"1000": "red"}},
            "red": {"after": {"1000": "green"}}
        }
    })");
    const xstate::result<xstate::machine> machine = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
    if (!machine.has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }

    xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
    const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*machine);
    if (!actor.has_value() || system.start(*actor) != xstate::run_outcome::settled) {
        return 1;
    }

    if (!tick(system, *actor, 500, "green") || !tick(system, *actor, 1010, "yellow")) {
        return 1;
    }
    return 0;
}

It prints:

after 500 ms: "green"
after 1010 ms: "yellow"

The light and the test are those of the first test of XState’s after.test.ts, with a simulated clock where XState’s test uses Vitest’s fake timers; xstate’s cases port that test (The ported cases). Time is counted in whole milliseconds, where XState’s clock takes fractions (Time in whole milliseconds).

Without the actor layer, a delay is data. The machine never reads a clock: entering a state with after returns a built-in delayed xstate.raise, and leaving it returns a built-in xstate.cancel. A simulated_clock the test owns takes every action a step returns (apply): it schedules a built-in delayed raise, applies a built-in cancel, and leaves a custom action to the test whatever its type or params. The test moves the time by a duration (increment, as XState’s increment), and pop_due releases each event whose time has come, which the test sends to the machine as a macrostep of its own (Delayed events and the simulated clock). The same test, on the pure functions:

/**
 Gives the clock every action a macrostep returned: it schedules the built-in
 delayed raises and applies the built-in cancels.
*/
void schedule(xstate::simulated_clock& clock, const std::vector<xstate::action>& actions) {
    for (const xstate::action& returned : actions) {
        clock.apply(returned);
    }
}

/**
 Moves the clock forward and delivers each event that comes due, as a
 macrostep of its own, scheduling what that macrostep returns.
*/
void advance(const xstate::machine& machine, xstate::snapshot& current,
             xstate::simulated_clock& clock, std::uint64_t milliseconds) {
    clock.increment(milliseconds);
    while (std::optional<xstate::event> due = clock.pop_due()) {
        auto [next, actions] = xstate::transition(machine, current, *due);
        schedule(clock, actions);
        current = std::move(next);
    }
}

int main() {
    const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
        "id": "light",
        "initial": "green",
        "states": {
            "green": {"after": {"1000": "yellow"}},
            "yellow": {"after": {"1000": "red"}},
            "red": {"after": {"1000": "green"}}
        }
    })");
    const xstate::result<xstate::machine> machine = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
    if (!machine.has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }

    xstate::simulated_clock clock;
    auto [current, actions] = xstate::initial_transition(*machine);
    schedule(clock, actions);

    advance(*machine, current, clock, 500);
    std::cout << "after 500 ms: " << boost::json::serialize(current.value) << '\n';
    if (current.value != boost::json::value("green")) {
        return 1;
    }

    advance(*machine, current, clock, 510);
    std::cout << "after 1010 ms: " << boost::json::serialize(current.value) << '\n';
    if (current.value != boost::json::value("yellow")) {
        return 1;
    }
    return 0;
}

It prints what the actor’s test prints:

after 500 ms: "green"
after 1010 ms: "yellow"

pop_due releases the due events one at a time, by deadline and then in the order they were scheduled, so an event that a delivered one schedules is ordered as XState orders it.

Testing actors

An actor runs a machine over time: it starts, receives events one at a time, keeps its snapshot, and works with its children. A test of an actor creates it from its machine, starts it, sends it events and checks its snapshot after each. In xstate an actor_system is XState’s createActor and its system in one: create_actor makes the actor, start and send deliver to it, and snapshot_of reads its snapshot. Each call that delivers runs the system until nothing is left to do before it returns, as XState’s send() processes at once, so the check that follows it sees all the event did. The call returns a result<run_outcome>: settled; out_of_fuel when an actor ran out of the fuel its budget gives (Every fuel budget); or, when the call is refused, xactor’s errc::invalid_argument, of the category webcpp.xactor, which changes nothing. A call is refused for an actor the system does not know, for an answer to a request no longer pending (Promise actors), and when it is made from inside a callback the test registered on the system, such as a mock (Actions). A test with plenty of fuel expects settled.

Stately’s second example tests a toggle that counts its activations. Its assign, a function in XState’s config, is count_activation here, registered as countActivation: it reads the context it is handed and fails when count is not an integer there (Updating context with assign). expect gathers the test’s checks of the snapshot, Stately’s expect calls, in one function that also prints what it checks:

/** Counts one more activation in the context. */
xstate::result<boost::json::object> count_activation(const xstate::action_args& args) {
    const boost::json::value* count =
        args.context.is_object() ? args.context.get_object().if_contains("count") : nullptr;
    if (count == nullptr || !count->is_int64()) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"count", count->get_int64() + 1}};
}

/** Whether the actor's snapshot has `value` and `context`; prints both. */
bool expect(const xstate::actor_system& system, xstate::actor_ref actor, std::string_view value,
            std::string_view context) {
    const xstate::snapshot* now = system.snapshot_of(actor);
    if (now == nullptr) {
        return false;
    }
    std::cout << boost::json::serialize(now->value) << ' ' << boost::json::serialize(now->context)
              << '\n';
    return now->value == boost::json::parse(value) && now->context == boost::json::parse(context);
}

int main() {
    xstate::implementations implementations;
    implementations.actions.emplace("countActivation",
                                    xstate::assign_action{.assignment = count_activation});
    const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
        "initial": "inactive",
        "context": {"count": 0},
        "states": {
            "inactive": {
                "on": {"activate": {"target": "active", "actions": "countActivation"}}
            },
            "active": {"on": {"deactivate": "inactive"}}
        }
    })");
    const xstate::result<xstate::machine> toggle_machine =
        xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
    if (!toggle_machine.has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }

    xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
    const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*toggle_machine);
    if (!actor.has_value() || system.start(*actor) != xstate::run_outcome::settled) {
        return 1;
    }

    // The initial state
    if (!expect(system, *actor, R"("inactive")", R"({"count": 0})")) {
        return 1;
    }

    // Send an event and test the transition
    const xstate::event activate{.type = "activate", .payload = {}};
    if (system.send(*actor, activate) != xstate::run_outcome::settled ||
        !expect(system, *actor, R"("active")", R"({"count": 1})")) {
        return 1;
    }

    // Send another event
    const xstate::event deactivate{.type = "deactivate", .payload = {}};
    if (system.send(*actor, deactivate) != xstate::run_outcome::settled ||
        !expect(system, *actor, R"("inactive")", R"({"count": 1})")) {
        return 1;
    }
    return 0;
}

It prints:

"inactive" {"count":0}
"active" {"count":1}
"inactive" {"count":1}

Each send returned settled once the system had done everything the event caused, so each expect after it saw the transition and the assign.

Mocking effects

An effect is what a machine asks of the world: send an email, write a log, fetch data. A test of the logic replaces each effect with a stand-in that records what was asked and answers as the test decides, so that the test is fast, isolated and the same on every run.

Actions

xstate’s actor system hands every custom action to the function on_action registers, with the actor that returned it, as the actor resolves it (Watching an actor). That function is the mock: it records each call, and the test checks the records. Stately’s test makes its mock with Vitest’s vi.fn() and checks it with toHaveBeenCalledWith; here the mock is a lambda that keeps the type and the params of each action it is handed:

int main() {
    const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
        "initial": "idle",
        "states": {
            "idle": {
                "on": {
                    "start": {
                        "target": "running",
                        "actions": {"type": "logMessage", "params": {"message": "Started!"}}
                    }
                }
            },
            "running": {}
        }
    })");
    const xstate::result<xstate::machine> machine = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
    if (!machine.has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }

    xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
    std::vector<std::string> calls;
    const xstate::result<void> acting =
        system.on_action([&calls](xstate::actor_ref, const xstate::action& returned) {
            calls.push_back(returned.type + ' ' + boost::json::serialize(returned.params));
        });
    if (!acting.has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }
    const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*machine);
    if (!actor.has_value() || system.start(*actor) != xstate::run_outcome::settled) {
        return 1;
    }

    const xstate::event start{.type = "start", .payload = {}};
    if (system.send(*actor, start) != xstate::run_outcome::settled) {
        return 1;
    }

    const xstate::snapshot* now = system.snapshot_of(*actor);
    const std::vector<std::string> expected{R"(logMessage {"message":"Started!"})"};
    if (now == nullptr || now->value != boost::json::value("running") || calls != expected) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "value: " << boost::json::serialize(now->value) << '\n';
    for (const std::string& call : calls) {
        std::cout << call << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}

It prints:

value: "running"
logMessage {"message":"Started!"}

A built-in log never reaches on_action: it reaches the function on_log registers, with its value and its label, and an event the machine emits reaches the listeners on_emitted registers. A test records them the same way (Watching an actor).

A mock only records. It runs inside an actor’s turn, while the system runs: it may read the system, with snapshot_of or status_of, but any call from it that changes the system, such as a send, a resolve or a registration, is refused with invalid_argument and changes nothing. A test whose mock must answer reads the records once the call that ran the system has returned, and answers then. XState accepts a send from an action, through its self, or from a subscriber, and handles it after the update in progress (A callback that calls the system back).

Promise actors

XState runs a promise in a fromPromise actor; a test replaces the promise with a mock and waits a tick for it to settle. xstate has no promise. A host_actor stands for one: its work is done by the host, outside the machines (Host actors). Once started, it is a pending host_request in host_requests(), with its src and its input, and the host answers it with resolve(request, output) or reject(request, error). In a test the test is the host: it checks what was asked once the call that started the request has returned, answers when it chooses with what it chooses, and has nothing to wait for. Here the machine invokes fetchData, a host actor, while it is loading, and the test answers with the data:

int main() {
    xstate::implementations implementations;
    implementations.actors.emplace("fetchData", xstate::host_actor{});
    const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
        "initial": "idle",
        "states": {
            "idle": {"on": {"fetch": "loading"}},
            "loading": {
                "invoke": {"src": "fetchData", "onDone": "success", "onError": "error"}
            },
            "success": {},
            "error": {}
        }
    })");
    const xstate::result<xstate::machine> machine = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
    if (!machine.has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }

    xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
    const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*machine);
    if (!actor.has_value() || system.start(*actor) != xstate::run_outcome::settled) {
        return 1;
    }

    const xstate::event fetch{.type = "fetch", .payload = {}};
    if (system.send(*actor, fetch) != xstate::run_outcome::settled) {
        return 1;
    }

    // The machine waits for the host, which the test plays.
    const std::vector<xstate::host_request> requests = system.host_requests();
    if (requests.size() != 1 || requests.front().src != "fetchData") {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "requests: " << requests.front().src << '\n';
    const boost::json::value output = boost::json::parse(R"({"data": "test"})");
    if (system.resolve(requests.front(), output) != xstate::run_outcome::settled) {
        return 1;
    }

    const xstate::snapshot* now = system.snapshot_of(*actor);
    if (now == nullptr || now->value != boost::json::value("success")) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "value: " << boost::json::serialize(now->value) << '\n';
    return 0;
}

It prints:

requests: fetchData
value: "success"

reject fails the request instead, and the invoke’s onError takes the error. A request whose actor has ended, because the state that invoked it was left, is no longer pending: answering it is refused with invalid_argument and changes nothing, as XState ignores a promise that settles too late.

Every fuel budget

An actor system runs on fuel (Fuel, parking and resume). Each host call opens executions with the fuel its budget gives, actor_system({.fuel = n}), and every microstep, every message an actor sends and every timer it arms costs one unit. When an execution runs out, its actor parks with what it has not done, the call returns out_of_fuel, and resume() gives every parked actor a new execution. While an actor is parked, the host’s own calls, start, send, clock_tick, resolve and reject, are held in the order made and return out_of_fuel, and resume() applies them once the parked actors have settled. So a run that is resumed until it settles must do what a run with plenty of fuel does, whatever the budget: the same macrosteps, in the same order for each actor, to the same end. That is what this test checks. XState has no fuel, so this test has no twin (The XState twins); xstate’s own actor test, actors_time, runs the same test on more scripts (The tests).

The family: app invokes a worker, a machine_actor (Invoking actors). On go the app sends ping to the worker, a send_to_action, and the worker counts it and answers its parent with pong, a send_parent_action, which the app counts (Sending events between actors); after 1000 ms the app finishes, which stops the worker.

xstate::implementations worker_implementations;
worker_implementations.actions.emplace("countPing", counting("pings"));
worker_implementations.actions.emplace("pong", xstate::send_parent_action{
                                                   .event = making("pong"),
                                                   .id = std::nullopt,
                                                   .delay = std::nullopt,
                                               });
const boost::json::value worker_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "worker",
    "context": {"pings": 0},
    "on": {"ping": {"actions": ["countPing", "pong"]}}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> worker =
    xstate::create_machine(worker_config, worker_implementations);
if (!worker.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::implementations app_implementations;
app_implementations.actors.emplace("worker", xstate::machine_actor{*worker});
app_implementations.actions.emplace("countPong", counting("pongs"));
app_implementations.actions.emplace("ping", xstate::send_to_action{
                                                .target = "worker",
                                                .event = making("ping"),
                                                .id = std::nullopt,
                                                .delay = std::nullopt,
                                            });
const boost::json::value app_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "app",
    "initial": "working",
    "context": {"pongs": 0},
    "states": {
        "working": {
            "invoke": {"src": "worker", "id": "worker"},
            "on": {"go": {"actions": "ping"}, "pong": {"actions": "countPong"}},
            "after": {"1000": "finished"}
        },
        "finished": {"type": "final"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> app =
    xstate::create_machine(app_config, app_implementations);
if (!app.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

run_with runs a script of host calls on a system with a given budget, resuming after each call until the system settles, and records what each actor did, by its id: every macrostep it settled, which the inspector (inspect) reports with the event that began it (Inspection), and its status at the end. clock_tick(1000) moves the system’s clock to 1000 ms, the time to move to and not an increment (Time), and the app’s timer, due then, fires.

/** What each actor did in a run, by its id: every macrostep it settled, then its status. */
using trace = std::map<std::string, std::vector<std::string>, std::less<>>;

/** A run: its trace, and how many times the host had to resume it. */
struct run {
    trace actors;
    std::size_t resumes = 0;
};

/**
 Resumes a system until no actor is parked; how many resumes it took, or
 nothing when a call failed or it never settled.
*/
std::optional<std::size_t> settle(xstate::actor_system& system,
                                  xstate::result<xstate::run_outcome> outcome) {
    constexpr std::size_t most = 100'000;
    std::size_t resumes = 0;
    while (outcome.has_value() && *outcome == xstate::run_outcome::out_of_fuel && resumes < most) {
        outcome = system.resume();
        ++resumes;
    }
    if (!outcome.has_value() || *outcome != xstate::run_outcome::settled) {
        return std::nullopt;
    }
    return resumes;
}

/** Runs the test's script on a system whose executions have `fuel` each. */
std::optional<run> run_with(const xstate::machine& app, std::uint32_t fuel) {
    xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = fuel});
    run made;
    std::vector<xstate::actor_ref> started;
    const xstate::result<void> inspecting = system.inspect(xstate::inspector{
        .started = [&started](xstate::actor_ref actor) { started.push_back(actor); },
        .settled =
            [&system, &made](xstate::actor_ref actor, const xstate::machine& /*logic*/,
                             const xstate::event& cause, const xstate::snapshot& settled) {
                made.actors[std::string(system.id_of(actor))].push_back(
                    cause.type + " -> " + boost::json::serialize(settled.value) + ' ' +
                    boost::json::serialize(settled.context));
            },
        .emitted = {},
    });
    if (!inspecting.has_value()) {
        return std::nullopt;
    }
    const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> root =
        system.create_actor(app, {.input = nullptr, .id = "app", .system_id = std::nullopt});
    if (!root.has_value()) {
        return std::nullopt;
    }

    const xstate::event go{.type = "go", .payload = {}};
    const std::vector<std::function<xstate::result<xstate::run_outcome>()>> script{
        [&] { return system.start(*root); },
        [&] { return system.send(*root, go); },
        [&] { return system.send(*root, go); },
        [&] { return system.clock_tick(1000); },
    };
    for (const auto& call : script) {
        const std::optional<std::size_t> resumes = settle(system, call());
        if (!resumes.has_value()) {
            return std::nullopt;
        }
        made.resumes += *resumes;
    }
    for (const xstate::actor_ref actor : started) {
        const xstate::result<xactor::status> status = system.status_of(actor);
        if (!status.has_value()) {
            return std::nullopt;
        }
        made.actors[std::string(system.id_of(actor))].push_back("status " +
                                                                std::string(name_of(*status)));
    }
    return made;
}

The test runs the script with plenty of fuel, and then with every budget from 1 to 40, and compares the records:

const std::optional<run> plenty = run_with(*app, 10'000);
if (!plenty.has_value() || plenty->resumes != 0) {
    return 1;
}
for (const auto& [id, entries] : plenty->actors) {
    for (const std::string& entry : entries) {
        std::cout << id << ": " << entry << '\n';
    }
}

for (std::uint32_t fuel = 1; fuel <= 40; ++fuel) {
    const std::optional<run> scarce = run_with(*app, fuel);
    if (!scarce.has_value() || scarce->actors != plenty->actors) {
        std::cout << "fuel " << fuel << " differs\n";
        return 1;
    }
    if (fuel == 1) {
        std::cout << "fuel 1: the same, after " << scarce->resumes << " resumes\n";
    }
}
std::cout << "every budget from 1 to 40: the same\n";

It prints:

app: xstate.init -> "working" {"pongs":0}
app: go -> "working" {"pongs":0}
app: pong -> "working" {"pongs":1}
app: go -> "working" {"pongs":1}
app: pong -> "working" {"pongs":2}
app: xstate.after.1000.app.working -> "finished" {"pongs":2}
app: status done
worker: xstate.init -> {} {"pings":0}
worker: ping -> {} {"pings":1}
worker: ping -> {} {"pings":2}
worker: status stopped
fuel 1: the same, after 14 resumes
every budget from 1 to 40: the same

With one unit of fuel per execution the host had to resume the system 14 times, and each actor did what it did with plenty. The records are compared actor by actor, not as one sequence. xactor queues every delivery: each actor has a first-in first-out mailbox, the actors that have work wait in a first-in first-out queue, and a turn hands one message to its actor. XState delivers an event to an idle actor at once, nested in its sender’s call, and queues it for a busy one. So the order between two actors may differ, while the order within each is XState’s (Interleaving across actors).

Model-based testing

A test written by hand checks the paths its author thought of. Model-based testing takes the paths from the machine: every state it can reach, and a shortest sequence of events that reaches it, each path a test to run against the system the machine models. Stately’s page closes with XState’s tools for it, xstate/graph, formerly @xstate/test.

xstate has no port of xstate/graph. A snapshot is a value and transition a pure function, so a test walks a machine itself: get_next_transitions lists the transitions a snapshot could take (Every transition a snapshot could take), as XState’s graph takes its events from the snapshot’s own event descriptors. The list holds every transition, so a type may come more than once, from several guarded transitions of a state or from a state and its ancestor, where XState’s descriptors are a set. shortest_paths walks breadth first. From each snapshot it sends each event type offered once, with get_next_snapshot, and keeps each snapshot it has not seen, known by its value and its context, as XState’s graph keys a snapshot. An eventless transition is no event to send: the macrostep takes it on its own. The machine runs, pauses, resumes and stops:

/** A snapshot a machine can reach, and the events of a path that reaches it. */
struct path {
    xstate::snapshot reached;
    std::vector<std::string> events;
};

/** A snapshot's identity in the walk: its value and its context, as XState's graph keys it. */
std::string key_of(const xstate::snapshot& reached) {
    return boost::json::serialize(reached.value) + boost::json::serialize(reached.context);
}

/**
 The shortest path to every snapshot a machine can reach, breadth first: from
 each snapshot, each event type get_next_transitions offers is sent once.
*/
std::vector<path> shortest_paths(const xstate::machine& machine) {
    std::vector<path> found;
    found.push_back(path{
        .reached = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(machine),
        .events = {std::string(xstate::init_event_type)},
    });
    std::set<std::string, std::less<>> seen{key_of(found.front().reached)};
    for (std::size_t next = 0; next < found.size(); ++next) {
        // A copy: what found holds may move when a path is added below.
        const path from = found[next];
        // Each type once, as XState's descriptors are a set: several transitions may offer it.
        std::set<std::string_view, std::less<>> types;
        for (const xstate::transition_definition* offered :
             xstate::get_next_transitions(machine, from.reached)) {
            if (offered->event_type.empty() || !types.insert(offered->event_type).second) {
                continue;
            }
            const xstate::event sent{.type = offered->event_type, .payload = {}};
            xstate::snapshot reached = xstate::get_next_snapshot(machine, from.reached, sent);
            if (!seen.insert(key_of(reached)).second) {
                continue;
            }
            std::vector<std::string> events = from.events;
            events.push_back(offered->event_type);
            found.push_back(path{.reached = std::move(reached), .events = std::move(events)});
        }
    }
    return found;
}

int main() {
    const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
        "initial": "idle",
        "states": {
            "idle": {"on": {"start": "running"}},
            "running": {"on": {"pause": "paused", "stop": "idle"}},
            "paused": {"on": {"resume": "running", "stop": "idle"}}
        }
    })");
    const xstate::result<xstate::machine> machine = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
    if (!machine.has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }

    const std::vector<path> paths = shortest_paths(*machine);
    if (paths.size() != 3) {
        return 1;
    }
    for (const path& one : paths) {
        std::cout << boost::json::serialize(one.reached.value) << ": [";
        for (std::size_t index = 0; index < one.events.size(); ++index) {
            std::cout << (index == 0 ? "" : ", ") << one.events[index];
        }
        std::cout << "]\n";
    }
    return 0;
}

It prints:

"idle": [xstate.init]
"running": [xstate.init, start]
"paused": [xstate.init, start, pause]

Each path is a test: start the machine, send the path’s events after its first, then check the state the system reached. The first entry, xstate.init, stands for the start, as in XState’s paths, and is not sent: from outside, XState’s macrostep selects no transition for it, where xstate’s selects transitions for it as for any other event (Events). The walk sends each event with an empty payload. A machine whose guards read the payload needs the events chosen for it, as XState’s getShortestPaths takes them in its events option.

When two events reach a snapshot in as many steps, the walk keeps the path of the event it tries first, in the order get_next_transitions lists them. Within one state that is the order in which XState formats the state’s transitions: its on events, then its onDone, invoke and after events, wherever the config writes those. Within on and within after, the keys come in the order JavaScript enumerates an object’s keys: a key that is an array index, such as 1 or 100, first, by number, then the others as the config writes them. Across states, an active atomic state’s transitions come before those of its ancestors, where XState’s graph takes the event descriptors of the active states root first. So in a machine whose initial state a goes to its sibling b on go and on stop, and whose root also takes stop to b, the walk reaches b by go, the first event a lists, and XState’s graph by stop, which the root lists.

How xstate is tested

xstate is a port, and a port is right when it does what the original does. So the tests that check behaviour XState also has do not state by hand what XState does, which could carry a translation error that nothing catches: they ask XState itself. XState runs every case, each ported from its own tests or written where they are silent, and what it records is what the suites hold xstate to (XState as the oracle, The ported cases); and XState runs a twin of every example of this page that it can run (The XState twins). The tests written by hand cover the rest: what XState has no test for, what the oracle cannot see, and a few of XState’s expectations, copied where no case can hold them (The tests). Every program of this page is a test too, built and run on every target (The examples).

Each is a target of b2, run from the root of a webcpp checkout:

b2 libs/xstate/test

The 39 tests, natively: the lightweight_test programs, the 2 Boost.Test suites that run the ported cases, each of the 24 public headers compiled alone, and core_alone and user_aggregates, which must compile (The tests). It needs a C++20 compiler and Boost’s headers, and no Node.

b2 libs/xstate/example

The 146 examples, each built, run, and its output compared with the one committed beside it (The examples).

b2 libs/xstate/test libs/xstate/example toolset=clang-wasip2 testing.launcher=wasmtime

The same for wasm32-wasip2: 37 tests, the Boost.Test suites being native only, and the 146 examples, each run by wasmtime (Targets). toolset=clang-wasip3 does the same for wasm32-wasip3: 37 tests and 146 examples.

b2 libs/xstate/test/oracle//oracle

The oracle lane: XState 5.33.2 runs every case, and what it records must be what the suites hold (XState as the oracle); and every twin runs on XState and must print what its program printed (The XState twins). It needs Node and npm. The continuous integration runs it from scratch, beside the lanes, in its job Own lane (xstate, oracle).

b2 libs/xstate/test/oracle//update-expected

Not a check: it writes XState’s output again, over the committed one (Regenerating XState’s output).

b2 compares timestamps, so a result that counts is built from scratch, with b2 -a. b2 libs/xstate/test//machine builds and runs one test alone, while working on it.

Targets

test/Jamfile and example/Jamfile declare the targets they are built for, webcpp.targets native wasip2 wasip3, and b2 builds each program for those alone:

Target How it is built and run

native

Any toolset not listed below. As the build makes it: with exceptions, unless its user asks for exception-handling=off, which links webcpp’s tools/throw_exception.cpp. The 2 Boost.Test suites are built for this target alone.

wasip2

The toolset clang-wasip2, the Clang of wasi-sdk for wasm32-wasip2, run by wasmtime. With exceptions, as WebAssembly’s exception handling, as on wasip3.

wasip3

The toolset clang-wasip3, for wasm32-wasip3, run by wasmtime. With exceptions, as WebAssembly’s exception handling.

That xstate works without exceptions is checked by the lint, which compiles every public header, and every test and example, which instantiate its templates, with exception-handling=off; a template that none of them instantiates is not checked.

<webcpp/xstate/config.hpp>, which every public header of xstate includes first, defines WEBCPP_XSTATE_NO_EXCEPTIONS when webcpp has no exceptions (WEBCPP_HAS_EXCEPTIONS is not defined: the compiler has none, or the program defined WEBCPP_NO_EXCEPTIONS), and a program may define it for xstate alone, to turn xstate’s exceptions off in a build that has them, as Boost.Asio’s BOOST_ASIO_NO_EXCEPTIONS does. xstate raises no exception of its own (where XState throws, it returns an error), so the macro changes nothing in it: it exists so that a program can set it for every webcpp library alike. The tests config, config_developer_defined and config_all_off check the three ways it is defined, and the lint refuses a throw in a public header, even in a template nothing instantiates: an exception goes through boost::throw_exception.

The WASI toolsets are b2’s clang, which a user-config.jam registers against wasi-sdk, as xactor’s page shows. The Boost.Test suites read the fixture files at run time, which a wasm program cannot without a directory its runtime opens for it, so they run natively; every other test, and every example, runs on native, wasip2 and wasip3.

The continuous integration runs xstate’s tests and examples in lanes, one toolset each: GCC 14 and 15, Clang 18 and 22, Apple Clang, MSVC 14.3 and 14.5, and wasip2 and wasip3. On Linux, GCC and Clang build with libstdc++, the system’s standard library there, so the lanes clang-linux-18 and clang-linux-22 run xstate with Clang on libstdc++. Each lane builds from scratch and records what b2 built and ran:

b2 -a --dump-tests --out-xml=<lane>.xml toolset=<toolset> libs/xstate/test libs/xstate/example

webcpp’s tools/report/report.py merges the files of every lane into the test matrix, published at https://webcpporg.github.io/report/, where each cell says whether a program passed in a lane, or how it failed. Beside the lanes, tools/lint/lint.sh runs clang-format and clang-tidy from wasi-sdk, with rules of webcpp’s own: the licence notice every source file opens with, the layout of JSON literals, the machine core’s boundary, which names the file and the line of any include of xactor or of the actor layer from the core, and the patterns webcpp bans, among them any real clock, file, socket or process a header could name, which no test can show xstate never reaches (guarantee 15).

XState as the oracle

test/oracle/ pins the npm package xstate at 5.33.2, exactly, with its lockfile, from which the first target that needs it installs it with npm ci; its Jamfile declares the lane with webcpp’s webcpp.cases and webcpp.twins. Its scripts run xstate’s test cases on it and write what XState produced:

  • oracle.mjs runs the machine cases. Each macrostep after the initial one runs through XState’s machine.transition, with an actor scope of the script’s own that records every action and every @xstate.microstep inspection event, and whose actor has a parent, so that a sendParent resolves as it does in an actor that has one. XState’s pure functions cannot serve: their actor has no parent, and throws on sendParent. The initial macrostep runs through machine.getInitialSnapshot, with the same scope; XState’s inspection does not report its first microstep, so the snapshots and actions of its microsteps are taken from getInitialMicrosteps. Delayed events go to XState’s own SimulatedClock.

  • actors.mjs runs the actor cases on XState’s actors, where a host actor is a promise the script settles when a step says so. After each step it writes, for every actor, the events it processed with the snapshot each left and the events it emitted, then every actor’s status and the host’s pending requests. An actor is keyed by its path of ids from the root, and, when an earlier actor had the same path, by its rank among them (root/n#2); the requests come in the order of the keys of their actors. No nesting of deliveries changes those keys. It never writes the order between two actors, which xactor’s queues may change (Interleaving across actors).

Both run XState’s development build, which XState’s own tests run. It makes checks the production build leaves out, and three of them are checks a JSON machine can meet: an event of the type * sent from outside, a transition that declares a truthy cond, a forwardTo whose target is no actor. xstate makes the same three, so its oracle must (The checks of XState’s development build): development.mjs refuses any other build, and every command runs node with --conditions=development. No library, suite or example uses the package, and its output is committed, so the suites run without node.

The ported cases

XState’s tests are TypeScript with inline functions. Each test that a machine written in JSON can express is ported to a case: under test/fixtures/cases/ for the machine core, and test/fixtures/actors/cases/ for the actor layer. A file holds the cases ported from one XState test file, or from a range of lines of a long one (invoke_1.json to invoke_5.json), under source, cases and excluded. A case names the test it ports, holds the machine’s config as JSON, and lists its steps. The first case of after.json, ported from after.test.ts, is the test of Time:

{
    "name": "transition after delay through yellow",
    "test": "after.test.ts > delayed transitions > should transition after delay",
    "machine": {
        "id": "light",
        "initial": "green",
        "context": {"canTurnGreen": true},
        "states": {
            "green": {"after": {"1000": "yellow"}},
            "yellow": {"after": {"1000": [{"target": "red"}]}},
            "red": {"after": {"1000": "green"}}
        }
    },
    "steps": [
        {"start": true},
        {"query": {"matches": "green"}},
        {"advance": 500},
        {"query": {"matches": "green"}},
        {"advance": 510},
        {"query": {"matches": "yellow"}}
    ]
}

A step of a machine case starts the machine (start, with an optional input), sends it an event (send), moves the clock (advance), resolves a state value (resolve) or asks a question of the snapshot (query: matches, has_tag, can, meta, next_transitions). A case may also expect the machine to be refused: expect_create_error when XState refuses it too, xstate_refuses with the error code when xstate refuses at creation what XState throws on only once it runs (A config is refused when it is created).

An actor case lists the actors its machine may run, machines, each with implementations of its own, and host actors. Its steps create or start the root (create, start, with an optional input and system_id), send to it or to a child (send, with to), move the clock (advance), answer a host request (resolve, reject), find an actor by its systemId (get) and stop the root (stop).

The implementations a case names come from a vocabulary written twice, entry for entry, test/oracle/vocabulary.mjs for XState and test/vocabulary.hpp for xstate: fixed assigns and guards (increment, push, context_at_least and others), the built-in actions a case declares with their options under actions, and any other name, which is a custom action.

A test that cannot be ported is not dropped in silence: each file lists the tests it leaves out, with the reason.

{
    "test": "after.test.ts > delayed transitions > should execute an after transition after starting from a persisted state",
    "reason": "persistence/rehydration: restores an actor from a snapshot taken via getSnapshot/getPersistedSnapshot"
}

The machine cases are 504 cases of 1,111 steps, 413 of them ported from XState’s tests, and leave 159 tests out: 36 of those are ported with the actor cases, and the others need a function JSON cannot hold, TypeScript’s type checker, enqueueActions, an actor reference held as data, callbacks or observables, persistence, machine.provide or XState’s options.maxIterations, which xstate does not read (tests of transient.test.ts, Bounding a macrostep); assert on spies, warnings or XState’s internal objects; or are skipped in XState’s own suite. XState’s SCXML suite is left out whole, because the published package exports no SCXML converter. The actor cases are 228 cases of 501 steps, 163 of them ported from XState’s actor tests (actor, interpreter, invoke, spawnChild, spawn, system, errors, emit, predictableExec, and the actor tests of input, after and the core’s files), and leave 153 tests out: callbacks, observables and transition functions, persistence, actor references as data, functions JSON cannot hold, and the places where the actor layer differs from XState.

Other files are xstate’s own, still checked against XState. The two review.json files, 43 machine cases and 30 actor cases, pin what XState does where its own tests are silent: among them a machine whose root is a history node, an event of the type *, a transition that declares cond, a value computed as undefined, a timer armed twice under one id, a history that is neither shallow nor deep, the order in which JavaScript enumerates the keys of delays, regions, events and state values, and, among actors, the systemId of a child born done and the snapshot a deferred failure reached. resolution.json, 12 actor cases, pins how XState resolves spawnChild, stopChild and sendTo in an actor; vocabulary.json, 16 actor cases, pins the vocabulary of the cases against XState; actor_actions.json, computed.json and invoke_pure.json, 47 machine cases, run the actions that name actors, the computed values and invokes through the pure functions; and each oracle has a smoke.json of its own.

The XState twins

The cases hold the library to XState; the twins hold this page to it. This page shows C++ only, and the comparison with XState that a reader no longer sees stays a test. Every program of example/xstate/ and example/actors/, the programs of this page, has a twin in test/oracle/twins/, under the same group and name: <name>.mjs, a Node program that does on XState 5.33.2 what <name>.cpp does on xstate, and prints what it finds the same way. Of the twins of this chapter’s programs, testing_<name>.mjs, 9 are tests of Node’s own runner, node:test, and assert with node:assert, where Stately’s page uses Vitest, so that each runs on Node alone.

A program is of one of three kinds:

  • Its twin agrees, and prints the program’s output, the one this page shows under the program. 114 twins agree.

  • Its twin diverges, on purpose. The program shows a place where xstate differs from XState, and the twin prints what XState does there. That output is committed beside the twin, as <name>.expected, and must differ from the program’s: an output equal to it is a fault, since that twin agrees. 22 twins diverge, and Where xstate differs from XState shows each output beside its program’s, with the reason for the difference.

  • It has no twin, because it shows what XState has no counterpart for: the macrostep cursor, fuel, a registry of inputs and outputs by invoke id or state id, a machine created again from its definition, an event read from JSON. 10 programs have none, and each has a line <group>/<name>: <reason> in test/oracle/twins/without-twin.txt.

So the 146 programs, 89 of example/xstate/ and 57 of example/actors/, are 114 that agree, 22 that diverge and 10 without a twin.

webcpp’s tools/oracle/twins.py runs the twins and compares, declared in test/oracle/Jamfile with webcpp.twins. It runs the twins in parallel, each in a process of its own:

  • on XState’s development build, node --conditions=development, which the oracle runs too (XState as the oracle);

  • with the report of Node’s test runner sent to the standard error (--test-reporter=spec --test-reporter-destination=stderr), so that only what the twin prints reaches the standard output;

  • with colour off, NO_COLOR set and FORCE_COLOR removed, whatever the shell asks for;

  • for at most 60 seconds, after which the twin and every process it started are killed, and the twin is reported.

What the twin prints on the standard output, every carriage return removed, must equal the program’s <name>.expected, or, for a twin that diverges, the twin’s own. A difference fails the target, and twins.py prints the diff; so does a twin that exits with an error or does not end in time. So does a mismatch of the directories: a program with neither a twin nor a line in without-twin.txt, a program with both, a twin or a line that names no program, an output of no twin, or a line that is not <group>/<name>: <reason>. A node that is not on the PATH, a directory that is not there, or a directory of examples with no program stops it at once, named. The twins run alone, in a few seconds:

b2 libs/xstate/test/oracle//twins

The output of a twin that diverges is never written by hand. A new one starts as an empty file beside the twin, and b2 libs/xstate/test/oracle//update-expected fills it with what XState prints (Regenerating XState’s output). That update rewrites only the outputs that exist, and refuses to write one equal to its program’s output: it reports that twin, which agrees, and leaves its output file as it was, for its author to delete.

The tests

xstate’s tests are under test/, each declared in test/Jamfile with one of webcpp’s rules. Most are programs of Boost.Core’s lightweight_test, declared with webcpp.run and run on every target. Each test case is a function, main calls them all and returns boost::report_errors(), and a case that cannot go on after a failed check returns; a helper, which cannot return from its case, calls webcpp::test::require, of test/require.hpp, which ends the program with the errors counted so far. So a test needs no exceptions to stop, and runs as it is in a user’s build without them.

Test What it checks

values

The error codes, state values, paths and events. Its matchesState rows are the expectations of XState’s match.test.ts, copied one row per expect().

machine

Creation, with XState’s ids, types and document order stated by hand; lookup; and every refusal, an implementation of each kind holding an empty function among them.

cursor

The cursor, which XState does not have: the microstep that settles and no other, an event that selects no transition, a copy that resumes, a cycle that never settles, and a failure that settles in error, reporting what it resolved before the failure apart from its actions. And rules of the machine core, stated by hand: a spawn whose input fails settles in error without the child; a sendTo to a systemId is returned for its caller to resolve; a sendTo to an invoke of the state being entered is bound at the end of that state’s entry actions, spawns and initial actions, the point bound_at counts to (action::bound_at); and the clock schedules only a built-in delayed raise (Delayed events and the simulated clock).

actors_lifecycle

What the oracle cannot see of an actor’s life: created, started, sent events, stopped, done or failed, what a failing macrostep hands over, the ids the system names its actors with, and the host’s stop of a child, which XState refuses too.

actors_sending

The events actors send each other and the system that delivers them: a sendTo, a sendParent and a send to the actor itself, an error sent as an event, and the systemIds that name actors while they run, with their refusals.

actors_children

The children actors invoke and spawn: a child’s output and error reaching its parent, its stop when its state is left, the order the children of a start start in, and the children of a macrostep that fails.

actors_time

Time and fuel. The timers due during a tick, delayed events and cancels, and the fuel each microstep costs; and parking: every budget from 1 to 40 resumed to the end doing what plenty of fuel does, for a child’s start, a deferred send or emit, a done or an error report, a host’s answer, a timer and a stop that reaches a grandchild; the host’s calls held behind a parked actor; a child done while its parent is parked.

actors_host

What the host sees and answers: host actors, their requests resolved and rejected, a late answer to a request, and the callbacks that hand over custom actions, logs, snapshots and emitted events, which cannot call the system back.
