WEBCPP_XSTATE_NO_EXCEPTIONS

Defined when xstate is built without exceptions: when webcpp has none (the compiler has none, or the developer defined WEBCPP_NO_EXCEPTIONS for every webcpp library), or when the developer defines it alone, to disable xstate’s in a build that has them.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/xstate/config.hpp>

#define WEBCPP_XSTATE_NO_EXCEPTIONS

Description

xstate raises no exception of its own: where XState throws, it returns an error, so the macro changes nothing in it. It is provided so that a program can set it for every webcpp library alike. An exception xstate raised would go through boost::throw_exception, and an API that throws would be absent while this is defined.

See Also

"How xstate is tested", in the guide.

Appendix A: From XState to C++

This appendix is for a reader who knows XState. It shows how each of XState’s JavaScript spellings is written in C++: a machine’s config, the functions the config holds, an event, an actor, a promise and an error. The machine itself does not change: its states, its transitions and what they mean are XState’s. What changes is how a program writes them, because C++ has no object literal, a JSON config holds no function, and xstate throws nothing.

Each section gives XState’s spelling first, in inline code, a table or a program, and then xstate’s, from an example program of this page. A program of XState’s shown here is the twin of the C++ program after it: the same program, which ran on XState 5.33.2 and printed what the C++ program prints (A twin for every example). The last section, XState’s names, goes from each of XState’s names to xstate’s.

Names keep XState’s words, in snake case: createMachine is create_machine, getNextSnapshot is get_next_snapshot, and snapshot.hasTag is snapshot.has_tag. The C++ examples write namespace xstate = webcpp::xstate;, and every value a machine holds, its config, its context, an event’s payload, an action’s params, an input and an output, is a boost::json::value.

A JavaScript object becomes a JSON config

XState’s createMachine takes the config as a JavaScript object, written in the program. xstate’s create_machine takes the same config as JSON, a boost::json::value the program parses from text, reads from a file or receives in a request. C++ has no object literal to write a config in, and as data a config can come from anywhere, Stately Studio’s export included, and needs no compiler (A JSON config).

The toggle of the quick start is an object in XState:

const toggleMachine = createMachine({
  id: 'toggle',
  initial: 'Inactive',
  states: {
    Inactive: {
      on: { toggle: 'Active' },
    },
    Active: {
      on: { toggle: 'Inactive' },
    },
  },
});

and JSON in xstate:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "toggle",
    "initial": "Inactive",
    "states": {
        "Inactive": {"on": {"toggle": "Active"}},
        "Active": {"on": {"toggle": "Inactive"}}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> toggle_machine = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!toggle_machine.has_value()) {
    std::cout << "refused: " << toggle_machine.error().message() << '\n';
    return 1;
}

Every member keeps its name and its meaning; JSON changes how it is written, and a function becomes a name:

XState’s object xstate’s JSON

id: 'toggle', a bare key and a string in single quotes

"id": "toggle", every key and every string in double quotes

after: { 2000: 'Inactive' }

"after": {"2000": "Inactive"}: a key is always a string

entry: assign(...), guard: ({ context }) => ...

"entry": "incrementCount", "guard": "countBelowMax": a name, and the function registered under it (Functions become implementations registered by name)

{ type: 'notify', params: { level: 2 } }

{"type": "notify", "params": {"level": 2}}, its params fixed in the config

not('isEmpty'), stateIn('#light.green')

{"type": "xstate.not", "guards": ["isEmpty"]}, {"type": "xstate.stateIn", "stateValue": "#light.green"} (Higher-order guards and stateIn)

a member that is undefined

the member left out (undefined in JSON)

The rules:

  • create_machine returns a result<machine>: the machine, or the reason the config was refused, which the program tests where a program of XState’s would catch what createMachine throws (Exceptions become result). It refuses every config XState refuses, and some XState accepts and fails on only later (A config is refused when it is created).

  • The keys of states, on and after are read in the order JavaScript enumerates an object’s keys, as XState reads them: a key that is an array index, such as "500", first, by number, then the rest as written (The config).

  • A machine never changes once created. XState’s machine.provide() is the same config created again with other implementations (A machine is immutable), and machine.toJSON() is to_json(machine), which create_machine_from_definition loads back (The definition).

  • Appendix B lists every place where a JSON config takes another form than XState’s object, each with its reason (What JSON imposes).

Functions become implementations registered by name

XState’s config may hold functions: an action, a guard, a delay, the logic of an invoked actor, and the functions that compute the initial context, an invoked child’s input and a final state’s output. JSON holds none, so xstate’s config names each one, and the program registers its C++ code under that name in an implementations, which create_machine takes with the config. XState already splits a machine this way when setup() registers implementations and the config refers to them by name: there, setup({ ... }).createMachine(config) becomes create_machine(config, implementations), and the config stays as it is (Implementations registered by name).

Stately’s setup example registers two assign actions, which the config names under on:

const counter = setup({
  actions: {
    increment: assign({
      count: ({ context }) => context.count + 1,
    }),
    decrement: assign({
      count: ({ context }) => context.count - 1,
    }),
  },
}).createMachine({
  context: { count: 0 },
  on: {
    inc: { actions: 'increment' },
    dec: { actions: 'decrement' },
  },
});

let [now] = initialTransition(counter);
for (const type of ['inc', 'inc', 'dec']) {
  [now] = transition(counter, now, { type });
  console.log(type, JSON.stringify(now.context));
}

xstate registers each as an assign_action, whose function returns the members to merge into the context; add, a function of the program, computes them:

/** The context's count plus `step`, as an assign merges it into the context. */
xstate::result<boost::json::object> add(const xstate::action_args& args, std::int64_t step) {
    const boost::json::object* context = args.context.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* count = context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("count");
    const std::int64_t* value = count == nullptr ? nullptr : count->if_int64();
    if (value == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"count", *value + step}};
}

const xstate::assign_action increment{
    .assignment = [](const xstate::action_args& args) { return add(args, 1); },
};
const xstate::assign_action decrement{
    .assignment = [](const xstate::action_args& args) { return add(args, -1); },
};
xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actions.emplace("increment", increment);
implementations.actions.emplace("decrement", decrement);

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "context": {"count": 0},
    "on": {
        "inc": {"actions": "increment"},
        "dec": {"actions": "decrement"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> counter = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!counter.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::snapshot now = xstate::initial_transition(*counter).first;
for (const std::string_view type : {"inc", "inc", "dec"}) {
    const xstate::event sent{.type = std::string(type), .payload = {}};
    now = xstate::transition(*counter, now, sent).first;
    std::cout << type << ' ' << boost::json::serialize(now.context) << '\n';
}

It prints:

inc {"count":1}
inc {"count":2}
dec {"count":1}

implementations has a member for each kind of function. actions, guards, delays and actors are keyed by name, as setup() keys them. The other three stand for functions XState’s config holds in place, so each is keyed by the place: context, one function, computes the initial context from the input; inputs computes a child’s input, under the id of its invoke; and outputs computes a final state’s output, under the id of that state, or the machine’s under the root’s id. Each member is taught in the section on implementations. Each function keeps its role in XState and takes a C++ shape:

XState xstate

An action creator, such as assign({ count: ({ context }) => context.count + 1 })

The built-in action of the same name, such as an assign_action, holding a function that returns what XState’s creator computes: here the members to merge, boost::json::object{{"count", ...}} (Built-in and custom actions)

An action that is a plain function, such as () => console.log('done')

No entry: an action name actions does not hold is a custom action, returned to the program, which performs it (Custom actions)

A guard, ({ context, event }, params) => boolean

A predicate: a function of an action_args, which returns result<bool>

A delay, ({ context, event }) => number

A delay_maker, which returns result<std::uint64_t>, in milliseconds

src: childMachine, src: fromPromise(...)

A machine_actor{child_machine}, or a host_actor{} (Promises become host actors)

context: ({ input }) => ({ ... })

implementations.context: a context_maker, a function of the input that returns result<boost::json::value>

An invoke’s input: ({ context }) => ..., a final state’s output: ({ context }) => ...

A value_maker, in inputs or outputs, which returns result<std::optional<boost::json::value>>, none for undefined

The rules:

  • Every implementation receives an action_args: args.context, args.event and args.params, XState’s ({ context, event }, params). It receives no actor and no system, where XState’s also receives self and system.

  • Every implementation returns a result, and fails by returning an error where XState’s would throw (Exceptions become result).

  • A name is checked when the machine is created. A guard, an after delay or an actor that the config names and implementations does not hold refuses the machine, where XState fails when it first needs the name, or never (A config is refused when it is created). An action name is not checked: one that actions does not hold is a custom action, by design.

  • params are fixed in the config. Where XState computes them with a function of the context and the event, xstate’s implementation reads the two from its action_args (Functions become names).

A flat event object becomes event{type, payload}

An event in XState is one object: its type, the string that names what happened, and its data, the other members beside the type. xstate’s event holds the two apart: type, a std::string, and payload, a boost::json::object holding every other member. Transitions match the type alone, and the payload is JSON, as every value a machine holds is (Events).

Stately’s feedback machine receives an event that carries the new feedback. XState writes the event as one object:

const [next, actions] = transition(feedbackMachine, initial, {
  type: 'feedback.update',
  feedback: 'Some other feedback',
});

xstate writes its type and its payload:

const xstate::event update{
    .type = "feedback.update",
    .payload = {{"feedback", "Some other feedback"}},
};
const auto [next, actions] = xstate::transition(*feedback_machine, initial, update);

An implementation reads the data from the payload. XState’s assigner reads event.feedback:

updateFeedback: assign({
  feedback: ({ event }) => event.feedback,
}),

xstate’s reads the member feedback of args.event.payload, and fails when the event does not carry it:

xstate::result<boost::json::object> update_feedback(const xstate::action_args& args) {
    const boost::json::value* feedback = args.event.payload.if_contains("feedback");
    if (feedback == nullptr) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"feedback", *feedback}};
}

The program prints the context before and after the event, and the number of actions the step returned:

{"feedback":"Some feedback","rating":5}
{"feedback":"Some other feedback","rating":5}
0 actions

The rules:

  • An event with no data, XState’s { type: 'toggle' }, is xstate::event{.type = "toggle", .payload = {}}.

  • An event that arrives as JSON in XState’s flat form, from a request or a file, is read by event_from_json and written back by to_json (Events).

  • The events xstate makes carry their data in the payload too: the output of a done event and the error of an error event, each beside actorId, and the input of xstate.init. XState’s event.output is the member output of args.event.payload (Done events).

  • An event carries no actor, since a payload is JSON (Actor references become actor_ref).

Actor references become actor_ref

XState’s createActor returns an actor, an object whose methods start it, send it events, read and subscribe to its snapshot, and stop it. In xstate, actors live in an actor_system the program creates, and create_actor returns an actor_ref, a number that names one actor of that system. Each method of XState’s actor becomes a member of the system that takes the reference first: actor.send(event) is system.send(actor, event). XState creates a system too, implicitly, for each root actor; xstate makes it explicit, because the system owns what the host decides: the fuel each call may spend, the time, and the systemIds its actors share (Creating an actor).

The quick start’s toggle, run as an actor. XState creates it and calls its methods, where toggle is the event { type: 'toggle' }:

const actor = createActor(toggleMachine);

actor.subscribe((snapshot) => {
  console.log('Value:',
    JSON.stringify(snapshot.value));
});

actor.start(); // logs "Inactive"
actor.send(toggle); // logs "Active"
actor.send(toggle); // logs "Inactive"

const now = actor.getSnapshot().value;
console.log('Now:', JSON.stringify(now));

xstate creates it in a system, and names it by the actor_ref that create_actor returned:

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 1000});

/** Whether a call that delivers ran to its end: no error, and no actor left parked. */
const auto settled = [](const xstate::result<xstate::run_outcome>& ran) {
    return ran.has_value() && *ran == xstate::run_outcome::settled;
};

const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*toggle_machine);
if (!actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

const xstate::result<void> subscribed =
    system.subscribe(*actor, [](const xstate::snapshot& snapshot) {
        std::cout << "Value: " << boost::json::serialize(snapshot.value) << '\n';
    });
if (!subscribed.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

if (!settled(system.start(*actor))) {  // logs "Inactive"
    return 1;
}

const xstate::event toggle{.type = "toggle", .payload = {}};
if (!settled(system.send(*actor, toggle))) {  // logs "Active"
    return 1;
}
if (!settled(system.send(*actor, toggle))) {  // logs "Inactive"
    return 1;
}

const xstate::snapshot* now = system.snapshot_of(*actor);
if (now == nullptr) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << "Now: " << boost::json::serialize(now->value) << '\n';

It prints:

Value: "Inactive"
Value: "Active"
Value: "Inactive"
Now: "Inactive"

The table of XState’s names gives each method of XState’s actor and the member of actor_system that does its work. The rules:

  • An actor_ref is a value, copied and compared as a number is, and keeps nothing alive. An address is never reused, so a reference to an actor that has ended still names it: status_of says how it ended, and an event sent to it is dropped, as XState drops an event sent to a stopped actor. A reference that names no actor of the system is refused with invalid_argument (webcpp::xstate::actor_ref).

  • XState’s actor.getSnapshot() returns a snapshot. snapshot_of(actor) returns a pointer to one, nullptr until the actor has started (The root is constructed on start).

  • XState’s actor.send returns nothing. system.send, like every call that delivers something, runs the system and returns a result<run_outcome>: settled, out_of_fuel or an error (Create an actor and send events).

  • A config names an actor by a string and never holds one: a child by its id, the parent as #_parent, and any actor by its systemId as #system:<systemId> (Targets that name actors).

  • XState’s snapshot.children holds its children’s references. xstate’s holds their ids and srcs, and child_of(actor, id) returns a child’s reference; XState’s actor.system.get(systemId) is system.get(systemId).

Promises become host actors

XState runs asynchronous work, a request to a server or a file to read, as a promise actor: fromPromise makes actor logic of a function that returns a promise, setup({ actors }) registers it, and an invoke or a spawn starts it. When the promise resolves, the parent receives xstate.done.actor.<id> with its output; when it rejects, xstate.error.actor.<id> with its error. A C++ library has no promise to await, and with no event loop and no thread of its own it cannot wait for one. So the work is the host’s. A host_actor, registered under the actor’s name, stands for the promise: once started, it is a pending request that the host lists with host_requests(), works on at its own pace, and answers with resolve(request, output) or reject(request, error), and the parent receives the same events (Host actors).

Stately’s user machine invokes a promise that fetches a user. XState registers the promise with fromPromise. This one does not fetch: it hands its resolve and reject to requests, an array of the program’s, so that the program settles it from outside, as a host answers:

const userMachine = setup({
  actors: {
    fetchUser: fromPromise(
      ({ input, self }) =>
        new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
          requests.push({ src: self.src, id: self.id, input, resolve, reject });
        }),
    ),
  },
}).createMachine({
  id: 'user',
  initial: 'idle',
  context: { userId: '42', user: null, error: null },
  states: {
    idle: { on: { FETCH: { target: 'loading' } } },
    loading: {
      invoke: {
        id: 'getUser',
        src: 'fetchUser',
        input: ({ context: { userId } }) => ({ userId }),
        onDone: {
          target: 'success',
          actions: assign({ user: ({ event }) => event.output }),
        },
        onError: {
          target: 'failure',
          actions: assign({ error: ({ event }) => event.error }),
        },
      },
    },
    success: {},
    failure: { on: { RETRY: { target: 'loading' } } },
  },
});

xstate registers a host_actor under the same name. user_id_of, assign_user and assign_error, the functions the config names, are the program’s own, shown in Host actors:

xstate::implementations implementations;
// The promise is the host's work: a host actor.
implementations.actors.emplace("fetchUser", xstate::host_actor{});
implementations.inputs.emplace("getUser", user_id_of);
implementations.actions.emplace("assignUser", xstate::assign_action{.assignment = assign_user});
implementations.actions.emplace("assignError",
                                xstate::assign_action{.assignment = assign_error});
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "user",
    "initial": "idle",
    "context": {"userId": "42", "user": null, "error": null},
    "states": {
        "idle": {"on": {"FETCH": {"target": "loading"}}},
        "loading": {
            "invoke": {
                "id": "getUser",
                "src": "fetchUser",
                "onDone": {"target": "success", "actions": "assignUser"},
                "onError": {"target": "failure", "actions": "assignError"}
            }
        },
        "success": {},
        "failure": {"on": {"RETRY": {"target": "loading"}}}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> user_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!user_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

The program rejects the first request and resolves the second. With XState it settles the promise, and then waits a turn of the event loop, after which the actor has heard of it; printRequests and print are functions of the program:

const actor = createActor(userMachine);
actor.start();
actor.send({ type: 'FETCH' });
printRequests(); // request fetchUser getUser {"userId":"42"}
requests.shift().reject('Network error');
await new Promise((settled) => setTimeout(settled, 0));
print(actor); // "failure", with the error

actor.send({ type: 'RETRY' });
printRequests(); // a new request
requests.shift().resolve({ name: 'David', location: 'Florida' });
await new Promise((settled) => setTimeout(settled, 0));
print(actor); // "success", with the user

With xstate the host lists the pending requests and answers one. The answer runs the system before the call returns, so nothing waits:

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*user_machine);
if (!actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.start(*actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.send(*actor, {.type = "FETCH", .payload = {}}).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::vector<xstate::host_request> requests = system.host_requests();
print_requests(requests);  // request fetchUser getUser {"userId":"42"}
if (requests.empty()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.reject(requests.front(), "Network error").has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
print(system, *actor);  // "failure", with the error

if (!system.send(*actor, {.type = "RETRY", .payload = {}}).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
requests = system.host_requests();
print_requests(requests);  // a new request
if (requests.empty()) {
    return 1;
}
const boost::json::object user{{"name", "David"}, {"location", "Florida"}};
if (!system.resolve(requests.front(), user).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
print(system, *actor);  // "success", with the user

It prints:

request fetchUser getUser {"userId":"42"}
"failure" {"userId":"42","user":null,"error":"Network error"}
request fetchUser getUser {"userId":"42"}
"success" {"userId":"42","user":{"name":"David","location":"Florida"},"error":"Network error"}

The rules:

XState xstate

fetchUser: fromPromise(...) in setup({ actors })

host_actor{} in implementations.actors

The promise function’s input

The request’s input, which an invoke’s input gives, or the function registered under the invoke’s id in implementations.inputs (An input computed from the context and the event)

The promise resolves with a value

system.resolve(request, output)

The promise rejects with an error

system.reject(request, error)

event.output in onDone, event.error in onError

The members output and error of args.event.payload

A promise that settles after its actor has stopped is ignored

An answer to a request no longer pending is refused with invalid_argument, and changes nothing

Exceptions become result

XState reports a failure by throwing. createMachine throws on a config it refuses, and an implementation that throws fails the actor that runs it: the snapshot’s status becomes 'error', and its error is what was thrown. xstate throws nothing, since it builds where exceptions are off (No exception of its own). A call that can fail returns a result<T>, Boost.System’s result, which holds the value or an error_code. An implementation that fails returns one, failure<T>(errc::implementation_failed) or any other error_code, and a machine that fails while it runs settles in a snapshot whose status is error and whose error is that code (Errors returned, not thrown).

The toggle above already tests the result its create_machine returned: where XState’s caller would catch, xstate’s tests has_value() and reads error().

An implementation reports its failure with a result too. Here a counter’s setCount fails on an event that carries no count. XState’s throws:

increment: assign(({ context }) => ({ count: context.count + 1 })),
setCount: assign(({ event }) => {
  if (!Number.isInteger(event.count)) {
    throw new Error('set needs a count');
  }
  return { count: event.count };
}),

xstate’s returns a failure:

xstate::result<boost::json::object> increment(const xstate::action_args& args) {
    const boost::json::object* context = args.context.if_object();
    const boost::json::value* count = context == nullptr ? nullptr : context->if_contains("count");
    if (count == nullptr || !count->is_int64()) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"count", count->get_int64() + 1}};
}

xstate::result<boost::json::object> set_count(const xstate::action_args& args) {
    const boost::json::value* count = args.event.payload.if_contains("count");
    if (count == nullptr || !count->is_int64()) {
        return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
    }
    return boost::json::object{{"count", *count}};
}

The program sends set without a count to a snapshot whose count is 1. XState’s getNextSnapshot would let the error out of the call, so XState’s program takes the step with an actor started from that snapshot, which keeps the error in its own:

const actor = createActor(counter, { snapshot: second });
actor.subscribe({ error: () => {} });
actor.start();
actor.send({ type: 'set' });
const failed = actor.getSnapshot();
console.log(failed.status, JSON.stringify(failed.context));

xstate’s get_next_snapshot returns the failed snapshot itself, as an actor’s would be (Failures are values):

const xstate::snapshot failed =
    xstate::get_next_snapshot(*counter, second, xstate::event{.type = "set", .payload = {}});
std::cout << (failed.status == xstate::status::error ? "error " : "active ")
          << boost::json::serialize(failed.context) << '\n';

It prints:

error {"count":1}

The failed step keeps the context it began from, a count of 1, though increment ran before setCount failed: a macrostep that fails settles with the snapshot it began from.

XState xstate

try { createMachine(config) } catch (error) { ... }

create_machine(config, implementations) returns a result<machine>; the program tests has_value() and reads error()

throw new Error('...') in an implementation

return xstate::failure<T>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);, or any other error_code

snapshot.status === 'error', snapshot.error

snapshot.status == xstate::status::error, and snapshot.error, an error_code whose message() is its name, such as implementation_failed

actor.subscribe({ error })

No error callback: status_of(actor) says the actor failed (Watching an actor)

The error of xstate.error.actor.<id>: what the child threw

The member error of args.event.payload: the failed child’s error, or the name of its code (Failures are values)

The rules:

  • A result is tested before it is read. * reads the value of a result that holds one, and value() of a failure calls boost::throw_exception, which ends a program built without exceptions (webcpp::xstate::result).

  • The actor layer refuses a call it cannot take, such as one that names no actor, with xactor’s invalid_argument, and changes nothing (Errors as values).

  • Boost.JSON’s accessors that check by throwing, such as at and as_int64, have counterparts that answer instead: if_contains and if_int64 with a pointer, try_at and try_as_int64 with a result (Handle context data).

XState’s names

Each function and type of XState that xstate ports, and its counterpart. Some of XState’s are internal to it, not exported by its package; the table marks them.

Appendix B: Where xstate differs from XState

xstate ports XState’s algorithm instead of defining semantics of its own, and XState itself judges the port: every case ported from XState’s tests runs on XState and on xstate, and xstate’s result must equal XState’s, microstep by microstep and actor by actor (How xstate is tested). Where the two differ, the difference is deliberate. This appendix gives every one, with its reason; the rule xstate keeps in its place is among xstate’s guarantees, or, for a rule of xactor that the actor layer keeps, among xactor’s. The differences are grouped by their reason:

  • What JSON imposes: a machine is JSON, which holds no function, no undefined and no reference to an actor.

  • What the actor model on xactor imposes: deliveries are queued instead of nested in the sender’s call, actors pay for their work with fuel, time is what the host brings, the actors of one actor_system live in one system, and a host’s callback runs inside an actor’s turn.

  • Where XState leaks JavaScript or has a defect: an accident of the language or of an implementation, which xstate does not reproduce.

  • Where imitating XState would make the API worse: failures as values, a config checked when it is loaded, a clock that hands its caller the due events, and one kind of listener of emitted events.

  • The checks of XState’s development build, which xstate always makes.

Each entry says what XState does, what xstate does, and why. Most show the difference with a C++ program and its twin, the same program written for XState (The XState twins): the C++ program, or the section that shows it, then what the twin printed on XState 5.33.2’s development build, the build XState’s own tests run, then what the C++ program printed. Both ran, and the outputs are theirs: the oracle lane, b2 libs/xstate/test/oracle//oracle, runs every twin again and fails when one no longer prints what is shown here. The twin of each program written for this appendix, a diff_<name>, is shown too, under the C++ program, so that both sides of the difference can be read.

What xstate does not have yet is not a divergence and is not listed here: What is not ported lists most of it, and Events one more part. Where XState awaits waitFor or toPromise, a host of the actor layer reads status_of and snapshot_of once its call returns, since every host call runs the system before it returns. Two of these gaps let a config load and then run otherwise than in XState, so they are named here as well. An invoke’s onSnapshot is read as transitions on xstate.snapshot.<id>, but no child sends its parent that event (XState’s syncSnapshot, in the overview’s list), so no child’s snapshot takes them (Invoking actors). And an event xstate.init or xstate.stop sent from outside selects transitions as any other event does, where XState’s macrostep takes no transition for the first and stops the machine for the second (Events).

What JSON imposes

An xstate machine is the JSON of XState’s createMachine config, read when the program runs (The config). That is what lets a program define a machine at run time, or load one that Stately Studio exported, and it makes a machine data: to_json writes its definition as XState’s machine.toJSON() does, and create_machine_from_definition loads it back, given the implementations and the context, which a definition does not hold; The definition says what else it leaves out, and so when the machine loaded back takes the original’s steps. JSON has no function, no undefined and no reference to an object, so every place where XState’s config holds one of them takes another form in xstate. Appendix A gives the C++ spelling of each (From XState to C++); the entries below give what changes beyond the spelling.

Functions become names

XState

A config holds functions: inline actions and guards, the action creators (assign, raise, sendTo and the others), params, an input or an output computed from the context, a context computed from the input, and logic given as an invoke’s src.

xstate

Every function is an implementation registered by name in implementations, as XState’s setup() registers them, and the config names it (Functions become implementations registered by name). Most keep what XState’s function does. Three cannot, and the config holds another form for each:

XState’s config holds xstate’s config holds instead

an inline action, or a function setup() registers as an action

a custom action: a name actions does not hold, which the core returns and the actor layer hands to on_action, where XState runs the function (Custom actions)

params: ({ event }) => ...

fixed params. The functions a built-in action or a guard is registered with read the event and the context from their action_args; a custom action carries its params alone (Custom actions)

src: someMachine, src: fromPromise(...)

the name of an entry of actors (An invoke’s src)
Why

A function cannot be JSON; a name can. Joining the two by name is how XState’s setup() already separates a machine’s logic from its implementations, so the config keeps XState’s shape.

Higher-order guards

XState

not, and and or are functions that wrap other guards, and stateIn one that tests a state value. JSON cannot hold them, and machine.toJSON() writes the transition without its guard.

xstate

They are JSON objects. The type names the combinator with the prefix XState gives its built-in actions, xstate., and the other members are the properties XState’s functions carry, guards and stateValue:

{"type": "xstate.not", "guards": ["isEmpty"]}
{"type": "xstate.and", "guards": ["isAdult", {"type": "hasRole", "params": {"role": "admin"}}]}
{"type": "xstate.or", "guards": ["a", "b"]}
{"type": "xstate.stateIn", "stateValue": "#light.green"}

to_json writes them where XState writes nothing, so a machine loaded back from its definition keeps them.

Why

JSON holds no function. The four forms are xstate’s own, since XState has no JSON for them.

Here SUBMIT is guarded by xstate.not of isEmpty. The program sends it without a name and with one, then reads the guard the definition writes:

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.guards.emplace(
    "isEmpty", [](const xstate::action_args& args) -> xstate::result<bool> {
        const boost::json::value* name = args.event.payload.if_contains("name");
        if (name == nullptr) {
            return true;
        }
        return name->is_string() && name->get_string().empty();
    });
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "form",
    "initial": "editing",
    "states": {
        "editing": {
            "on": {
                "SUBMIT": {
                    "target": "submitted",
                    "guard": {"type": "xstate.not", "guards": ["isEmpty"]}
                }
            }
        },
        "submitted": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> form = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!form.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::snapshot editing = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*form);
const xstate::snapshot unnamed = xstate::get_next_snapshot(
    *form, editing, xstate::event{.type = "SUBMIT", .payload = {{"name", ""}}});
const xstate::snapshot named = xstate::get_next_snapshot(
    *form, editing, xstate::event{.type = "SUBMIT", .payload = {{"name", "Ana"}}});
std::cout << "SUBMIT without a name: " << boost::json::serialize(unnamed.value) << '\n'
          << "SUBMIT with a name: " << boost::json::serialize(named.value) << '\n';

const boost::json::value definition = xstate::to_json(*form);
boost::system::error_code missing;
const boost::json::value* guard =
    definition.find_pointer("/states/editing/on/SUBMIT/0/guard", missing);
std::cout << "the definition's guard: "
          << (guard == nullptr ? "undefined" : boost::json::serialize(*guard)) << '\n';
The twin, on XState
import { getInitialSnapshot, getNextSnapshot, not, setup } from 'xstate';

const form = setup({
  guards: {
    isEmpty: ({ event }) => !event.name,
  },
}).createMachine({
  id: 'form',
  initial: 'editing',
  states: {
    editing: {
      on: {
        SUBMIT: { target: 'submitted', guard: not('isEmpty') },
      },
    },
    submitted: {},
  },
});

const editing = getInitialSnapshot(form);
const unnamed = getNextSnapshot(form, editing, { type: 'SUBMIT', name: '' });
const named = getNextSnapshot(form, editing, { type: 'SUBMIT', name: 'Ana' });
console.log(`SUBMIT without a name: ${JSON.stringify(unnamed.value)}`);
console.log(`SUBMIT with a name: ${JSON.stringify(named.value)}`);

// The definition as JSON, as a file would hold it.
const definition = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(form.toJSON()));
const guard = definition.states.editing.on.SUBMIT[0].guard;
console.log(`the definition's guard: ${JSON.stringify(guard)}`);
XState prints
SUBMIT without a name: "editing"
SUBMIT with a name: "submitted"
the definition's guard: undefined
xstate prints
SUBMIT without a name: "editing"
SUBMIT with a name: "submitted"
the definition's guard: {"type":"xstate.not","guards":["isEmpty"]}

The context function

XState

context: ({ input, spawn, self }) => ... receives the input, a spawn function and the actor itself, and a context may hold an actor it spawned.

xstate

implementations.context receives the input only (Initial context from the input). A context is JSON and holds no actor; a child is spawned by an invoke or a spawn_child_action.

Why

A reference to an actor is not data (Targets that name actors), and the machine core runs no actor: it includes nothing of xactor, holds a machine’s actors and children as data, and resolves a spawn into an xstate.spawnChild action for its caller to run, which the actor layer does (Spawning actors).

An invoke’s src

XState

src is the name of an actor setup() registered, or the logic itself: a machine, or fromPromise(...).

xstate

src is a string that names an entry of implementations.actors. Any other src refuses the machine with invalid_config, and a name with no entry with unknown_actor (A config is refused when it is created). A host_actor stands for fromPromise: the host answers it (Host actors).

Why

Logic cannot be JSON.

Targets that name actors

XState

sendTo takes an actor reference, a string (a child’s id, #_parent, #_internal, #_<id>) or a function that returns one; a send to a systemId is written sendTo(({ system }) => system.get('notifier'), ...). An event or an input may carry an actor reference, as a parent passes self to a child that must answer it.

xstate

A target is a string: a child’s id or #_<id>, #_parent, #_internal, or #system:<systemId>, the actor registered under that systemId, which the actor layer resolves when the action resolves. When no actor holds the systemId, a sendTo goes to the actor itself, as XState’s does when the function returns undefined, and a forwardTo fails (The checks of XState’s development build). Events and inputs carry no actor: a child answers its parent through #_parent, and any other actor is named by its id or its systemId.

Why

JSON holds neither a reference nor a function.

Custom actions

XState

An actor runs each action’s implementation, a function, when the action executes. The function receives the context, the event, the actor and its system, and the action’s params, which may themselves be computed from the context and the event.

xstate

An action that implementations.actions does not hold is a custom action (Custom actions). The machine core returns it as {type, params}, as XState’s pure transition() returns the actions to execute, and the actor layer hands each one, in order, to the callback on_action registers, with the actor that returned it, and nothing else; a log reaches on_log the same way (Watching an actor). Where XState’s function receives the context and the event, the callback receives neither. What a custom action needs from them must be in its fixed params, or reach the host through an emit_action, whose event_maker reads both.

Why

A function cannot be JSON, and what a machine does to the world belongs to the program that runs it.

undefined

XState

JavaScript tells undefined from null. The event xstate.init always has a member input, undefined when the actor was given none, and an implementation that returns undefined leaves a log without a value, a child without an input or a snapshot without an output.

xstate

JSON has null only. A value_maker, the implementation that computes a log’s value, an input or an output, returns a result<std::optional<boost::json::value>>, and none, the empty optional, stands for undefined: the member is left out, as XState leaves it out (When a value is undefined). xstate.init carries input only when the input is not null, so a null input and no input are the same.

Why

The JSON xstate reads and writes cannot hold undefined, and a member left out is how XState itself writes one.

A state’s null meta, and a description that is not a string

XState

A state’s meta that is null is kept: getMeta() lists it, and machine.toJSON() writes it. A state’s description is kept whatever its type, and written too, although XState’s own type declarations make it a string.

xstate

A null meta is no meta: get_meta does not list it, and to_json leaves it out. A description that is not a string is left out of the machine, and so of its definition (What creation refuses). A transition’s meta and description are kept as XState keeps them.

Why

A null is how JSON writes no value, so it stands for no meta, as it stands for no context (A context that is not an object). A state’s description is text, as XState’s declarations make it, and state_node::description holds it as a string; a transition’s is kept as the JSON the config gives.

What the actor model on xactor imposes

xstate’s actor layer runs machines as XState’s actors on xactor, webcpp’s actor system (xactor’s model): one scheduler, which holds a first-in first-out mailbox for each actor and a first-in first-out queue of the actors that have work, and hands one message to its actor per turn; fuel paid for every microstep, every message an actor sends and every timer it arms; timers owned by actors; and time the host brings. That makes a run deterministic, bounds every call the host makes, and reuses xactor’s scheduler, fuel and timers instead of building a second actor system beside it (How the layer runs). Within one actor, everything happens in XState’s order. Between actors, and around the host’s calls, the entries below differ.

Entries of the other groups concern the actor layer too. Of JSON’s: custom actions handed to on_action (Custom actions), a host actor in place of a promise (An invoke’s src) and targets named by strings (Targets that name actors). Of XState’s defects: a root that sends to its parent (sendParent without a parent), an emitted event of the type * (An emitted event of the type *), the children of a failing macrostep (The children of a failing macrostep), the timers of an ended actor (Timers of an ended actor), a timer that falls due during clock_tick (A timer that falls due during clock_tick), the host’s stop of a family with a failed member (The host’s stop of a family with a failed member) and a sendTo whose child is gone (A sendTo whose child is gone). Of the API’s: a failed actor’s error and the error event it sends its parent (Failures are values), and the listeners of emitted events (Listeners of emitted events).

Interleaving across actors

XState

An event sent to an idle actor is delivered at once, nested in the sender’s call stack. start() starts an actor’s children first, each running its initial actions, and then runs the actor’s own.

xstate

xactor queues every delivery, the message in its actor’s mailbox and the actor in the queue of actors with work, and a turn hands one message to its actor, so a delivery never runs inside its sender’s call. Each actor receives what one sender sends it in the order sent, and handles it in XState’s order; but when an actor hears from two senders and one send is caused by the other’s, the order between the two may differ, and so may the order of callbacks across actors. So an actor’s start hands over its own initial custom actions before its initial children handle theirs. In the same way, a parent handles the last sends of a child that is done once the child has released its systemId, where XState, delivering them nested, has not released it yet; and a child born done or failed, started by its parent, finds the systemIds as the parent’s macrostep left them, where in XState a sibling may have ended, or an actor a nested send reached may have claimed one, before that start.

Why

Queues instead of a call stack make a run deterministic and replayable, keep one actor’s work from nesting inside another’s, and let fuel bound each turn. The tests compare each actor’s own sequence, never the order across actors (XState as the oracle).

Here an app whose entry is the custom action appStarted invokes a kid whose entry is kidStarted, and the host prints each custom action it is handed:

const boost::json::value kid_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "entry": "kidStarted"
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> kid = xstate::create_machine(kid_config, {});
if (!kid.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actors.emplace("kid", xstate::machine_actor{*kid});
const boost::json::value app_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "entry": "appStarted",
    "invoke": {"id": "kid", "src": "kid"}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> app = xstate::create_machine(app_config, implementations);
if (!app.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<void> acting = system.on_action(
    [](xstate::actor_ref, const xstate::action& custom) { std::cout << custom.type << '\n'; });
if (!acting.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*app);
if (!actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.start(*actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
The twin, on XState
import { createActor, setup } from 'xstate';

const kid = setup({
  actions: { kidStarted: () => console.log('kidStarted') },
}).createMachine({
  entry: 'kidStarted',
});
const app = setup({
  actors: { kid },
  actions: { appStarted: () => console.log('appStarted') },
}).createMachine({
  entry: 'appStarted',
  invoke: { id: 'kid', src: 'kid' },
});

createActor(app).start();
XState prints
kidStarted
appStarted
xstate prints
appStarted
kidStarted

Fuel

XState

Nothing bounds a call unless the config asks for it: createActor, start() and send() return once every macrostep they run has settled, so one that reaches an actor whose eventless transitions never settle never returns. For a root whose initial macrostep never settles, that call is createActor, which runs the macrostep (The root is constructed on start). The bound XState has is the config’s options.maxIterations: once that many microsteps have followed the event’s own with the machine still active, the macrostep throws an error whose message begins Infinite loop detected, even when it would settle there. transition lets the error out, and an actor catches it into its snapshot, whose status is then 'error'.

xstate

Every microstep costs one unit of the execution’s fuel, as does every message an actor sends and every timer it arms. When an execution runs out, the actor parks and the call returns out_of_fuel; resume() gives every parked actor a new execution. While an actor is parked, the host’s start, send, clock_tick, resolve and reject are held, in order, and applied by a later resume(), so no event starts before the macrostep in progress has settled. stop is never held: it is how the host ends an actor that would never settle. xstate does not read options.

Why

The program that runs a machine decides how much work an event may cost, from outside, one microstep at a time, so a machine loaded at run time cannot hang it (Fuel, parking and resume). A bound written in the config is its author’s, and ends the macrostep as a failure; fuel is the host’s, and a parked actor resumes where it stopped. The core’s pure functions, get_next_snapshot among them, run without a bound, as XState’s do when the config sets none; a caller that must bound the work drives the macrostep cursor itself, one microstep per next() (the cursor’s fuel).

Here a root’s initial macrostep never settles: ping and pong lead to each other. Each execution has 100 units of fuel. The twin gives its config an options.maxIterations of 1000, without which its createActor never returns; with it, createActor throws inside and leaves the actor in error before start():

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "initial": "ping",
    "states": {
        "ping": {"always": "pong"},
        "pong": {"always": "ping"}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> ping_pong = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!ping_pong.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 100});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*ping_pong);
if (!actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<xstate::run_outcome> started = system.start(*actor);
if (!started.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << "start(): " << outcome_name(*started) << '\n';
const xstate::result<xstate::run_outcome> resumed = system.resume();
if (!resumed.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << "resume(): " << outcome_name(*resumed) << '\n';
if (!system.stop(*actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<webcpp::xactor::status> ended = system.status_of(*actor);
if (!ended.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << "stop(): " << (*ended == webcpp::xactor::status::stopped ? "stopped" : "running")
          << '\n';
The twin, on XState
import { createActor, createMachine } from 'xstate';

const pingPong = createMachine({
  initial: 'ping',
  // Without it, createActor never returns: it runs the initial macrostep.
  options: { maxIterations: 1000 },
  states: {
    ping: { always: 'pong' },
    pong: { always: 'ping' },
  },
});

const actor = createActor(pingPong);
actor.subscribe({ error: () => {} });
actor.start();
console.log('start(): ' + actor.getSnapshot().status);
actor.stop();
console.log('stop(): ' + actor.getSnapshot().status);
XState prints
start(): error
stop(): error
xstate prints
start(): out_of_fuel
resume(): out_of_fuel
stop(): stopped

The start and the resume each run as many microsteps as their execution pays for, and the actor parks again; the host’s stop ends it. XState’s actor failed in createActor, and stays in error after stop().

The core shows the same two bounds. In the cursor’s example of a cycle, the caller gives SPIN 1000 units of fuel, one per next() of the cursor, where the twin gives the config an options.maxIterations of 1000:

XState prints
transition throws: Infinite loop detected
the stable state is still "idle"
xstate prints
out of fuel after 1000 microsteps, at "right"
the stable state is still "idle"

And in the example of an eventless cycle, the caller pays for five microsteps, printing each, where the twin gives the config an options.maxIterations of 5:

XState prints
transition throws: Infinite loop detected
xstate prints
"ping"
"pong"
"ping"
"pong"
"ping"
not settled after 5 microsteps

XState’s transition throws and returns no snapshot of the cycle; its caller keeps the snapshot it passed. xstate’s caller holds the cursor, a value: the snapshot inside the cycle, the stable one it began from, and the choice to drop the event, report it, or resume with more fuel.

The root is constructed on start

XState

createActor constructs the root at once: its initial macrostep runs, getSnapshot() returns its snapshot, and its system holds the systemIds of its initial children, all before start().

xstate

create_actor creates the actor and runs nothing. Its construction runs on start, so until then snapshot_of returns nullptr and get finds none of its children’s systemIds; its initial children also take their session numbers then (One system per actor_system).

Why

Construction runs a macrostep, which costs fuel, and fuel is paid inside an execution, which only a host call that delivers something opens (start, send, clock_tick, resolve, reject, resume). create_actor delivers nothing.

Here the root invokes a worker registered under the systemId worker, and describe prints the root’s state value and whether worker is registered, before the start and after it:

/** Prints the actor's state value, if it has a snapshot, and whether "worker" is registered. */
void describe(std::string_view moment, const xstate::actor_system& system, xstate::actor_ref app) {
    const xstate::snapshot* now = system.snapshot_of(app);
    const std::string value = now == nullptr ? "no snapshot" : boost::json::serialize(now->value);
    const std::string_view worker = system.get("worker").has_value() ? "registered" : "unknown";
    std::cout << moment << ": " << value << ", worker " << worker << '\n';
}
const boost::json::value worker_config = boost::json::parse("{}");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> worker = xstate::create_machine(worker_config, {});
if (!worker.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actors.emplace("worker", xstate::machine_actor{*worker});
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "initial": "running",
    "states": {
        "running": {"invoke": {"id": "w", "src": "worker", "systemId": "worker"}}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> app = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!app.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*app);
if (!actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
describe("before start", system, *actor);
if (!system.start(*actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
describe("after start", system, *actor);
The twin, on XState
import { createActor, createMachine, setup } from 'xstate';

const worker = createMachine({});
const app = setup({ actors: { worker } }).createMachine({
  initial: 'running',
  states: {
    running: { invoke: { id: 'w', src: 'worker', systemId: 'worker' } },
  },
});

function describe(moment, actor) {
  const registered = actor.system.get('worker') !== undefined ? 'registered' : 'unknown';
  const value = JSON.stringify(actor.getSnapshot().value);
  console.log(`${moment}: ${value}, worker ${registered}`);
}

const actor = createActor(app);
describe('before start', actor);
actor.start();
describe('after start', actor);
XState prints
before start: "running", worker registered
after start: "running", worker registered
xstate prints
before start: no snapshot, worker unknown
after start: "running", worker registered

One system per actor_system

XState

createActor makes a system of its own for every root: its systemIds, system.get and the sends to a systemId. An actor’s session id, its id when it is given none, is x:<n>, where n counts every actor the process created, across all its systems.

xstate

The roots of one actor_system share one system. A systemId names one actor across all of them: a child of one root is refused a systemId that another root’s family holds, and create_actor refuses one too, with system_id_taken. A root’s session id counts the actors its own actor_system created before it, a spawn whose claim of a systemId was refused included, so the two agree when a process runs one actor_system with one root. With fuel, a root created while another is parked takes its number before that root’s children are all created. A program that wants XState’s arrangement gives each root an actor_system of its own (The system).

Why

An actor_system owns one xactor scheduler, with its registry of systemIds and its counter of actors. Nothing of it is global: xstate keeps no global or static mutable state.

Time in whole milliseconds

XState

SimulatedClock and the delays take fractions of a millisecond. An after key that JavaScript reads as a number is that many milliseconds, "1.5", "-1" and "1e3" among them, and any other key names a delay, "2fast" among them.

xstate

xactor’s clock, which clock_tick moves, and the core’s simulated_clock count whole milliseconds, and a delay is a std::uint64_t. An after key is a number of milliseconds only when it is digits alone. Any other key that starts with a digit, a sign or a dot, such as "1.5", "-1", "1e3" or "2fast", refuses the machine with invalid_config, even when a delay of that name is registered, and the remaining keys name delays.

Why

xactor’s timers count whole milliseconds (xactor’s timers), which keeps every deadline an exact integer; a fraction has no timer to hold it, and a negative delay has no meaning. A key is read as a number only when it is digits alone, as every such key is a whole number of milliseconds.

A tick earlier than the last

XState

SimulatedClock.set throws for a time before the current one, and the time stays where it was.

xstate

clock_tick accepts it: the time moves back, the timers due by then are released, and a timer armed afterwards counts from the earlier time, so it can fall due at a time the clock has already passed once. The core’s simulated_clock refuses the same move (The core’s clock hands over the due events). A host that wants XState’s behaviour passes a time that never decreases.

Why

The actor layer’s time is xactor’s, the time the host brings: xactor reads no clock, and its rule is that a tick earlier than the last moves now back (xactor’s guarantee 18 and guarantee 34). The actor layer, whose timers are xactor’s, keeps that rule as it is. The core’s simulated_clock is a port of XState’s SimulatedClock, and keeps its refusal.

Here the time goes to 1000 and back to 10, and then an actor enters a state that leaves after 100 ms:

const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "initial": "green",
    "states": {
        "green": {"after": {"100": "yellow"}},
        "yellow": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> light = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!light.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
if (!system.clock_tick(1000).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<xstate::run_outcome> back = system.clock_tick(10);
if (!back.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << "clock_tick(10): " << outcome_name(*back) << '\n';
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*light);
if (!actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
// The timer of green is armed now, 100 ms from 10.
if (!system.start(*actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
for (const std::uint64_t time : {1050, 1100}) {
    if (!system.clock_tick(time).has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }
    const xstate::snapshot* now = system.snapshot_of(*actor);
    if (now == nullptr) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "at " << time << ": " << boost::json::serialize(now->value) << '\n';
}
The twin, on XState
import { SimulatedClock, createActor, createMachine } from 'xstate';

const light = createMachine({
  initial: 'green',
  states: {
    green: { after: { 100: 'yellow' } },
    yellow: {},
  },
});

const clock = new SimulatedClock();
clock.set(1000);
try {
  clock.set(10);
  console.log(`set(10): the time is ${clock.now()}`);
} catch (error) {
  console.log(`set(10) throws: ${error.message}`);
}
const actor = createActor(light, { clock });
actor.start();
for (const time of [1050, 1100]) {
  clock.set(time);
  console.log(`at ${time}: ${JSON.stringify(actor.getSnapshot().value)}`);
}
XState prints
set(10) throws: Unable to travel back in time
at 1050: "green"
at 1100: "yellow"
xstate prints
clock_tick(10): settled
at 1050: "yellow"
at 1100: "yellow"

XState’s timer counts from 1000 and fires at 1100; xstate’s counts from 10, so the tick to 1050 releases it.

A callback that calls the system back

XState

A subscriber, an actor.on listener or an inspector may call the system: a send from one of them is accepted, and the actor handles the event once the update in progress is done.

xstate

The host’s callbacks, a subscribe or on_emitted listener, on_action, on_log and the inspector, run inside an actor’s turn, while the system runs. A call from one of them to a member of actor_system that changes the system, create_actor, start, send, clock_tick, resolve, reject, resume, run_until_idle, stop, or a registration (subscribe, on_emitted, on_action, on_log, inspect), returns xactor’s errc::invalid_argument, of the category webcpp.xactor, and changes nothing. The const members, which read the system, snapshot_of, status_of, get and the others, are free. A host that must act on what it heard records it in the callback and acts once the call that ran the system has returned (Watching an actor).

Why

Every host call that delivers runs the system and returns the outcome of that run, settled or parked. A call made inside the run cannot know that outcome, and running the system again from inside a turn would nest one run in another, where xactor runs one turn at a time, each to its end.

Here a listener prints each snapshot it hears, and sends NEXT when it hears "b"; print_value prints the state value after each of the host’s own sends:

/** Prints the state value an actor's snapshot holds, after `moment`. */
void print_value(const xstate::actor_system& system, xstate::actor_ref actor,
                 std::string_view moment) {
    const xstate::snapshot* now = system.snapshot_of(actor);
    if (now == nullptr) {
        return;
    }
    std::cout << moment << ": " << boost::json::serialize(now->value) << '\n';
}
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "initial": "a",
    "states": {
        "a": {"on": {"NEXT": "b"}},
        "b": {"on": {"NEXT": "c"}},
        "c": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> steps = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
if (!steps.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*steps);
if (!actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::actor_ref stepper = *actor;
bool heard_b = false;
const xstate::result<void> subscribed =
    system.subscribe(stepper, [&system, &heard_b, stepper](const xstate::snapshot& heard) {
        std::cout << "heard " << boost::json::serialize(heard.value) << '\n';
        if (!heard.matches("b")) {
            return;
        }
        heard_b = true;
        const xstate::result<xstate::run_outcome> sent =
            system.send(stepper, {.type = "NEXT", .payload = {}});
        if (!sent.has_value()) {
            const boost::system::error_code& refused = sent.error();
            std::cout << "  the listener's send: " << refused.message() << ", "
                      << refused.category().name() << '\n';
        }
    });
if (!subscribed.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.start(stepper).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.send(stepper, {.type = "NEXT", .payload = {}}).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
print_value(system, stepper, "after the host's send");

// The host acts on what the listener recorded once its own call has returned.
if (heard_b && !system.send(stepper, {.type = "NEXT", .payload = {}}).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
print_value(system, stepper, "after the host's second send");
The twin, on XState
import { createActor, createMachine } from 'xstate';

const steps = createMachine({
  initial: 'a',
  states: {
    a: { on: { NEXT: 'b' } },
    b: { on: { NEXT: 'c' } },
    c: {},
  },
});

const actor = createActor(steps);
actor.subscribe((snapshot) => {
  console.log(`heard ${JSON.stringify(snapshot.value)}`);
  if (snapshot.value === 'b') {
    actor.send({ type: 'NEXT' });
    console.log('  the listener sent NEXT');
  }
});
actor.start();
actor.send({ type: 'NEXT' });
console.log(`after the host's send: ${JSON.stringify(actor.getSnapshot().value)}`);
XState prints
heard "a"
heard "b"
  the listener sent NEXT
heard "c"
after the host's send: "c"
xstate prints
heard "a"
heard "b"
  the listener's send: invalid_argument, webcpp.xactor
after the host's send: "b"
heard "c"
after the host's second send: "c"

Where XState leaks JavaScript or has a defect

Some of what XState does is an accident: of JavaScript, of V8, or of an implementation that XState’s own tests do not reach. xstate does not reproduce the accident: it does what the accident gets in the way of, or states as a rule what XState gets by chance.

sendParent without a parent

XState

The pure functions run a machine as an inert actor, which has no parent, so transition() throws on a sendParent, which a running child resolves to its parent.

xstate

The machine core returns it as XState returns it for an actor that has a parent: xstate.sendTo to #_parent. Delivering it is the caller’s work. In the actor layer, a root that sends to its parent fails with unknown_target, as a root actor of XState fails.

Why

Whether a machine has a parent depends on where it runs, not on the machine, and the pure functions describe the machine.

Here FINISH takes a sendParent of DONE, and the program prints each action transition returns:

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actions.emplace(
    "reportDone", xstate::send_parent_action{
                      .event = [](const xstate::action_args&) -> xstate::result<xstate::event> {
                          return xstate::event{.type = "DONE", .payload = {}};
                      },
                      .id = std::nullopt,
                      .delay = std::nullopt,
                  });
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "child",
    "on": {"FINISH": {"actions": "reportDone"}}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> child = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!child.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const auto [next, actions] = xstate::transition(*child, xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*child),
                                                xstate::event{.type = "FINISH", .payload = {}});
for (const xstate::action& returned : actions) {
    std::cout << returned.type << ' ' << boost::json::serialize(returned.params) << '\n';
}
The twin, on XState
import { createMachine, getInitialSnapshot, sendParent, transition } from 'xstate';

const child = createMachine({
  id: 'child',
  on: { FINISH: { actions: sendParent({ type: 'DONE' }) } },
});

try {
  const [next, actions] = transition(child, getInitialSnapshot(child), { type: 'FINISH' });
  for (const returned of actions) {
    console.log(returned.type, JSON.stringify(returned.params));
  }
} catch (error) {
  console.log(`transition() throws: ${error.message}`);
}
XState prints
transition() throws: Unable to send event to actor '#_parent' from machine 'child'.
xstate prints
xstate.sendTo {"targetId":"#_parent","event":{"type":"DONE"}}

An emitted event of the type *

XState

emit hands an event to the listeners of its type and to the listeners of *. For an event whose type is *, the two lookups find the same listeners, and each hears the event twice.

xstate

on_emitted hears every event an actor emits, as XState’s actor.on('*') does, and an event of the type * reaches each listener once.

Why

A listener hears an event once; hearing it twice is a defect of the lookup.

Here PING emits an event of the type * to one listener:

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actions.emplace(
    "emitStar", xstate::emit_action{
                    .event = [](const xstate::action_args&) -> xstate::result<xstate::event> {
                        return xstate::event{.type = "*", .payload = {}};
                    },
                });
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "on": {"PING": {"actions": "emitStar"}}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> emitter = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!emitter.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*emitter);
if (!actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<void> listening = system.on_emitted(
    *actor, [](const xstate::event& heard) { std::cout << "heard " << heard.type << '\n'; });
if (!listening.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.start(*actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.send(*actor, xstate::event{.type = "PING", .payload = {}}).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
The twin, on XState
import { createActor, emit, setup } from 'xstate';

const emitter = setup({
  actions: {
    emitStar: emit({ type: '*' }),
  },
}).createMachine({
  on: { PING: { actions: 'emitStar' } },
});

const actor = createActor(emitter);
actor.on('*', (heard) => console.log(`heard ${heard.type}`));
actor.start();
actor.send({ type: 'PING' });
XState prints
heard *
heard *
xstate prints
