A spawned child without an id

XState

spawnChild(src) without an id keys the child "undefined", JavaScript’s spelling of the missing value, and a stopChild of it then leaves that key in the snapshot’s children.

xstate

The id of a spawn_child_action is fixed or computed by an id_maker, and one left out is the empty string: the child is keyed under "", and a stop_child_action of "" removes it from the snapshot’s children.

Why

A C++ string has no undefined: an id left out holds the empty string, a key a stop can name.

In both, every child spawned without an id has the same key, as does a child given that key as its id ("" here, "undefined" in XState). A second such spawn takes the key from the first child, which keeps running, but its parent can no longer name it, to send it an event or to stop it. Give each spawned child an id of its own, or a system_id to find it by.

Here two children are spawned without an id, each with a system_id, and the key names the second:

const boost::json::value child_config = boost::json::parse(R"({"id": "child"})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> child_machine = xstate::create_machine(child_config, {});
if (!child_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actors.emplace("childMachine", xstate::machine_actor{*child_machine});
implementations.actions.emplace("spawnFirst", spawning("first"));
implementations.actions.emplace("spawnSecond", spawning("second"));
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "entry": ["spawnFirst", "spawnSecond"]
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> parent_machine =
    xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!parent_machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> parent = system.create_actor(*parent_machine);
if (!parent.has_value() || !system.start(*parent).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::snapshot* current = system.snapshot_of(*parent);
if (current == nullptr) {
    return 1;
}
boost::json::array keys;
for (const auto& [id, src] : current->children) {
    keys.emplace_back(id);
}
std::cout << boost::json::serialize(keys) << '\n';
const std::optional<xstate::actor_ref> keyed = system.child_of(*parent, "");
for (const std::string_view name : {"first", "second"}) {
    const std::optional<xstate::actor_ref> child = system.get(name);
    if (!child.has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }
    const xstate::result<xactor::status> status = system.status_of(*child);
    if (!status.has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << name << ": " << name_of(*status)
              << ", keyed: " << (keyed == child ? "true" : "false") << '\n';
}
The twin, on XState
import { createActor, createMachine, setup, spawnChild } from 'xstate';

const childMachine = createMachine({ id: 'child' });

const parentMachine = setup({
  actors: { childMachine },
  actions: {
    spawnFirst: spawnChild('childMachine', { systemId: 'first' }),
    spawnSecond: spawnChild('childMachine', { systemId: 'second' }),
  },
}).createMachine({
  entry: ['spawnFirst', 'spawnSecond'],
});

const parent = createActor(parentMachine);
parent.start();
const children = parent.getSnapshot().children;
console.log(JSON.stringify(Object.keys(children)));
for (const name of ['first', 'second']) {
  const child = parent.system.get(name);
  const keyed = Object.values(children).includes(child);
  console.log(`${name}: ${child.getSnapshot().status}, keyed: ${keyed}`);
}
XState prints
["undefined"]
first: active, keyed: false
second: active, keyed: true
xstate prints
[""]
first: active, keyed: false
second: active, keyed: true

Equal deadlines

XState

SimulatedClock sorts its timers with a comparator that never returns 0, so the order of two timers with the same deadline is whatever V8’s sort makes of it: the order they were scheduled in.

xstate

The order is a rule: by deadline, then by the order the timers were scheduled in, in the core’s simulated_clock and in the actor layer’s clock_tick.

Why

The result is XState’s; xstate states it instead of leaving it to a sort.

The children of a failing macrostep

XState

When a macrostep fails after it spawned children, because an implementation throws or a later action claims a systemId another actor holds, the children it spawned stay constructed and are never started, their systemIds still registered.

xstate

The actor fails, and the children the macrostep created and did not start are stopped, which releases their systemIds. When the actor falls back to the snapshot the macrostep began from, the started children it had asked to stop are its own again, as that snapshot lists them.

Why

A child that is never started and never stopped would hold its systemId for good, and no later actor could claim the name.

Timers of an ended actor

XState

When an actor stops, is done or fails, its cancelAll cancels the timers its _scheduledEvents lists: one per id, the latest armed under it, until a timer of that id fires and removes the entry. So of two timers armed under one id, the earlier still fires, or the later once the earlier has fired, and its event is delivered when its target still runs.

xstate

xactor drops every timer of an actor that ends.

Why

An actor that has ended sends nothing.

A timer that falls due during clock_tick

XState

SimulatedClock fires a timer armed during a tick, for a deadline the tick has already reached, only while its flush has timers left to visit.

xstate

clock_tick(now) releases the timers due by now one at a time, in the order of their deadlines, and a timer armed meanwhile and due by now is released in the same call.

Why

Whether a due timer fires cannot depend on how many timers the flush had left to visit.

The host’s stop of a family with a failed member

XState

actor.stop() stops the root actor, its system and, in the words of XState’s documentation, the actors in that system. It reaches a child only through a running parent, though, so the children of a failed actor keep running.

xstate

system.stop(root) stops the whole family at once, the children of a failed member included. A parent’s stopChild of a failed child keeps that child’s children running, as XState does.

Why

The host’s stop is how a program ends a family of actors; one that leaves some of them running does not end it.

A sendTo whose child is gone

XState

A sendTo that names an invoke of the state being entered is bound to its child once the state’s entry, spawns and initial actions are resolved (retryResolveSendTo). When no child has that id at that point, XState relays the event to undefined, which throws a TypeError.

xstate

The actor fails with unknown_target when the send is delivered.

Why

A send to an actor that is not there is an error of the machine, and xstate reports it as one, with the code it reports for every other target that names no actor.

A context that is not an object

XState

A context is a JavaScript object. A falsy context in the config, null, 0, false or "", starts the machine with {}, and any other is kept. An assign merges with Object.assign, which spreads a string or an array into numbered members, so "ab" becomes {"0": "a", "1": "b"}, and leaves out a number or true; whatever a context function returns is merged into an empty object the same way.

xstate

A config whose context is null, or that has none, starts the machine with {}, as XState’s falsy context does. Any other value that is not an object, false, a number, a string or a list, is kept as written, and an assign on it fails with implementation_failed, where XState starts the machine with {} for a falsy one and merges the update into any other with Object.assign (Initial context). A context function, implementations.context, returns a result<boost::json::value>: a value that is not an object fails the initial macrostep with implementation_failed, and a failure it returns fails it with its own code (Initial context from the input).

Why

Truthiness and the spreading of a string are properties of JavaScript. A JSON machine whose context is not an object has a fault, and xstate reports it where it shows instead of turning the value into another. A null is how JSON writes no value, so it stands for no context.

Here four configs, whose contexts are null, false, 5 and "ab", each take an ADD that assigns x, and a context function returns "ab"; describe prints a context, or the error of a snapshot that failed:

/** {x: 1}, XState's assign({ x: 1 }). */
xstate::result<boost::json::object> add_x(const xstate::action_args& /*args*/) {
    return boost::json::object{{"x", 1}};
}

/** A context function that returns a string, () => 'ab'. */
xstate::result<boost::json::value> make_ab(const boost::json::value& /*input*/) {
    return boost::json::value("ab");
}

/** A snapshot's context, or its error when it failed. */
std::string describe(const xstate::snapshot& now) {
    if (now.status == xstate::status::error) {
        return "error, " + now.error.message();
    }
    return boost::json::serialize(now.context);
}
xstate::implementations adder;
adder.actions.emplace("add", xstate::assign_action{.assignment = add_x});
const boost::json::value base = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "on": {"ADD": {"actions": "add"}}
})");
const boost::json::value contexts = boost::json::parse(R"([null, false, 5, "ab"])");
for (const boost::json::value& context : contexts.get_array()) {
    boost::json::object config = base.get_object();
    config["context"] = context;
    const xstate::result<xstate::machine> machine = xstate::create_machine(config, adder);
    if (!machine.has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }
    const xstate::snapshot initial = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*machine);
    const xstate::snapshot added =
        xstate::get_next_snapshot(*machine, initial, {.type = "ADD", .payload = {}});
    std::cout << "context " << boost::json::serialize(context) << ": " << describe(initial)
              << ", after ADD " << describe(added) << '\n';
}

xstate::implementations maker;
maker.context = make_ab;
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> made =
    xstate::create_machine(boost::json::object{}, maker);
if (!made.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << "a context function that returns \"ab\": "
          << describe(xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*made)) << '\n';
The twin, on XState
import { assign, createMachine, getInitialSnapshot, getNextSnapshot, setup } from 'xstate';

function describe(snapshot) {
  if (snapshot.status === 'error') {
    return `error, ${snapshot.error}`;
  }
  return JSON.stringify(snapshot.context);
}

const adder = setup({ actions: { add: assign({ x: 1 }) } });
for (const context of [null, false, 5, 'ab']) {
  const machine = adder.createMachine({
    context,
    on: { ADD: { actions: 'add' } },
  });
  const initial = getInitialSnapshot(machine);
  const added = getNextSnapshot(machine, initial, { type: 'ADD' });
  console.log(`context ${JSON.stringify(context)}: ${describe(initial)}, after ADD ${describe(added)}`);
}

const made = createMachine({ context: () => 'ab' });
console.log(`a context function that returns "ab": ${describe(getInitialSnapshot(made))}`);
XState prints
context null: {}, after ADD {"x":1}
context false: {}, after ADD {"x":1}
context 5: 5, after ADD {"x":1}
context "ab": "ab", after ADD {"0":"a","1":"b","x":1}
a context function that returns "ab": {"0":"a","1":"b"}
xstate prints
context null: {}, after ADD {"x":1}
context false: false, after ADD error, implementation_failed
context 5: 5, after ADD error, implementation_failed
context "ab": "ab", after ADD error, implementation_failed
a context function that returns "ab": error, implementation_failed

Where imitating XState would make the API worse

XState reports a failure by throwing, accepts a config whose faults it finds only when an event reaches them, has its clock call the functions that fall due, and calls the listeners of an emitted event by a lookup of its type. Imitating the first two would let a program learn of a failure later than it can, or not at all; the clock would run the machine from inside the clock’s call, and the lookup would order the listeners by something other than the program. These entries say what xstate does instead.

Failures are values

XState

An implementation that fails throws. transition() and getNextSnapshot() let the error out; getInitialSnapshot() and an actor catch it into the snapshot, whose status is 'error', with the value and the context from before the event. A child that fails sends its parent xstate.error.actor.<id>, whose error is the value the implementation threw.

xstate

An implementation returns a result. A failure, implementation_failed or any other error_code the implementation returns, settles the macrostep with the snapshot it began from, its status error and its error that code, from the pure functions as from an actor, and the failing microstep returns no action. A cursor that drives microsteps one at a time also gets the actions the failing microstep resolved before it failed (When an implementation fails). A machine child that fails sends its parent xstate.error.actor.<id>, whose error is the child’s error_value when an error event no transition handled failed it, so a grandchild’s error climbs unchanged, as in XState, and otherwise the name of its error code, such as "implementation_failed" (Done and error events). The failed child’s snapshot keeps that code in error, and the error it reported in error_value, where XState’s keeps the value alone.

Why

xstate throws no exception, and builds where exceptions are off; a failure that comes back as a value is one the caller cannot miss: it is in the snapshot it receives, and that snapshot is the one an actor of XState keeps. An implementation fails with an error_code, which carries no value of its own, and an event’s members are JSON: the code’s name is the JSON that says which failure it was.

Here an assign fails on GO, first under the pure transition, then in an actor:

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actions.emplace(
    "count",
    xstate::assign_action{
        .assignment = [](const xstate::action_args&) -> xstate::result<boost::json::object> {
            return xstate::failure<boost::json::object>(xstate::errc::implementation_failed);
        },
    });
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "m",
    "initial": "idle",
    "context": {"count": 0},
    "states": {
        "idle": {"on": {"GO": {"target": "busy", "actions": "count"}}},
        "busy": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> machine = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!machine.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const auto [next, actions] =
    xstate::transition(*machine, xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*machine),
                       xstate::event{.type = "GO", .payload = {}});
std::cout << "transition() returns: " << status_name(next.status) << ", "
          << boost::json::serialize(next.value) << ", " << next.error.message() << ", "
          << actions.size() << " actions\n";

xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*machine);
if (!actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.start(*actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.send(*actor, xstate::event{.type = "GO", .payload = {}}).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::snapshot* failed = system.snapshot_of(*actor);
if (failed == nullptr) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << "an actor's snapshot: " << status_name(failed->status) << ", "
          << boost::json::serialize(failed->value) << ", " << failed->error.message() << '\n';
The twin, on XState
import { assign, createActor, getInitialSnapshot, setup, transition } from 'xstate';

const machine = setup({
  actions: {
    count: assign(() => {
      throw new Error('count failed');
    }),
  },
}).createMachine({
  id: 'm',
  initial: 'idle',
  context: { count: 0 },
  states: {
    idle: { on: { GO: { target: 'busy', actions: 'count' } } },
    busy: {},
  },
});

try {
  transition(machine, getInitialSnapshot(machine), { type: 'GO' });
} catch (error) {
  console.log(`transition() throws: ${error.message}`);
}

const actor = createActor(machine);
actor.subscribe({ error: () => {} });
actor.start();
actor.send({ type: 'GO' });
const failed = actor.getSnapshot();
const value = JSON.stringify(failed.value);
console.log(`an actor's snapshot: ${failed.status}, ${value}, ${failed.error.message}`);
XState prints
transition() throws: count failed
an actor's snapshot: error, "idle", count failed
xstate prints
transition() returns: error, "idle", implementation_failed, 0 actions
an actor's snapshot: error, "idle", implementation_failed

In the example of a failing guard, the guard of an eventless transition fails after the microstep of GO. The C++ program drives the macrostep with the cursor, which reports that microstep, its actions and that it settled; XState has no cursor, and its twin’s actor prints only what it ran and how the macrostep ended, which the C++ program prints too:

In the example of error events, a payment fails under a checkout that has no onError, and the shop above it takes the checkout’s error. The error event is the same, and so is the error the checkout reported; xstate’s snapshot of the checkout also holds the code it failed with, which XState’s does not have:

XState prints
shop {"type":"xstate.error.actor.checkout","error":{"code":"declined"},"actorId":"checkout"}

A config is refused when it is created

XState

createMachine accepts configs it fails on later, or runs wrongly: an initial that names no child throws when the machine starts; a guard with no implementation throws when an event first evaluates it; a named after delay with no implementation counts as no delay, and the state is left at once; a state whose default entry leads back to it overflows the stack when it is entered; an entry, exit or actions that is null, which toArray reads as a list that holds null, throws a TypeError when that list runs, and a history’s target that is null, read the same way, when the default is needed; an invoke of an actor setup() does not hold warns, in the development build, and fails when something reads the child.

xstate

create_machine refuses each of these with an error and no machine, as it refuses every config XState refuses at creation (What creation refuses lists them all). It also refuses members that createMachine accepts, such as a history target that is not a string or a list of strings, the root’s too, and a tags that is null or holds anything but strings. One config that XState accepts, xstate accepts too: a history state at the root, whose default target has no parent to be resolved against, so a microstep that needs it fails with unknown_target where XState throws (History states).

Why

A machine is loaded from data when the program runs. The moment it is loaded is the moment its author can be told what is wrong with it, not when an event reaches the broken part, long after and perhaps in production.

Here report gives create_machine a config of each of these kinds but the null history target. The twin creates each with createMachine, then runs what reaches its fault and prints the first line of what that throws, or what it returns:

/** Prints whether create_machine accepts `config`, and the error when it refuses it. */
void report(std::string_view label, const boost::json::value& config) {
    const xstate::result<xstate::machine> created = xstate::create_machine(config, {});
    if (!created.has_value()) {
        std::cout << label << ": refused, " << created.error().message() << '\n';
        return;
    }
    std::cout << label << ": created\n";
}
const boost::json::value no_such_initial = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "m",
    "initial": "nowhere",
    "states": {"a": {}}
})");
const boost::json::value unknown_guard = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "m",
    "initial": "a",
    "states": {
        "a": {"on": {"GO": {"target": "b", "guard": "isReady"}}},
        "b": {}
    }
})");
const boost::json::value unknown_delay = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "m",
    "initial": "a",
    "states": {
        "a": {"after": {"slow": "b"}},
        "b": {}
    }
})");
const boost::json::value endless_entry = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "m",
    "initial": "a",
    "states": {
        "a": {
            "initial": "h",
            "states": {
                "h": {"type": "history", "target": "#m.a"},
                "x": {}
            }
        }
    }
})");
const boost::json::value null_exit = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "m",
    "initial": "a",
    "states": {
        "a": {"exit": null, "on": {"GO": "b"}},
        "b": {}
    }
})");
const boost::json::value unknown_actor = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "m",
    "invoke": {"id": "w", "src": "worker"}
})");
report("an initial that names no child", no_such_initial);
report("a guard with no implementation", unknown_guard);
report("a delay with no implementation", unknown_delay);
report("a default entry that leads back", endless_entry);
report("an exit that is null", null_exit);
report("an invoke of an unknown actor", unknown_actor);

import { createActor, createMachine, getInitialSnapshot, getNextSnapshot } from 'xstate';

// Prints that createMachine accepts `config`, then what `call` makes of the
// machine, or the first line of what it throws.
function report(label, config, name, call) {
  const machine = createMachine(config);
  console.log(`${label}: created`);
  try {
    console.log(`  ${name}: ${call(machine)}`);
  } catch (error) {
    console.log(`  ${name} throws: ${error.message.split('\n')[0]}`);
  }
}

const noSuchInitial = {
  id: 'm',
  initial: 'nowhere',
  states: { a: {} },
};
const unknownGuard = {
  id: 'm',
  initial: 'a',
  states: {
    a: { on: { GO: { target: 'b', guard: 'isReady' } } },
    b: {},
  },
};
const unknownDelay = {
  id: 'm',
  initial: 'a',
  states: {
    a: { after: { slow: 'b' } },
    b: {},
  },
};
const endlessEntry = {
  id: 'm',
  initial: 'a',
  states: {
    a: {
      initial: 'h',
      states: {
        h: { type: 'history', target: '#m.a' },
        x: {},
      },
    },
  },
};
const nullExit = {
  id: 'm',
  initial: 'a',
  states: {
    a: { exit: null, on: { GO: 'b' } },
    b: {},
  },
};
const unknownActor = {
  id: 'm',
  invoke: { id: 'w', src: 'worker' },
};

report('an initial that names no child', noSuchInitial, 'getInitialSnapshot', (machine) =>
  JSON.stringify(getInitialSnapshot(machine).value),
);
report('a guard with no implementation', unknownGuard, 'GO', (machine) =>
  JSON.stringify(getNextSnapshot(machine, getInitialSnapshot(machine), { type: 'GO' }).value),
);
report('a delay with no implementation', unknownDelay, 'the initial snapshot', (machine) =>

The core’s clock hands over the due events

XState

SimulatedClock holds functions: setTimeout keeps one with its delay, and set and increment move the time and call each function that falls due, in the order of the deadlines. set throws for a time before the current one.

xstate

The core’s simulated_clock holds events. apply schedules each built-in delayed xstate.raise a step returns and applies each built-in xstate.cancel, a custom action being the caller’s whatever its type or its params, and schedule holds any event. set and increment only move the time, and pop_due() takes out the earliest event that is due, which the caller delivers as a macrostep of its own. set refuses a time before the current one with invalid_config, and the time stays where it was (Delayed events and the simulated clock).

Why

The machine core computes what a step does and leaves every effect to its caller, which delivers each event. A clock that called a function would run the machine from inside the clock’s call; one that hands over each due event lets the caller apply what its delivery returns before it takes the next, so a delivered event can cancel a later one, as it can in XState. A refusal is a value, as every failure is (Failures are values).

Listeners of emitted events

XState

actor.on(type, handler) adds a listener of one type, or of every type with *. An emitted event reaches the listeners of its type first and then those of *, each group in the order it was added.

xstate

on_emitted adds a listener that hears every event the actor emits, as XState’s actor.on('*'), and an actor’s listeners hear in the order they were added. A listener that stands for one of a type tests the type itself; adding those first keeps XState’s order.

Why

One kind of listener, heard in the order the program added it, is the whole rule. A type is one test in the listener, and the order follows from the program instead of from a lookup.

Here the listener of every type is added first, then a listener of PING, and GO emits PING:

xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actions.emplace(
    "ping", xstate::emit_action{
                .event = [](const xstate::action_args&) -> xstate::result<xstate::event> {
                    return xstate::event{.type = "PING", .payload = {}};
                },
            });
const boost::json::value config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "on": {"GO": {"actions": "ping"}}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> emitter = xstate::create_machine(config, implementations);
if (!emitter.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*emitter);
if (!actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::result<void> hearing_any =
    system.on_emitted(*actor, [](const xstate::event& heard) {
        std::cout << "the listener of every type heard " << heard.type << '\n';
    });
if (!hearing_any.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
// XState's actor.on('PING', ...): a listener that tests the type itself.
const xstate::result<void> hearing_ping =
    system.on_emitted(*actor, [](const xstate::event& heard) {
        if (heard.type != "PING") {
            return;
        }
        std::cout << "the listener of PING heard " << heard.type << '\n';
    });
if (!hearing_ping.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.start(*actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.send(*actor, xstate::event{.type = "GO", .payload = {}}).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
The twin, on XState
import { createActor, emit, setup } from 'xstate';

const emitter = setup({
  actions: {
    ping: emit({ type: 'PING' }),
  },
}).createMachine({
  on: { GO: { actions: 'ping' } },
});

const actor = createActor(emitter);
actor.on('*', (heard) => console.log(`the listener of every type heard ${heard.type}`));
actor.on('PING', (heard) => console.log(`the listener of PING heard ${heard.type}`));
actor.start();
actor.send({ type: 'GO' });

the listener of PING heard PING
the listener of every type heard PING
xstate prints
the listener of every type heard PING

The checks of XState’s development build

XState

Of XState’s two builds, the development build, which XState’s own tests run and node --conditions=development selects, makes checks that the production build leaves out, and throws where one fails. It also warns, on the standard error, about an event descriptor whose * is not its last token.

xstate

xstate makes the checks a JSON machine can meet, in every build, and writes no warning:

  • An event of the type * that a macrostep takes from outside fails the macrostep with invalid_event, the snapshot it began from in error. An event of that type that the machine raises itself takes the wildcard transitions, as in XState.

  • A transition that declares a cond, the name XState v4 gave guard, refuses the machine with invalid_config when the cond is truthy, as JavaScript reads it.

  • A forwardTo whose target resolves to no actor fails with unknown_target: one with an empty target, when it resolves, and, in an actor, one to #system:<systemId> when no actor holds the systemId.

Why

Each check stops an error that the production build lets through to do something worse. The production build ignores the cond, so the transition is taken unguarded; it runs an event of the type *, a type XState keeps for the wildcard descriptor; and it forwards an event whose target is undefined to the sender itself, which forwards it again, without end. xstate’s tests compare it with the development build (XState as the oracle), and xstate behaves as that build does. A warning changes nothing that a machine does, and xstate writes to no stream: what it has to tell its caller comes back as a value.

The program makes the three checks, one config each:

const boost::json::value with_cond = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "m",
    "initial": "a",
    "states": {
        "a": {"on": {"GO": {"target": "b", "cond": "ready"}}},
        "b": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> refused = xstate::create_machine(with_cond, {});
std::cout << "a transition that declares cond: "
          << (refused.has_value() ? "created" : refused.error().message()) << '\n';
const boost::json::value listener = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "m",
    "on": {"*": {"actions": "heard"}}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> anything = xstate::create_machine(listener, {});
if (!anything.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::snapshot after_star =
    xstate::get_next_snapshot(*anything, xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*anything),
                              xstate::event{.type = "*", .payload = {}});
std::cout << "an event of the type * from outside: " << status_name(after_star.status) << ", "
          << after_star.error.message() << '\n';
xstate::implementations implementations;
implementations.actions.emplace("relay", xstate::forward_to_action{
                                             .target = "#system:nobody",
                                             .id = std::nullopt,
                                             .delay = std::nullopt,
                                         });
const boost::json::value relay_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "relay",
    "on": {"PING": {"actions": "relay"}}
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> relay =
    xstate::create_machine(relay_config, implementations);
if (!relay.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
xstate::actor_system system({.fuel = 10'000});
const xstate::result<xstate::actor_ref> actor = system.create_actor(*relay);
if (!actor.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.start(*actor).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!system.send(*actor, xstate::event{.type = "PING", .payload = {}}).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::snapshot* forwarded = system.snapshot_of(*actor);
if (forwarded == nullptr) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << "a forwardTo to no actor: " << status_name(forwarded->status) << ", "
          << forwarded->error.message() << '\n';

Then it sends four events to a state whose two descriptors each hold a * before their last token, mouse.*.* and mou*se.*. The twin prints each warning XState’s development build writes, under the event that made it:

const boost::json::value pointer_config = boost::json::parse(R"({
    "id": "pointer",
    "initial": "idle",
    "states": {
        "idle": {"on": {"mouse.*.*": "deep", "mou*se.*": "starred"}},
        "deep": {},
        "starred": {}
    }
})");
const xstate::result<xstate::machine> pointer = xstate::create_machine(pointer_config, {});
if (!pointer.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xstate::snapshot idle = xstate::get_initial_snapshot(*pointer);
for (const std::string_view type : {"mouse.x", "mouse.x", "mou*se.x", "mouse.*.*"}) {
    const xstate::snapshot next = xstate::get_next_snapshot(
        *pointer, idle, xstate::event{.type = std::string(type), .payload = {}});
    std::cout << "the event " << type << ": " << boost::json::serialize(next.value) << '\n';
}
The twin, on XState
import { createActor, createMachine, forwardTo, getInitialSnapshot, getNextSnapshot } from 'xstate';

try {
  createMachine({
    id: 'm',
    initial: 'a',
    states: {
      a: { on: { GO: { target: 'b', cond: 'ready' } } },
      b: {},
    },
  });
  console.log('a transition that declares cond: created');
} catch (error) {
  console.log(`a transition that declares cond: throws: ${error.message}`);
}

const anything = createMachine({
  id: 'm',
  on: { '*': { actions: 'heard' } },
});
try {
  const start = getInitialSnapshot(anything);
  const afterStar = getNextSnapshot(anything, start, { type: '*' });
  console.log(`an event of the type * from outside: ${afterStar.status}`);
} catch (error) {
  console.log(`an event of the type * from outside: throws: ${error.message}`);
}

const relay = createMachine({
  id: 'relay',
  on: {
    PING: { actions: forwardTo(({ system }) => system.get('nobody')) },
  },
});
const actor = createActor(relay);
actor.subscribe({ error: () => {} });
actor.start();
actor.send({ type: 'PING' });
const forwarded = actor.getSnapshot();
console.log(`a forwardTo to no actor: ${forwarded.status}, ${forwarded.error?.message}`);

// The development build warns about these descriptors on the standard
// error; each warning is printed here, under the event that made it.
const warnings = [];
console.warn = (message) => warnings.push(message);
const pointer = createMachine({
  id: 'pointer',
  initial: 'idle',
  states: {
    idle: { on: { 'mouse.*.*': 'deep', 'mou*se.*': 'starred' } },
    deep: {},
    starred: {},
  },
});
const idle = getInitialSnapshot(pointer);
for (const type of ['mouse.x', 'mouse.x', 'mou*se.x', 'mouse.*.*']) {
  const next = getNextSnapshot(pointer, idle, { type });
  console.log(`the event ${type}: ${JSON.stringify(next.value)}`);
  for (const warning of warnings.splice(0)) {
    console.log(`  warns: ${warning}`);
  }
}
XState prints
a transition that declares cond: throws: State "m.a" has declared `cond` for one of its transitions. This property has been renamed to `guard`. Please update your code.
an event of the type * from outside: throws: An event cannot have the wildcard type ('*')
a forwardTo to no actor: error, Attempted to forward event to undefined actor. This risks an infinite loop in the sender.
the event mouse.x: "idle"
  warns: Wildcards can only be the last token of an event descriptor (e.g., "event.*") or the entire event descriptor ("*"). Check the "mouse.*.*" event.
  warns: Infix wildcards in transition events are not allowed. Check the "mouse.*.*" transition.
  warns: Wildcards can only be the last token of an event descriptor (e.g., "event.*") or the entire event descriptor ("*"). Check the "mou*se.*" event.
the event mouse.x: "idle"
the event mou*se.x: "starred"
  warns: Wildcards can only be the last token of an event descriptor (e.g., "event.*") or the entire event descriptor ("*"). Check the "mouse.*.*" event.
  warns: Wildcards can only be the last token of an event descriptor (e.g., "event.*") or the entire event descriptor ("*"). Check the "mou*se.*" event.
the event mouse.*.*: "deep"
  warns: Wildcards can only be the last token of an event descriptor (e.g., "event.*") or the entire event descriptor ("*"). Check the "mou*se.*" event.
xstate prints
a transition that declares cond: invalid_config
an event of the type * from outside: error, invalid_event
a forwardTo to no actor: error, unknown_target
the event mouse.x: "idle"
the event mouse.x: "idle"
the event mou*se.x: "starred"
the event mouse.*.*: "deep"

The first three lines of XState’s are the messages its checks throw. Its production build makes none of them: it creates the machine that declares cond, runs the event of the type * and ends its macrostep active, and never returns from the send() that forwards to no actor.

The warnings come from the matching of a descriptor that ends in .* and holds another *. XState warns that a wildcard may only be the last token of a descriptor, and, when a token that is * alone comes before the last and the event’s tokens before it equal the descriptor’s, as the mouse of mouse.x equals that of mouse.*.*, also that infix wildcards are not allowed. A state warns about each such descriptor of its own but the one equal to the event’s type, the first time it looks up the transitions of a type. It keeps what it found for each type, so the same type sent again writes nothing unless the search reaches a state that has not looked that type up yet, such as a parent the first send did not reach. Every descriptor matches as in the production build, and as in xstate (Event descriptors): mouse.*.* only the event of that exact type, and mou*se.*, a partial descriptor whose first token is mou*se, mou*se.x.

The example of event descriptors ends with an event of the type * from outside, which XState’s development build throws on and xstate fails with invalid_event:

XState prints
feedback.good -> "thanks"
feedback.bad -> "apology"
feedback.bad.rude -> "apology"
feedback.meh -> "form"
feedback -> "form"
feedbacks -> "other"
mouse.click -> "other"
* -> An event cannot have the wildcard type ('*')
xstate prints
feedback.good -> "thanks"
feedback.bad -> "apology"
feedback.bad.rude -> "apology"
feedback.meh -> "form"
feedback -> "form"
feedbacks -> "other"
mouse.click -> "other"
* -> invalid_event

Appendix C: Rationale

This appendix gives the decisions that shape xstate, each with its reason, the alternative it was weighed against where there was one, and what it costs. The chapters teach what each decision makes of the library, so a section here says why and points to the chapter rather than teach it again. Where a decision makes xstate behave otherwise than XState, Appendix B gives the case (Where xstate differs from XState).

Why it is built this way

Three aims shape xstate, and each decision below serves at least one of them:

XState’s machines, unchanged

A config written for XState, or exported from Stately Studio, runs in a C++ program and does there what it does in XState, transition for transition. A team keeps one machine for both languages, and XState itself can judge the port.

A host in control

The program that runs a machine may not have written it, and stays in charge of it all the same: of the work an event may cost, of time, of what a failure becomes and of every effect on the world, with the same run for the same inputs.

A library in Boost’s manner

Portable to every C++20 compiler and to WebAssembly, usable in every build a program makes, one without exceptions included, and built, tested and documented as Boost’s libraries are.

The first aim gives the JSON config, the implementations registered by name, the actor layer that runs machines as XState’s actors, and the oracle. The second gives errors as values, the cursor and fuel, and determinism. The third gives header-only, no exception of its own, and Boost’s tools. Where the first two pull apart, the host’s control wins: XState runs a macrostep without a bound, and delivers an event nested in its sender’s call, where xstate bounds every macrostep with fuel and queues every delivery. Appendix B lists each such place, with its reason (Where xstate differs from XState).

A JSON config

A machine is the JSON of XState’s createMachine config, a boost::json::value read when the program runs (The config).

  • A machine is data. It is loaded from a file, a request or a store, with nothing to compile, so a program runs machines that did not exist when it was built: one a user wrote, one Stately Studio exported, one a request carried.

  • It is XState’s format. The config is the one a person writes for XState’s createMachine, and to_json writes a machine’s definition as XState’s machine.toJSON() writes it (The definition). The same config runs on XState and on xstate, and that is what lets XState judge the port: every case of the oracle is a config both run (The oracle and the twins as evidence).

  • Boost.JSON holds it. It is Boost’s JSON library, and its object keeps its members in the order they were written, which xstate needs to read states, on and after in the order XState reads them.

The alternative is a machine described in C++, by a builder or by a table of types. The compiler checks it, but it is code: it cannot come from a file or from Stately Studio, and XState cannot run it. Such a machine is what compile-time libraries such as Boost.MSM already provide (Static actors left to compile-time machines).

The cost is what JSON cannot hold. A function, undefined and a reference to an actor each take another form (What JSON imposes, and From XState to C++ for the spelling). And a mistake in a config is found when the program loads it, not when the program is compiled: so create_machine checks all it can at that moment, and refuses some configs that XState accepts and fails on only later (A config is refused when it is created).

Implementations registered by name

What JSON cannot hold, the code of an action, a guard, a delay or an actor, and the functions that compute a context, an input or an output, is C++ registered in implementations under the name the config gives it (Implementations).

  • XState already does it. setup() registers implementations by name, and the config refers to them by name, with JSON params. A machine written that way keeps its config unchanged in xstate (Functions become implementations registered by name).

  • Names are checked once. A guard, an after delay or an actor that the config names and the implementations do not hold refuses the machine when it is created, before any event reaches the part that would fail (A config is refused when it is created).

  • Effects stay the program’s. An action name the implementations do not hold is a custom action, which the machine returns with its params, for its caller to perform (Custom actions). The machine says what is to be done, and the program decides how.

An implementation receives the context, the event and the params, its action_args, and returns a result. It receives no actor and no system, where XState’s does: an effect that needs them is a custom action, which the host performs. The cost falls there: a custom action carries only its fixed params, so what it needs of the context or the event is in them, or travels in an emitted event (Custom actions).

Header-only

xstate is headers, as xactor is, and nothing of either is built, versioned or linked. The first chapter gives the first reason, portability (Why header-only): the same headers build the same way with every C++20 compiler, natively and for WebAssembly, with no binary to match to each. Two more follow:

  • The program’s flags are the library’s. The headers are compiled with the program, so a build without exceptions, or with a sanitizer, gets the library built the same way, which a prebuilt library cannot promise.

  • xactor is generic. Its scheduler, its turns, its actor logic and its drivers are templates over the program’s message type, and a template is a header in any case (xactor’s model).

The one part a program compiles is Boost.JSON’s definitions: one of its translation units includes <boost/json/src.hpp>, which is how Boost.JSON itself is used without a compiled library (Requirements). Boost.System and Boost.Asio are headers too, so no Boost library is built, neither by a program nor by webcpp, whose Boost.Test suites use its header-only form.

The cost is compile time: each translation unit compiles what it includes. A program that only steps machines includes <webcpp/xstate.hpp> alone, which brings in nothing of xactor or of Boost.Asio (Two layers).

Errors returned, not thrown

Every call that can fail returns a result<T>, Boost.System’s result with an error_code; an implementation fails by returning one; and a machine that fails while it runs settles in a snapshot whose status is error (Errors as values).

  • A failure cannot pass unseen. A caller reaches a value only through its result, and the failure of a run is in the snapshot the caller receives: the snapshot XState’s actor keeps when an implementation throws, which xstate’s pure functions return too.

  • Every build can use it. A value works where exceptions are off (No exception of its own), and an exception does not.

  • A code travels. An error_code carries its category, compares with the codes of xstate::errc and xactor::errc, and holds a code of any other library as well: an implementation may return the code its own call failed with, and the snapshot keeps it as it is.

The alternatives fall short. std::expected is C++23, and xstate is C++20. Boost.System’s result is the type Boost.JSON’s own checking accessors, such as try_at, return. And a failure carried by an exception would not reach a caller in the builds xstate is made for.

The cost: an error_code carries no value, where XState’s implementation may throw any value. A machine child that fails in an implementation tells its parent the name of its code, "implementation_failed", where XState’s tells what was thrown (Failures are values).

No exception of its own

xstate throws no exception and catches none (guarantee 15), and neither does xactor (xactor’s guarantee 20).

  • Programs turn them off. Many builds disable exceptions: embedded and real-time programs, games, and WebAssembly for a host that lacks exception handling. A header-only library is compiled with the program’s flags (Header-only), so it must work under the strictest of them; one that needed exceptions would make every program that uses it turn them on. Whether a program uses them stays its own choice.

  • No hidden exit. A call that throws nothing returns through its result, so every way out of it is one its caller sees (Errors returned, not thrown).

The lint keeps it so: it compiles every public header, and every test and example, which instantiate its templates, without exceptions (Targets), while every program, built for wasm32-wasip2 as for every target, is built with them. Where Boost’s own code would throw, a build without exceptions calls boost::throw_exception, which the program defines. In such a build that call is a defect, never a condition, and webcpp’s definition reports it and aborts (Requirements).

The macrostep cursor and fuel

The machine core’s one primitive is the macrostep cursor, whose next() runs one microstep; XState’s pure functions are the cursor run to its end (The macrostep cursor). The actor layer drives the cursor under fuel. Every microstep, every message an actor sends and every timer it arms costs one unit, paid from one reservoir for each execution, and an actor that runs out parks until resume() (Fuel, parking and resume, and xactor’s fuel).

  • A host must bound the work. XState runs a macrostep to its end inside one call. A program that runs machines it did not write cannot know that each one settles: a cycle of eventless transitions never does, and a server answers within a budget whatever machine it runs.

  • The bound is the host’s. XState’s options.maxIterations is a member of the config, set by the machine’s author and unset by default, and it throws when it is reached (A macrostep that never settles). xstate’s bound is set by the program that runs the machine, and stopping keeps the work: the cursor is a value, which resumes exactly where it stopped.

  • The unit is XState’s step. A microstep is the smallest step of XState’s algorithm, so a run stops only between two of them, never inside one.

  • One reservoir for each execution. Fuel counted for each message would bound the length of a chain of messages but not a fan-out, whose every branch would start with almost the whole budget. One reservoir, from which every actor of an execution pays, bounds its total work whatever its shape (xactor’s fuel).

The cost: a host chooses a budget, and an execution that spends it ends with out_of_fuel and a parked actor, which holds the host’s later deliveries until resume() (Appendix B, Fuel). XState has no counterpart, so the examples of the cursor and of fuel have no twin.

Determinism

The same inputs give the same run. xactor runs actors on one thread, one message per turn, from a first-in first-out mailbox for each actor and one first-in first-out queue of the actors that have work. Neither library reads a clock, a file or a network: time is a number the host brings with clock_tick, or, in the machine core, a simulated_clock its caller moves. And neither holds static mutable state (xactor’s rules of determinism, How the layer runs).

  • A run can be reproduced. A test replays a run by repeating its inputs, and a failure seen once is seen again. The oracle compares each actor’s events and snapshots with XState’s (XState as the oracle), and two schedulers fed the same deliveries record equal envelope logs, under either driver (xactor’s envelope log).

  • Time is an input. A delayed transition is tested without waiting, and the program decides what time is: the wall clock, a simulated one, or the time of a run it replays (Delayed events and time).

  • One thread needs no lock. The actors share nothing another thread could change, so they need no synchronisation, and they run the same everywhere: every example prints on wasm32-wasip2 and wasm32-wasip3 the output it prints natively (The examples).

The cost: XState delivers an event to an idle actor at once, nested in its sender’s call, and xactor queues it, so the order of events across actors can differ from XState’s, though never within one actor (Interleaving across actors). And the host owns the clock: a timer fires only when the host calls clock_tick.

The actor layer on xactor

xstate runs machines as XState’s actors on xactor, webcpp’s actor system, rather than on a second actor system of its own. Each actor that runs a machine is an xactor actor whose logic drives the machine’s cursor under its turn’s fuel. The layer adds what xactor leaves out: a child’s done and error events reaching its parent, invoke, the systemId registry, emitted events and inspection (The actor layer, What is not ported).

  • XState separates the two. A machine is logic, and an actor system runs it. xactor already is such a system, with a mailbox for each actor, a scheduler, timers, children that stop with their parent and the fuel of an execution, under XState’s names: actor_logic, create_actor, spawn_child, actor_ref. A second system inside xstate would duplicate all of it.

  • Machines inherit xactor’s guarantees. Determinism and the bound on work hold for a machine’s actor as for any actor of xactor (Determinism, The macrostep cursor and fuel).

  • Each library stands alone. xactor knows nothing of xstate, and a program uses it on its own for actors written in C++ (xactor’s page). The machine core knows nothing of xactor: <webcpp/xstate.hpp> includes none of it, which a check of the build keeps so, and a program that only steps machines does not depend on xactor.

The cost: XState’s actors are reached through xactor’s model, so the deliveries are queued and the work is paid for, which Appendix B lists entry by entry (What the actor model on xactor imposes).

Static actors left to compile-time machines

xstate interprets machines that are data; it does not compile a machine into C++ types. A program whose machine is known when it is written can write it with a compile-time state machine library, such as Boost.MSM, and run it as an xactor actor whose logic holds the machine (xactor’s static actors).

  • Those libraries already do it well. A compile-time machine is what they are for: the compiler checks the transition table, and nothing is read or interpreted when the program runs. A third such library inside xstate would duplicate them.

  • xactor needs no adapter. An actor logic is any class with a handle, so a logic holds a machine as a member and hands each message to it. xactor depends on no such library, and any library whose machines take typed events joins the same way.

The cost: a static machine cannot come from JSON or from Stately Studio, and XState cannot run it, so nothing compares it with XState.

Boost’s way of building and testing

xstate is built, tested and documented as Boost’s libraries are, as every library of webcpp is, so that people who know these tools can review it:

  • b2 is the build, of everything: the tests, the examples and this page, from the root of a webcpp checkout, and a b2 project uses xstate through /webcpp/xstate//xstate (Building with b2).

  • Boost.Core’s lightweight_test runs the tests, a header of its own, so that a test runs as it is on every target, and in a user’s build without exceptions; Boost.Test runs the 2 suites that register a test case for each ported case, natively, in its header-only form, so the build compiles no Boost library (The tests).

  • Every target is tested. The tests and the examples run natively and for wasm32-wasip2 and wasm32-wasip3, each with exceptions, and the lint compiles every public header, and every test and example, without them, so that a library that works without them is a checked fact rather than a claim. Every public header also compiles on its own, and the machine core is checked to include nothing of xactor (How xstate is tested).

  • Every program of this page is a test. b2 libs/xstate/example builds each one, runs it and compares what it printed with the output committed beside it, on every target, and the page includes that source and that output, so neither can drift from the library (The examples).

  • The documentation is one page of AsciiDoc, built with Asciidoctor.js on Node, which the oracle needs already, so the build needs neither Ruby nor Java; its reference is written by MrDocs from the Doc Comments of the headers, and a message of Asciidoctor’s fails the build.

The continuous integration runs all of it with GCC, Clang, Apple Clang and MSVC, and for wasm32-wasip2 and wasm32-wasip3 (Targets).

The oracle and the twins as evidence

XState itself proves xstate. Every case ported from XState’s tests, and every case written where they are silent, runs on XState 5.33.2 and on xstate, and xstate’s result must equal XState’s, microstep by microstep and actor by actor; and every program of this page that uses xstate runs on XState too, as its twin (How the port is proven, How xstate is tested).

  • A port is right when it does what the original does. An expectation written by hand states what its writer believed XState does, and a mistake in it would hold xstate to the mistake. What XState produces is what XState does.

  • The development build is the judge, as it is of XState’s own tests; where its checks can meet a JSON machine, xstate makes them too (The checks of XState’s development build).

  • What XState produced is committed, so the suites run without Node, and the oracle lane runs XState again and fails when what it produces is no longer what the suites hold (Regenerating XState’s output).

  • The twins hold this page to XState. A program shown here that XState can run has run on XState and printed what the page shows. Where xstate differs on purpose, the twin’s output is XState’s own, and Appendix B shows the two (Where xstate differs from XState).

The cost is Node, for the oracle and for this page; and the programs that show what XState does not have, the cursor and fuel among them, have no twin, so only their own committed output proves them (The XState twins).

Appendix D: Glossary

An alphabetical guide to the terms this documentation uses. Each entry says what the term means here, what XState calls it, what it is in the code of xstate, and which section explains it.

Most terms are XState’s and keep XState’s meaning; xstate adds C++ names for them. A few are xstate’s own, for things XState does not have: the cursor, settled, fuel, an execution, a parked actor and xactor; and a host actor, with its host request, stands where XState runs a promise. xactor’s own terms name the parts of the actor system the actor layer runs on, and its page defines them: the scheduler, a turn, an actor logic, a mailbox, an envelope and the envelope log, a driver and a static actor. The last subsections show the terms at work in programs: a machine, an actor system, and an actor system that runs out of fuel.

Terms

Action

An effect a machine names on a state’s entry or exit, or on a transition, and runs when it passes there. Actions are fire-and-forget: the machine names them and moves on. A few are built in, and the library knows what each means (built-in action); every other one is a custom action, which the machine hands to its caller. A microstep returns its actions in XState’s order: the exit actions of the states it leaves, the actions of its transitions, then the entry actions of the states it enters.

XState: a name, an action object { type, params } or an inline function; transition() returns them as action objects.
xstate: a name or {"type": ..., "params": ...} in the config, an implementation in implementations.actions, and an xstate::action (type, params) when it is returned. An inline function cannot be JSON, so it becomes a named action.
See Entry, exit and transition actions.

Actor

A running process that receives events, sends events to other actors, and changes its behaviour with what it receives. Nothing else reaches its state: other actors only send it messages. In xstate an actor runs a machine (a machine actor) or stands for work the host does (a host actor), inside an actor system. The host creates a root actor and starts it, which runs its initial macrostep; a machine creates its children by invoking or spawning them.

XState: an actor, from createActor(logic), named by an ActorRef; what it runs is its actor logic.
xstate: an actor of an xstate::actor_system, named by an xstate::actor_ref; create_actor and start for a root; machine_actor and host_actor for what a child runs, by its src.
See Actors in Core concepts and Creating an actor.

Actor layer

The half of xstate that runs machines as XState’s actors: the host creates an actor from a machine, starts it, sends it events and reads its snapshot, and the layer executes what the machine core returns. It creates the child of a spawn, delivers the event of a send, arms a timer for a delayed raise or send, and hands a custom action to the host. It runs on xactor: each actor that runs a machine is an xactor actor whose logic steps the machine.

XState: createActor and the system it creates, which XState’s package holds beside its machines.
xstate: <webcpp/xstate/actors.hpp>, whose xstate::actor_system holds the actors.
See The actor layer and Actors: xstate on xactor.

Actor system

The actors that run together and what they share: the registry of systemIds, the scheduler that delivers their messages, and the host’s listeners. The host creates actors in it, and creating one runs nothing. Starting an actor, sending it an event, moving the time, answering a request and resuming each run the system until no message is left, and return out_of_fuel when an actor is left parked; while one is parked, every one of these calls but resuming is held instead (parked actor).

XState: the system each root actor creates, actor.system, with system.get(systemId).
xstate: xstate::actor_system, built with the fuel of one execution (xstate::budgets); the roots created in one actor_system share one system, where XState makes one for each root (One system per actor_system).
See The system.

After transition

See delayed transition.

Always transition

See eventless transition.

Assign

The built-in action that changes the context. Its implementation returns a partial object, which is merged into the context as Object.assign merges it. Once a machine has started, it is the only way its context changes. An assign is never returned to the caller: its effect is already in the snapshot.

XState: assign({ ... }), which spreads whatever the context is, so a context "ab" becomes {"0": "a", "1": "b"} beside the update.
xstate: xstate::assign_action, whose assignment, an xstate::assigner, returns the partial update as a result<boost::json::object>; an assign on a context that is not an object fails with implementation_failed (A context that is not an object).
See Assign and Updating context with assign.

Atomic state

A state without child states, a leaf of the machine’s tree, such as green in a traffic light. Each active branch of a machine ends in an atomic state or a final one.

XState: type: 'atomic', which a state without states has.
xstate: the same; node_type::atomic.
See Parent states in Core concepts and Selecting a transition.

Built-in action

An action whose meaning the library knows: assign, raise, log, sendTo, sendParent, forwardTo, cancel, spawnChild, stopChild and emit. The library resolves its params when its microstep runs; every one but assign is then returned to the caller, or to the actor layer, which carries it out, under a type that starts with xstate. (the names that start with xstate.).

XState: the action creators assign, raise, sendTo and the rest.
xstate: the alternatives of xstate::action_implementation, registered by name in implementations.actions; a returned one has action::builtin set.
See Built-in and custom actions.

Child actor

An actor another actor, its parent, started by invoking it in a state or spawning it with an action. The parent knows it by its id, may send it events, and hears when it is done or fails. A child stops when its parent stops it, when the state that invoked it is left, or when its parent is done or stopped.

XState: snapshot.children, by id.
xstate: snapshot::children, a list of (id, src); actor_system::child_of(parent, id) and parent_of(child).
See Invoking actors, Spawning actors and Stopping a child.

Clock

What holds delayed events until their time comes. A machine never reads a clock: the time is its caller’s. With the machine core, a simulated_clock the caller owns holds the built-in delayed raises a step returned and releases each once the time the caller sets reaches it; a custom action is the caller’s, whatever its type or params. In the actor layer, each delayed event is a timer of the actor that armed it, and the host moves the time with clock_tick(now). Time counts whole milliseconds.

XState: the clock option of createActor, setTimeout by default, and SimulatedClock for tests.
xstate: xstate::simulated_clock (apply, schedule, cancel, increment, set, pop_due); actor_system::clock_tick(now).
See Delayed events and the simulated clock and Delayed events and time.

Compound state

See parent and child states.

Config

The JSON that describes a machine: its states, their transitions, and the names of the actions, guards, delays and actors it uses. It is the object a person writes for XState’s createMachine, or exports from Stately Studio. A config holds no function: where XState takes a function, xstate takes a name, and the function is registered under that name in the implementations.

XState: the object given to createMachine(config).
xstate: a boost::json::value, read by create_machine(config, implementations), which refuses every config XState refuses, some earlier than XState does, with an error code and no machine.
See The config.

Context

The data a machine keeps beside its finite state: a count, the fields of a form, what a child returned. It is a JSON value: the config’s context, or {} when the config gives none or null, or what a context function makes of the input. It then changes only through assign.

XState: snapshot.context. A falsy context in the config, such as false, becomes {}, and what a context function of the input returns is merged into {}.
xstate: snapshot::context, a boost::json::value. A config’s context that is not an object, null aside, is kept as written, and an assign on it fails with implementation_failed. The context function is implementations.context, a context_maker, which returns a result<boost::json::value>; a value that is not an object fails the initial macrostep with implementation_failed (A context that is not an object).
See Context.

Core

See machine core.

Cursor

xstate’s one primitive: a value that runs a macrostep one microstep at a time. Each call of next() runs exactly one microstep and says whether it settled the macrostep. The caller decides how many microsteps to pay for, keeps the cursor between calls, and may copy it: a copy resumes exactly where the original stopped. Each pure transition function is the cursor run to its end.

XState: none. XState runs a macrostep to its end inside transition() or actor.send().
xstate: xstate::macrostep, from begin(machine, snapshot, event) or begin_initial(machine, input); next() returns a progress (step, settled).
See The macrostep cursor.

Custom action

An action the implementations do not hold. The machine does nothing with it: it returns it to the caller, with its name and the params the config gave, in the order XState would run it, and the caller runs it. This is how a program’s own effects, sending a mail or writing a row, leave a machine.

XState: an action whose implementation is a function of the program, which a running actor calls and transition() returns as an action object.
xstate: an xstate::action whose builtin is false; in the actor layer, handed to the on_action listener.
See Custom actions.

Deferred effect

What an actor of the actor layer does only once its macrostep has settled: the delivery or the timer of a send, the timer of a delayed raise, a cancel, an emit, the stop of a started child and the start of a new one. The actor first publishes its snapshot, then runs them in the order its actions deferred them; on its start, the starts of its active children come first, as XState’s start() starts them before the actor’s own initial actions.

XState: the work its actions put off with actorScope.defer, which an actor runs once its snapshot is updated.
xstate: inside the actor layer; the host sees their outcome.
See Sending events between actors and Watching an actor.

Definition

A machine written back as JSON, in the form XState’s machine.toJSON() writes. It lists every state, transition and action by name, but leaves out the context, the eventless transitions and a history state’s default target, and two states may share an id in it when a key holds a dot. A machine loaded back from it, given its context, takes the original’s steps and writes the same definition, its version included, whenever the original has none of those and no entry or exit names a custom action xstate.raise or xstate.cancel: a definition cannot tell such an action from the raise and cancel an after adds, and the loader drops it.

XState: machine.toJSON(), which leaves out a higher-order guard.
xstate: to_json(machine), which writes the higher-order guards too, and create_machine_from_definition(definition, implementations, context), which refuses with invalid_config a member of another type than XState writes, such as an entry that is not a list.
See The definition.

Delayed event

An event raised or sent with a delay, delivered when its time comes rather than at once. A delayed raise comes back to the machine itself; a delayed send goes to another actor. Either may carry an id, which a cancel names to drop it before it fires. The delay is a number of milliseconds or the name of a delay implementation.

XState: raise and sendTo with { delay, id }, cancel(id), and setup({ delays }).
xstate: the delay and id of raise_action and of the send actions, cancel_action, and implementations.delays. The machine returns the action. With the machine core, a simulated_clock holds a built-in delayed raise, while a delayed send is the caller’s to deliver: the clock keeps only its id, when it has one, as XState’s scheduler keys every delayed event by its id. In the actor layer, a timer of the sender holds either.
See Delayed raise, ids and cancel.

Delayed transition

A transition taken when its state has been active for a given time, unless the state is left first. A state’s after adds, on entry, a delayed raise of the event xstate.after.<delay>.<state id> and, on exit, the cancel of it, so the timer of a state already left never fires.

XState: after: { 1000: 'next' }.
xstate: the same after in the config; entering the state returns an xstate.raise with a delay, and leaving it an xstate.cancel.
See Delayed transitions.

Description

See meta.

Development build

The build of XState that makes checks its production build leaves out, and throws where one fails; it also warns, on the standard error, about an event descriptor whose * is not its last token. XState’s own tests run on it, and so does the oracle xstate’s tests compare with. xstate makes the checks a JSON machine can meet, in every build, and writes no warning.

XState: the build node --conditions=development selects.
xstate: invalid_event for an event of the type * a macrostep takes from outside, invalid_config for a transition with a truthy cond, and unknown_target for a forwardTo whose target resolves to no actor.
See The checks of XState’s development build.

Document order

The order of a depth-first walk of a machine’s tree: the root first, and each node followed by all its descendants before its next sibling. Siblings come in the order JavaScript enumerates the keys of their parent’s states: a key that is an array index, such as "2" or "10", first, by number, then the others as the config writes them. Unless two nodes share an id, a microstep exits states in reverse document order and enters them in document order, the regions of a parallel state included: both libraries sort them by XState’s order, which falls behind a node’s place in document order after a node that takes an id an earlier node holds. JavaScript enumerates the keys of a state’s on and after the same way as those of states, and XState and xstate read them so: a state whose after writes 1000 before 500 returns on entry the raise of 500 before that of 1000.

XState: StateNode.order, from states read with Object.keys.
xstate: the index of a node, as in machine::node(index); state_node::order, XState’s order, the number of distinct ids among the nodes before it.
See State nodes and ids and Nested states and the root.

Done event

The event that says something finished. When a compound state’s final child is entered, the machine raises xstate.done.state.<state id> for the compound state, with that child’s output; when every region of a parallel state is final, it raises the parallel state’s, with no output. The state’s onDone takes it. When a child actor is done, its parent receives xstate.done.actor.<child id>, with the child’s output and its actorId, and the invoke’s onDone takes it.

XState: the same two events.
xstate: the same; an onDone is a transition on the event’s type.
See A parent state is done, Done events and Done and error events.

Emitted event

An event an actor emits to the listeners outside it, not to another actor. Emitting changes nothing in the machine.

XState: emit(event), heard with actor.on(type, handler).
xstate: emit_action, returned as xstate.emit; in the actor layer, heard with actor_system::on_emitted(actor, listener), which hears every type, as XState’s actor.on('*', ...) does.
See Emitting events and Watching an actor.

Error code

What xstate returns where XState throws. A fallible function returns a result<T>, holding either its value or a boost::system::error_code: an xstate::errc, of the category webcpp.xstate, or xactor’s errc::invalid_argument, of the category webcpp.xactor, which xstate::errc does not have. actor_system returns invalid_argument for a start, a send, a stop, a status_of, a subscribe or an on_emitted whose address names no actor, for the host’s stop of a child, for an answer to a request no longer pending, and for a call from a host callback that changes the system; create_actor refuses a systemId another running actor holds with xstate::errc::system_id_taken. The const readers snapshot_of, child_of, parent_of, id_of and get refuse nothing: they answer a null pointer, none or an empty view for what they do not find. Nothing throws, since xstate builds without exceptions. A config XState would refuse is refused by create_machine, and an implementation that fails leaves the snapshot in the status error, with its error code.

XState: an exception, or a snapshot whose status is 'error'.
xstate: xstate::result<T>, the codes of xstate::errc, such as invalid_config, unknown_target and system_id_taken, and snapshot::error.
See Errors as values, Failures are values and errc.

Error event

The event a parent receives when a child actor fails: xstate.error.actor.<child id>, with the child’s error and its actorId. The invoke’s onError takes it. When no transition takes it, the parent fails in turn: its status error, its error code actor_failed, and the child’s error in snapshot::error_value.

XState: the same event; an unhandled one puts the parent’s snapshot in the status 'error'.
xstate: the same, with the error code actor_failed.
See Done and error events.

Event

Something that happened, which a machine reacts to: a type, which selects the transitions, and a payload, which implementations read. Events come from the caller or another actor, from the machine itself (a raised event, a done event), or from a clock (a delayed event).

XState: an event object, { type: 'submit', ...payload }.
xstate: xstate::event (type, payload); event_from_json reads XState’s flat form and to_json(event) writes it.
See Events.

Event descriptor

The key of an on, which says the events its transitions take: an event type, the wildcard * for every event, or a prefix ending in .* (mouse.* takes mouse.click). A state tries the transitions of the exact type first, then those of the matching wildcard descriptors, the longest first.

XState: the event descriptor, in the same three forms.
xstate: the same; an event of the type * sent from outside fails its macrostep with invalid_event, as XState’s development build throws on it.
See Event descriptors.

Eventless transition

A transition no event triggers. After the event’s own microstep, and after every later one, the machine takes the always transitions its active states enable, before any raised event; each guard is evaluated with the last event taken. Only after a microstep of eventless transitions that changed nothing (no active node, history, context, status or child) does it skip them, and take the next raised event or settle. A guard usually decides where an eventless transition goes, as in a choice between two states.

XState: always.
xstate: always, selected as XState selects them. A cycle of them never settles, and only fuel bounds it.
See Eventless transitions.

Execution

Everything one input from the host causes: the messages and the timers that follow from it, through any number of actors, paid from one reservoir of fuel, the budget’s. In xactor, a delivery or a tick from the host opens one, and every message it causes belongs to it. In the actor layer, each host call that delivers something (start, send, clock_tick, resolve, reject, resume) opens executions of its own, each with the whole budget: one for each input it applies and, for resume, one for each parked actor it continues; their microsteps are paid from it too. So the budget bounds an execution, and one call may spend it more than once.

XState: none; XState has no fuel.
xactor: an execution named by a correlation_id, whose fuel fuel_of(correlation) tells; xactor::budgets, which xstate::budgets names, sizes it.
See Fuel, parking and resume, and an execution in xactor’s glossary.

Final state

A state that, once entered, completes its parent. When a final state at the machine’s top level is entered, the machine is done: its status becomes done, the children it has left are stopped, and, as an actor, it reports its output to its parent.

XState: type: 'final'.
xstate: "type": "final"; status::done and snapshot::output.
See Final states.

Fuel

The units a caller pays a machine’s work with, so that no event costs more than the caller allows. With the machine core, the caller pays for each next() of the cursor, and stops when it has no more, keeping the cursor to resume it later. In the actor layer, each execution has the budget’s fuel: every microstep costs one unit, and so does every message an actor sends and every timer it arms; an actor that cannot pay parks. A cycle of eventless transitions never settles, and fuel is its only bound.

XState: none. XState runs each macrostep to its end; the config’s options.maxIterations, when set, makes a macrostep throw once that many microsteps have followed the event’s own with the machine still active, even when it would settle there. xstate does not read that option.
xstate: the caller’s own count with the core; xstate::budgets::fuel in the actor layer, with run_outcome::out_of_fuel and resume().
See Fuel in Pure transitions, Fuel, parking and resume, Fuel in Where xstate differs, and the fuel example.

Guarantee

A rule a library keeps whatever its caller does, numbered: xstate’s, those of its actor layer numbered from A1, and xactor’s, on xactor’s page. A guarantee keeps its number and its anchor, and a comment of the code or of a test cites it by that anchor, as (doc: #xstate-invariant-13) does; the build fails on a citation that names no anchor of this page.

XState: none as a list; XState’s tests, which xstate’s cases port, pin its behaviour.
xstate: the anchors xstate-invariant-<n> and xstate-invariant-a<n>.
xactor: the anchors xactor-invariant-<n> of xactor’s page.
See Guarantees.

Guard

A condition that decides whether a transition is taken. Of the transitions an event selects in a state, the first whose guard passes is taken, and a transition without a guard always passes. A guard reads the context, the event and its params, and changes nothing. XState’s higher-order guards, not, and, or and stateIn, are functions in XState; xstate writes them as JSON.

XState: guard: 'isValid', implemented in setup({ guards }), and not(...), and([...]), or([...]), stateIn(...).
xstate: "guard": "isValid", implemented in implementations.guards as a predicate, and {"type": "xstate.not", "guards": [...]} and its siblings. A guard the implementations do not hold is refused at creation with unknown_guard.
See Guards, Higher-order guards and stateIn and Higher-order guards in Where xstate differs.

History state

A pseudo-state that remembers which children of its parent were active when the parent was left, and returns to them when a transition targets it. A shallow history remembers the parent’s children; a deep one, every descendant. Until it remembers something, it goes to its own target, or to the parent’s initial state.

XState: type: 'history' with history: 'shallow' or 'deep', or, on a state without type or children, a truthy history alone; snapshot.historyValue.
xstate: the same in the config, where a history of false, null, "" or 0 is falsy, as in JavaScript; snapshot::history, by the history state’s id.
See History states.

Host

The program that runs an actor system: it creates the root actors, starts them, sends them events, moves the time, answers the requests of the host actors and stops the roots. Its callbacks hear what the actors do, and each runs inside an actor’s turn: it may read the system, and a call from it that changes the system returns invalid_argument and changes nothing (listener).

XState: the code that calls createActor, actor.start() and actor.send().
xstate: the caller of the members create_actor, start, send, clock_tick, resolve, reject, resume and stop of actor_system.
See Creating an actor and Watching an actor.

Host actor
